The Association
THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION is an organ-
ization of officers, graduates, and friends of Washington
University devoted to the furtherance of the University's work
and the extension of its usefulness and influence throughout
the community. Its principal activity is the maintenance of a
series of public lectures and lecture courses; to these lectures
members of the Association are admitted free. Eligible to
membership are all officers, graduates, and former students
of any department of the University, and other persons
who may be nominated by the Executive Council of the
Association. The annual membership fee is three dollars.
THE BULLETIN of the Washington University Association
is designed to provide a medium for the publication of a
selection of lectures from the Association's courses and for
the occasional publication of other papers of a special local
or educational interest; to record the corporate interests of
the University and its scholarly activities; and to serve as an
organ for the interests of the Alumni. The Association is
not responsible for opinions expressed by lecturers and con-
tributors. THE BULLETIN is, for the present, published
annually, on the University anniversary. Each member of
the Association is entitled to receive one copy; others may
obtain copies at fifty cents, postpaid, by addressing the Secre-
tary of The Washington University Association, St. Louis, Mo.

NUMBER FOUR
APRIL, 1906
EDITORIAL
On January thirty-first the non-professional departments of the
University completed their first year in the new buildings. The
year has necessarily been largely a period of readjust-
ment, of putting the physical surroundings into order,
of adapting administrative machinery to new conditions,
and of disposing of the loose ends of things that at first
The First
Year of a
New Era.
still dangled awkwardly overhead. Meanwhile the regu-
lar work has gone on without interruption and with some perceptible
increase in efficiency, in spite of certain temporary inconveniences,
especially in connection with the library and laboratories. The rare
beauty and attractiveness of the buildings and site grow increasingly
apparent with better acquaintance. The new shell is still, undeniably,
a little large for the animal; but the September matriculation showed
an increase of some twelve per cent over the enrollment of the previous
term. Both the men's dormitories are in use this year, and have added
immeasurably to the attractiveness of undergraduate life and the esprit
de corps of the student body. In a word, the University by this time
finds itself well domesticated in a home of singular nobility and dignity,
excellently fitted to promote scholarly work, a delightful social life, and
a sense of corporate solidarity.
With these externals of the University so successfully provided
for, the time has come when we may expect to see several larger and
more serious questions of internal policy and educational
methods come to the fore and, after due consideration,
receive settlement. These questions should, therefore,
now be considered, not merely by those officially charged
with the ultimate responsibility for them, but by all the
graduates and friends of the University; for the Uni-
The
Problems
of the
Future.


## p. 6 (#14) ###############################################

versity can permanently flourish only in the degree in which it enlists
the interest and coöperation of all the people in the community who are
capable of understanding the ideals of a university and its meaning to
society. It ought to be understood that the University in the last
analysis belongs to the people of St. Louis and the section of which
St. Louis is the metropolis; that in the long run it will be what the
community makes it; that the future greatness or the future mediocrity
of its standing, its usefulness, and its influence will afford a fairly
accurate gauge of the intellectual quality, the public spirit, and the
historical far-sightedness of the whole generation of men and women
who now carry on the affairs of this corner of the world. And since
real interest can come only through understanding and through par-
ticipation in working out the unsettled questions, it is, we venture
to think, worth while at such a juncture as this to bring to mind some
of the University's ambitions, its needs, and its problems.
There seems to be reasonable ground for doubting whether the
local public, and even the University's friends, generally realize how
large a contract it is to undertake to maintain a real
university of the modern type, planned upon a scale
sufficient to enable it to correspond to the character and
to serve the needs of a community so large and so im-
portant as St. Louis and the surrounding territory.
The
University
of a Great
City.
There is some danger lest, dazzled by the immense
improvement in the outward conditions and the material equipment
of Washington University, which has been made possible by a few
generous benefactors, we suppose that the old College has already
been adequately reconstructed into the new University. In reality,
there has not yet been an inward expansion of the scope and extension
of the activities of the University commensurate with either its
physical expansion or its possibilities of usefulness. It is, for example,
questionable whether the principal seat of learning in a great city-
whatever be the case with the country college-can properly perform
its function if it serve merely as a place for putting a number of youth
through the undergraduate course of study. This, certainly, will
always be its fundamental and probably its most important work. But
it hardly seems appropriate that a city university, which stands practi-
cally as the crown of an immense and elaborate system of public and
private schools and as the principal center of knowledge and research in
a community of huge industrial interests and of widely-extending social
influence, should be not much more than a glorified country college


## p. 7 (#15) ###############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
7
with an exceptional equipment. In view of its strategic position and
of the extent of the social group which it serves, Washington Uni-
versity should be enabled to offer to all who come to it instruction
even of the most advanced and specialized character in all subjects;
it should be a training place for teachers in the high schools and
colleges of the Southwest; and it should be a place of extensive and
profound original research in the natural and historical sciences, in
technology, and in medicine. These things are as yet hardly possible.
Except in two or three departments, the University is now obliged to
turn away advanced graduate students. The faculty is properly
determined to encourage no sham graduate work, and for real study
of such sort means are lacking; the instructors are too burdened with
elementary instruction to give the time necessary to the supervision
of minute specialized study; and neither the University Library, nor
any other in this part of the country, affords material for such com-
plete investigation of the literature of any specific topic as is pre-
supposed in the writing of a doctoral dissertation. For similar
reasons, the research work of the members of the Faculties is still
greatly hampered and confined. The real university, in the full sense
of the word, the great seat of learning, the repository of the sources
and materials of investigation and discovery, the home of productive
and many-sided scholarship, the center of far-reaching intellectual
influences, such as should befit the chief city of the heart of the con-
tinent: for this we have still to look to the future. It does not seem
that such a community as this ought to be satisfied with anything less.
When we turn from these future possibilities of strictly university
work to present conditions in the Undergraduate Department, the
circumstance which seems most in need of consideration
The
-the one which almost invariably elicits expressions of
Number of surprise from visitors to the University is the dispro-
Under-
portion between the attractions and privileges which the
graduates. University offers and the number of students who come
to take advantage of them. We do not think it anything
but a statement of the obvious to say that, considered as a college for
undergraduates, Washington University, in such matters as scholarly
standing, the character of its requirements, the extent of its equipment,
the architectural beauty of its buildings, has a somewhat exceptional
position in this part of the West. But although the number of students
rises steadily, the total, even after the removal to the new site, remains
relatively small. There has not yet come that sudden and marked


## p. 8 (#16) ###############################################

8
THE BULLETIN OF
increase which most of the important American colleges have already
experienced and which we ought, for the best of reasons, to expect.
An enrollment of 244 regular students in both College and Engineering
School-184 men and 60 women-with 44 special students-makes
up a very limited undergraduate body, as college enrollments go in
America in these days. The fact is, indeed, fortunate for those
students now in the University; for it means that they receive an
amount of individual attention from heads of departments that would
be wholly impossible in other and more crowded institutions. Yet
we hardly suppose that the graduates and friends of the University
will, for that reason, wish it to remain among the numerically small
colleges. Those who do not so wish ought, therefore, to inquire into
the causes of the present disproportion between attractions and attend-
ance.
One of the possible causes there is, which hardly any friend of
the University would wish to see removed: the character of the
University's standards. The requirements for admission and gradu-
ation are still susceptible of decided improvement; but it has been,
and is, a part of the University's tradition to hold its standards well
above the prevailing average. A recent statistical investigation has,
for example, shown that an unusually large percentage of students
in the School of Engineering-and especially of Freshmen at the end
of their first term-are conditioned or "flunked," in comparison with
the percentage of conditioned students in other technical schools. It
may be taken as the fixed policy of Washington University to refuse
to increase its numbers by "letting down the bars" to ill-trained candi-
dates for its degrees. Another possible cause for the limited number
is of quite a different sort, and is not intrinsically incapable of elimina-
tion. Surrounded by institutions where instruction is free or ex-
tremely inexpensive, in a community where the tradition of free
education has firmly seized the popular consciousness, Washington
University maintains a tuition fee higher than that of any college
west of the Alleghenies. Those authorized to judge of the matter do
not appear to deem it practicable, in the University's present circum-
stances, to reduce the fee; but that its reduction, if it were made
possible, would help to bring about a considerable increase of attend-
ance-especially of students of serious purpose but limited means can
hardly be doubted. Yet, after all, the present charges are far below
the value and the actual cost of the privileges which the University
lays before its students; and there are many who are abundantly able
to pay such charges. Neither of the causes mentioned, therefore, fully
accounts for the facts under consideration. For the rest, the Univer-


## p. 9 (#17) ###############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
9
sity must rely for its future growth largely upon the loyal efforts of
its friends and, above all, of its graduates, in making its advantages
known, in talking of its excellences in season and out of season, in
enlisting the sympathy of all who can appreciate its characteristic
ideals-its faith that the way to truth is through openness of mind and
liberty of inquiry, its demand for honesty and thoroughness of work,
its insistence upon the eventual transformation of knowledge into
efficiency in action and serviceableness to society.
+++
Mr. Andrew Carnegie has placed in the hands of a Board of
Trustees the munificent sum of ten million dollars, the income from
Professorial
Pensions.
which is to be devoted to the pensioning of retired
professors in a large number of American colleges.
Although the gift has generally elicited the hearty
approval and appreciation of the academic public, not
a few college professors seem to feel some reluctance to avail them-
selves of the benefits of this endowment. There need, however, be
no more hesitancy in accepting a yearly allowance from the Carnegie
Fund than in accepting a salary at the hands of a college treasurer. The
endowment of an institution of learning represents nearly always the
gift of an individual or the accumulated gifts of many. Part of the
income of these gifts is devoted to the payment of professorial salaries.
The Carnegie pension fund is likewise a gift from an individual, to
be devoted to the payment of professorial salaries. The pensions will,
it is true, be rather a continuation of salary for services previously
rendered than a payment for services concurrently performed. But
the original services are, in nearly all American colleges, so inade-
quately compensated, that the annual allowances made possible by
Mr. Carnegie's generosity can only be regarded as deferred payments.
It is, therefore, to be expected that the new foundation will be cordially
accepted as an important aid toward the correction of one of the
grave imperfections of the entire educational system in America-the
meagreness of the remuneration of the teaching profession in all its
grades. Incidentally, the fund will help to solve a troublesome problem
of college administration. Hitherto many colleges have felt obliged
to continue professors in active service long after their period of full
efficiency was past, since the abrupt dismissal of venerable and faith-
ful servants of the institution, who had no means of livelihood beside
their salaries, was out of the question. The establishment of a system
of retiring-allowances will make it possible to bring new blood into
a department when it is needed, without injustice to the older men.

The
Significance
of the Salary
Question.
The question of university salaries is significant, not as a question
of benevolence or even of justice to college professors, but as a question
of educational efficiency. The present and the increas-
ing disparity between the salaries of university teachers
and the incomes obtainable in other professions and in
business, tends to discourage an increasing number of
young men of exceptional ability from entering upon
the academic career. It is, also, because of their
cramped financial condition that men already occupying college chairs
so often dissipate their energies in the effort to add to their income
by any and every kind of semi-professional work which promises
financial returns especially by the needless multiplication of elemen-
tary text-books. A profession so exacting in its requirements of
preparation should promise at least a reasonable compensation, so that
men of good ability may continue to give their thought and life to
the acquirement and dissemination of knowledge, without being con-
stantly distracted by the res angusta domi and the prospect of poverty
in old age.
Recent
Progress.
The only serious question which Mr. Carnegie's gift may raise is,
whether colleges and universities will not lessen their efforts for
adequate endowments, excusing themselves and consoling
their faculties with the thought that, although instruct-
ors are very insufficiently paid while in active service,
there will be some provision for their declining years.
There is possibly some slight danger, in this as in other cases, that
Mr. Carnegie's otherwise admirable and well-conceived generosity
may tend to weaken local energies and the local sense of responsibility
in the communities and institutions that benefit by his gifts. It is,
however, manifest that the Carnegie Fund will not prove permanently
adequate even for the purposes for which it is designed; this will
become particularly apparent when ten or fifteen years have mortgaged
all the available annual income from the fund. Scant provision will
be left for the men who reach the retiring age after that time. And
in any case, what is chiefly needed for the adequate treatment of the
salary problem is not so much a multiplication of pension funds as
an establishment of a proper standard of actual salaries. Much more
encouraging, therefore, than even Mr. Carnegie's benefaction, is the
fact that certain American universities have, within the past year,
vigorously set about the increase of revenues devoted to the payment
of salaries. Harvard has raised, by the subscriptions of its alumni,


## p. 11 (#19) ##############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
11
the sum of $2,339,000 as a Teachers' Endowment Fund, the whole
income from which is to be devoted to the enlargement of salaries.
This fund has made possible an increase of $600 in the salaries of all
teachers in Harvard College, from the grade of assistant professor in
his first term to the maximum salary of a professor; so that professors
now receive a salary of $4000 upon appointment, and ultimately $5500.
It is reported also that the University of Illinois has, under its new
President, been given authority by the State Legislature to raise the
maximum of its professorial salaries to $3500. These things are
noteworthy, not because a number of deserving and learned gentlemen,
in Cambridge, Urbana, and elsewhere, will hereafter be enabled to
practice an honorable profession with greater cheerfulness and com-
fort; but because the changes in question are parts of a general move-
ment, as a result of which we may hope that the country which boasts
of being the richest in the world and the most devoted to education
may eventually come to assign to the teacher's profession a scale of
compensation sufficient to give to that profession a proper degree of
attractiveness, of efficiency, and of dignity.


## p. 12 (#20) ##############################################

COLLEGE ENTRANCE REQUIREMENTS
EDMUND H. SEARS
Principal of Mary Institute, Washington University
In the days of John Adams and George Washington it
was a simple and easy matter to gain admission to an Amer-
ican college. A slight knowledge of Latin and the ordinary
English branches was all that was needed; but as time passed
and the nation grew and developed, a more rigorous training
was required. A gentleman who entered Harvard College
about 1830 told the writer that his preparation included an
excellent knowledge of mathematics, Latin, Greek, and He-
brew, together with extensive reading in the best English
literature; and for a number of decades the standard denoted
by this range of preparation was not materially changed.
Hebrew was not commonly taught in preparatory schools
and was perhaps not actually demanded by the admission re-
quirements of any college; but a fairly exact training in
Latin, Greek, and elementary mathematics, together with a
smattering of English, history, and geography, was the gen-
erally accepted standard.
With the national awakening that came after the Civil
War, education, both higher and secondary, received critical
attention. Its standards were pronounced too low. Its
courses were considered narrow. Radical reforms were de-
manded, and, little by little, they were brought about. Com-
parisons with the educational systems of England and Conti-


## p. 13 (#21) ##############################################

COLLEGE ENTRANCE REQUIREMENTS
13
nental Europe were frequently, though not always intelli-
gently, made; and changes in methods of instruction and in
the range and character of the studies pursued, both in the
schools and the colleges, were effected.
That these changes have been in some respects beneficial
must be fully and freely admitted. Educational methods
have been improved. New studies have been added to the
college preparatory curriculum, natural science and the mod-
ern languages now receiving a recognition that was not even
dreamed of a few decades ago. But with gains have also
come losses which are so serious that they merit careful con-
sideration.
First of all it is to be noted that the very awakening that
came after our ardent civil conflict wrought harm as well
as good. It gave to the people of the land a larger vision,
higher ambitions, and a more earnest and enlightened interest
in all branches of human endeavor. But along with this
growth and progress have come so many distractions and
such a strenuous and feverish manner of living that it may
well be questioned whether our moral and spiritual tone has
not materially suffered. Certainly it would seem true that
our young people now have such varied and absorbing inter-
ests that their minds are diverted from intellectual pursuits
and discouraged from forming intellectual tastes. Before
the days of tennis, golf, canoeing, automobiling, unseason-
able, and indeed almost unceasing, social activity, boys and
girls had time to read in their own homes. Almost of neces-
sity they turned to books for amusement in their leisure
hours; and the books that were at hand were usually better
than the exciting and ephemeral modern novel. The Bible
was read and studied in those days; history, travel, and


## p. 14 (#22) ##############################################

14
EDMUND H. SEARS
poetry were not neglected. Books of adventure were few
in number and were of a healthy tone. By reading good
books attentively boys and girls acquired a real desire for
mental recreation, a respectable familiarity with some of
the best things in our literature, and a knowledge of good
English style that was not without its influence upon their
own manner of expression. An acquaintance with gram-
mar and correct idiom came almost of itself under these
conditions. But in these days, what boy knows his Bible
or has any familiarity with Shakspere beside that which he
gains wearily in the class-room as a part of the drudgery
of college preparation?
A direct result of this lack of true intellectual activity
and of the formation of intellectual tastes is the spirit of
mental indolence that prevails in these pursy times. Young
people seem averse to solid intellectual effort. The exhila-
ration of sport makes them eager to exercise their bodies,
but education offers no seduction to the mind. Knowledge
must be gained through toil, and toil of this kind is distasteful.
The trouble begins in the kindergarten, where the mind is
to be interested before any demands are made upon it. Sim-
ilarly, throughout the years of school-life, pupils are haunted
by the delusion that the teacher must do the work for them,
unless they can steal the results of their companions' labors.
Hence there is placed upon the teacher of today a pressure
that has ever to be sharply resisted. It is the teacher who
is expected to do all the work while the pupil looks lazily on.
Vicious consequences follow when teachers have not the cour-
age and resolution to stand out against this indolent habit of
mind. Sometimes, indeed, their best efforts are thrown away
through the foolishness of parents who, with no exercise of


## p. 15 (#23) ##############################################

COLLEGE ENTRANCE REQUIREMENTS
15
judgment or discrimination, indulge their children with pri-
vate tutors.
It is not strange, therefore, that when teachers have to
labor under such adverse conditions there is a lamentable
and far-reaching lack of thoroughness in their work. Old
and worn-out methods have quite largely disappeared from
the secondary schools, but unhappily those that have taken
their place are only too often loose and slip-shod. There
used to be too much grammar drill in the teaching of Latin;
now there is so little that college professors and school teach-
ers of long experience pronounce robust and accurate Latin
scholarship a rare attainment. Latin composition in the
schools used to be nothing more than a practical exercise in
Latin grammar; now the college admission standard re-
quires that pupils should put connected English sentences
into Latin, which they do in a manner that is simply farcical,
owing to the feeble drill they have had in the very elements
of the language, and to their almost absolute ignorance of
the complicated structure of the Latin period. Mathematical
teaching suffers from the lack of persistent attention to men-
tal arithmetic and the fundamental processes. Much time
is devoted to theory in algebra and to originals in geometry;
but such training is profitless, sometimes even mischievous,
when based upon a very imperfect mastery of common frac-
tions and the multiplication table. The methods pursued in
natural science, intelligent as they are when compared with
those prevailing a generation since, do not properly insist
from the very outset on a rigorous training of the powers of
observation. The compound microscope in botany and the
algebraic formula in physics are made to stand directly in the
way of the closest and most searching study of natural phe-


## p. 16 (#24) ##############################################

16
EDMUND H. SEARS
nomena. It was with the naked eye, not with the aid of a
microscope, that Agassiz made his scientific recruits find out
all that days of study would tell them about the simplest ob-
jects. It is not by the help of mathematics that Nature's
laws, as they are daily manifesting themselves in phases with-
out number, can be accurately noted. Again, both in Eng-
lish and in history the training of the schools is lamentably
deficient. Bad spelling, bad punctuation (sometimes the ut-
ter lack of it), and a slovenly style characterize the written
work of the average school-boy who is preparing for college;
and his knowledge of history is sadly marred by the effort to
make him master in a short time far more than his mind can
assimilate.
Another evil that deserves mention, and one which is to
a large extent responsible for the loose methods of instruc-
tion that have just been noticed, is the multiplicity of sub-
jects that college preparation now requires. If requirements
were too few and too simple a generation ago, it is a question
whether they are not now altogether too numerous and too
exacting. Certainly they make the work of preparing boys
and girls for college a painful drudgery. Teachers and pu-
pils work under high pressure, and mental confusion is very
frequently the result in the pupil's mind. The wide range of
his mental exertions tends to perplex and bewilder him, and
he does not easily find any study which he can pursue in a
spirit of simple enjoyment. It is not enough that he should
translate Latin well and understand its constructions; he must
know quantity, rhythm, and psychological discriminations in
syntax. Mathematics leads him into baffling subtleties; for
he must prepare to pass examinations that will contain the
most ingeniously devised traps for his feeble understanding.


## p. 17 (#25) ##############################################

COLLEGE ENTRANCE REQUIREMENTS
17
When he turns to history, he finds himself face to face with
large constitutional problems and mysterious questions of
origin and cause; while the area of knowledge that he is
required to master is year by year increased, until it would
seem as if the college professor expected him to know the
whole story of human experience, ancient, mediæval, and
modern. In the English classics he blissfully fancies that he
may find some rest for a wearied brain; but he soon discov-
ers that these authors are not to be read for their own sake,
but for the historical allusions in which they abound and the
preparation of ignorant essays upon very learned themes.
In translating a modern language there is indeed some en-
tertainment, but unhappily the training in French and Ger-
man has to be done with vast hurry, with unrest and nervous
apprehension; for the college catalogues require in one year
a preparation which it would take three years of sane and
rational work to accomplish. The result of it all is that
the student in the preparatory school loses all thought of
learning for learning's sake and looks upon the whole sys-
tem as a contrivance solely devised to enable him to pass his
examinations. All that he learns he learns for the sake of
the examinations, not because the knowledge gained has any
intrinsic value or use; and, sad to say, this view but too often
gains ascendency in the mind of the teacher also, destroying
his enthusiasm and making him a drudge and a machine.
It would be easy to enumerate other defects in our present
system of secondary education, but enough has been said to
indicate those that are most radical. That the defects really
exist, few who are fitted to pronounce judgment would deny.
What then shall be done to remedy them?
To this question many answers could be given. Every

EDMUND H. SEARS
intelligent educator would doubtless be glad to lop and prune
this vine that seems long to have been growing awry; but the
pruning knife will hardly be applied with the necessary thor-
oughness and vigor till we realize that we have been making
a huge mistake. We have been trying to grow an European
plant in an uncongenial American soil.
That our young people of both sexes have a freedom that
is foreign to European standards of conduct has become the
merest commonplace. This was intimated in the brief enu-
meration of existing evils in our educational system that has
just been given. Even in that cursory account of abuses to
be remedied the peculiar intellectual and social atmosphere
in which our boys and girls grow up had inevitably to be
mentioned. To it was attributed much of the weakness that
belongs to our educational structure; and the longer one
studies the subject, the more just does that conclusion appear.
Again and again do American scholars declare that the
American youth of eighteen is two or three years behind the
German youth of the same age in scholarship; and, this
granted, they deplore the fact as a reproach to our educa-
tional methods and seek for a remedy.
Now the fact thus pointed out is really a fact. This can
hardly be denied. But why should it be deplored? The
German boy is a product of the profoundly intellectual Teu-
tonic civilization. The American boy is a product of the
intensely nervous, restless, and stimulating American life.
He does not take kindly to books; in some parts of our coun-
try, notably in New England, he takes less kindly to them
now than he did half a century ago. Academic learning has
no charms for him; yet he is alert, wide-awake, quick to take
suggestions, and a learner from his earliest years. His


## p. 19 (#27) ##############################################

COLLEGE ENTRANCE REQUIREMENTS
19
senses are well-developed; his mind is active; he is gaining
impressions and acquiring knowledge every day of his life.
On the field of sport, on the river, on mountain trails, he is
gaining confidence in himself, quickness of decision, resource-
fulness in emergencies, and courage in action. The spirit of
progress is in him and he is always striving to find better
methods of doing the things that are given him to do, in
this respect reflecting the spirit that has characterized the
native American since the early pioneers pushed their way
westward into the trackless forests. Hence it is that the
youth of America are so clever at sports and, unhappily, so
often unsportsmanlike; for they develop a sport to an unpre-
cedented degree of perfection, and then add trickery to make
victory sure. The English youth played Rugby foot-ball
generation after generation in the same unvaryingly rough,
hard, uningenious, manly fashion. The American youth took
the game from them, made it wonderfully scientific, and
finally ruined it by dirty tricks and brutal play.
Nor is this active, high-strung American intelligence by
any means incapable of high scholastic accomplishment.
When the American student does show a zest for academic
learning he pursues his end with the same enthusiasm, the
same energy, and the same success that characterize his en-
deavors in other fields. The American specialist is worthy
of respect. In some fields he presses the great German mas-
ters hard; in some, especially where practical skill is, above
all things, required, he attains an excellence that is all his
own. Not to speak of such things as surgery and dentistry,
excellence in which is hardly of the academic type, we may
well bear in mind American achievements in some branches
of scientific research, the unsurpassed quality of our best lit-


## p. 20 (#28) ##############################################

EDMUND H. SEARS
erary and scholastic reviews, and the unsurpassed accuracy
of some American classical students in reading ancient manu-

observed when the practical, unacademic American mind ap-

critical that an advanced Latin specialist ought to speak Eng-
lish correctly and that a big-brained man of science should
have more cultivation than the average mechanic; but end-

dent American.
Now, American conditions of life being what they are, a
sound system of education should be a natural outgrowth
from them. The youth of our country do not take kindly
to being made into scholars. Why, then, try to make highly
accomplished scholars out of them? By all means give them
the opportunity of becoming men of learning and thorough
specialists, seeing that many will use such opportunities to
the best advantage; but what sense is there in demanding of
the secondary schools that which the colleges and univer-
sities fail to accomplish? Make the scholarship of the schools
as thorough and advanced as that of the German schools, it
is demanded, and then our universities will attain to the
standards of those of Germany. So the schools are put under
a tremendous pressure to build up a disciplined Teutonic
scholarship in the alert but crude and unacademic American
mind; and when the task is wretchedly done, with toil and
worry and heart-burning, the youth goes to college and there
tries to undo what his teachers at school did their best to
accomplish; for at college he elects easy courses, finds that
it is bad form to "dig," and prides himself on never getting
higher than "C," the grade of the gentleman!

It is by no means asserted that he does not profit, and
profit greatly, from his college course, even though he does
elect easy studies and maintain but an indifferent standing.
The intellectual quickening imparted by the college atmos-
phere, by association with the bright and not wholly unre-
sponsive minds of fellow-students, by teachers of ripe cul-
ture and broad learning, and by studies in themselves inter-
esting and stimulating, such as economics and laboratory
research, inevitably mature the mental powers, and give a
tone of vigor and manly strength to the understanding; but
these moulding processes do not turn out a scholar, unless
the man that is submitted to them possesses from the start
the scholar's ambition and the scholar's unquenchable ardor
in the pursuit of learning.
It is quite true that the easy-going, unambitious student
is found in every university in every land. He is as easily met
at Berlin, Bonn, and Leipsic as at Cambridge, New Ha-
ven, and Chicago. An ardent thirst for knowledge is not a
universal characteristic of the youth of any country; and the
German student who loves beer and duelling better than
Greek roots and chemical reactions is too well known to need
mention. It may be thought, therefore, that there is no
point in calling attention to the large class of American col-
lege students who have no decided intellectual tastes and
make but a poor use of their opportunities; yet that this class
of students is a very large and apparently an increasing one
is a fact of no little significance and has a most important
bearing upon the whole question under discussion, for some
of the very colleges and universities which are most exact-
ing in their standards of admission, and most pretentious in
their claims to an advanced and distinguished scholarship, are

EDMUND H. SEARS
generating quite the largest number of these student drones.
Hence it may be pertinently asked: Why all this painful
and Titanic endeavor after a hitherto unattained and an
ever-increasingly high standard of excellence in the college
preparatory training? Cui bono? Who profits by it? Par-
turiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus.
Yet surely, it may be objected, you would not give the
school-boy a poorer preparation just because he frequently
turns out to be an indifferent college student. No, perish
the thought! I would give him a better one, a very much
better one, than he is now getting. I would give him the
very best possible one, just because he so often fails to add
materially to his stores of knowledge after passing within
the university pale; but I would improve his preparatory
training by simplifying it, by making it mean a thorough
knowledge of a few things and not by modelling it largely af-
ter the standards of the German gymnasium and other pre-
paratory schools. I would make school training mean ability
to spell correctly, to write idiomatic English, and to have a
clear and accurate knowledge of a few subjects.
And what kind of a training will best produce this result?
Regarding that question there will always be unending vari-
ety of opinion, just as there is today. Agreement in such a
matter is practically impossible; but it is helpful to remember
that the thing desired is not merely a disciplined intelligence,
but one that is fitted to grapple with the studies of a univer-
sity course. Discipline alone is not enough. That might
be gained by the study of Chinese and advanced algebra;
but such a training, however thorough, would not have suffi-
cient breadth; it would not give the student adequate power
to pursue the courses which are opened to him in any well-


## p. 23 (#31) ##############################################

23
organized college. Bearing in mind, then, that the school-
boy is to be fitted to take up university work, we can
never very widely depart from the traditional and time-

history, these are the branches that, beyond question, must
dominate in all sound preparatory training. But why
should three languages, or two and an equivalent for a third,

should not as thorough a familiarity with Latin, as can be

and non-mathematical minds be distracted and muddled by
the more theoretical parts of algebra and by original propo-

could solve by their own unaided thinking? Algebra through
quadratics and plane geometry without originals would be a
sufficient requirement for the average student who has no
aptitude for mathematics. A thorough training in English

lish be judged by subtle questions that savor far more of
psychology than of rhetoric, and by the power to write a
learned and well developed essay on such a scholastic theme
as a comparison between Wordsworth and Keats? Some
careful study of English masterpieces there must certainly
be, but it is a great pity that what ought to be an agreeable
pastime is made into irksome toil that kills, instead of encour-
aging, the love of literature. It is with much hesitation,

preparatory course in English literature ought to be. Until

add to his confusion, he is required to read some hundreds
of pages in the larger historical works, a task which he per-
forms in nine cases out of ten in an absolutely perfunctory
manner and with absolutely no recollection of what he reads.

EDMUND H. SEARS
glad to drop them out of his consciousness as soon as circum-

No doubt such a scheme of college preparation as I have
roughly outlined would be held by many to mean a deplorable
lowering of the standards of the schools, and hence of the col-
leges and universities, which rest their own teaching upon
the training given in the schools; but I claim that the result
would be just the opposite. It is indeed not a little strange
that the higher educational institutions of the country should
never have tried to raise their standards of admission by the
intensive rather than the extensive method; that is, by de-
manding a high degree of proficiency in a few subjects. By
rigorously applying this method, they could get minds as
well trained as they chose to have them; they could secure
students who could spell correctly, write idiomatically, know
the essential facts of ancient or of English and American
history, and show that they were well grounded in elemen-
tary mathematics, an ancient and a modern language, and
perhaps also in a science. The matter would be absolutely
in their own hands. They could rule out loose and unsound
preparatory work as rigidly as they wished, and could thus
make sure of a sound training on which to build up a truly
admirable college scholarship and help to produce speci-
alists of first rank. But in racing with each other for
numbers, in demanding of the schools a preparation which
the conditions of American life make it well-nigh impossible
for them to give, and in setting their own pretentious admis-
sion standards at defiance by accepting hordes of wretchedly
trained students, they are contributing one more to the many
shams that disgrace our American civilization.


## p. 27 (#35) ##############################################

COLLEGE RECOGNITION OF HIGH SCHOOL WORK*
MARSHALL S. SNOW
Professor of History and Dean of the College, Washington University
The public high school in its present state is a compara-
tively recent development in the great free school system of
our country, especially in these Western and Southwestern
States.
In New England and the Middle States, even, although
the high school had an early existence in many of the larger
towns and cities, its function was a limited one and seldom in-
cluded that of preparing its pupils for admission to college.
The endowed academies and the many private schools were
the usual feeders of Harvard, Yale, and Columbia. The
last twenty-five years have seen great changes in this respect.
In the Eastern States many of the old academies have disap-
peared, together with a host of small private fitting schools.
The older and stronger academies like Andover and Exeter
have survived only by the generosity of wealthy alumni who
have provided the increased endowments necessary in order
to meet the greater demands now made upon all secondary
schools, and to meet also the competition of the high schools
which have been established everywhere and have been liber-
ally supported by an appreciative public. The same is true
in a modified way in our part of the country and in our own
State. Ten or twelve years ago (I do not try to give exact
*Read before the Missouri College Union, November 4, 1904.


## p. 28 (#36) ##############################################

28
MARSHALL S. SNOW
figures) there were perhaps fifteen public high schools in
Missouri that were able to send their pupils properly pre-
pared to enter the State University, even when the standard
of admission was much lower than it is now. To-day there
are perhaps one hundred and twenty or thirty such schools
whose graduates are accepted by the State University, which
demands much more than formerly, upon presentation of the
certificate of the principal.
More than ever, therefore, are we of the colleges bound
to look to the high schools for the members of our Freshman
classes, and more close than ever before has become the rela-
tion and interdependence of the two. It is perfectly natural,
then, that at such a time as this these relations should be
before us for consideration. To me has been assigned as the
topic for a brief discussion, "College Recognition of High
School Work."
A certain indefiniteness lingers about this title. It may
refer (1) to the admission to college of graduates of high
schools upon the certificates of principals; or (2) to an accept-
ance of work in the high school which may be only par-
tially sufficient for admission; or (3) it may mean such recog-
nition of the work of the high school as will secure to the
student who has been admitted to the Freshman class credit
for courses, prescribed or elective, which are included in the
curriculum of the college.
1. The "certificate plan," as it is sometimes called, has
been so generally adopted by all of our colleges that little need
be said upon the first of the above definitions. It is not in-
tended, I take it, to enter now into any argument for or
against this widely accepted plan. We receive students from
certain accredited schools into our Freshman classes without


## p. 29 (#37) ##############################################

COLLEGE RECOGNITION OF HIGH SCHOOL WORK
29
an examination, upon the presentation of the proper papers
certifying as to their fitness to carry on college work.
The requirements of our colleges are, to be sure, not uni-
form, and the standards are sufficiently different in some
cases to make the certificate accepted by one college differ
somewhat from that which is received by another, but these
differences are constantly lessening and the tendency is to-
wards uniformity. The North Central Association of Col-
leges and Secondary Schools, an organization with which
the colleges of this Union of ours are in affiliation and full
sympathy, has now a commission at work which will before
long conclude its labors. When this commission has given
to us the results of its work of some years, we shall have a
standard system of college and school affiliation to which we
can easily and gradually adjust ourselves. I think we shall
not have to wait long for this conclusive aid.
2. In regard to the second possible meaning of our
subject: Shall we accept partial certificates, as they may be
termed? That is, shall we give credit without examination
for such work as the principal of the school may be willing
to approve, and require an examination on the other subjects
not covered by the certificate, or possibly admit the candidate
to the college with conditions?
My answer to these questions would be "No." My view
is that no certificates at all should be received except from
schools which have been formally approved by us, either upon
our own examination and inspection, or such inspection as
we may have agreed to accept as ours. Now if any school
is found to have a place on our accredited list, it must be one
entirely competent to answer our requirements, and no prin-
cipal of such a school should grant a certificate unless the


## p. 30 (#38) ##############################################

30
MARSHALL S. SNOW
candidate is, in his opinion, ready to meet the full require-
ment. To win a certificate making entrance to college eas-
ier, or, at any rate, more comfortable, is a proper stimulus
to an ambitious student. This incentive is greatly weakened
and the value of the certificate much lessened, if the candidate
feels that he may take his chances on certain examinations,
or take an entrance condition, -a poor substitute, by the way,
for careful previous preparation, and a handicap at the very
beginning of his college course. If a school is not prepared
to fit properly candidates for admission to college, let the col-
lege withhold the certificate privileges until the school is
fully ready. In this way only, in my opinion, can a proper
respect for the certificate plan be maintained.
In treating of these two phases of our subject I have said
nothing of the recognition of specific studies which are pur-
sued in the secondary school, and this for two reasons: first,
no uniform requirements for admission have yet been agreed
upon by our colleges, although the approach to uniformity
is greater every year; and it does not seem to be my duty
upon this occasion to discuss that particular question; and
second, as a matter of fact, nearly every subject of gener-
ally recognized value which is taught in the high schools of
good standing, is, in one way or another, already recognized
in the elastic conditions of admission to our colleges, and
to specify would be to name about all of them. We are all
agreed, I doubt not, that Latin, Greek, French, German, pos-
sibly Spanish, history (general and of special periods or
countries), civics, as it is called, algebra, geometry, chemis-
try, physics, biology (which may include botany, zoology and
physiology), carefully taught as preparatory subjects, are
proper for recognition in this sense by our colleges. I pass


## p. 31 (#39) ##############################################

31
now to the last of the three ways in which the subject may be
approached.
(3) What credit, if any, should be given upon the col-
lege record of scholarship for work previously done in the
high school or academy?
This inquiry leads us dangerously near the burning
question of a shortened college course, abbreviated, it may
be, by allowing work done in the secondary school to count
towards a year, more or less, of college work. Perhaps it
was intended, in suggesting this subject, that the question of
a possible shortened course should be considered. Upon this
particular point, however, I may say, I am now of the same
opinion as I was two years ago when, in a paper upon the
"Length of the College Course," I said:
"I am speaking to teachers in Missouri colleges, and I
have in mind our own needs, our own situation, and the
quality of the material that makes up our Freshman classes,
and so I do not hesitate to say that for us, for many years to
come, in all probability, no formal, general shortening of the
college course is advisable. Our greater need is to broaden
and strengthen the work which we do now, whether we ad-
here to the old-fashioned required course, or whether we have
adopted one of the many forms which the so-called elective
system has assumed."
I do not think it wise to make much account in the college
of work done in the secondary school, and it follows natu-
rally that I am not in favor of trying to do more than second-
ary or preparatory work in the high school. From my ex-
perience of many years in dealing with Freshmen I am forced
to the opinion that more careful and thorough instruction and
study in the preparatory courses is the needed thing; not an


## p. 32 (#40) ##############################################

32
MARSHALL S. SNOW
extension of courses of study. When the work in elemen-
tary English is so well done in the high school that the first
year in the college will not have to be taken up with the most
elementary instruction, as is now the case in colleges all over
the country; when the elements of algebra and geometry are
so taught and mastered that the college courses follow easily
and naturally, and when the elementary principles of science
are so fixed and grounded that the broader field upon which
college courses open can be only a joy and satisfaction;
when the foundation in classical instruction and in the mod-
ern languages shall be so well laid that formal elementary
grammar may in the college give place to the attractions of
literature and philology; when the teaching of history shall
go beyond dry text-books and give results which make for a
genuine preparation for the college work; then, in my opin-
ion, it will be time enough to talk about counting high school
work as equivalent to college work, and asking for recogni-
tion upon the college books. I need not say that I have no one
school in mind in making these apparent strictures upon the
preparatory school work. I am only repeating what has
been said on all sides, in all parts of the country, these many
years back, and has been confirmed by my own observation
and experience. I am firmly of the opinion that there is need
of greater thoroughness and severer drill on what may be
called "the essentials" in preparatory education, a thorough-
ness which is in danger of being sacrificed in the desire to
offer and to study many subjects, and to undertake more ad-
vanced courses before the more elementary ones have been
really mastered.
Again, the plan and method of the high school make it
difficult for work to be done beyond a certain point, as similar


## p. 33 (#41) ##############################################

COLLEGE RECOGNITION OF HIGH SCHOOL WORK
33
work is to be done in the college. Especially is this true if
the aim of the pupil in the secondary school, and of his teach-
ers also, is to crowd college work into the same period which
is naturally to be assigned to preparation for the Freshman
class. But granting that more time is to be allowed, I still
believe that an additional year in the high school cannot be
an equivalent for the corresponding year in the college. In
•the school the student is still in the atmosphere of constant
supervision. He is still a school-boy. He cannot, from the
very nature of things, learn the lessons of freedom combined
with self-restraint that should come with the college life and
opportunity. His work will of necessity be the work of the
school and not of the college, and I assume that we are all
agreed that the difference is, or should be, a real one, and one
that reflects no discredit on the secondary school. You will
understand that I am speaking of the high school as it is-
the average school and not of a high school which may by
and by be the result of a process of evolution by no means
complete as yet. There is an old saying that "you can't put
a quart into a pint cup," and this homely adage may, with all
propriety, be quoted for the benefit of some who would play
the rôle of reformer in the relations between the high school
and the college.
My view of this question, however, is not such a sweeping
one as to shut out all possibility under existing conditions of
allowing some credit for work already done in the high
school. For instance, in English some secondary schools do
work of such excellence as to make much of that of the
Freshman year as it is usually laid out a waste of time, and it
may be regarded as only fair that their work should receive
credit. It may be that here and there a school will be found
3


## p. 34 (#42) ##############################################

34
MARSHALL S. SNOW
in which such facilities are afforded in the natural sciences
as to warrant a certain credit on the college record book; but
generally speaking, our high schools have all they can do to
satisfy any reasonable college requirements.
In summing up, therefore, what has been presented to
you, as suggested by this third application of my subject-
and this third definition is probably that which I was expected
to discuss-let me say:
1. That most of our high schools would do well to
endeavor to strengthen the work which they are doing as
strictly preparatory schools, and not allow themselves to be
led into the error of neglecting the most essential things by
the attractiveness of those which may seem to reach into
higher work.
2. That even under the most favorable conditions school
work seldom is regarded as college work; and that, there-
fore, only now and then in exceptional instances should credit
be given in the college for school work.
3. That whatever courses the school has to offer, they
should be directed to training and strengthening the mental
powers of its pupils, so that when they do enter college they
may easily and happily accustom themselves to their new en-
vironment.
4. And, finally, that we should keep in mind all the while
that our problem is that which comes close to us here in Mis-
souri, under conditions which have to be met almost daily
in a practical way, and not that which concerns the general
needs of the United States at large.

A PLEA FOR A MORE LIBERAL SYSTEM OF
EDUCATION IN ARCHITECTURE
HENRY KERR McGOODWIN
Instructor in Architecture, Washington University
There is probably no branch of technical education of
which the results are of more general and immediate public
importance than those involved in the training of the archi-
tect. That training affects, directly and indirectly, the com-
fort and convenience, the physical and moral health of the
whole people; for it affects our efficiency in organizing the
mass of humanly wrought material with which civilized life
must surround itself. Stated broadly, the business of the
architect is to put men's surroundings in order; to seek and
to establish just relations among the objects of men's crea-
tion, to introduce harmony of arrangement among them.
More specially it is to "design" the most convenient, whole-
some and beautiful streets, parks, play-grounds, homes, hos-
pitals, offices, factories, churches; to save light and air and
material; and to avoid all waste of effort, of energy, of re-
sources, by his skill in these designs. In short, it is the
architect's business to make the best possible surroundings
for human work, play, rest, and worship, surroundings best
designed to satisfy sense and sensibilities and to save money,
labor, time, and health. The proper architect inherits a good
feud; for he is the born enemy of all waste and disorder in
the things built with men's hands. So he is the friend and ally
of every man, and every man has a very near interest in what


## p. 36 (#44) ##############################################

36
HENRY KERR MCGOODWIN
he does and in his being taught to do it in the best way. If
he be untaught or ill-taught, the public must suffer, con-
sciously or unconsciously. The disorder which results to a
community by reason of an inefficient police force is a baga-
telle compared to that which results by reason of an ineffi-
cient architectural profession.
It is by reason of this identification of his purposes and
his work with the general good of civilized men that the
architect may justly claim, and will generally receive, a place
in the public esteem and the public interest. There now ap-
pear hopeful signs that architectural art in America may re-
ceive the general attention merited by its importance; that
Americans may again reach the point of civilization of their
Colonial times; that they may regain a sense of the dignity
and necessity of having rightness and nobility in the "things"
of daily life,-a general realization of the fact that æsthetic
law is an inseparable part of the law of the universe, a part
as potent as any other in the life of man, and in his advance
toward sanity, wisdom, and happiness. The remarkable in-
crease in the number of our schools of arts, and especially of
architecture, may be taken as one of these signs. The equally
remarkable increase in the number of students in them is
another sign. These schools and their students cannot fail
to have a very important influence on the future civilization
of this continent.
So far as the architectural schools are concerned, it may
be fairly said that their methods and results are as yet tenta-
tive. The oldest one of them was organized less than half a
century ago, and its work has probably not been important
for much more than the latter half of that time. The others
are much younger still. So the time of their activity has been


## p. 37 (#45) ##############################################

A PLEA FOR MORE LIBERAL EDUCATION IN ARCHITECTURE 37
hardly sufficient for the perfection either of their means or of
their methods. In fact, certain defects appear to be inherent
in their methods. It is with the purpose of indicating these
and of suggesting remedies for them that the following dis-
cussion is presented.
The most important defects appear to be, first, the inac-
cessibility of the school training to all but those young men
who are in a position to devote a very considerable sum of
money and nearly all their time and effort during a number
of years to the pursuit of their studies; second, the gradua-
tion of the student from the school and the severing of his
intimate relations with it at a time when he is still immature
and half-trained, and yet when he has just begun to have a
valuable influence in it; third, the lack of sufficiently intimate
relations between schooling in architecture and the practice
of it.
As a remedy for these defects it is proposed that the
architectural schools admit to their courses, as candidates
for their degrees, any students who can by thorough exami-
nation show fitness to do any part of the work in the pre-
scribed courses; that no limit or a low limit be placed on the
amount of work that must be completed in a given time; that
advancement from stage to stage of the work be automatic,
certain values being given for a certain quality of work done,
and a certain accumulation of values being required for ad-
vancement; that the work be done under the general super-
vision of the factulties and under their personal instruction or
that of accredited instructors; that when a student, after any
length of time, has acquired all the values prescribed in the
curriculum of the school with which he is affiliated, its de-
gree be conferred upon him.


## p. 38 (#46) ##############################################

38
HENRY KERR MCGOODWIN
If it should appear from the following reasoning that
these defects in our methods of educating the architect do
exist, and that the proposed scheme would remedy them,
there would seem to be no formidable reason why it should
not be put into general operation by the schools. The sug-
gestion does not involve any necessary increase of resources.
It is rather to render existing resources more efficient and
more accessible.
The suggested scheme should remedy the first of the de-
fects pointed out by making it possible for the student to be
self-supporting, since it would permit him to do his work in
connection with the school slowly enough to serve concur-
rently as draftsman or to do other practical architectural
work. No other question touching the art of architecture
seems so important in this country today as that of making
a thorough training accessible to all architects and requiring
such training of them. The question of the adoption or
invention of an "American" architectural style, which has
sometimes generated much heat in the profession, seems, by
comparison, a trivial one. This matter is one of interest and
importance, surely; but the settlement of it is likely to take
its own course in any event. We need not trouble ourselves
about the invention of a new style outright; for no style has
ever been invented on purpose," and there is no likelihood
that we should succeed. The choice of one or another exist-
ing style for adaptation and development may be fortunate or
unfortunate in helping or hindering the natural tendencies
in the progress of our art; but it is not probable that even an
unfortunate choice could long persist, or could materially
alter the tendency of style to follow lines set by the needs and
natures of the people and by the character of the problems to
be solved.


## p. 39 (#47) ##############################################

A PLEA FOR MORE LIBERAL EDUCATION IN ARCHITECTURE 39
What is vastly more important than the question of the
architect's choice of a style or form of expression is that he
should "make architecture," should express the truth, should
be able to attack and solve the innumerable problems pre-
sented to him. Now it is just in this matter of finding solu-
tions to architectural problems that the preliminary training
of the schools governs all the architect's results in practice;
for it is to the end of fitting him to attack and solve problems
in composition, -arrangement, -that this training is directed.
If all our architects were thoroughly trained in these more
fundamental matters of their art it is likely that heated dif-
ferences of opinion as to style would rapidly disappear.
Such a system would remedy equally well the second and
third of the defects pointed out above. At present the meth-
ods of the schools make it necessary for the student to devote
his time continuously to the work required of him. This
work covers in most cases a period of four years, of which
only three are devoted to architectural studies. The more
important schools offer, and urge students to take, a fifth
year of study. One now offers a sixth year also, but very
few students are in a position to make use of these exten-
sions.
Now the architectural skill which can be acquired in
three or four years is on all hands recognized as insufficient,
not so much because enough teaching cannot be given in that
time as because under such circumstances the teaching must
progress so much faster than the development of the student,
who consequently fails to comprehend what he is taught. It
is further impossible for him to gain the greatest possible
benefits from teaching received in so limited a time, because
under such conditions teaching cannot be closely enough


## p. 40 (#48) ##############################################

40
HENRY KERR MCGOODWIN
related to practice. Manifestly no one who is given a whole
body of principles without application to practice, and who
afterward undertakes to apply them without careful guid-
ance, can either comprehend or apply them with the fullest
intelligence.
In the great majority of cases the consequence to the
architect is that as a student he understands his principles
imperfectly or not at all, and that when he comes to practice
he helplessly regards them as things purely "academic,"
which the practitioner cannot and need not live up to. Yet
nothing could be more absurd than that any architectural
school should teach any methods or principles whatever that
are not necessary and right in practice. But that the average
graduate in practice should be at a loss to make proper and
complete use of what he has been taught is the natural and
inevitable result of the faults in the present methods of teach-
ing him. The young architect is thus at a disadvantage
such as the medical student would suffer if he were obliged
to finish his courses of study without accompanying hospital
or clinical work.
The schools cannot hope to remedy these defects without
a radical departure from their methods. They cannot, of
course, undertake to engage in the actual construction of
architectural works in order to properly correlate precept and
practice, but they may change current methods so as to allow
and encourage, or even require, students to engage in prac-
tice in architects' offices. Thus the change would not only
make education accessible to every young architect, by en-
abling the student to be self-dependent, but would result in
the greatest efficiency of training.
It is noteworthy that by far the most intelligent work


## p. 41 (#49) ##############################################

A PLEA FOR MORE LIBERAL EDUCATION IN ARCHITECTURE 41
done in the schools is that of students who have had a number
of years of practical experience and who maintain as stu-
dents the closest relations with practice possible under present
scholastic conditions. This is so generally the case that
instructors invariably urge their students to spend vacation
periods in architects' offices. This attempt to remedy wrong
methods can be but partly efficacious, since the student can
thus obtain only as many months as he needs to have years
of practice concurrent with consistent and carefully directed
study.
At present our young architects obtain the practical expe-
rience necessary before they may safely undertake the execu-
tion of independent works, by serving for some or many
years as assistants in architects' offices. The disadvantages
of acquiring this experience apart from guidance in the prin-
ciples which should influence it, have been pointed out. Fur-
thermore, many school graduates, and, unfortunately, these
have the greatest aptitude for securing commissions,-go
into practice soon or immediately after graduation, entirely
immature in their understanding of the most important ma-
terials of their art, with results to which American architec-
ture bears mute but eloquent testimony.
Certain steps have already been taken in the direction of
the proposed changes. One of the most important of the
American schools has this year put into operation a system
under which the required courses in design may be taken
either in the drafting rooms of the school or in one of a num-
ber of accredited "ateliers" conducted by practicing archi-
tects of the City of New York; that is, it is no longer regarded
as imperative by the faculty of this school that the most im-
portant architectural study be pursued within the walls of the


## p. 42 (#50) ##############################################

42
HENRY KERR MCGOODWIN
institution. If this be a wise action with regard to the most
important subject, why should it not be extended to any or all
of the others? The same institution has begun to specifically
encourage candidates for its advanced degree in Architecture
to pursue their studies for it in Europe; and it has made its
system of advancement through the stages of undergraduate
work automatic, basing it on the accumulation of values
accorded a certain quality of work.
Another movement in the same direction has assumed
such magnitude as to bid fair to become, if indeed it has not
already become, the most important yet begun in architec-
tural education in this country. This is the free course of
study offered by the Society of Beaux Arts Architects, an
American organization of graduates of the Ecole des Beaux
Arts in Paris. During the last two years or more this society
has, through its educational committee, organized and con-
ducted courses of training in the most important subjects of
an architectural study, design, freehand drawing, arch-
æology and modelling. These courses are open to any stu-
dent who can do the work laid out by the Society, under the
direction and criticism of one of its members or of any other
accredited instructor. The work done is assembled and
exhibited periodically in New York. It is examined and
ranked competitively by juries of able practicing architects
and instructors. Advancement of the student is dependent
on the acquisition of prescribed values for quality of work
done. When a certain total of values in the various classes
has been won, a diploma certifying that fact is given. The
Society also supports a valuable competitive scholarship for
foreign study. The winner of this scholarship is admitted
to advanced work in the Ecole des Beaux Arts without


## p. 43 (#51) ##############################################

A PLEA FOR MORE LIBERAL EDUCATION IN ARCHITECTURE 43
examination, a concession not made by that school to any
other educational institution.
The work done under this organization, principally by
students engaged at the same time as draftsmen, has been
astonishingly important. To one who has seen the quality
of this work and the ambitious enthusiasm of the young men
doing it, it would seem absurd to contend that the same men
could not under similar conditions do other work necessary
to the completer education of the architect. It seems most
unfortunate that these talented and ambitious young men
do not find, at any American architectural school, the open
door inviting them to undertake such completer training.
The schools are thus losing far the larger part of the most
valuable material they might have, and most of this material
must remain undeveloped. What could be more ruinously
wasteful to a nation which needs so urgently as ours the
benefit of every latent power that might help to set right its
physical works and its intellectual and moral ideals?
It seems to the writer that if it were possible for this
Society to so extend its work as to include all the subjects
most necessary for his training, the student of architecture
would do wisely to pursue his education in this course rather
than in any existing school excepting the Ecole des Beaux
Arts. But it is manifestly as impossible for the ateliers of
practicing architects, in which the work projected by the
Society is done, to give all of the necessary courses, as it is
impossible for the schools to organize within themselves
means of practical experience for their students. The nature
of the limitations of both the schools and the independent
ateliers suggests the remedy above indicated, which would
combine the resources and advantages of both.


## p. 44 (#52) ##############################################

44
HENRY KERR MCGOODWIN
By such a combination many young men would find it
possible to obtain a very thorough training when they can
now obtain a very imperfect one at best. The standard of the
efficiency produced by the schools would inevitably be raised.
Even if some students preferred to take their academic train-
ing, as now, in a comparatively short period devoted entirely
to study, the influence on these of a body of mature men who
preferred to combine practice with schooling and to remain
in connection with a school for six or eight or a dozen years,
would be invaluable; an influence similar to that of the
ancien in the ateliers of Paris, which is well recognized as
the most valuable feature of the training to be had in them.
Undoubtedly there would be an increasingly large proportion
of students who would prefer to remain connected with a
school for a long period, doing their work slowly and ma-
turely, gaining the greatest possible benefit from their studies
combined with the practical work which would maintain
them, bringing to bear on both a liberal understanding and a
ripened judgment. A much enlarged usefulness and an in-
creased prestige could not fail to result to the schools.
The details of the scheme proposed above are of course
only tentative. Such details would of necessity vary consid-
erably in different schools. But the general features of it
need not be considered wholly experimental nor the results
wholly problematical. Such a system has been in operation
at the Ecole des Beaux Arts for upward of three-quarters of
a century; and it may be asserted without any fear of exag-
geration that the graduates of this institution have produced
the only body of consistent and vital architectural work ex-
ecuted during that time.
There seems every reason to believe that the time is ripe


## p. 45 (#53) ##############################################

A PLEA FOR MORE LIBERAL EDUCATION IN ARCHITECTURE 45
for the adoption of such a system by American schools of
architecture, and that those adopting it would render a most
far-reaching service by doing so, a service of profound im-
portance in the development of American art and American
civilization.
Since this paper was written, the Society of Beaux Arts Architects has
proposed still further to extend its work and to undertake in New York the
establishment of an American National School of Architecture, on lines similar
to those of the Ecole des Beaux Arts, by combining the system of instruction
in the æsthetics of architecture now conducted by the Society, with scientific
courses to be offered, at least at first, in some existing school in New York, if
any can be induced to open its doors on some such terms as outlined above.
The following is quoted from an open letter written by Mr. Lloyd Warren,
Chairman of the Educational Committee of the Society:
"Will you allow me to state succinctly the aims and scope of this work?"
(the present educational work of the Society).
"Its object, primarily, is to bring within the reach of the mass of workers
in the architectural profession a course of instruction in those principles of
design which the Paris school has considered essential in the practice of the
art of architecture.
"The possible scope of the Society could unquestionably be much enhanced
by the addition of the scientific part of architectural education to the purely
æsthetic side which it now treats. We wait with impatience the time when
some one of the New York seats of learning will so far unbend as to extend
the aid of its architectural department to the mass of (architectural) workers.
"Which one of our institutions will have the merit of accomplishing this
great thing?"

"As the Herald has stated, and has been endorsed by those best fitted to
