## p. 46 (#54) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL
GOVERNOR OF MISSOURI*
WALTER R. SMITH
Instructor in American History, Washington University
The interest which has been aroused in the Lewis and
Clark Expedition in recent years has led to a number of de-
scriptive articles and books, and to the publication of three
expensive editions of the notes taken by the leaders during
the trip; yet the personality of William Clark has remained
curiously obscure. No biography, or even respectable ac-
count of his career, has ever been written. His character as
soldier, statesman, Indian agent, and citizen deserves the
highest praise, and his services were so important that an
extended chronicle of them would add immensely to our
knowledge of the history of the early West. He was for
seven years the Territorial Governor of Missouri when Mis-
souri was on the frontier, leading in the progress of western
life toward higher civilization and American statehood.
Louisiana had already been admitted into the Union as the
first state beyond the Mississippi; but Louisiana was an old
French settlement and had been destined for statehood from
the time of the Purchase. It remained for Missouri to indi-
cate the development of the great West of the Louisiana Pur-
chase and the attitude of the national government toward it.
During Clark's governorship Missouri was for the first time
a focus of national interest, and to the end of this critical
period he was the most prominent figure.
*Lecture delivered before the Washington University Association, Nov. 9, 1905.


## p. 47 (#55) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL GOVERNOR 47
Clark was a Virginian, born in Caroline County, August
1, 1770. He was the youngest of a family of nine, five broth-
ers and four sisters. His parentage was that of the Vir-
ginia planter type, not distinguished but thoroughly respeс-
table. His earliest traceable ancestor was John Clark, who
came from England to the struggling Virginia colony when
it was still young, and married a Scotch lass who is said to
have been a "red-haired beauty." This accounts for the
prevalence in the Clark family of red hair, of which William's
was the most striking example. The first ancestor of Wil-
liam Clark of whom definite records are obtainable was
Jonathan Clark, who died in 1834, leaving a considerable es-
tate and four small children. The eldest of these was John
Clark, the father of William. He married his second cousin,
Annie Rogers, who belonged to another prominent family of
Virginia planters. To this couple were born nine children,
all five of the sons becoming prominent soldiers and the four
daughters the wives of leading citizens. The eldest of the
sons, Jonathan Clark, became a lawyer, a politician, a brig-
adier-general in the Revolutionary army, and a wealthy man
of business. John Clark entered as a lieutenant in the
army, was captured at Germantown, and for five years kept
in prison where he contracted consumption, from which he
died at the close of the war. Edmund Clark left school at
the age of eighteen to accept a lieutenancy in the Revolution-
ary army, in which he rose to the rank of captain. The ser-
vices of the remaining brother, George Rogers Clark, are too
well known to need mention, and the only reason William
himself was not in the Revolutionary army was that he was
too young to carry a musket.
Scarcely anything is known of the early life of William.


## p. 48 (#56) ##############################################

48
WALTER R. SMITH
Born on the eve of the Revolution, his earliest memories
must have been of the inspiration and terror of those dread
and hallowed days. As one after another of his brothers
and brothers-in-law donned the uniform of an officer and
went out to battle, his military instincts were stirred and his
ambition aroused. But if he was favored with an atmos-
phere of patriotism and courage, he was at the same time de-
prived of the educational advantages of his brothers and the
refining influences that under other circumstances would
have been his in such a home. His education was further
hindered at the close of the Revolution by his father's re-
moval to the Falls of the Ohio, now Louisville, Kentucky,
where George Rogers Clark had erected a fort.
Into the midst of wilderness perils at this place William
was introduced at the age of fourteen. The Clark home
was one of a cluster of cabins about the fort, and the Clark
estate, christened Mulberry Hill, soon became the center of
hospitality for the whole region. It was frequented by all
the distinguished pioneers of the country, particularly the old
Revolutionary soldiers, and the bright, enterprising, red-
headed "Billy" was a general favorite. He was doubtless
an enchanted listener to the tales of war and adventure re-
lated by his elders, and grew up with little thought of any
other career than that of a soldier. This idea was further
encouraged when at the age of seventeen he was made a mem-
ber of the Society of the Cincinnati, and his certificate was
signed by General Washington.¹ Amid such surround-
ings he naturally became a skillful hunter and an expert
woodman, and learned early to command and to use his in-
genuity in overcoming the obstacles inseparable from frontier
Coues, Lewis and Clark, Vol. I, p. 68.

life. At this period he also laid the foundations of that
knowledge of Indian character so useful to him in later years.
In his nineteenth year William began his military career
by joining an expedition under Colonel John Hardin against
the Indians north of the Ohio. The next year he was sent on
a mission to the Creek and Cherokee Indians, thus at the age
of twenty beginning his responsible dealings with them. At
twenty-one he served as an ensign and acting lieutenant un-
der General Scott against the Indians of the Wabash. Dr.
James O'Fallon, writing to Colonel John Clark, says: "Your
brother William is gone out as a cadet with General Scott on
the expedition. He is a youth of solid and promising parts,
and as brave as Caesar." In 1793 he was commissioned
first lieutenant in "Mad" Anthony Wayne's western army,
where he soon won favor. He was first engaged as engineer
in constructing forts along the line of march. Late in the
winter he was sent on a perilous expedition up the Wabash
to Vincennes, during which his progress was for several
weeks blocked by ice. In 1794 he was entrusted with the
important command of convoying a large quantity of cloth-
ing and provisions from Cincinnati to Fort Greenville. The
equipment consisted of seven hundred pack-horses with a
guard of only eighty men. En route the vanguard was at-
tacked by Indians and five men were killed, but Lieutenant
Clark hastened forward and led such a furious charge that
the Indians were scattered in flight. The success of this
expedition won the praise and favor of General Wayne, un-
der whom he soon afterwards fought in the battle of Fallen
Timbers. During the next year Lieutenant Clark was twice
sent on important military missions to the Spaniards along

the Mississippi and got his first impressions of Missouri at

lieutenant immediately won the confidence and wholesome re-

signed from the army July 14, 1796, with the brevet rank of

This six years of military service under men like Scott
and Wayne had familiarized him with the conduct of West-
ern warfare and developed his natural talent for military
leadership. It had also shown his trustworthiness and dip-
lomatic gifts, and had brought him to the notice of the prom-
inent men of his time. More important still, it had won for
him the admiration of his junior officer, Meriwether Lewis,
and developed a friendship which later was to ripen into a
comradeship as rare as it was beautiful.
After his resignation from the army Clark retired to his
Kentucky farm, where he spent the next seven years. Dur-
ing this period he was frequently in the East and became well
acquainted with President Jefferson. This was the other
friendship so influential in his career. It was while here
upon the farm that he received the offer of a share in the
Lewis and Clark expedition.
The survey and exploration of the West had been long a
favorite idea with Mr. Jefferson. While in Paris he had
aided John Ledyard to obtain a passport through Russia in
order that he might board a ship to Nootka Sound and then
cross to the Missouri River and descend to St. Louis. When
Ledyard failed he proposed to the American Philosophical
Society in 1792 that it should raise a subscription to engage
a competent frontiersman who should, with a single scien-
tific companion, ascend the Missouri and cross the Rockies


## p. 51 (#59) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL GOVERNOR
51
to the Pacific. The subscription was raised, and Captain
Meriwether Lewis and a French botanist, André Michaux,
set out to make the trip; but the botanist was recalled by
the French Government, and the enterprise failed. Mr. Jef-
ferson having been elected to the Presidency, an opportunity
arose in 1803 to make the expedition a national enterprise.
The occasion was the need of establishing trading houses
with the Indians on the upper Missouri; the cause was the
desire to know more of the western wilderness which Jef-
ferson and his commissioners were about to purchase for the
United States. On recommendation by special message the
necessary appropriation was made by Congress and placed at
the disposal of the President, who again selected Captain
Lewis as the leader. It was to be a military expedition, nom-
inally under the orders of the Secretary of War, but really
in control of President Jefferson. Lewis was asked to name
a lieutenant who should assume charge in case of accident to
himself. Lewis wanted a partner rather than a lieutenant,
however, and on June 19th wrote to his old friend Clark, of-
fering him a full share in the enterprise, "its fatigues, its
dangers, and its honors." He further assured Clark that
there was no other man on earth with whom he would "feel
equal pleasure in sharing them." Clark promptly accepted,
and each began making the necessary preparations.
The greatness of the Lewis and Clark expedition histo-
rians are just beginning to realize and the lay public has
hardly yet begun to suspect. No other expedition in history
has equalled it in the length of time required, the distance of
travel, the constancy of peril, and the success of execution.
It started from the mouth of the Missouri River on May 14,
1804, and did not return until September 23, 1806-two


## p. 52 (#60) ##############################################

52
WALTER R. SMITH
years, four months and ten days. For one year and a half
they were buried in the depths of the wilderness, without a
word of cheer or a single communication with civilization.
The trip covered nearly 8000 miles. They were in almost
constant peril from wind and wave, wild beasts, Indians, dis-
ease, or famine; yet so skillful and circumspect were they
that not a single man was killed and only one died from dis-
ease. They came in contact with almost two score of Indian
tribes, many of them predisposed to hostility, but so adroitly
were these managed that only one skirmish occurred, two
Indians being killed in this while trying to steal horses. The
success of the expedition was so complete and perfect that
both leaders immediately sprang into national prominence.
The company was composed of the two captains, equal in
command and responsibility, and forty-one picked men-
soldiers, hunters, rivermen, and interpreters, of whom four
were chosen sergeants. The outfit consisted of three boats
loaded with tools, clothing, food, ammunition, and Indian
presents such as tomahawks, knives, medals, flags, mirrors,
paints, and richly ornamented articles of dress. These things
were done up in twenty-one bales and boxes so distributed
that in case of accident no one article would be wholly lost.
The first of the boats was a keel boat fifty-five feet long,
drawing three feet of water and carrying one large sail and
twenty-two oars. It had a deck in the bow and one in the
stern, while the middle part was filled with lockers which
could be raised to form breastworks in case of attack. The
other two boats were open pirogues of six and seven oars re-
spectively. Two horses were led along the shore, to be used
in hunting and carrying in the game.
At four o'clock of a rainy Monday afternoon in May,


## p. 53 (#61) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL GOVERNOR
53
1804, this picturesque assemblage left their encampment at
the mouth of Wood River, rowed across the Mississippi, and
began paddling against the turgid current of the Missouri.
The detailed account of their observations, progress, and ad-
ventures fills six fat volumes. Slowly and painfully they
toiled their way upward, day after day rising with the dawn,
and night after night drawing their boats into some shel-
tered nook where they could build a campfire and carry on
petty warfare with the mosquitoes and kindred pests of the
river bottoms. They safely breasted the tempestuous June
rise, paused to fire salutes on the Fourth of July, stopped
again to bury in the solitudes of the forest the beloved Ser-
geant Floyd, and finally reached the present site of Bismarck,
South Dakota, where they were compelled to spend the win-
ter among the Mandan Indians. From this point they sent
back a part of their force to report progress, and in the spring
of 1805 continued their voyage into Montana. Leaving the
headquarters of the Missouri they plunged into the wild
canons of the Rockies, crossed the divide, and ferreted out
the sources of the Snake River. Down this stream they
floated into the Columbia, thence on the Columbia to its
mouth, where, on the 15th of November, they beheld "the
waves like small mountains rolling out in the sea." On the
shore of the Pacific they wintered, living principally upon
fish, horses, edible roots, and other Indian delicacies. In the
spring of 1806 they again entered the tortuous defiles of the
Rockies, encountering famine and hostile Indians. They
separated in parties to test the various possible routes and
finally came together on the headwaters of the Missouri,
down which stream they floated to the Mississippi. On Sep-
tember 23, 1806, they drew up their boats to the landing at


## p. 54 (#62) ##############################################

54
WALTER R. SMITH
St. Louis, fired a last salute, and stepped ashore to receive
the joyous welcome of their friends, most of whom had given
them up for lost.
The perfect harmony and success of this expedition forms
the most creditable chapter in the history of American fron-
tier life. It not only opened up a pathway across the conti-
nent and paved the way for the Americanization of the Ore-
gon country, but it was a scientific expedition of great merit.
The part of William Clark in it was not less important than
that of its nominal leader, Lewis. Lewis was the better ed-
ucated and had received special training for taking astro-
nomical and botanical observations but Clark was the military
and practical leader. Mr. Reuben Gold Thwaites, in writing
of their journals, speaks of the "poetic temperament of
Lewis, who loved flowers and animals and in his notes dis-
coursed like a philosopher who enjoyed the exercise of writ-
ing," and "the rugged character of Clark, who wrote in
brief, pointed phrase, spelled phonetically, capitalized chaot-
ically and occasionally slipped in his grammar. Clark
was pre-eminently the Indian diplomat, and in his multitu-
dinous pow-wows with the Indians laid the foundations of
that remarkable influence he was ever afterwards able to
exert over the western tribes. The combination of qualities
possessed by the two leaders left little to be desired, and their
successful comradeship was to continue in higher offices.

On March 3, 1807, Lewis was made Governor of the Ter-
ritory of Louisiana, and Clark was made Indian Agent and
Brigadier-General in command of military affairs. Louisi-
ana Territory then consisted of all the Louisiana Purchase
north of the thirty-third parallel. It contained a population

of less than 20,000, scattered all the way from the southern
boundary of Arkansas to the Dakota mountains. All the
outposts were in danger from hostile Indians and had to be
given such protection as the Governor and the General could
provide. Clark's headquarters were in St. Louis, whence
we find him issuing to protect a settlement, or strengthen a
fortification, or treat with the Indians. For example, in
1808, to stop the depredations of the Osage Indians, he vis-
ited them, founded Fort Osage at the mouth of the Osage
River, and made a treaty preliminary to Lewis's great treaty
of 1808, by which the Indians gave up a large slice of terri-
tory in the central part of the state. The force at Clark's
command was small, however, and his duties mainly routine.
It was during this period (January 5, 1808,) that he married
Miss Julia Hancock, at Fincastle, Virginia, and brought his
bride to St. Louis. A little later he purchased half a block
of property on the corner of Main and Pine Streets, and
moved there to live. On this corner was a small stone
store which he converted into an Indian office. He soon
became prominent in local affairs and was elected a member
of the Board of Trustees of the city. As such we find him
signing an ordinance as President pro tem, in 1811, defining
the boundaries of the city. He also formed a partnership
with Manuel Lisa and Sylvester Labbadie to engage in the
fur trade, each partner putting in $9000. He was also a
member of the Board of Trustees which inaugurated the
public school system of the State of Missouri.
In September, 1809, Governor Lewis either committed
suicide, or was murdered, on his way to Washington City and
General Clark was offered the governorship. This he mod-
estly refused, on account of his lack of political experience,


## p. 56 (#64) ##############################################

56
WALTER R. SMITH
and General Benjamin Howard was appointed. Howard
served until the breaking out of the war of 1812, when he
resigned to enter the army, and General Clark was appointed
to succeed him as governor. Being absent from the Terri-
tory he did not enter upon the duties of his office until the
following July, the Secretary of the Territory, Edward
Bates, acting as governor in the meantime.
Just previous to Clark's appointment the Territory had
been reorganized. Its name was changed from the Terri-
tory of Louisiana to the Territory of Missouri and it was ad-
vanced to the second grade of territorial government. The
old districts were reorganized into five counties: St. Charles,
St. Louis, Ste. Genevieve, Cape Girardeau, and New Madrid.
The government consisted of a Governor, a Secretary, three
Judges, all appointed by the President, and a bicameral Leg-
islature. This Legislature consisted of a popularly elected
House of Representatives and a Legislative Council. There
was to be one representative for every six hundred free
white male inhabitants, and this representative must be of
full age, a freeholder in the county he represented, and a res-
ident of the Territory at least one year previous to his elec-
tion. The House of Representatives was to choose eighteen
men, out of whom the President, with the advice and consent
of the Senate, was to select nine members for the Upper
House or Legislative Council. The Legislature was to
meet annually in St. Louis and the first sessions were held in
the house of Joseph Robidoux on Main Street between Wal-
nut and Elm.
The Legislature which William Clark met for the first
time in July, 1813, was composed of nine Councillors and
thirteen Representatives. They were a rugged, frontier lot,


## p. 57 (#65) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL GOVERNOR 57
but much had to be done in the way of primal legislation, and
they went at it with vigor and common-sense, if not with
training and polish. Two new counties were created, Wash-
ington and Arkansas, and a census of the free white male in-
habitants was ordered. This census, taken early in 1814,
gave Arkansas 214; Washington 1010; St. Charles 1096;
New Madrid 1548; Ste. Genevieve 1701; Cape Girardeau
2062; St. Louis 3149. This indicates a total population of
about 25,000 in 1814, showing an increase of 4000 over the
federal census of 1810. The population was a heterogeneous
mixture of French, Spanish, and English, with a varied as-
sortment of half-breed Indians, negro slaves, and adventur-
ers from many lands. There were outlying settlements in
Arkansas, at Boone's Lick, on Salt River, and far up the
Missouri. The chief source of income was the fur trade, al-
though lead-mining, salt-making, and agriculture were be-
ing rapidly developed. The people were typical pioneers, un-
couth in speech and dress, rude in manner, reckless and ad-
venturous, brave and hospitable. They were willing to abide
by and carry out a government of rude justice and order, but
had little need of the refinements of legislation.
The duties of the Governor were more military than
civil. The outlying posts had to be protected and our Indian
wards looked after. Just before Clark's nomination for the
governorship, a number of outrages having been committed
by the Indians on Boone's Lick and other exposed settle-
ments, it was thought that a pilgrimage of the chiefs to
Washington to see their "Great Father" would have a happy
effect. So in the spring of 1812 General Clark set out from
St. Louis with the chiefs of the Great and Little Osages, the
Sacs, the Foxes, the Shawnees, and the Delawares. It was


## p. 58 (#66) ##############################################

58
WALTER R. SMITH
a skillful move and so cemented his control of the tribes west
of the Mississippi that he was able to keep them neutral dur-
ing the war then threatening. It was also Clark's vigilance
and his spies among the Indians east of the Mississippi that
enabled the government to follow the machinations of Brit-
ish agents and foil the grand schemes of Tecumseh and the
Prophet for a general confederation of Indian tribes against
the Americans.
The winter of 1813 and 1814 Governor Clark spent in
preparing for an expedition to Prairie-du-Chien, 600 miles
up the Mississippi at the mouth of the Wisconsin River. It
was to co-operate with that of his nephew, Major Croghan,
against Mackinaw. Clark left St. Louis early in 1814 with
five armed barges and two hundred volunteers. They ar-
rived at Prairie-du-Chien and found it evacuated; but the
fiery energy of Tecumseh and the shrewdness of the British
agents, together with the failure of Croghan's attempt upon
Mackinaw, made the situation so perilous that Governor
Clark returned to St. Louis for reinforcements. These were
finally procured and sent out under Lieutenant Campbell; but
they were ambushed on the way and had to return to St.
Louis, leaving Prairie-du-Chien to be captured by the British.
The war of 1812, however, did not bear heavily upon
Missouri, and at its conclusion Governor Clark, Governor
Edwards of Illinois, and Auguste Chouteau, made a treaty
of peace and friendship with the hostile tribes.
As Governor of Missouri Territory, Clark had to keep
careful watch over widely scattered frontier forts, appoint
the "factors" and other officers, look after supplies, and do his
best to see that marauding Indians and lawless whites were
brought to justice. As Indian agent he had to keep the peace


## p. 59 (#67) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL GOVERNOR
59
between warring tribes when possible, look after the execu-
tion of the Indian treaties, which neither the United States
Government nor the Indians were careful to keep, and dis-
tribute the funds and supplies of the Government to the vari-
ous tribes. He saw the population of Missouri grow from
about, 25,000 at the beginning of his governorship to 66,000
at the close. The frontier was pushed gradually westward,
the settled districts extending from a fringe twenty miles
wide along the Mississippi to the central part of the state,
with numerous settlements near the western border. Since
his training and instincts were military, he interfered little
with the work of legislation. During his whole official ca-
reer he never vetoed a law, but sometimes objected to a bill,
and by diplomacy had it changed before it passed the Legis-
lature.
In 1816, Missouri was advanced to the third stage of
territorial government, and Clark was re-commissioned Gov-
ernor.
The growth of the community was rapid. Whole
trains of wagons, loaded down with household "plunder,"
headed westward. Mr. Flint, a careful writer of the period,
states that as many as one hundred persons passed through
St. Charles in a single day for Boone's Lick, Salt River, and
other western settlements. A new era of prosperity was
inaugurated in 1817 when the General Pike, the first steam-
boat to reach St. Louis, puffed up the Mississippi. County
after county appeared on the map, the number growing from
five to fifteen during Clark's governorship. At one session
of the Legislature, in 1818, the seven new counties of Jeffer-
son, Franklin, Wayne, Lincoln, Madison, Montgomery, Pike,
and Cooper, were organized. The people began to clamor
for statehood, and in spite of a financial panic brought on

by speculation in cheap land, the Legislature applied to Con-
gress in 1818 for authority to frame a constitution and es-
tablish a state government.
Accordingly, on March 6, 1820, a national law was ap-
proved providing for a constitutional convention in Mis-
souri, to be composed of forty-one delegates, who were to
meet in St. Charles on the second Monday in June. Their
work was completed by July 19th, and the first Constitution
of Missouri was promulgated without sending it back for the
approval of the people by popular vote. An election was
called for the autumn of 1820, and William Clark became a
candidate for Governor under the new constitution. At this
time his wife was sick unto death and wanted to go back to
her Virginia home to die. The grief-stricken husband left
the state at the opening of the campaign, to return with
Mrs. Clark, and published a letter in the newspapers dated
July 2, 1820. It was addressed "To the People of Missouri,"
and ran as follows: "Fellow Citizens: My name is before
you as a candidate for the office of Governor of the new State
of Missouri. A necessary absence, the cause of which is
known to many of you, will prevent me from being among
you till the election is over; but this circumstance does not
give me uneasiness, except as it might be construed by some
into an indifference for your good-will. Otherwise I think
it of no importance for me to be present. The choice of a
governor is your business and not mine; and so far as my
fitness for that place may be the subject of inquiry, that mat-
ter may be discussed as well in my absence as in my presence.
I should take no part in the discussion even if I remained at
home, but leave it to those whose business it is to decide
upon my pretensions." Then, speaking of his services as

Governor, he continues: "My long residence has given me
a personal acquaintance, which time has ripened into friend-
ship, with most of the old inhabitants and early settlers; and
to them I refer for answers to any inquiries which may con-

duct is more amply before you. During the last seven years
I have been Governor of the Territory, and the period has
been one of uncommon danger to the inhabitants, and of
peculiar difficulty to the executive department. Our country
was engaged in war with the British and their Indian allies,
and this remote and isolated territory was exposed to a more
than equal share of the common danger, and with a less than
equal share of the common means of defense. It presented
a frontier of many hundred miles in circumference, thinly
sprinkled with inhabitants and surrounded with Indian na-
tions stimulated to war by their own love of blood and plun-
der and the wicked arts of British emissaries. The territory
was accessible to their excursions by the large rivers which
traverse it, and by means of which an immense force, de-
scending the Illinois, Missouri, and Mississippi, might con-
centrate at any moment and with the utmost secrecy, rapidity,
and silence, in the heart and center of our country. The
general government had no regular troops to spare for our
defense; and to a system of policy more than to arms and
to the proper employment of some rangers and militia, the
territory was reduced to depend for its safety.
Still I
flatter myself that the system adopted was not without suc-
cess, and although some remote settlements were tempor-
arily dispersed and some valuable citizens lost their lives, yet
the country upon the whole enjoyed comparative safety and
suffered less than any new country has ever yet suffered
during the progress of an Indian war."*

but they afforded good campaign material and were used in
Clark's absence with such good effect that he was defeated
by a large majority.
After the death of Mrs. Clark the General returned to St.
Louis where, a year later, November 28, 1821, he married
Mrs. Harriet K. Radford. There had been five children
born of the first marriage, four of whom were living. Of
the second marriage two children were born, only one living
to maturity. December 15, 1825, Clark wrote thus of his
family in a characteristic letter to Mr. Jefferson: "I have
five sons the oldest of them Meriwether Lewis of 17 years of
age is a cadet at West Point; he is a youth of Capacity & Ap-

Clark still remained Indian agent and lived quietly in St.
Louis the remainder of his life. He was a good business man
and had accumulated enough wealth to live in dignity and
comfort. His character was so well balanced and mild that
he made few enemies, and his home was the center of hospi-
tality. In 1827, when the city desired to give a ball to the
soldiers stationed at the new military post of Jefferson Bar-
racks, General Clark's home was chosen for the purpose.
Nearly every distinguished visitor to the city was entertained
in his home. A typical instance of his kindliness is given by
Colonel McKenney in his memoirs. Colonel McKenney was
prominent in the Indian affairs of the west, and visited
St. Louis with the French Count de Lillier. A small party
was given for them at General Clark's, which the Count
was too sick to attend. Knowing that the hotel had poor
accommodations, the Clarks invented a ruse to have the
Count driven to their own home, which he was not allowed
to leave until he had fully recovered.
General Clark's public career was by no means ended
with his defeat for Governor. In 1822 the new office of
Superintendent of Indian Affairs was created and he was
appointed by President Monroe to fill it, which he did dur-
ing the remaining sixteen years of his life. During this
period a large number of Indian treaties were completed, the
most important being the one with the Osages in 1825, that
with the Sioux of the same year, and the one in 1830, known
as the Treaty of Prairie-du-Chien. In 1824 he was com-

missioned Surveyor-General of the states of Illinois and

a superb draughtsman, as shown by his volume of maps in

After residing in St. Louis thirty years, General Clark
died here in his sixty-ninth year at the home of his son,
Jefferson K. Clark, on the first day of September, 1838. His
almost three score and ten years had been full of intelligent
labor and its rewards. His funeral was a demonstration of
the respect and affection of the community for its most ven-
erable citizen, and was the most impressive the city had ever
known. The next edition of the "Missouri Saturday News"
appeared in mourning and contained a feeling obituary by its
editor, Charles Keemle.
William Clark's greatest service to the country was in his
dealings with the Indians in the West. No other citizen of
the United States has ever had such personal influence over
so large a number of tribes. From the Mississippi to the
Pacific, from Canada to the Gulf, he was known, and his
word was respected among them. His name appears in the
American state papers on Indian affairs as the leading nego-
tiator of thirty-seven treaties with the Indians, and wherever
it appeared it carried peculiar weight with the red men. Mr.
Coues states with reference to his influence: "Probably no
officer of the government ever made his personal influence
more widely and deeply felt; his superintendency grew to be
a sort of lawful autocracy, wielded in the best interests of all
concerned, on the strong principle of even-handed justice;
his word became Indian law, from the Mississippi to the


## p. 65 (#73) ##############################################

65
Pacific. Thousands of Indians had made his personal ac-
quaintance when he traveled among them; and in later years
there could have been few who did not regard his signature
as 'medicine' of the most salutary sort.""
Clark was universally known among them as the "Red-
Head," and St. Louis became simply the Red-Head's town.
No Indian chief ever visited St. Louis without calling upon
the Governor. Their attitude towards him is summed up in
the speech of a Sac chief in a council called in 1821 by Major
Benjamin O'Fallon: "American Chief! We have opened
our ears to your words and those of the Red-Head brother!
We receive you as the son of the Red-Head; inasmuch as we
love him, we will love you and do not wish to offend you."
Probably no higher compliment was ever paid him than that
by his opponents for the governorship in 1820 when they
accused him of being partial to the Indians. Frontier respect
for Indian rights was very slight and Clark stood between the
greedy and fraudulent trader and his barbarian victim. He
understood perfectly the simple outlines of the Indians' char-
acter and could see their side of the case. He won their favor
by diplomacy, their respect by his fairness and firmness, and
their love by his kindness. He stood by his own word and
compelled the Indians to stand by their agreements. His In-
dian office and his home were always open to them. A fine
and curious incident is reported by William Walker, agent to
the Wyandotte Indians. Passing through St. Louis he called
upon Superintendent Clark to get letters to the various Indian
agents in the West. While there he was informed that three
Flathead chiefs were in the house sick and that one had died
a few days before. They were from west of the Rocky

A key to Clark's policy with the Indians can be given in
his own words in a letter to Mr. Jefferson, dated St. Louis,
December 15, 1825: "In my present situation of Superin-

enabled to meliorate the condition of those unfortunate peo-

ness and their rapid decline-It is to be lamented that the
deplorable situation of the Indians do not receive more of the
humain feelings of the nation.""

Indian life. During his thirty years of service as Indian
agent he labored to build up an Indian museum. Back of his
house on the southeast corner of Pine and Main Streets

His interest in the museum and the Academy, however,

At the time of Lewis's death he was on his road to Wash-
ington, one of his aims being to look after the publication
of the journals. The work next devolved upon Clark. He
took it up forthwith and after much persuasion secured the
services of a young Philadelphia lawyer, Nicholas Biddle,
afterwards president of the Bank of the United States, to
edit the notes. A publisher was then sought and soon
found in Mr. Conrad of Philadelphia, but as the work went
to press Mr. Conrad failed in business. It was next under-
taken by Bradford & Inskeep, who likewise made an assign-
ment while the book was in press. After numerous vicissi-
tudes it was given to the public in February, 1814, and it
was six months before General Clark was able to get hold
of a borrowed copy. The affairs of Bradford & Innskeep
were in litigation for several years and General Clark re-
ceived no financial reward for his pains. Such was the
early history of the journals which have been recently so
eagerly sought by publishers as to call for the three expen-
sive editions previously mentioned.
The public career of General Clark was long and varied
and is an example of our best type of public service. For
fifty years, from his very boyhood, he was in the employ of
the Government. He started in the army as a private and
ended a brigadier-general; he started in civil life as a mes-
senger to an Indian tribe and ended as Governor of Mis-
souri Territory and Superintendent of Indian Affairs for the
United States. He was faithful in small trusts and was
given larger ones; he served his country and his neighbors,
and was quite able to take care of himself. There was no
such pathetic end to his career as there was to that of his
elder and more brilliant brother, George Rogers Clark, who


## p. 69 (#77) ##############################################

GENERAL WILLIAM CLARK, TERRITORIAL GOVERNOR
69
died in poverty and distress. In his long official life he was
never accused by his fiercest opponents of using his office
for selfish ends, although the Indian agency, which he held
for thirty years, offered temptations that few others have
been able to resist.
In character Clark was mild and diplomatic, yet per-
severing and determined. He never courted difficulty and
never shrank from danger. He preferred smooth sailing
on a calm sea, but could face a storm with resolute courage.
He was military by instinct and training, yet most of his life
was spent in calming the bickerings and strife of the frontier
and in avoiding trouble with the Indians; and, strange to
say, his very success accounts for the semi-obscurity into
which his name has fallen. There were few angles and
barbed edges to his character and few eccentricities for the
scanty chroniclers of his day to seize upon and perpetuate.
Although without educational training, living in a rude
community where he was surrounded by imperious and quar-
relsome neighbors who freely indulged in brawling and duel-
ling, his demeanor was polished and courtly, his temper even
and smooth, his nature kindly and sympathetic, and his life,
almost without enmities, full of labor and service to his
country.


## p. 70 (#78) ##############################################

LAW AND PUBLIC OPINION
I. H. LIONBERGER
Lecturer on Law of Corporations, Law School, Washington University
Professor Dicey, in his most admirable book upon Law
and Public Opinion, has traced with interesting detail the
changes wrought in the laws of England during the nine-
teenth century. The impression made by the book is pro-
found. In the light of its revelations it is difficult to believe
that in Dr. Johnson's time philosophers deemed the English
Constitution and the English law of the eighteenth century
the most perfect product of human experience. Today that
Constitution seems iniquitous and that law a dilapidated re-
pository of worn-out traditions, obsolete principles, and most
cruel and oppressive punishments.
There were then more than one hundred capital offences.
The most trifling crimes against property were punished by
death. Debtors were imprisoned, not only after judgment,
but pending trial. Procedure in all courts of justice was
technical, slow, and expensive. Personal liberty as we know
it was not dreamed of. Wages and prices were fixed by law.
Privilege and monopoly were deeply intrenched. Jews and
Catholics were excluded from the franchise. Politics were
so corrupt that it is not an exaggeration to say that the
kingdom was governed by bribery. Graft obtained in all
public departments. The civil list was surcharged with sine-
cures conferred upon favorites, or friends, or relatives, or
dependents, of the party momentarily in power. Seats in
Parliament were openly bought and sold. The franchise


## p. 71 (#79) ##############################################

LAW AND PUBLIC OPINION
71
was restricted to a very small fraction of the population.
The great towns were not represented in Parliament.
Yet at such a time, under such institutions, Burke and
Blackstone and Dr. Johnson lived, and while they lived, con-
tinued to applaud the Constitution and laws of their country.
With rhetorical splendor they painted the glory of those in-
stitutions, which they deemed the consummation of wisdom,
of justice, and of expediency. Acutely alarmed by the ap-
pearance of social discontent, they denounced innovation as
dangerous to the State, subversive of liberty, and calculated
to disturb the firm foundations of the best and most happy
society ever constructed by the wit and heart of man.
That these great men voiced the dominant and common
opinions of their time, there can be no doubt. Men of prop-
erty and privilege ruled the realm because the people wished
it. The people were coarse, brutal, ignorant, stupid; insen-
sible to abstract right, indifferent to special wrong; cruel by
practice and inclination. They liked a lord, and firmly be-
lieved that public affairs might best be intrusted to the great
landed interests. Dr. Johnson was never so eloquent as in
his tract entitled "Taxation no Tyranny." His essay ex-
pressed a common opinion. What was good enough for old
England was good enough for its colonies. The iniquity of
adding imprisonment to unmerited bankruptcy never entered
men's minds. Blackstone's eulogy of the law, addressed to
the gentlemen of England, is in one sense the most stupid
book ever uttered by the human mind. Its massive volumes
contain no word of criticism, no suggestion of improvement.
The general scheme and policy of laws long since swept aside
as being improper for a free people, are nowhere condemned.
These great men were real representatives of the people


## p. 72 (#80) ##############################################

72
I. H. LIONBERGER
whose opinions they expressed. Their indifference to wrongs
which today seem atrocious was general throughout all
classes of society. Changes in the law did not precede, but
followed changes in public opinion. Reforms were gradu-
ally effected. Not for fifty years did a marked spirit of re-
form manifest itself. The Reform Bill, Catholic emancipa-
tion, the Corrupt Practices act, were the results of a long
agitation strenuously conducted. Bentham, Cobden, and
Bright roused the fear and animosity of men for a long time.
A great while was required to amend and humanize the
criminal code. A good code of civil procedure was not
adopted for nearly a century. Great men were still the
stanchest conservatives. Gladstone opposed the emancipa-
tion of slaves. Bright made one of his most eloquent ora-
tions in denunciation of a bill regulating child labor in facto-
ries. Shaftesbury spent $100,000 in order to secure his elec-
tion to the Parliament in which he inaugurated the beneficent
measures which have been identified with his name.
Such has been the course of England's progress; not sud-
den, violent, complete; but slow, intermittent, and unequal.
Men were never of one mind in the doing of good. The
greatest differed. There were blind conservatives and blind
liberals. The leaders were not always wiser than the mob.
Men of common opinions and uncommon abilities guided the
destinies of the nation and framed laws from time to time as
they felt the impulse of the constituencies. The people va-
cillated; today earnest followers of Cobden and Bentham, to-
morrow zealous supporters of the paternalism of Shaftesbury.
The laws reflected this vacillation. The union between the
two-between law and opinion-was close and continuous,
as it must ever be among a free people.


## p. 73 (#81) ##############################################

LAW AND PUBLIC OPINION
73
Our own country has had a history no less interesting and
no less significant. What we have thought and believed
from time to time has found expression in the laws adopted
from time to time. We have not always been righteous nor
wise. It is a mistake to assume that the Declaration of In-
dependence was the inspiration of a new and perfected soci-
ety which firmly believed and practiced the great principles
which it eloquently expressed. Men were not free, nor
equal, in America. There were many sorts of slaves, black
and white. Indentured servants, men, women, and children-
redemptioners, felons, and negroes were alike held in bond-
age. Unfortunate debtors were imprisoned before, pending,
and after trial. The criminal laws were harsh and cruel.
Punishments were humiliating and inhumanly severe. Petty
larceny was punished by whipping and branding; passing
counterfeit money, by clipping both ears, branding, impris-
onment, and fine. The insane were treated with barbarous
cruelty and confined in loathsome dungeons. The franchise
was withheld from the poor. A landless man had no rights.
Several States imposed a religious qualification upon voters.
Laws were unequal. By special enactment, without cause
assigned, a husband might be divorced from a wife; and in
the same manner property rights might be divested and re-
appropriated. Taxes were unequal; total exemption was
conferred upon all sorts of favored enterprises.* The no-
tion that taxation without representation was tyrannical, was
a pure fiction, so far as local law was concerned. Judge
Marshall decided that no such system obtained in the Ameri-
can System of Jurisprudence. The famous ordinance of
1787, which Webster regarded as a greater declaration than

I. H. LIONBERGER
the Declaration of Independence, provided for the arbitrary
government of a vast region lying north of the Ohio and east
of the Mississippi rivers. In terms it authorized the Presi-
dent of the United States to appoint commissioners who
might adopt such laws and establish such tribunals as they
deemed proper. No inhabitant of that region had the right
to vote, yet he was taxed and governed. After the Louis-
iana purchase, the territory of Missouri was governed by the
District Court of Indiana, under a special act of Congress,
although its inhabitants were alien in race and accustomed
to a peculiar law.
Individual liberty, as we know it, was not recognized.
The State of Alabama fixed the price and weight of loaves
of bread by statute. Not for seventy-five years did the odi-
ous institution of slavery arouse the righteous wrath of the
average Northerner, and during that period, and long after,
the public opinion of the South approved and sanctioned in-
voluntary servitude.
These things and many more we may read upon the pages
of our own history. They show that in America as in Eng-
land, he who would find the solid basis of our laws and in-
stitutions must search not the declamations of orators, nor
poems, nor treatises, nor philosophical essays, nor even the
platforms of principles promulgated by rival party organiza-
tions dependent upon the public suffrage; but the laws of the
land, for they only declare from time to time the convictions,
the prejudices, the opinions of society.
The time is not yet ripe for the systematic study of these
opinions so expressed. The American Bar Association re-
quires of its president an annual address upon the laws of
the various states of the Union, and much admirable work


## p. 75 (#83) ##############################################

75
has already been done; yet it still remains to arrange and an-

been enacted by the most diligent lawmakers of history. At
least 20,000 pages of law are enacted each year. Forty-four
sovereign states and the Congress of the United States con-
tribute to this vast reservoir of human experience. Never
before has passion, prejudice, and opinion found such instant
and complete expression.
I regret that I cannot within the appropriate limits of
this essay present the results of a hasty examination of the
laws of one of these commonwealths. Missouri has had a
various and interesting history. Its laws have faithfully re-
flected the opinions dominant at the time of their adoption.
These opinions have fluctuated. The policy of the state has
changed from time to time. The experiences of one gener-
ation have distinctly not become the intuitions of the next.
The same lessons had to be learned over and over again.
The first Constitution of the state prohibited the incor-
poration of more than one bank of issue. It was adopted
while the Bank of the United States afforded a pattern of
excellence which all men admired. It guarded the currency
of the people against adulteration, and provided necessary
safeguards against disasters of then recent experience. Yet
in the course of time men became impatient of restraint.
They had forgot both the miseries of their ancestors and the
causes which produced them. The Constitution was amended,
and ten banks of issue were created. In the nick of time a
panic occurred which checked the new spirit of adventure.
Banks opened, issued, and suspended. New laws were en-
acted. State bank issues were shortly afterwards destroyed
by federal taxation.


## p. 76 (#84) ##############################################

76
I. H. LIONBERGER
Ordinary banks, that is, banks without power to issue
notes, had a similar experience. They were at first timidly
created, with limited powers, under the name of savings in-
stitutions. Their value to the community becoming evident,
they were encouraged and endowed with larger powers.
When panics excited the fears, or losses the indignation, of
the people, they were restricted and held within narrow
bounds. Prosperity led in turn to relaxation. Safeguards
deemed essential after some bitter experience, such as the
maintenance of a proper reserve, were abandoned by a new
generation forgetful or unmindful of the abuses of the past.
Anomalies crept into the law. Recently a new class of com-
panies, emancipated from all restraints, have been created,
which are permitted to disregard the plainest dictates of ex-
perience. They have powers never dreamed of, privileges
never before conferred, capabilities never yet tested. They
may do what ordinary banks may do, yet are emancipated
from the restraints imposed upon banks. They have all the
powers of savings institutions, yet are trammeled by none of
the restrictions enjoined by the history of such institutions.
They are required to keep no reserve; they may invest their
resources in such manner and in such securities as they deem
proper. They may utter debentures, go on bonds, and accept
trusts. Every safeguard heretofore deemed essential for the
protection of depositors has been omitted from their charters.
The policy and opinion of the state with respect to works
of internal improvement is even more interesting. The
Constitution of 1820 pledged the state to the encouragement
of such works. For forty-five years this policy was consist-
ently adhered to. Charters of all sorts were freely granted.
All sorts of aid were granted. Some companies were ex-

empt from taxation, others were granted state bonds. Το
some, lands were given. Counties were permitted to sub-

After a few years the fruits of this delirium were gath-

stantly reflected in new laws. The constitution was changed.
For forty years the people remembered their indiscretions.
Then came a change. The lesson was forgot. A law has
just been passed authorizing cities of the state to build at
public expense free railroad bridges. The old frenzy, under
a different guise, has broken out among the people.
What has occurred in Missouri, has occurred elsewhere.
The Granger movement swept over the whole west and re-
sulted in excesses as dangerous to the general welfare as the
indiscretions committed under the cry of Internal Improve-
ment.
The general opinion with respect to municipal charters
has been no less fluctuating. Today a strong executive, an
undivided responsibility is preferred; tomorrow a weak exec-
utive and a divided responsibility. The city of St. Louis has
had no less than thirteen charters, each of which reflects the
political wisdom and distressing experience of a particular
time.

Money has from the beginning engaged a large measure
of public interest and the most various, divergent, and oppo-
site views have from time to time been entertained.
Fiat
money, free silver, the gold standard, each has had its advo-
cates in every time, and each its opportunity provided by the
law of the land. The tariff has been as fruitful of legisla-
tion. Even Webster changed his views.
Perhaps the most remarkable illustration of the wide di-
vergence between abstract right and temporary opinions with
respect to what is just, is afforded by acts recently adopted
for the government of American colonies or dependencies.
Americans fought for liberty, bled for it, sung its praises
for generations upon generations; yet, after a century's expe-
rience of its blessings, deliberately perpetrated, with respect
to the Philippine Islands, the very wrong for which they de-
nounced and fought King George and his parliament.
With respect to private liberty and the public opinion,
much might be said. The inalienable right to life, liberty, and
the pursuit of happiness is no longer to be taken for granted.
By a law of New York, bakers were prohibited to work ex-
cept within hours prescribed by the state. Missouri regu-
lates the working hours of miners. We are beginning to
extend to men the "protection" of which in Bright's time
women and children of tender age were thought to be in no
need.
Further illustrations of the remarkable trend and twist
of public opinion and public law are unnecessary. The two are
inseparable. The law is the mirror; the opinion the reality.
The people are not always, never in fact for a long time,
wise. A famous philosopher defined a fool to be a person who
could not profit by experience. Peoples-free peoples-are


## p. 79 (#87) ##############################################

LAW AND PUBLIC OPINION
79
in this sense fools. Each generation must have its fling.
The same lessons must be learned over and over again. Peo-
ple are not always just. They do what they complain of.
They have the keenest sense of personal injustice, but are
indifferent to the rights of others. Constitutions avail noth-
ing against popular excitement. They still restrain the
whim, but not the will, of the people.
The national character is restless, impatient, bold, and at
times brutal; and never before in the history of mankind has
the constitution of society allowed such instant and complete
expression of its passing whims. No one realized this por-
tentous fact more fully than the wise men who framed our
organic laws. Obvious in all of them is the profound con-
viction that the people are not to be trusted. Whether, to
use a fine phrase of Gladstone, these great men were inspired
by trust of the people tempered by prudence, or mistrust of
the people tempered by fear, they still followed the dictates
of a profound statesmanship in setting up governments of
limited and restricted authority. To the limitations of fun-
damental law we owe such measure of liberty and security
as we enjoy,-not to the free will of the constituents of this
great Republic.
Whether in the course of time there has been a gradual
amelioration of law, it is most difficult to determine. A cen-
tury after the Declaration of Independence a law for the gov-
ernment of dependencies was enacted by the Congress of the
United States, which violates every principle of that declara-
tion. There are visible in the jurisprudence of every state
under-currents of sentiment, prejudice, and passion, which
each year find vent in unjust and unwise laws. Courts must
still enforce constitutional limitations imposed for the protec-


## p. 80 (#88) ##############################################

80
I. H. LIONBERGER
tion of private right and individual liberty. Progress, if
there be progress, is not so marked as to be distinctly prov-
able. Experiments are still tried; errors are still committed.
Waves of popular emotion from time to time sweep over
the country and break upon the barriers set by experience.
Fundamental guaranties are not always able to resist the im-
pact of repeated shock. Individual right and individual lib-
erty are not now, and they have never been, secure against the
gradual encroachments of the majority. Collectivism, or
socialism, or communism, has never ceased to have its advo-
cates and its victims. Class prejudices and class legislation
go hand in hand. In times of excitement and in times of dis-
tress many iniquities are attempted; some are accomplished.
No student of laws can find occasion for despair in the
legislation of this country; nor can he find room for unmixed
satisfaction.

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY*
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
Professor of Philosophy in Washington University
No general question could well be more interesting to
Americans in this first decade of the twentieth century
than the question of the present status of democracy through-
out the world. When we survey the unusually absorbing
and stirring spectacle of contemporary world-politics, we
hardly find any very considerable realization of the hope
which seems to have been cherished by some of the founders
of our Republic-we hope that the system of self-govern-
ment which they initiated upon these shores would speedily
become the prevailing type of government amongst all civil-
ized nations. Representative government has, indeed, been
widely extended; even the most backward and corrupt of
European autocracies seems upon the eve of conversion into
an imperfect parliamentary system. Yet only one other great
power in the world, and that one of diminishing political
significance, is avowedly a republic; and of the numerous
professed republics lying to the south of us in this hemi-
sphere, few are democracies in anything but name. In short,
to one who looks abroad with somewhat superficial glance
the situation seems decidedly confused; multitudinous cross-
currents and conflicting tendencies show themselves, but there
is certainly no steady tide setting towards the general estab-
lishment of thorough-going republicanism. What makes
*Address delivered before the Monday Evening Club of Kirkwood, February
19, 1906.
6


## p. 82 (#90) ##############################################

82
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
the outlook the more confused is the frequency with which
nominal monarchies prove to be most truly democratic, while
nominal republics realize very imperfectly the ideal of gov-
ernment of the people, by the people, and for the people.
More significant is the question how far the experiment
of democracy has worked in practice, in those countries
where it has been tried. We have lately been forced to
much searching of our own national conscience with respect
to this question. We have had evidence put before us tend-
ing to the conclusion that our governments, both federal and
municipal, have long been governments by self-perpetuating
oligarchies for the sake of special interests, rather than
governments by public opinion for the sake of the general
well-being. Certainly nothing remotely resembling self-
government can be said to have existed in the local affairs
of St. Louis during the past decade. Furthermore, the
exigencies arising from our curiously accidental and unex-
pected assumption of the responsibilities of a colonial empire
have led us into courses of action which are declared, cer-
tainly with plausibility, to show that we as a nation care
very little about democracy and retain no enthusiasm for
its diffusion. We have, it is said, lost our grip upon the
principles of the Declaration of Independence, and the doc-
trines of the founders. By some this is regarded as a sign
of a deplorable degeneration; we are said to have grown
brutalized and materialized, to have squandered our glorious
birthright as the protagonists of popular liberty for the sake
of a little cheap prestige and a certain amount of com-
mercial profit. On the other hand, there are not wanting
those who tell us that this change of attitude which has
apparently followed upon our colonial expansion is a con-


## p. 83 (#91) ##############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
83
summation greatly to be rejoiced over. The Declaration has
before this, but now with more frequent repetition, been said
to be an exploded piece of metaphysics, where it is not an
inaccurate piece of history; our disposition practically to
recognize its irrelevancy to modern conditions, while under-
taking the rule and tutelage of "new-caught, sullen peoples"
unfit for self-government, is praised as evidence that we
"have done with childish days" and are entered upon national
maturity.
It is this last question-the question of theory-which is
primary for any one who would undertake an appraisal of
the present position of democracy in the world. Before we
ask how the system operates as a working scheme, we ought
to ask how the theory of it works under the conditions of
contemporary thought. How do the principles of, and the
general arguments for, democracy stand, after more than
a century's reflection? This question as to the theoretical
status of democracy at the beginning of the twentieth cen-
tury is more fundamental than any of the others. The plan
for this lecture originally contemplated a discussion not only
of this theoretical issue, but also of the effect upon the work-
ing of popular government of various more external econ-
omic and social conditions of modern life; but it appears that
such a discussion would require a treatise rather than a
lecture, and we shall therefore not get beyond the first ques-
tion upon the order of the day.
It will help us to avoid confusion of ideas if we note one
or two distinctions, before proceeding to the main subject.
These distinctions are very familiar and obvious; yet in cur-
rent controversy they seem rather often to be forgotten. In
the first place, then, the term democracy may signify either


## p. 84 (#92) ##############################################

84
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
a state of feeling exhibited in the social relations of indi-
viduals, or a form of government. In the former sense,
democracy-the democratic spirit-has been wittily charac-
terized by Mr. Chesterton. "The democratic emotion," he
says, "like most elementary and indispensable things is a
thing difficult to describe at any time. But it is peculiarly
difficult to describe it in our enlightened age, for the simple
reason that it is peculiarly difficult to find it. It is a certain
instinctive attitude which feels the things in which all men
agree to be unspeakably important, and all the things in
which they differ (such as mere brains) to be almost un-
speakably unimportant. The nearest approach to it in our
ordinary life would be the promptitude with which we should
consider mere humanity in any circumstance of shock or
death. We should say, after a somewhat disturbing dis-
covery, 'There is a dead man under the sofa.' We should not
be likely to say, 'There is a dead man of considerable personal
refinement under the sofa.' We should say, 'A woman has
fallen into the water.' We should not say, 'A highly edu-
cated woman has fallen into the water.'" Now with this
democratic social spirit, or democratic emotion, we are not
here primarily concerned. We are to talk about political
democracy-about the system of thorough-going represen-
tative government based upon widely extended suffrage
and designed to be readily responsive to the popular
will. The two things, political democracy and social dem-
ocracy, may easily exist apart. Thus Russia, in its political
system, is the least democratic Christian power in Europe;
England in many respects in the promptness and complete-
ness with which the public opinion of the majority can get
itself translated into law-is politically more democratic


## p. 85 (#93) ##############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
85
than our own country. But in its social spirit Russia is said
to be one of the most democratic countries in the world;
while England, in the prevailing social attitudes of nearly all
classes of its society, is one of the countries most destitute
of the democratic emotion. It attaches unspeakable im-
portance to the things in which men differ, rather than to
the things in which they all agree.
Again, it is hardly necessary to say that political democ-
racy and liberty are not synonymous terms; nor that dem-
ocracy is not always a means for assuring liberty. There are
various aspects of liberty; and we may, if we like, call the
wide diffusion of the privilege of participating in the tasks
of government, political liberty. But political liberty can
never, in practice, mean anything but the rule of the ma-
jority, of fifty-one men over forty-nine. And the more
important kinds of liberty-liberty of thought, of speech, of
the press, of action-ought, within the limits imposed by the
requirements of public order and security, to be guaranteed
to everybody; indeed, if it were necessary to choose, we
should have to consider it more unimportant for the progress
of mankind to give this kind of liberty to minorities than to
majorities. To such liberty political democracy sometimes
proves no less unfavorable than other political systems; we
know very well what is meant by the tyranny of a majority.
There is a third sort of confusion of ideas which one
sometimes finds in popular discussions of political issues;
though the distinction to be made here is so broad that it
might be assumed to be self-evident. The question of dem-
ocracy, namely, is occasionally confused with the question
of independence. This confusion is partly due, perhaps, to
the fact that our own American Revolution happened to be,


## p. 86 (#94) ##############################################

86
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
at one and the same time, a struggle for independence and a
struggle for political democracy. A community is independ-
ent when it has a government of its own not controlled in
any degree by the action of any other community geographic-
ally or racially separate from itself. A community is demo-
cratic when its members generally have a voice in the de-
termination of the laws by which they are to be governed.
Thus Ireland enjoys, in the main, a high degree of political
liberty but is not independent; Venezuela is independent
but has no real political liberty; India is neither democratic
nor independent. The tendency to confuse these things shows
itself chiefly in discussions concerning our treatment of our
colonies; and the distinction may be illustrated by a reference
to the case of the Philippines. It is abstractly conceivable
that our duty to the Filipinos is to make them independent
but not democratic; that is, to cut them loose from Washing-
ton at an early date, but in the meantime to promote the es-
tablishment among them of a sort of benevolent despotism,
like that which (with some disguises) Diaz exercises in
Mexico, or that which Rajah Brooke used to exercise in
Sarawak. On the other hand, it is conceivable that our duty
may be to give the Filipinos democracy without independ-
ence; that is, to maintain their connection with our political
system, but to admit them as individuals to a full enjoyment
of the political privileges of American citizens. It is also
abstractly conceivable that our duty for the present is to
give them neither democracy nor independence.
With these possible ambiguities obviated, we may pro-
ceed to consider the subject before us.
The first thing that must be said of democracy certainly
is that a large part of its original theoretical or philosophical


## p. 87 (#95) ##############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
87
foundations has fallen into decay. The movement towards
popular government in the eighteenth century which ex-
pressed itself in a series of modifications of the British Con-
stitution, in the establishment of the North American Re-
public, in the French Revolution, and later in the Wars of
Liberation in South America, was entirely a product of its
time. It was the expression of certain eighteenth century
preconceptions, the putting into practice of a system of ideas
which dominated the consciousness of the men of that period
all the more effectually because they were often vague and
ill defined. There then prevailed, in other words, a peculiar
and distinctive way of thinking, a certain fashion in cate-
gories, which was applied to all the favorite subjects of re-
flection of the time, and gave the tone to men's opinions in
half a dozen apparently disconnected fields of thought. What
this set of presuppositions-this current philosophy of the
"Enlightenment"-was, I shall try presently to indicate. I
do not, however, desire to maintain that without the preva-
lence of just this philosophic fashion there would have been
no democratic movement in eighteenth century politics and
society. But it is quite certain that, without that philosophy,
the reasons by which the movement was justified and ex-
plained, and the principles upon which the subsequent recon-
struction of governmental systems was based, would have
been altogether different. There might have been a French
Revolution; but there would have been no Déclaration des
Droits de l'Homme, and the catchwords of French politics
for the next hundred years would not have been Liberty,
Equality, and Fraternity. There might have been an Ameri-
can Revolution; but there assuredly would have been no such
Declaration of Independence, and the political philosophy
