ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
which has lain in the back of the head of the average Ameri-
can citizen and largely determined his convictions and his
vote, would have been of quite another cast. Now mean-
while, the principal intellectual business of the nineteenth
century has been the acquisition of a new group of funda-
mental concepts which are essentially incompatible with
those of the eighteenth and have rendered the latter obso-
lete. The philosophy of the Enlightenment has, indeed, per-
sisted as a potent force throughout the century recently
ended, and has often found place in men's minds side by side
with the newer ideas, the younger children of the intellect,
which were destined eventually to strangle it. But by the
beginning of the twentieth century the new system of pre-
suppositions has come to be tolerably mature and pretty well
in command of the common consciousness of educated men.
And consequently democracy, as a thing which historically
happens to have been begotten of the eighteenth century
spirit, must now reckon with the new Zeitgeist. It is not
true, I think, that the reckoning need be fatal to our belief in
democracy. A practical scheme which owes its origin to
one set of reasons may often be wisely continued for another
set of reasons; a sound ideal has often, when it first came
into the world, been defended by bad arguments. But at
all events a readjustment must be made; we must honestly
inquire how far the theoretical grounds for democracy have
been affected by the fresh discoveries and the new intellectual
fashions that we owe to the reflection of the past hundred
years. It will suffice, for this occasion, to mention three such
changes, the bearing of which upon our political philosophy
we are called upon to consider.


## p. 89 (#97) ##############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
89
I.
The eighteenth century had, in the main, no philosophy
of history; or rather, to speak more precisely, it had a
peculiar philosophy of history of its own, essentially charac-
terized by the absence of any idea of social evolution. It was
commonly assumed, by the English and French thinkers of
that period, that the historical course of events was mostly
a series of regrettable mistakes and aberrations—and of un-
natural mistakes, too, due to the craft and artifice of design-
ing men, rather than to any inherent necessity. It was com-
monly supposed that there was in each province of human
thought just one standard type of true belief and right prac-
tice which was really natural or according to Nature; just
a single universally valid and rational religion, which was
the Religion of Nature; just a single defensible moral code,
which was called la loi naturelle, the Law of Nature; just
a single reasonable economic system, which was called
Physiocracy, the Rule of Nature; and just one proper scheme
of political organization, which was that based upon a formu-
lation of the "natural rights" of man as man. These standard
schemes were called "natural" because they were supposed to
be universal and simple; that is, they were supposed to be
truths that would be obvious to the natural understanding
of the least sophisticated man at any time, in any place. They
were therefore, it was felt, the things that ought to have
prevailed uninterruptedly at all periods of history. It was,
indeed, a familiar eighteenth century notion that they had
so prevailed at the beginning of human history, in the "State
of Nature," which was to some philosophers, long before
Rousseau, an actual historic reality, and to others at least a
sort of archetype of what ought to have been the reality.


## p. 90 (#98) ##############################################

90
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
That mankind had ever departed from the State of Nature,
the Religion of Nature, and the Law of Nature, was there-
fore a thing that had to be explained; and it could be ex-
plained only by supposing that the natural light of reason
which shines equally in every man had somehow been ob-
fuscated by the deliberate trickery of a comparatively small
number of selfish misleaders of mankind-by ambitious con-
querors and crafty priests. History, when so considered, as
a sequence of perverse departures from the order of Nature,
came to seem relatively meaningless; the eighteenth century
philosophers could, for the most part, have uttered the words
of Browning's Paracelsus:
"I saw no use in the past; only a scene
Of degradation, ugliness and tears;
A sullen page in human chronicles,
Fit to erase."
And as for the future, the reformer conceived his function
to be, not to carry a step farther a gradual and continuous
process long since operative in society, but rather to hew off
all the artificial accretions upon the State of Nature, and
thus to bring back mankind suddenly and definitely to the
enjoyment of its proper and natural felicity:
"'Twas then, the studious head or gen'rous mind,
Follow'r of God or friend of human kind,
Poet or Patriot, rose but to restore
The Faith and Moral Nature gave before;
Relum'd her ancient light, not kindled new."
And since the thing to be restored was, whether in morals or
politics or religion, the one, simple, clear-cut system that is
according to Nature, the restoration could allow for no vari-
ations and no exceptions. In the matter of political systems,
for example, it sufficed to say that a man was a man for all


## p. 91 (#99) ##############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
91
that; that every man was endowed by Nature, or his Creator,
with certain inalienable rights; that these rights include the
right to liberty; and that this implies (in the language of the
French Déclaration) "the right of all citizens to take part,
personally or through their representatives, in the formation
of the laws" by which they are governed. Here was the last
word of political truth; here were the essentials of a consti-
tutional scheme which, since it was according to Nature, must
be equally appropriate to all peoples at all times.
Now just as "Nature" was the sacred and never-suffi-
ciently-to-be-uttered word of the greater part of the eight-
eenth century, "Evolution" came to be the sacred and
never-sufficiently-to-be-uttered word of the nineteenth.
And though there is no apparent antithesis between the two
terms, it is a fact that in their influence upon men's attitudes
toward practical problems the one term contradicts all that
is implied by the other. That which is good "according to
Nature," in the mid-eighteenth century sense, must be some
body of truths or system of practices that is single, univer-
sally valid, absolute; that which is good according to the
"laws of social evolution," is highly variable, contingent, rela-
tive to time and place and circumstances. To the one view
past history seems meaningless, unprogressive, and rather
accidental than rationally necessary; to the evolutionary
view, the past of the race, and beliefs, ideals, and institu-
tions which it has developed, appear significant, rationally
sequential, and instructive. Thus the dying Paracelsus came
to see it:
"Not so, dear child
Of after-days, wilt thou reject the past,
Full of deep warnings of the proper tenure,
Thereby thou hast the earth."


## p. 92 (#100) #############################################

92
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
And for the reforms of the future, the eighteenth century
appeal to Nature implied that they should consist in the
simple and easy process of getting rid of a few established
artificialities and thereby reaching finality, bringing in the
"perfection of the species" once for all; the present-day recog-
nition of social evolution as a fact and a necessity implies that
the problem of reform is complex, many-sided, variable, and
its solution necessarily gradual and provisional. Some
such idea of the evolution of society through a sequence
of inevitable and consecutive stages has been more or less
familiar since the time of Lessing and of Herder. What it
necessarily means for the modern theorist about politics and
society was clearly realized by John Stuart Mill as early as
1830. Mill, trained as he was by his father and Bentham in
the eighteenth century habit of mind-tells us in his auto-
biography that, about that time, he began to learn certain
new conceptions from the German and French philosophy of
the period. "Among other ideas which the general turning
upside-down of the opinions of European thinkers had
brought uppermost were these in particular: That the human
mind has a certain order of possible progress, in which some
things must precede others, an order which governments and
public instructors can modify to some but not to an unlimited
extent; that all questions of political institutions are relative,
not absolute, and that different stages of human progress
not only will have, but ought to have, different institutions;
that government is always either in the hands, or passing into
the hands, of whatever is the strongest power in society, and
that what that power is, does not depend on institutions but
institutions on it; that any general theory or philosophy of
politics presupposes a previous theory of human progress, and


## p. 93 (#101) #############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
93
that this is the same thing with a philosophy of history."
There, in one sentence, you have an adequate statement
of the bearing of an evolutional view of society upon one's
attitude toward the practical questions as to the rightness
or wrongness of different types of political institutions. Be-
fore considering more directly how this should affect our
present judgment concerning democracy, I must remind you
of another of the new ideas of the nineteenth century, which
is closely connected with that with which we have been
dealing.
II.
The representative thinkers of the century of the great
revolutions were professed cosmopolitans; they knew man
only as Man, and based their reasonings upon the assump-
tion of his essential uniformity the world over. Racial
differences, national peculiarities, were regarded as historical
accidents to which no philosophic mind could attach much
importance. In the past, no doubt, these differences had been
regrettable facts; but in the future, all men were to be alike
in a common rationality. In a word, it was only the ubiquitous
things in human nature that interested the political theorists
of that age. On the other hand, the concept of race and
nationality is one of the greatest discoveries of the nine-
teenth century-although it was, indeed, first made in Ger-
many in (by the calendar) the last two decades of the
eighteenth. The idea that each people has a distinctive and
permanent character of its own, a national genius, and that
this must express itself in distinctive art and literature and
institutions, has grown to be a commonplace. The category
of race has, indeed, come to be somewhat badly overworked
in modern thought-in literary criticism, in the philosophy


## p. 94 (#102) #############################################

94
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
of history, and in political controversy. Racial self-con-
sciousness has been intensified to the point of morbidness,
and nations have taken to the systematic inbreeding of their
special peculiarities, in a fashion detrimental to their intel-
lectual and moral sanity. But whatever be the contemporary
exaggerations of the idea of nationality, the fact remains
that it is an idea of which the eighteenth century mind was
virtually innocent, but one which every latter-day theory and
movement must reckon with. "I have never known any
men," Joseph de Maistre, the great reactionary opponent of
the revolutionary spirit used to say; "I have known only
Italians, and Frenchmen, and Russians, and Englishmen."
And history and anthropology and the experience of events
have ever since been teaching us that the saying was an
epigrammatic way of putting a highly practical truth. The
factor of_race cannot be ignored in the framing of insti-
tutions. You cannot even deal successfully with a class of
German children, in a school or a social settlement, in the
same way in which you would deal with a class of Italian
or Irish or Anglo-American children.
The result of the conjunction of these two new ideas-the
idea of a necessary sequence of stages of social evolution, and
the idea of deep-seated differences of racial or national
genius-has, as you see, been to destroy the unity of that
eighteenth century generic Man for whom the reformers of
that period proposed to draw up constitutions. He has, so
to say, been split into pieces in two directions-longitudinally
and cross-wise-and it has become evident that the different
pieces cannot be treated in the same manner. The institu-
tions appropriate to a given stage of culture are quite certain
to be inappropriate to an earlier stage of culture; and the in-


## p. 95 (#103) #############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
95
stitutions appropriate to the genius of a given race may be-
I do not, in this case, say "must be"-inappropriate to the
genius and traditions of a different race. We shall never
again, probably, see such a spectacle as could be observed in
London towards the end of the eighteenth century-the
great Mr. Jeremy Bentham sitting in his comfortable study
in Westminster, confidently preparing drafts of constitutions
and codes of laws for several different nations whose coun-
try he had never visited, and to whose local conditions, pecul-
iarities, limitations, and aptitudes he gave never so much as
a thought.
What this involves, with respect to the future of dem-
ocracy, is obvious. No man who has assimilated the ruling
ideas of the last century can ever again share that pleasant
and dogmatic confidence, possessed by many of the Fathers
of the Republic, that the democratic system is the one proper
kind of government, to the adoption of which all the nations
ought speedily to come. Our question can no longer be: Is
a republican regime based upon universal male suffrage, and
all the rest of it, better than any other possible regime? The
question hereafter must rather be: What kind of government
is best suited to the needs of a given community? If some
measure of self-government is suitable to the case, how great
ought that measure to be? Every case must be judged on
its own merits; and the kind of institutions that is best in
each instance can be determined only after a patient consid-
eration of the racial character, the intellectual possibilities,
the past history, the prejudices and traditions, of the people
by whom the institutions are to be used. We shall, similarly,
be less impatient than our fathers used to be with those
European brethren of ours whose established institutions


## p. 96 (#104) #############################################

96
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
still fail to conform to the model of our own perfect and won-
derful Republic. We may feel impatient with the mediaeval-
isms of the German Emperor's public utterances, and dis-
approve of certain Prussian restrictions upon the personal
liberty of the subject; yet we may at the same time recognize
that Germany for the past thirty years, and in particular for
the past eighteen, has had a government which has suited
the needs and the tastes, and advanced the interests, of the
German people singularly well-that, indeed, even from an
absolute standpoint, Germany has been incomparably better
governed than either France or the United States during the
same period. But for the very same reason, we may also
recognize the fact that the political arrangements most ser-
viceable to a nation at one stage of its history may not always
continue to be the most desirable; and we may therefore
sympathize heartily enough with the endeavors of the Social-
ists and other Liberal parties in Germany to bring about a
more thorough-going system of representative government.
III.
But at about this point I seem to hear the voice of some
stout old adherent of the principles of the Fathers, one
reared from his youth upon the sounding periods of the
Declaration of Independence. "Can," I seem to hear him say,
"can any scheme of government be right-at least for a
civilized Christian nation-which does not fully assure to
all citizens their natural rights, which does not rest clearly
and unmistakably upon the consent of the governed?" And
I am thereby brought to note another development of nine-
teenth century thought which affects still more seriously
and directly the older theoretical foundations of political


## p. 97 (#105) #############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
97
democracy. The doctrine of natural rights and the corrol-
lary theory that the civil state is based entirely upon a volun-
tary contract of association and copartnership between indi-
viduals who have a natural right to keep out of such an
association if they do not like its terms:-this, too, is a piece
of eighteenth century philosophy which emerges into the
twentieth very much the worse for wear. It found its first
clear and influential modern formulation in the "Treatises of
Civil Government" of John Locke (1689); it was afterwards
repeated, modified, or amplified in a hundred different fash-
ions down to the time of the French Revolution; and it still
powerfully affects the minds of considerable masses of men.
But it has long been the object of much destructive criticism,
and it is out of harmony with several of the most distinctive
preconceptions of modern thought. For it is, in the first
place, permeated with the eighteenth century individualism;
it conceives of a man as only accidentally and extrinsically re-
lated to any organized society. The individual is represented
by it as a little, separate, self-sufficient moral atom, carrying
about on his person wherever he goes some sort of inalienable
or undetachable rights. But we have long been learning to
conceive of the individual human being as quite essentially
a member of a continuing social organism; as having no truly
human or moral status except by virtue of his distinctive place
in a connected historic process and in an organized society.
That society, it is true, is nothing more than a collection of
individuals, and it is organized for the sake of the better ful-
filment of the life of its individual members. But just as
truly are the members nothing, in any moral sense, save
through their relations to other members and to the whole,
and through their participation in the historic tasks in which
7


## p. 98 (#106) #############################################

98
Arthur O. LOVEJOY
human nature progressively expresses and realizes itself
from generation to generation. A man, therefore, gets his
rights from society, not from "Nature" nor from himself;
and they are only so far inalienable as their realization proves
not incompatible with the general and permanent interests
of the rest of society.
Again, the doctrine of natural rights, if taken literally
and strictly, is as what has just been said implies-nothing
more or less than the philosophy of anarchism. If a man
has an inalienable natural right to liberty, that means that
he may do aught that he pleases and that any other person
who attempts to interfere with his action, or to punish his
past acts, behaves immorally. If a man has an inalienable
right to life, it means that we may not rightfully hang him,
or compel him to enter the military service, under any con-
ceivable circumstances. If a man has an inalienable right to
his property, it means that the state may not, without his
consent, legitimately put streets across that property or run
water pipes through it or dictate what may be built upon it.
We have, of course, never really applied our natural rights
theory in practice; we hang people upon due occasion, we
take their property away from them by what is called due
process of law, we make them refrain from purchasing cer-
tain artificial fluids on certain days, we compel them to send
their children to school, to sit upon juries, to pay taxes even
for public expenditures of which they do not approve; and,
when a sufficient emergency arises, we draft them into the
army. What is more to the point, we compel the minority
of white male citizens, all women and children, and, in some
states, all male negro citizens who cannot expound the Con-
stitution to the satisfaction of registration officials, to be


## p. 99 (#107) #############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
99
governed by laws made without their consent. All these
things we do and most of them we shall continue to do; and
we explain our inconsistency with the language of the
Declaration by saying that a man is to be understood to be
entitled to his natural rights only in so far as they do not
interfere with the natural rights of some other man. But
there never was a weaker logical evasion than that con-
tained in this notion of the compounding of natural rights.
The effect of the collision of two inalienable rights could only
be like the effect of a collision of an irresistible force with an
immovable body. What would happen, under the hypothesis,
is one of the things that nobody could find out; which merely
shows that the hypothesis itself is absurd and self-contradic-
tory. And if the rights are not absolute and inalienable, we
require some principle, other than the statement of each of
the two rights taken separately, to determine the proportions
to be observed in the compounding of them.
As a matter of fact, that determining principle is neither
obscure nor unfamiliar. Even in the expressions of the
political philosophy of the eighteenth century there is to
be found, side by side with the natural rights doctrine, and
imperfectly harmonized with it, the doctrine that the good-
ness or badness of systems of government is to be judged, not
by what they come from, but by what they come to; not by the
degree in which they give expression to abstract rights, but by
the degree in which they realize certain concrete ends. The
English philosophical radicals-the school of reformers that
has Bentham for its founder-based their belief in represen-
tative government purely upon such a utilitarian criterion.
And utilitarian in the broader sense all modern political rea-
soning has more and more been growing; the utilitarian habit


## p. 100 (#108) ############################################

100
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
of mind-the tendency to judge institutions and policies in
the light of their total practical consequences, and their
ulterior bearing upon the general welfare-has become
little less than universal. It is, obviously, possible to
judge of utilities too narrowly. Governments exist as
means for the realization by human individuals of
whatever things good for human nature can best be
brought about directly or indirectly by collective action.
Among the things that are very good for human nature are,
certainly, political liberty and the feeling of direct personal
responsibility for the acts and character of the state to which
one belongs. But these are not the only goods; nor are they
the most essential. Civil liberty-which may, under certain
circumstances, be quite incompatible with political liberty, or
the rule of the majority; order and security; progress in cul-
ture, in domestic and civic virtue, and in commercial integ-
rity; continuity of national development; the multiplication
of the means for the enjoyment of noble pleasures and the cul-
tivation in the community of the power of such enjoyment;
the production of a better breed of citizens from generation
to generation, and the general maintenance and elevation of
the standard of civilization; these are ends far more im-
portant to the state than can be the guaranteeing to each rel-
atively sane adult male of the privilege of dropping a ballot
into a ballot box every year or two. The latter, it is true,
may be, and often is, the best means of ensuring the realiza-
tion of the former ends; but it is not invariably so, and the
question whether it is, and how far it is, in any given com-
munity, can only be answered after an impartial consider-
ation of the circumstances of that community. Governments,
in a word, do not derive their just powers from the consent


## p. 101 (#109) ############################################

DEMOCRACY IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY
101
of the governed. All governments derive their actual
powers from the content of the governed-or at least, from
the fact that no preponderating section of the governed is
too violently discontented. But that is a question of power,
not of right. Governments can derive just powers from
nothing but the fact that they make for justice-in that Pla-
tonic sense of the word in which it is synonymous with the
unity, the health, and the good ordering of the whole body
politic.
Such, then, are the three changes in the ruling categories
of modern thought which have affected the status of the
theory of democracy. They all, no doubt, present themselves
rather as truisms than as paradoxes, by this time; yet they
are not without practical bearings upon questions connected
with the present working of democracy that are still subjects
of lively discussion. A due consideration of them will, for
example, affect our attitude towards the problem of colonial
policy-will make us less certain that the Constitution ought
to follow the flag, if the flag persists in establishing itself in
tropical climes somewhere east of Suez. A similar considera-
tion will affect our view of such a matter as female suffrage.
There can no longer be any talk about women's right to vote;
the only question to be considered is whether the granting
of the electoral franchise to women will on the whole, at this
stage of human progress, make for a preponderance of good
with respect to all the interests of human society involved-
the harmony of the family, the preservation of the distinctive
qualities that we have come to admire in the feminine char-
acter, better legislation, greater stability and continuity of
public policy. When the question is put in such a form as
this, it is less easy to answer, and there is less occasion for


## p. 102 (#110) ############################################

102
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
heat in the discussion of it; but the answer will be more likely
to rest upon sound reasons. Again, the considerations men-
tioned may incline us to look with great regret and disap-
proval upon the hasty way in which the generation just before
ours set about the enfranchisement of the negro, and to
sympathize with the attempt to disfranchise all illiterate
negroes. I do not desire to express any very explicit opinion
upon any of these questions; the drawing of morals for
special cases may be left to the judgment of my hearers. I
wish merely to suggest certain issues, in the treatment of
which we still have occasion to be mindful of the relativity
of all political doctrines, the need to make allowances for
differences of stage of culture, of traditions and of race, and
the obligation to judge of institutions and policies by a patient
examination of their probable effect upon the permanent
interests of civilization.

AESCHYLUS' TREATMENT OF THE TIME ELE-
MENT IN THE AGAMEMNON
FREDERIC A. HALL
Collier Professor of Greek, Washington University
Why should a choral ode of such unusual length consti-
tute the early part of this play?
An answer will be found, I think, in the consideration of
four points: first, the prologue; second, the character of the
ode; third, the time of the herald's entrance and the nature
of his report; and, fourth, the time of Agamemnon's arrival.
The play has 1673 verses, divided about equally between
the chorus and all the other characters. The play is there-
fore one of the longest extant and the choral passages take
a larger proportion than is elsewhere found. We should not
be surprised to find long choral passages scattered through
the play; but that a single ode of 200 verses should stand
almost at the beginning suggests some special purpose.
Let us look at what precedes the ode-the prologue.
Darkness is just withdrawing. The stars are already nod-
ding on their day-time couches. It is early dawn. In the
foreground stands the palace of Agamemnon, King of Argos;
here and there are statues of the gods-Zeus, Apollo, Hermes
and others sacred to the people. As the trumpet announces
the opening there is seen upon the flat roof of the palace a


## p. 104 (#112) ############################################

104
FREDERIC A. HALL
man reclining, with head resting upon his arms, his attention
riveted upon something in the distance. A deathlike stillness
prevails, for all know that this day Aeschylus will depict the
woes of Atreus' house. Just what his plan may be few are
aware, but the author's reputation arouses expectation. In
time the man is seen to move, to stretch, to turn from side
to side as if to rest his body grown stiff and weary with unin-
terrupted watching. But though he seeks change and ease
from cramped position he never turns his face from that dis-
tant object.
At last he breaks the gloomy silence.
"Ye gods above release me, pray, from further irksome
task. Night by night for a year and more have I lain upon
this roof searching, vainly searching, victory's flash of fire
my lord would send from Troy-that beacon light to tell
of Troy's downfall. I cannot sleep, I dare not sing, lest it
should come and go unseen of me. Oh! when will things in
Argos be as once they were a noble king upon the throne
and by his side a virtuous queen, the pride of loyal subjects?
I chill with terror as I think how Argos once was, is now, and
yet must be; for woe brings woe and woe must come because
in Atreus' house woe has been and still remains. But grant
release, I pray, from toil unending and exhausting."
With this soliloquy, spoken slowly, often broken with
turn and stretch and yawn, he settles down again, intently
gazing for the first gleam of that desired beacon.
But twenty verses have been uttered thus far. Two min-
utes would suffice if one were to speak them as fast as he
could or perhaps naturally would. I imagine that several
times that number of minutes were actually used in their de-
livery. The question is not in how brief time could they be


## p. 105 (#113) ############################################

TREATMENT OF THE TIME ELEMENT IN THE AGAMEMNON 105
spoken, but rather how much time could be spent upon them
with increased effect?
In general it is unsafe to compare modern acting with
ancient as there are more points of contrast than of compari-
son. Yet I suppose that the Greeks would be no slower to
take advantage of such an opportunity as this than was Joe
Jefferson in Rip Van Winkle, when, in the waking scene, he
uses several minutes and yet speaks few sentences. The
scene in both cases, to seem real, must be very deliberate;
action rather than words, for the action conveys more than
words could. The watchman then, no doubt, occupied sev-
eral minutes in the delivery of those first twenty verses.
As he resumes his former attitude the audience fully
understand for what he looks-that blaze to be seen from the
Arachnæan promontory proclaiming the capture of Troy.
With him they now fix their eyes upon that distant point and
with him wait for minutes, seeming hours. But he, trained
by long service, catches the first ray of light as the pile is
fired upon that lofty peak, and, with a loud hurrah, jumps to
his feet and wildly dances upon the housetop; then hastily
descends and rushes into the palace to announce to Clytem-
nestra that her husband, Agamemnon, has captured Troy.
After a brief pause fifteen old men are seen coming from
the city side. They are bowed with age and support their
bending knees with staves. Their hair is white; their faces
creased with care. Their very presence turns the current
of thought back to Agamemnon's glorious reign, for they
were his trusted councillors, the senators of the State. Dur-
ing the king's absence of ten years they have seldom met
together, for their queen had depended upon Aegisthus for
advice. Not alone are the spectators taken, in their medi-

This sacrifice of Iphigenia, given in minutest detail, ab-

at Argos, slain like a kid; they see the fleet again set sail for
Troy; they remember that success must come at last, but they

the crime. The spectators with the chorus are now filled
with anxiety, lest with this news of victory, if such it shall
prove to be, some calamity may be treading close upon the
heels of their victorious king.
The poet has, then, made the chorus review the whole
history of that ten years' siege; the events before the prepara-
tion as seen by the prophet Calchas; the assembled army;
the setting out; the detention at Aulis; the sacrifice of Iphi-
genia; the awful threats of Artemis. Thus for a half-hour
or more the spectators have had their attention riveted upon
events dating far back and covering a period of ten years,
so that they are oblivious to the fact that it was only last
night that Troy fell and that this day they have learned the
news. Accordingly when Clytemnestra turns, at the close
of the choral passage, and, having completed her devotions,
listens to what the chorus wish to ask, there is no shock to
learn through her that last night Troy met its fate and that
already this early morning's light has brought the welcome
tidings.
Nor is any one concerned with the impossible when, at
verse 500, the herald is seen hurrying from the shore to the
city to confirm by word of mouth what the beacon light has
heralded in advance. He, too, instead of laying stress upon


## p. 111 (#119) ############################################

TREATMENT OF THE TIME ELEMENT IN THE AGAMEMNON 111
the recency of Troy's fall, dwells upon the fact of his long
absence, rehearses at length the trying experiences upon land
and water, and expresses his joy at standing once more upon
the ground he had yearned for years to see. Thus he, as the
chorus, lays emphasis upon incidents of the past, and when,
in verse 800, Agamemnon enters, slowly riding cityward,
accompanied with his retinue of captured slaves and with
wagons laden with booty, no offense is given to the multitude
of listeners in the reflection that the king could not return
from Troy in less than the space of a day. The element of
time has been removed.
Here is the situation stated briefly:
Troy fell at night. At break of the following day a light
was seen from Mount Arachnæa as a pile of gathered brush
blazed skyward. An hour later a messenger came rushing
upon the stage as though he had come in person from Troy.
Half an hour after the herald's arrival, Agamemnon, seated
upon his chariot, drove into the orchestra as having traveled
with the dignity becoming his station all the way from
Troy.
I think that I have given a fair answer to the question
with which this paper began. Aeschylus arranged the play
so that the time of Troy's fall and the return of the victori-
ous king, though impossibly near in reality, would not mar
the effectiveness of the play as presented upon the stage.
One who reads the tragedy as a piece of literature will
have small concern about the impossibilities in the situation;
but will be ready with the ancients to recognize Aeschylus'
masterly hand as an artist in so hiding the historical relation
of events as to make all seem probable and harmonious.

THE ETHNOLOGICAL IN MATTHEW ARNOLD
ROBERT STINSON STARBIRD
Instructor in English in Washington University
One of the notable characteristics of Matthew Arnold's
criticism is his habit of summing up an argument in a seem-
ingly happy definition or in a general term and then in turn
using this catchword or phrase as a ground for further dis-
cussion. Illustrations of this practice are numerous: Gray
"never spoke out;" Celtic Literature "could not have been
written by fools or for any foolish purpose;" the working
principles of life are, "first, never go against the best light you
have; second, take care that your light be not darkness;"—
one might go on almost indefinitely.
This habit of Arnold's is peculiarly seductive. Not only
does the insistent return to the catchword throughout any
given essay seem to prove the truth of the argument, but the
nicety with which the specious term is made to fit the case
over and over again seems in itself to prove the original
truth of the catchword-a truth, by the way, which is rarely
established. All the illustrations which I have given are
merely the sayings of somebody, who may or may not have
taken the trouble to prove them.
It is not my purpose to speak generally of this habit,
however, but to consider one phase of it,-Arnold's practice
of hitting off a turn of thought, a custom, or a tendency in


## p. 113 (#121) ############################################

THE ETHNOLOGICAL IN MATTHEW ARNOLD
113
literature as characteristic of some particular age or of some
particular people, what might be called his ethnological
habit.
Instances of this sort of procedure are familiar to every
one. Culture is defined as "a study of perfection," a term
general enough to suit even Arnold, one would think; but it
must be made still more vague by being ethnologized (if I
may be allowed the term). Culture, he says, is a point mid-
way between two extremes between which "moves our
world," Hellenism and Hebraism. These two terms are in-
deed defined (Hellenism is "spontaneity of consciousness;"
Hebraism is "strictness of conscience"); but the point is
that Arnold is not ready to proceed with his argument until
he has got his material summed up in a specious ethnological
allusion.
Again, in the essay "On Translating Homer," Arnold
lays stress upon the peculiarities of particular periods. The
essay falls neatly into a discussion of the four distinguishing
characteristics of Homer: his rapidity, his plainness and di-
rectness of expression, his plainness and directness of ideas,
and his nobility. The four great English translations of
Homer are then considered, and each one is declared to fall
short of the original because some peculiar tendency of the
age in which the translation appeared prevented the poet
from reproducing some one of these excellences of Homer.
For instance, one translation is said to fail because of "the
curious complexity of Chapman's Elizabethan English," and
another because of "the oratorical, antithetical, heroic Eng-
lish of the Augustan Age of Queen Anne." The fault is
convincingly traced to some fundamental, or at least tempo-
rarily prevalent, human instinct.
8


## p. 114 (#122) ############################################

114
ROBERT STINSON STARBIRD
But Arnold not only outlines his themes upon a basis of
Hellenism and Hebraism, of Elizabethan characteristics, and
those of the Age of Anne; he falls back, in the discussion of
minor details, upon what he considers self-evident truths con-
cerning the tendencies of ages and the inherent qualities of
races.
Such terms as Asiatic prose, Attic prose, Corinthian
style, Greek spirit of beauty, Hebrew spirit of sublimity are
frequent. "If you want to know plastic art, you go to the
Greeks; if you want to know science, you go to the Aryan
genius;" "the English lack lucidity, the French lack mor-
ality, the Germans lack civil courage" -all these references
are introduced rather casually as axiomatic.
It is when such an allusion becomes the apparent basis
for a conclusion in one of Arnold's essays that we get the
peculiar confusion which I have pointed out and which I wish
to discuss in some detail, -a confusion that arises, in the first
place, from a failure to prove his ethnological assertion and, in
the second, from a failure to apply it closely to his argument.
Such a case we have in the assertion concerning Pope and
Dryden that "their age was one of prose and reason."
Perhaps this particular example is as good as any to illus-
trate Arnold's rather slovenly management of facts. The
whole argument, if I grasp it correctly, can be reduced to a
syllogism:
The builders of an age of prose and reason cannot pro-
duce poetry;
Dryden is "the puissant and glorious founder" of prose,
and Pope its high priest;
Hence, they were not poets.
Accepting for the moment the first member (which is
certainly far from axiomatic) let us examine the second.


## p. 115 (#123) ############################################

THE ETHNOLOGICAL IN MATTHEW ARNOLD
115
How does Arnold prove that Dryden and Pope were the
founders of an age of prose and reason?-by two argu-
ments. The first says: Chapman wrote "intolerable" prose;
Milton wrote "inconvenient" prose; Dryden wrote in "true
English prose" (whatever that phrase may mean)-hence,
Dryden is the puissant founder of prose. And, applying
the major premise, we understand that he could be nothing
else. The second argument is that "the nation felt the im-
perious need of a fit prose." Then follows a definition of fit
prose, and then two extracts from the poets named. From
Dryden, he selects
"A milk white hind, immortal and unchanged,
Fed on the lawns and in the forest ranged;"
and from Pope,
"To Hounslow Heath I point, and Banstead Down
Thence comes your mutton, and these chicks my own."
Arnold shows that the essential qualities of prose appear
in these two poetic selections and that the selections do not
stand the test of poetry. Hence these selections are prose;
and hence all the rest of Dryden's and Pope's poetry is prose!
Now, the age may have been one of prose and of reason,
and Dryden and Pope may have been quite responsible for
the horrible fact. But this argument hardly proves the case.
As a simple matter of fact, neither of the selections is char-
acteristic of its author and either may be compared with iso-
lated commonplaces in other poets which are stupid enough.
And, further (it is almost unnecessary to indicate), to quote
two such passages as a basis for saying that Dryden and


## p. 116 (#124) ############################################

116
ROBERT STINSON STARBIRD
Pope were without "high seriousness," "poetic largeness,"
"freedom," "insight," and "benignity" is a lazy attempt to
prove by ridicule what perhaps might be proved by serious
thought but what is evidently an open question. If Arnold
had honestly quoted two lines more from "The Hind and the
Panther," we should have had
"Without unspotted, innocent within,
She feared no danger, for she knew no sin."
Which is, if I understand the term, at least "a criticism of
life." And if he had been minded to do justice to Dryden
rather than to his hobby, he might have selected a passage
even more happy. To let mutton and chicks stand as the sum
and substance of Pope is of course too absurd an idea to merit
attention.
However, it is not my purpose to show that Arnold's
opinion of Dryden and Pope is wrong (for he is probably
right), but simply to indicate that his argument is fallacious.
In formulating his premise Arnold has no difficulty, for in-
stinctively he jumps at a generality which is alluring because
it seems to be a fundamental fact; but in proving it he has
quite as much trouble as he does in explaining "the grand
style." He does not prove it or even try to. He is sure that
he is right. Consequently he states the premise, then by ridi-
cule affirms the conclusion, and then by way of gaining force
repeats the unproved premise and calls the task done.
Let us go back for a moment to the major premise. Here
Arnold is so sure that he refuses to argue. The poetry of
Dryden and Pope has not the manner or the matter or the
accent of real poetry (he gives examples)-"it has not and


## p. 117 (#125) ############################################

117
cannot have them; it is the poetry of the builders of an age of
prose and reason." This is refreshing and cheerful in the
extreme. It might be possible to show that Pope and Dryden
do not come come up to specifications as poets-but cannot is
a big word to use unless further proof is adduced. The
point is that the repetition of this assertion at the close of the
argument-especially in this solemn and apparently convinced
manner-is Arnold's method of getting a hearing. Gener-
alizing broadly about "ages" and "periods" is very alluring
and seductive, and if done persistently and with solemn assur-
ance it is likely to carry conviction as it does here.
The curious fact about this particular argument, how-
ever, is this: the generalization seems to have nothing to do
with it. The premise is merely asserted; the conclusion is
proved by an independent process, that of ridiculing example;
and the original assertion is then repeated. Thus both the
premise and the conclusion seem to be established. So far as
the argument itself is concerned, the original premise is use-
less, although it might, perhaps, be formulated as a general
law by an elaboration of the argument, that is, by giving a
conclusively large number of examples of prosaic, rational
poetry written in ages admittedly of prose and reason.
seems to be introduced merely as a rhetorical flourish.

Perhaps another example will show even more clearly the
unattached nature of such generalizations in Arnold's argu-
ments. The essay on the "Literary Influence of Academies,"
after a brief history of the French academy, takes its start
with the ethnological generalization that the English spirit
is characterized by energy and honesty, the French spirit by
openness of mind and flexibility of intelligence. Then
through a tortuous page Arnold shows that the first quality


## p. 118 (#126) ############################################

118
ROBERT STINSON STARBIRD
-he is at a loss to find a use for the second except to hope
good things from it-that energy leads to proficiency in po-
etry and science, and that the French qualities lead to prose.
(I am slightly in doubt as to his meaning in this latter argu-
ment because he seems to have assigned these same qualities
to the Greeks, who excelled in poetry.) Arnold is then
started: Our prose is bad; French prose is good. And
these assertions he proves by example throughout the re-
mainder of the essay, showing, from time to time, why and
how a central authority would be of assistance to us in the
writing of prose.
These examples, by the way, like those used in the case
of the unfortunate eighteenth century, are anything but
"urbane." From Burke he selects passages out of the "Reflec-
tions on the French Revolution," a work which even a great
many blunted English "geniuses" believe Burke to have writ-

Arnold presents a desirable piece of English prose, he is care-
ful to indicate that it possesses the qualities of poetry-a
piece of logic which, taken together with the gratuitous state-
ment that genius produces poetry, leaves no hope for our en-
ergetic English genius of ever attaining any distinction in
prose.
But granting the truth of Arnold's estimate of our prose
and poetry, (and usually, I must confess, I believe Arnold in
spite of his arguments), what has the English spirit to do
with the case? The argument is this: Our prose is bad;
French prose is good; the French people have an academy;
we have none. Hence our prose is bad because we have no
academy. Of course it is not stated quite so baldly as this,
but this arrangement is not unfair, because I have granted


## p. 119 (#127) ############################################

THE ETHNOLOGICAL IN MATTHEW Arnold
119
the whole case. The question arises, however, what was
Arnold's idea in introducing the almost irrelevant ethnologi-
cal allusion! It adds nothing to the argument as did the gen-
eralization about the age of Pope, although, like that gener-
alization, it might be derived from the conclusion by an elab-
oration of the argument-that is, inductively.
I have suggested that this use of ethnological terms
seems a mere rhetorical flourish. I am convinced however
that Arnold used this device not because of its rhetorical ef-
fect, but because he felt instinctively a fundamental relation
between the product of a literary man and the life of that
man, between the literary output of an age and some char-
acteristic movement of that age, and between literature as a
whole and life as a whole. In fact he says as much quite
plainly. He calls poetry a criticism of life,-a vague enough
phrase but one for which the reader readily supplies a mean-
ing, although, to be sure, the reader, like Arnold, is likely
to be somewhat at a loss for concrete terms in which to ex-
press the vagary. Arnold characterizes an age with much
facility, and we feel usually that his estimate is just, notwith-
standing the fact that he rarely adduces anything like proof.
He hits off easily the distinctive marks of a race, and here,
unfortunately, the critics have frequently taken him to task.
And he accounts for the work of an individual writer either
upon a basis of that man's disposition or upon a relation
(and this preferably) of the man with his age or his race.
I have called this ethnological tendency a fallacy, not be-
cause Arnold's positions are always wrong or even at times
wrong, but because he seems to imagine that he is establish-
ing his assertions as facts by a mere confusion of argument.
The argument is seldom kept coherent when this element is


## p. 120 (#128) ############################################

120
ROBERT STINSON STARBIRD
introduced. Usually the characteristic is first set forth as a
general statement without proof, a specific case is mentioned,
and a conclusion is drawn. Thus by deduction the argument
is formally presented. One would think that the next logical
step would be the establishing of the premises. But ordina-
rily such is not the method Arnold pursues. The conclusion
is established independently, usually by concrete examples,
and the major premise is once more dragged in. And we
are left in doubt as to whether Arnold intends to prove merely
the conclusion or the general fact the ethnological premise.
As a rule the confusion results in a piece of rhetoric that
seems to establish both.
I have indicated that the argument on the "Literary In-
fluence of Academies" would, if read backward and elabor-
ated, possibly prove the traits which Arnold asserts of the
English mind. And I am convinced that Arnold himself
must always have argued in this direction. His whole idea
seems to be that our literature is due, first, to our tendencies
as a people and, second, to the particular stage of develop-
ment in which we happen to be when any given piece of lit-
erature is produced; and his ultimate aim is, not so much to
account for the character of our literature, as to use the
literature which he discusses as a measure for estimating the
English character and for determining the constituent parts
of our character. Whenever, therefore, we find in Arnold's
work an argument as illogical as the two which I have dis-
cussed (and there are others equally bad), we must supply
from his other essays additional specific facts concerning the
output of the English mind and endeavor with these to sub-
stantiate the general proposition concerning the ethnological
tendency to which he refers. We must first read forward a


## p. 121 (#129) ############################################

THE ETHNOLOGICAL IN MATTHEW ARNOLD
121
large number of his essays in order to see the virtues and the
faults of our literary and social productions and then read
them all backward to discover and prove that they arise from
certain qualities inherent in us as Englishmen.
Arnold's purpose in this analysis is of course evident.
When we have analyzed the peculiarities of our race and of
our time and have compared them with the peculiarities of
other races and of other times we are to apply the doctrines
of "The Function of Criticism at the Present Time" and of
"Culture and Anarchy"-namely, select all that is best
(would that Arnold's definition of "best" were more specific!)
in every race and in every time, make a composite character
of ourselves, and be perfect. Then will follow naturally, of
course, a people unexceptional and a literature perfect. Ar-
nold had a great future in store for the Englishman.
The lesson to the reader of Arnold must also be evident:
Arnold's work is a whole; one idea seems to pervade it; let
us perfect our race. Arnold's work read piecemeal is mislead-
ing because many of his positions seem accidental when they
are not read in the light of his whole work. For instance,
his facile classification of authors into first, second, and third
ranks is easily mistaken for dogmatic pedantry; his insist-
ence upon the value of the classics is likely to be interpreted
as old-fogyism; and his numerous ethnological assertions,
such as "the difference between the Bible and the Koran is
the difference between Isaac and Ishmæl" seem, when isolated
to be merely rather felicitous and weakly clever associations
of ideas. But, read in the light of Arnold's whole purpose,
they show the sincere, all-absorbing desire to bring about that
"perfection" which he has so earnestly labored for in "Sweet-
ness and Light."

THE SCHOOL AND THE INDIVIDUAL
EDGAR JAMES SWIFT
Professor of Psychology and Pedagogy, Washington University
It was not very long ago, as history measures time, that
a Suabian school-master pointed with pride to the results of
his fifty-one years of teaching. He had given "911,00 can-
ings, 121,000 floggings, 209,000 custodes, 136,000 tips with
the ruler, 10,200 boxes on the ear, and 22,700 tasks by heart."
It was also recorded to his credit that "he had made 700
boys stand on peas, 6000 on a sharp edge of wood, 5000
wear the fool's cap, and 1700 hold the rod."
Our early
school-masters were certainly not troubled with philosophic
doubts about the action of matter upon mind, whatever ideas
they may have had regarding the mind's reaction.
"Students," said Crabbe's schoolmaster,
"like horses on the road,
Must be well lash'd before they take the load;
They may be willing for a time to run,
But you must whip them ere the work be done;
To tell a boy, that if he will improve,
His friends will praise him, and his parents love,
Is doing nothing he has not a doubt
But they will love him, nay, applaud without;
Let no fond sire a boy's ambition trust,
To make him study, let him see he must."
But mental ills that had already broken out by no means
exhausted the therapeutical efficacy of the rod; its generous
application was also regarded as a kind of antidote for threat-
'Barnard's English Pedagogy, Second Series, p. 327.
Ibid., p. 328.


## p. 123 (#131) ############################################

THE SCHOOL AND THE INDIVIDUAL
123
ening psychical aspirations. So we find the good Colet,
Dean of St. Paul's, ordering a gentle boy of ten to be flog-
ged, not because he deserved it, as he remarked to Erasmus
who was present, but because "it was fit to humble him."
Erasmus's own teacher was very proud of him, but being a
conscientious man he did not wish his affection to deprive
the boy of the benefit of the stimulus approved by the best
pedagogy, and so he flogged him just to see how he could
bear the pain.
Today we are passing through a transitional period.
Flogging's sceptre no longer brings the small boy to his
knees in reverence, though there are those who are sure that,
so far as being "shaped" is concerned, the boy has been the
loser at both "ends," by thus handicapping Destiny. However
that may be, school flogging, like many other social customs,
has had its day, and passed. Its popularity was due to a
mistaken idea of the nature of sin and to failure to under-
stand the part that racial instincts play in the life of boys.
These were pardonable errors one hundred years ago because
the body of knowledge upon which the newer view rests had
not yet been gathered and worked out. The favor that
whipping finds today is due to the tendency to follow lines
of least resistance, a psychical no less than a physical prin-
ciple. It is very easy to force a semblance of obedience and
attention to work. That is a mere matter of superior
strength, real or imagined. But to create a desire for work, -
that is quite a different problem. And then the desire to
rule, to govern, to sit in judgment over others, is a racial in-
stinct whose birth antedates man. We condemn it only

In earlier days the strongest boy in the school had to be
whipped before he and his friends would consent to be in-
structed, and I am not sure but they were wiser, in their un-
conscious way, than the children of light. Accommodation
by their teachers to an unessential factor in the conditions
demonstrated unfitness. By and by a teacher came into
the school who started a fire with the whips while the larger
boys looked on in amazement, wondering whether the end
of the world was at hand, and unwilling to do anything lest
their action might precipitate the catastrophe. Boys and
girls react in much the same terms as are expressed by one's
action toward them.
There is a delightful little book by William Hawley
Smith, "The Evolution of Dodd." If you have chanced to
read it you will remember how Miss Stone, the village
teacher, ran through all the precepts and maxims that she
had committed to memory during her pedagogical training,
to see which one would apply to Dodd entering the school
room one morning, walking up to her desk with the dignity
that only six year olds can assume, scraping a huge piece of
black loam off his left boot with the toe of his right, just by
way of variety, and rubbing it into the floor with his heel.
You remember the tortured existence of the teachers. One
after another came, but not to stay. Dodd was the one case
that pedagogical precepts seemed not to have taken into ac-
count. One day eighteen year old Amy Kelly was engaged.

Transitional periods at best are very perplexing. No

to do in an emergency. Fortunately, perhaps, the same un-

Extreme reform always ushers in unwonted power. So the
efforts of school boys to find out just what the abolition of
corporal punishment means, to trace the boundaries of their
new possibilities, to see how far they may go without reaching
the jumping-off place, need not surprise us. Naturally these
excursions of discovery keep the teacher's mind in a more or
less chaotic state. If she could only make use of the time-
honored birch rod she could very soon demonstrate to them
the confines of the new freedom. And so we find the teach-
ers in some of the schools in which corporal punishment has
been prohibited petitioning for a return to the good old ways,
and one of the Boston papers, in a recent issue, pleads for the
reinstatement of "judicious punishment."
Age has so long thought itself identical with wisdom that
we cannot, at times, help wondering why its scintillations fail
to dazzle the eyes of youth, yet strangely enough the gratitude
that some eminent men express in their maturity is not for

To be guided in elementary education by the promptings
of the very natures that are to be trained sounds quite illog-
ical to the adult mind accustomed to look with complacent
adulation upon its own deliverances. We are still greatly,
even if unconsciously, influenced by the old idea that the na-
ture of children is intrinsically bad. They must be made
over, remodeled on a better pattern-the adult pattern-with
large parts of them left out. And so we set up a psychical
operating-table in every school room, and proceed to cut each
child according to our measure, forgetful of our own defi-
ciencies, lopping off one individual trait after another until
we have made him commonplace enough to fit into the tra-
ditional pedagogical mould.

Variability is a fundamental biological principle. With-
out it there is no selection, for the simple reason that there
is nothing from which to select. Conformity to a mean re-
duces all to common mediocrity. Improvement posits vari-
ation, and this is just the quality that finds least favor in our
schools today. Individuality may not receive quite the same
treatment that it did from Dr. Parr of the Norwich school
who, when informed by one of his teachers that a certain
pupil seemed to be showing signs of genius, exclaimed, "Say
you so? Then begin to flog him tomorrow morning," but
it causes hardly less commotion in the orthodox pedagogical
breast. Non-conformists are always hard to dispose of. In
school they are particularly objectionable because they do not
easily fit into a system. We arrange pupils under a few gen-
eral types and those who do not conform to our classification
we call lazy, or dull, or bad; but these are only names to in-
dicate certain deviations from the convenient standard of the
school, and have no necessary validity beyond its walls. How
fortunate this is becomes evident when we learn that Koezle
counted 914 faults of children enumerated by various school-

One of the most distinguished British physiologists and

It is curious that everything that enters the school-room
at once becomes rigid. The method of the recitation has
been elevated into a fetich before whose image individuality
yields to unbecoming humility. The belief that there is one
road to knowledge is fundamentally wrong. There are as
many ways of getting ideas as there are individuals. No one
has a monopoly on the manner in which children arrive at
the number concept, though some have tried to patent the
process. Mental flexibility is essential to intellectual growth,
and ability to adapt oneself to the innumerable ways in
which mind matures marks the born teacher. Possession
of this power explains the success of some with little educa-
tion and its absence makes useless in the class-room the pro-
found knowledge of the specialist. It was Turgot, I think,
who once said that "the first thing for a philosopher to do is
to get a system of philosophy, and the second thing for him
to do is to discard it." This is eminently true of method.

Methods serve him only who has risen above them. To be

The mere breaking away from habit rejuvenates the mind.
Uniformity, in teachers and pupils alike, arrests mental pro-

Freedom from routine and formality seems to have char-
acterized the teachers who impressed themselves upon those
whose subsequent eminence has enabled us to learn of their
boyhood days. Dr. Hutcheson, to whom Adam Smith felt
so deeply indebted, was a decided radical. It was he who
first broke away, at Glasgow, from the almost sacred tradi-
tion of lecturing in Latin. He worked with his students,
ridding them of antiquated beliefs by first liberating his own
mind, and he continually stimulated them to do something a
little better than they had thus far done by suggesting possi-
ble lines of study and thought.
He is a fortunate man who, from the kindergarten
through the university, has had more than one or two real
teachers. Abundant knowledge and good character, to-
gether with logical clearness in exposition, are commonly
thought sufficient, yet the failure of teachers possessed of all
these qualities to attract and inspire the boys and girls who
later became eminent men and women is a fact the signifi-
cance of which cannot be ignored. The right of children
to their own individual natures is grudgingly accorded the

School-teachers are fond advocates of the coercion-drudg-
ery theory, but casual inspiration counts for little. Anyone
can drive, but few are capable of leading, and the desire for
self-justification is natural. The time to give information is
when it is asked for. That is the psychological moment, and
the teacher who cannot create the desire for knowledge
should speculate in other futures than those of human beings.
The school may not be able to make poets or scientists or
philosophers, but it can certainly spoil them.
It is a very trite remark that if education is to be effect-
ive the child must react upon it, but in this statement there is
always an implicit assumption that reaction is of one sort.

commonly afflicted, only it has it in a little worse form. We
incline to think in formulæ, and having once found the magic

words, our pedagogical soul feels the peace "which passeth

the boys had been reproved or kept after school for not
mastering it. Much of the work that children call play is
just as hard as any that is given them in the school-room.
The attitude of the teacher makes the difference. Primitive
man did not distinguish between work and play, and children
do not until the distinction is forced upon them. Orthodox
pedagogy, under the spell of the mysterious efficacy of severe
mental strain, wants to make everything conscious, unmind-
ful of the fact that many times the learning processes are most
effective when there is no conscious effort. Every little
while children must be mentally eviscerated in order that the
degree of mental digestion may be observed and a percentage
value given. This is thought to hold the pupils to a higher
standard of work; but, on the other hand, the human mind,
fortunately perhaps, adapts itself with remarkable facility
to continued misfortune and settles down into indifferent ac-
quiescence.
The assertion that the cases which have been cited are
exceptional, and for that reason without evidential value, is
not sufficient; for, first, it is clear that the teachers did not
recognize them as exceptional; i. e., did not understand them,


## p. 141 (#149) ############################################

THE SCHOOL AND THE INDIVIDUAL
141
but, instead, regarded them as just commonplace boys; sec-
ond, the claims that they are exceptional is an admission of
the unrecognized right of individual differences to a funda-
mental place in education, and this is the position of the
writer.
Forced attention accomplishes nothing. Intellectual ef-
fort is effective only when it springs from an irresistible im-
pulse in the individual to do the thing, and that impulse can
never be stirred by external constraint or restraint. The ef-
fective line of approach to children is through their racial in-
stincts and individual dispositions. These are their vulner-
able points, easily taken without loss to either side, and, when
once communication is opened, it is astounding how many
native tendencies may be made allies in promoting intellectual
and moral growth. It is against those who are indifferent to
these instinctive tendencies of childhood and youth that
Wordsworth hurls his scorn-
"Those mighty workmen of our later age,
Who, with a broad highway, have overbridged
The forward chaos of futurity,
Tamed to their bidding, they who have the skill
To manage books, and things, and make them act
On infant minds as surely as the sun
Deals with a flower; the keepers of our time,
The guides and wardens of our faculties,
Sages who in their prescience would control
All accidents, and to the very road
Which they have fashioned would confine us down,
Like engines; when will their presumption learn,
That in the unreasoning progress of the world
A wiser spirit is at work for us,
A better eye than theirs, most prodigal
Of blessings, and most studious of our good,
Even in what seems our most unfruitful hours." "
"Wordsworth's Complete Poetical Works, The Prelude, p. 267.

THE NEAR FUTURE OF AMERICAN SOCIETY*
EDWARD ALSWORTH ROSS, PH. D.
Professor of Sociology in the University of Nebraska
The sharpest corner American Society has turned since
the destruction of slavery was turned in the early nineties
when the last homestead in the rain belt was taken up. This
event closed the expansive, free land epoch that has extended
through our nascent period and ushered in the era of limited
natural opportunities and intensive development. Hitherto
the discontented American has enjoyed an option-to move
up or to move on. He can no longer move on and as "room
at the top!" is the gospel for the exceptional man it is hard
to escape the conclusion that for the ordinary man the circle
of opportunities is destined to be relatively narrower.
Our population has always sloped westward, lying deep
in the older sections and thinning out toward the sunset.
But when the onrushing tide of migration broke into spray
on the hundredth meridian, the viewless coast of the fertile
expanse beyond the Mississippi, the backwash began to pro-
portion population to the man-supporting power of the differ-
ent sections. As West and South thus acquire their due
quota of people, factories and cities will multiply in them, and
the interchange of goods between crowded East and farming
West will become less exaggerated. Consumers will spring
*Abstract of a lecture delivered before The Washington University Asso-
ciation, December 14, 1905.


## p. 143 (#151) ############################################

THE NEAR FUTURE OF AMERICAN SOCIETY
143
up at the Western farmer's door. Home markets will di-
versify crops and the soil will no longer be worn out in grow-
ing only exportable staples like wheat, cotton, and tobacco.
Once the East with its ships and mills, the Center with
its furnaces and forges, the South with its slave-worked
plantations, the West with its farms and the Far West with
its ranches and mines, constituted distinct basins in which
unlike types of society developed. Henceforth they will more
and more merge into a single great national basin filled with
one rich and highly diversified social life.
Electricity is diffusing the city into the country. Tele-
phones, free mail delivery, and interurban lines are revolu-
tionizing the farmer's life. The "clod-hopper" and the "cob-
ble-trotter" types are both doomed. The state is bound to
bulk bigger than it does today and the net of regulation it
casts over business will have a finer mesh. As corporate
undertaking spreads and the army of shareholders swells to
many times its present size, corporations will have to allow
their inner workings to be radiographed upon the screen of
publicity. Government will become a giant purveyor of ex-
act and statistical information. Philanthropy and education
will be fostered with a more generous hand. The public on-
slaught on disease will develop from desultory bushwhacking
into a vast scientific warfare and state aid to research will
reach proportions yet undreamed.
Within recent years the sheer cash standard of human
work wrought out among heavy spenders has triumphed in
our great cities and spread with alarming rapidity to the
minor centers. Not a day passes but new communities and
new interests surrender to commercialism. Naturally
enough the result has been a whetting of greed and there-


## p. 144 (#152) ############################################

144
EDWARD ALSWORTH Ross
upon an unprecedented carnival of boodle, graft, fraud, and
monopoly extortion.
Relief from this Mammonism must come from a change in
the standard of human worth. The only graduated test of
man's worth that can dispute the sway of pecuniary standard
is-not birth, or prowess, or culture, or even character, but
-efficiency. When tomorrow's morrow, graft-stricken and
desperate, lights Diogenes' lamp and looks about for an hon-
est man, it will find him in the trained expert, fortified with a
professional ethics, who, next to a living for wife and babes,
cares for nothing so much as the "Well done, old man!" of
his brother experts.
Our crowded colleges are rearing a breed that will not
dance before the golden calf. From schools of business, jour-
nalism, social work, and the public service moral ozone will
spread into new quarters. Over against the dollar standard
of success professional schools, associations, and periodicals
will raise the standard of workmanship. In the public ser-
vice the trained sanitarian, statistician, teacher, engineer, or
warden will oust the henchman.
Those who experience this antiseptic professional train-
ing will not be left to fight the battle alone. The toiling mil-
lions value men in terms of efficiency and instinctively pay
homage to workmanlike traits. Hitherto they have been too
unconscious and mute to have a hand in shaping the reigning
standards of worth. Now, however, the deeps begin to
heave and stir. The great and growing movement of asso-
ciation among laboring men promises to release into society
a purifying current of opinion. When through fellowship
and converse the workers come to themselves they will per-
haps pluck up the courage to champion their own sound ideals
against the tinsel idols of our day.

THE UNDEVELOPED RACES IN CONTACT WITH
CIVILIZATION*
G. STANLEY HALL, PH. D., LL. D.
President of Clark University
Man has always been the great exterminator. From pre-
historic times to the present, there has been a long and grow-
ing list of animals he has extirpated. The buffalo is nearly
extinct; and the giraffe, the higher apes, the moose, and
many other species are going slowly but surely the way of
the great auk.
There is also a long list of races of primitive people
that have been utterly exterminated, whose blood cries to
us from the ground, such as the Tasmanians, the Mohegans,
the Mohawks, and the Boethuk. Besides these, the Samoy-
eds, the Patagonians, Australians, Hawaiians, and the
natives of Madagascar are slowly fading under the white
man's diseases, weapons, drink, lust, and his love of land
and of all the products of the mines. What is to be the fate
of the two-fifths of the population and one-third of the sur-
face of the globe now in a condition of more or less depend-
ence and subserviency to the white race? Shall these
*Abstract of lecture delivered before The Washington University Association,
Monday, November 27, 1905.
10


## p. 146 (#154) ############################################

146
G. STANLEY HALL
peoples be swept out of existence as weeds in the human gar-
den or shall their own indigenous culture be developed in
order that they may some time be relays to take up the torch
of civilization and culture when the dominant races of the
present shall have passed away? Fifty years ago the great
powers thought of dividing Japan between them and would
have done so could they have agreed upon the terms of par-
tition. To the ancient Romans, the Germans of the days of
Tacitus were barbarians, as were the residents of England
in the period of Roman occupation. What would the world
be had they been exterminated or permanently crushed and
enfeebled? And many races that now seem doomed to
extinction have as much promise of future development as
these races did then.
We have in the Congo basin today a rapid exhaustion
and depletion of an indigenous population consisting of prob-
ably fifteen or twenty million and covering an area of more
than one-third of the United States, under the rapacious
rule of Leopold the Second. Accessible tribes are being re-
duced to a condition as bad as slavery and often worse. There
are punitive expeditions, native soldiers commanded by un-
controlled native officers let loose upon villages that have not
furnished their quota of supplies, which now require an un-
interrupted labor often of two or three hundred days a year
to obtain. Here, as in Mexico in the days of Cortez, and in
Peru in the days of Pizarro, life is being sacrificed at a
tremendous rate, although in Spain at that day, and in Bel-
gium now, the laws upon the statute books for the protection
of the aborigines are models of humanity, philanthropy, and
Christian good will. The trouble is that the worst elements
of modern civilization are let loose in colony life. Avarice,


## p. 147 (#155) ############################################

THE UNDEVELOPED RACES IN CONTACT WITH CIVILIZATION 147
greed, and lust are doing their work to an amazing and in-
credible extent. Some nations have a genius for coloniza-
tion, and some seem to have an invincible stupidity in this
work. England heads the former, and she has taught jus-
tice, security, and respect for law in all her wide dominions;
but even here greed rules. The Indian peasant is taxed for
the girdle about his loins, and for everything he can pro-
duce, the rate of taxation amounting sometimes to over
thirty per cent and rarely below twelve, a state of affairs
which is simply ruinous. The sequestration of the famine
fund aggravated the vast loss of life throughout the East
Indian domain, and millions of people periodically perish
who might be saved.
The American Indian we are now striving to make over
into a cheap imitation of the white man. The contrast at
the Louisiana Purchase Exposition between the Indian
school on the hill and the primitive tribes on the slope below
was designed to be a lesson in the value of education and
civilization, but it was hardly a fair and honest representa-
tion. The Indian, although a man of the stone age, is per-
haps the noblest of all savages. His myths and traditions,
the more we come to understand them, prove to be interest-
ing and often sublime; yet we treat these people on the reser-
vations much as the Spaniards treated the Cubans in the
concentrado camps. They must cut their hair and refrain
from their dances which are holy sacraments to them, and
they are forbidden to paint or to leave the reservation. What
we should do is to make them good Red Men, encourage their
native industries, traffic in skins, the making of canoes, bas-
ketry, pottery, weaving, etc., which have just as much edu-
cational value in them as Sloyd, if not more. We should not


## p. 148 (#156) ############################################

148
G. STANLEY HALL
break up the tribal spirit and not force the white man's
burden at every point to the extinction of the best elements.
We should teach them to respect themselves and their tra-
ditions, and should ourselves respect the integrity of their
families, their tribes, and their reservations. Why are an-
thropologists, who know the Indian, always excluded from
the Mohawk Conference?
Again, the negro is now the ward of the nation. Our
deplorable carpet bag policy has made him feel enmity toward
his former master in the South who understands him, and
has taught him that his friends are in the North. We have
deepened the color line and made it also a party line. Booker
Washington's work has done more than all else that has ever
been attempted to point out the right way. The negro
should not in most places in the South be compelled to waive
the right to vote, but should be taught to gather some prop-
erty and to make himself an intelligent citizen. The negro
has some excellent traits which the whites lack. No race
ever had a freer, richer emotional life, greater docility and
power of adaptation, more cheerfulness in the most adverse
conditions, a more intense religious nature, or a keener and
more sympathetic appreciation of nature. These elements
should be developed and are capable of being made the basis
of a civilization which will be very different from that of the
whites if it ever comes. The negro here has retrograded in
the last ten years, especially in the South. He ought to
interest himself in the problems of Africa, his motherland,
not because deportation is practicable, which it is not, but
that the race may slowly solidify and gather itself up for
some great advance in the future under leaders of its own
blood and color. Men like Blyden, Booker Washington,


## p. 149 (#157) ############################################
