du Bois, and many others are beginning to realize the magni-
tude of this problem. There should be somewhere an African
museum, library, or bureau, where both ethiopic information
and exemplifications of negro culture should be gathered.
Negro leaders here should speak out more clearly than any
one of them has yet done against the enormity of the crime
of rape.
The true policy in regard to every primitive people is
educational in the largest statesmanly view of this great
word, which far transcends even the present highest inter-
pretation of politics. Happily there are the beginnings of
other solutions. Japan has developed indigenous culture,
although mingled with and vitalized by the culture of other
nations. When science is a part of the grist ground in the
tremendous mill of the Chinese educational system, Europe
will have to look out for her laurels. In South Africa we
have lately had in one English domain a splendid exemplifi-
cation of what native training should be. Under this system
the black children are taught their own languages, which
are reduced to writing, and record the best of their tradi-
tions; their tribal organization is maintained and utilized
in the administration of justice; and only those who have
passed through the elementary stages of this work and are
likely to become leaders are allowed to study English subjects
or even the English language.
Many parts of the civilized world today are threatened
more or less acutely with the problem of race suicide. Where
would this country be if dependent upon the offspring of the
primitive stock and if all immigrants were excluded for a
generation or two? It may be that when stirpiculture is
more developed and when we have realized that a little


## p. 150 (#158) ############################################

150
G. STANLEY HALL
heredity is worth more than a ton of education, we shall
learn how to develop indigenous stocks as grafts and relays.
The savage body is usually far more vigorous than that
of civilized man. It is better proportioned and better devel-
oped. The savage emotions are keener, more intense. These
are more closely connected with heredity than the intellect
which is largely a product of individual training. The human
race should realize that the most precious thing in all the
world is health, vigorous native stocks, and stirps, and if
these are eliminated the world of the future will be in the
condition in which the modern world would have been if the
Romans had crushed the life out of all the peoples under their
dominion, as we are crushing it out in our colonies. The
twelve or fifteen hundred million people on the earth today
are but a small fraction of those who will people it in the
future as the generations of men go on. The best standard
of virtue is to so live that the sacred torch of heredity may
be transmitted undimmed to this boundless future.

THE SHELBURNE ESSAYS
SHELBURNE ESSAYS, by Paul Elmer More [W. U., 1887]. First,
Second, and Third Series. G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York and
London, 1905.
These three volumes by a graduate of the University have already
been widely recognized as constituting one of the most serious and
weighty contributions to literary criticism that have been made in
America in recent years. In what temper of mind, and with what con-
siderable pretensions Mr. More approaches the task of the critic is well
enough indicated by the quotation from Lowell that stands upon the
title-page of the first volume: "Before we have an American literature
we must have an American criticism." It is the kind of criticism
that may help to make an American literature possible in the future,
that Mr. More would help to provide. We have here, therefore, no
irresponsible impressionism, no mere "record of the adventures of a
mind at large among master-pieces." Mr. More's criticism, in short,
has traditions and it has standards; its purpose is to chasten as well as
to interpret, and it is apparently not much in sympathy with the con-
tention that
"There are nine and sixty ways
Of constructing tribal lays,
And every single one of them is right."
It seems to be rather a point of honor with Mr. More to be a
little out of harmony with the enthusiasms of his time; thus in the
height of the Kipling craze he entered the field to point out, with some
analytical carefulness, "the limitations which debar" the author of The
Seven Seas "from ranking with the truly great poets of England;" and
in the day when Omar clubs multiplied, he insisted upon the (fairly
obvious) ethical imperfections of the philosophy of the Rubaiyat-and
later repents, in a footnote, of having been led by "the silly talk of the
day to pass too lightly over the extraordinary beauty and humanity of
Fitzgerald's work." So, again, though having for Emerson a "rever-
ence this side of idolatry," Mr. More devotes his essay upon that
moralist to pointing out-it was high time that somebody should do
so-the "perilous dizziness of the brain" which "Emersonianism" has
wrought "in our religion, our politics, and our literature"-through the


## p. 152 (#160) ############################################

152
THE SHELBURNE ESSAYS
infatuate optimism, the blindness to those "unconcerning things, matters
of fact," which, especially in the climate of Boston, the Emersonian
influence tends to produce. This temper of suspicion towards current
fashions in literature and thought, though it has its dangers, is essen-
tially a great virtue in a critic, if it be the genuine expression of a
trained and steady sense for permanent values, the product of a wide
and penetrating knowledge of the great things in the literatures of
many peoples and many times. And this, for the most part, is the
meaning of such an attitude in Mr. More's case; if he avoids the
mere dithyrambic outcry of admiration, even in the presence of the
immortals, he can not be charged, either, with any flippant iconoclasm.
His criticism, though easy and wholly unacademic in manner, is emi-
nently learned. This, indeed, is its distinguishing quality. Mr. More
shows, perhaps, less painstaking patience in the induction of evidence,
in the psychological analysis of temperament, and in the inquiry into
the historical conditions and antecedents of great writers, than do
some other critics of our time-Mr. Brownell, for example. But it
would be hard to find any other critical writer of today who can
so illuminate a subject by wide-ranging comparisons, who can so in-
structively correlate a manifestation of one or another quality of style
or thought in English books with other manifestations of the like
quality in other literatures, especially French, Italian, Greek, and
Oriental. And for this reason, Mr. More's critical work is precisely
of the type that is most likely to serve as the means for a needed
cross-fertilization of our American literature, for the correction of the
more unhealthy sort of provincialism, and for the establishment amongst
us of that mental habit of comparison of seeing beyond the immediate
object of one's momentary interest or admiration-to which our good-
natured, childlike, and fad-loving reading public are peculiarly unac-
customed. In one respect Mr. More has, doubtless, an altogether unique
position among contemporary critics-namely, in that he comes to the
criticism of modern, and especially English, literature, from an earlier
study of, and especial interest in, the literature and philosophies of
India and even from a two years' practice of the hermit life, of
something approaching the vita contemplativa, withdrawn from virtu-
ally all (save canine) society, in a retreat near the secluded Vermont
village from which these volumes take their name.
Before the appearance of the present essays Mr. More was known
as the writer of The Great Refusal, a singular romance with a certain
curious charm, permeated with the Buddhistic philosophy of self-
negation-and as the translator of the Indian Epigrams of Bhartrihari.


## p. 153 (#161) ############################################

THE SHELBURNE ESSAYS
153
Such a preparation for literary criticism is, at all events, decidedly
unusual, and it shows its effect very plainly in some characteristics of
Mr. More's work. It is not merely that he is constantly bringing the
English writings with which he deals into contrast or comparison with
Oriental ideas or writings; it is, much more, that he has come chiefly
to value in any piece of literature certain qualities which his sympathy
with Hindu thought, and especially with Buddhism, has taught him to
appreciate. It is the presence ce of these qualities which, for him, makes
the great writer-for such presence means that the writer is one of
those who, at least at moments, have seen below the surface of life,
have been "twice-born." The essence of these qualities lies in detach-
ment from the game of existence, a certain disillusion, a sense of the
transiency and unreality of things and the emptiness of the ends men
set their hearts upon. The great poet must have, not merely the moral
power of seeing and caring for "the righteousness that rules in the
hurly-burly of a contentious life," but "that other spirit that turns
from the passion and toil of existence as from a wasteful illusion, and
whose eyes are set on solitude and a triumph of peace beyond earthly
victories." "Poetry to accomplish its nobler mission must both
evoke and lay the passions. Through the din of personal struggle
and personal emotions must break at times the voice of something
deeper within us, calling us to rest. In the clash of worldly
ambitions it happens now and then to a man to pause while a feel-
ing of unreality comes over him, and for a moment he knows that
his concern in the drama is purely fictitious, and that there is a witness
looking down with disdain on the strutting part he plays. No man
ever achieved anything great in this world without these moments of
deeper insight, and without a certain contemptuous indifference to his
own fate. No poet ever causes the hearts of his hearers to expand
with the larger joy who does not lift the veil occasionally, and destroy
the illusion he is himself creating." So for Mr. More, the supreme
thing in Shakespere is that great "cry of disillusion, after the storm
of passion and ambition in Macbeth." This note Mr. More likes to
discover, and he finds it in diverse and surprising contexts, in widely
dissimilar writers in Thoreau, Hawthorne, Freneau, Carlyle, Emerson,
and many others. But, as Mr. More hardly sufficiently observes, such a
mood, in the greater of our English writers, is for the most part a
thing of moments, a dark foil to the bright and stirring business of
life, in which they are, after all, chiefly interested. When the mood
becomes a conscious and settled philosophy, it proves singularly sterile
and wholly unfavorable to the development of literature. It is sterile,


## p. 154 (#162) ############################################

154
THE SHELBURNE ESSAYS
this philosophy of disenchantment, because it is essentially negative;
it tells us what is unreal and what is worthless, but can define the real
and the good only by pointing to what they are not; and looking
equally upon all human passion and struggle with the eye of detach-
ment, it can possess no scale of comparative values for determining the
relative worth of one passion or activity as over against another. Ac-
cording to the predisposition of the holder of such a view of life, it
adjusts itself equally well to one or another ethical temper-it inclines
necessarily and logically no more to one than to another. With
Schopenhauer it ends in a caustic pessimism, touched with pantheistic
feeling and humanitarian pity; with James Thomson it ends in the
bitterness of a cosmic despair; with the Omar of Fitzgerald it ends in
the pleasant counsels of the voluptuary. With Mr. More it implies
something different from any of these: a demand for austerity, self-
renunciation, the rigorous discipline of the will, the cultivation of
spiritual self-sufficiency and quietude of mind. In this Mr. More
shows himself responsive to the characteristic spirit of Indian Bud-
dhism, and expresses the tone of it better than most of our modern rep-
resentatives of the Oriental influence, who usually have had more
affinity with the more sentimental and less austere form of the nega-
tive philosophy that is found in the Vedanta. But one can not but
ask, here, as in the case of Buddhism itself: For the sake of what real
and positive good are the common interests and affections of life to
be renounced? Is not "attachment" to even the pettiest thing in life
better than mere "detachment," which in the end is logically synony-
mous with inactivity and death? In this connection it must be observed
that Mr. More attempts unsuccessfully to read some sort of concrete
worth and meaning into the Buddhist conception of the goal of life,
Nirvana. The subject is too large a one to be discussed here; but
Mr. More, in writing as he does in Vol. I, p. 241, can hardly have
been duly mindful of such passages as Sutta Nipata, 1073-1076.
Such seems to be the philosophy of life which shows itself behind
Mr. More's criticism. It, too, perhaps has its uses for our hurried
and over-strenuous American life; and it is certainly an historically
significant incident in the story of the intellectual relations of America
and the Orient. But it is a philosophy which, if one may speak dog-
matically, is mainly unsound and illogical; and it is certainly no
natural product or interpretation of the spirit of our American and
democratic life. For it is incapable of assigning any significance to
personality, of finding anything of essential import and ultimate value
in the social relationships, of recognizing that there is some, though not


## p. 155 (#163) ############################################

THE SHELBURNE ESSAYS
155
an equal, degree of worth in every play of consciousness, in every
vital activity, in every purposive movement of the will. And the
result of this philosophy in Mr. More's criticism is seen in his in-
adequate treatment of Browning, who is the touch-stone by which a
critic's sense for these things, and his general soundness of vitality,
may be judged. It is a satisfaction, therefore, to find in the latest-
written of the Shelburne Essays a less frequent preoccupation about
the detection of expressions of the vanity of the common life of man.
For when he forgets this preoccupation-as in the admirable essays on
Sainte Beuve, on Cowper, and on Whittier-Mr. More shows a pene-
tration and a freshness of insight into the diversities of life and char-
acter that lead us to expect from him in the future still more note-
worthy work-criticism not less serious, nor less exacting in its
standards, but still more human, fuller-bodied, more variously sympa-
thetic.

THE BULLETIN OF
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
THE WORK OF THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY
ASSOCIATION
On account of the earlier date of publication of this year's
BULLETIN it is not possible to give here a complete report of the
work of The Washington University Association for the current
season. Of the four parts into which the work falls, the BULLETIN
itself represents something more than a quarter; and it is here to
report for itself. The three other divisions of the Association's
activities are the giving of a series of single evening lectures in St.
Louis, for the profit of the members, the students of the University,
and the general public; the maintenance of short educational lecture
courses, usually given in the University buildings; and the offering
of University Extension courses in centers outside of St. Louis.
I. SINGLE LECTURES.
The Council of the Association determined at the beginning of
the year to make the single lectures of the year for the most part
the occasions for bringing before the members and the University
public lecturers of eminence from outside the city-men distinguished
for authoritative scholarship or for the originality, importance, and
thought-provoking quality of the ideas which they had to present.
Consequently most of the single lectures given thus far have been
by non-resident speakers. It is not, however, the policy of the present
Council to adhere undeviatingly to the rule of bringing speakers from
a distance; and it has already seized the opportunity to present two
from this city. The execution of the plan for the year has necessarily
involved the expenditure of considerably greater sums for single lectures
than in any previous year of the Association's history. It seemed to
the Council, however, that such a plan would add to the attractiveness
of the privilege of membership in the Association, and would, in par-
ticular, enable the Association to add notably to the educational
opportunities available at the University, by giving the students the
chance to hear some of the men in the country who are best worth
hearing, whether resident in or outside of St. Louis. It is unfortu-
nately necessary to report that the results, in this respect, have hardly
justified the expenditure, or fulfilled the hopes of the Council. Al-


## p. 157 (#165) ############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
157
though, in the opinion of most of those who have been present, the
lectures given have been of uncommon interest and value, the attend-
ance of members has been small, of students still smaller, and of the
general public (who were admitted to three of the lectures upon
payment of an admission fee) decidedly limited. This has, it is true,
been due in part to an unusual sequence of unpredictable pieces of
ill-fortune. One important lecture was given on one of the stormiest
evenings of the year. In two cases lecturers who had been secured
were compelled, almost at the last moment, to announce their inability
to keep their engagements; and this necessitated the hasty rearranging
of the programme and in one case the omission of a lecture altogether.
The migratory character of the course has also been unfavorable to
large and regular attendance; lectures have been given in three different
halls in widely separated sections of the city. It is greatly to be hoped
that the University may at an early date possess a permanent center
for its activities and those of the Association, near the heart of the
residence district of the city. It is not for the present at all prac-
ticable to hold evening lectures or extension classes in the University
buildings a fact sufficiently evidenced by the restricted attendance
even at the afternoon lecture courses, which have all been given in
University Hall. Even exceptional attractions will not suffice to
induce large numbers of people to come so far to hear lectures, at all
events, so long as the street car service remains so hopelessly infre-
quent and unreliable, and the termini of the lines are so instructively
illustrative of the nature of the Sirbonian bog.
Of the lectures given, two that by Mr. Dole, at the beginning of
the year, and that by Dr. Peters, given by the Association and the
St. Louis Society of the Archaeological Institute of America conjointly
-were open only to members and invited guests; and each was fol-
lowed by an informal reception in the galleries of the Art Museum.

FACULTY LEGISLATION
FOR THE UNDERGRADUATE DEPARTMENT
[A condensed statement is here given of the various actions of the
Faculty which affect the general administration of the Undergraduate
Department, taken at meetings from May 1, 1905, to March 1, 1906.]
GENERAL FACULTY.
May 3, 1905. The Faculty voted to suspend its rules in regard to
cheating and to adopt the "Honor System" as proposed by the members
of the student body. By this system all cases of cheating, or illegitimate
use of another's work, on the part of a student of the Undergraduate
Department will be dealt with by a special committee consisting of
two Seniors, one Junior, one Sophomore, and one Freshman.
The Faculty voted to adopt the recommendations of the special
committee on advertising. These recommendations were in part:
1. That the Undergraduate Department publish monthly, from
August to June inclusive, a news-letter to be called "Washington
University Record"; this publication to contain official announcements


## p. 160 (#168) ############################################

160
THE BULLETIN OF
of the Undergraduate Department and such matter as would be of
interest to faculty, students, and alumni of the University.
2.
That the system of examining accredited schools be revised
and extended.
The Chancellor announced that the Board of Directors of the
University had approved the recommendation of the Library Com-
mittee in regard to the purchase of reference books for the library,
amounting in value to $2500.
October 5, 1905. The Chancellor announced that a joint committee
from the Board of Directors and the Faculty of the Undergraduate
Department had adopted mottoes to be carved upon the front and rear
of University Hall. The mottoes are as follows:
For the front, DISCERE SI CUPIAS, INTRA: SALVERE
JUBEMUS.
For the rear, CEDUNT HORAE; OPERA MANENT.
November 1, 1905. The Chancellor announced that the joint
committee of the Board of Directors and the Faculty appointed to con-
sider the matter of mottoes had recommended for inscription upon the
open book of the University emblem the words PER VERITATEM VIS,
and that this motto had been adopted.
The Faculty voted that it would view with satisfaction the sub-
stitution of the "Association" for the "Rugby" game of football in
American colleges and schools.
The Western Military Academy was placed upon the list of
accredited schools for both the College and the School of Engineering.
FACULTY OF THE COLLEGE.
June 7, 1905. The Faculty enacted the following requirements
with regard to conditioned students:
I. When a student's work has been otherwise satisfactory, but
has proven deficient through illness or other unavoidable cause, it
shall be marked "incomplete."
Such deficiency may be made up by the presentation of the un-
completed parts of the work of the course, or in such other way as
the instructor may direct. When the work is thus made up the in-
structor shall mark the student for the course according to the usual
grades.
2. Students shall be marked (except in the case named in Clause
1) as "conditioned" in all cases in which the work is not up to passing
grade. Conditions shall be removable by re-examination or by a


## p. 161 (#169) ############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
161
repetition of the course, or a specified part thereof, and in no other
way, except that when two courses are so continuous that the regu-
lations of the University do not permit the student to receive credit
for the first course alone, the instructor may, if he desires, remove the
conditions upon the students creditably passing the second course.
3. The instructor in reporting conditions shall in each case indicate
whether the course shall be made up by re-examination or by repetition
of the course, or a part thereof.
4. No student shall drop or change a course after having taken
it for six weeks without receiving a condition, and may drop or change
a course during the first six weeks only with the permission of the
dean and the instructor.
5. Conditioned students who are required by the instructor to
repeat a course must arrange to take such a course when next offered.
Conditioned students who are required by the instructor to take a
second examination, shall, when the condition has been imposed at
the end of the first term, take such examination before May Ist fol-
lowing, and when the condition has been imposed at the end of the
second term, they shall take such examination before September 30th
following. Students who fail to appear at the examinations thus
specified, or who fail to pass when they have taken them, shall repeat
the course when next offered.
No grade except that of C shall be given when conditions are
removed.
6. At the end of each term the dean shall present to the Faculty
a separate report of those students whose conditions exceed three
hours of work per week, and the Faculty shall then determine how
many courses the student shall be permitted to carry for the succeeding
term.
January 10, 1906. The Faculty voted:
I. That either of the following be accepted as one year's work
towards the A. B. degree.
(a) Satisfactory completion of the Junior Course in the Law
School.
(b) Satisfactory completion of one-half of the Junior Course,
plus satisfactory completion of one-half of the Middle Class Course in
the Law School.
2. That the privilege of pursuing such courses in the Law
School be restricted to members of the Senior Class in the College
whose average grade in the two previous terms has not fallen below B.
3. That the work of the student in the Law School must be of a
II


## p. 162 (#170) ############################################

162
THE BULLETIN OF
high grade, and not lower than that which would receive the mark
of B in the College.
4. That whenever the College is prepared to offer courses equiv-
alent to any of those now offered in the Law School, students shall be
credited upon the Law School record with such courses.
5. That College students taking courses in the Law School, as
before mentioned, during their senior year, shall be registered in the
College and pay the regular undergraduate tuition fee.
6. That this arrangement be regarded as a tentative one, which
may be amended or abandoned, if, in the opinion of the Faculty, such
course should seem wise.
FACULTY OF THE SCHOOL OF ENGINEERING AND ArchitectURE.
June 14, 1905. The Faculty adopted the same regulations re-
garding conditioned students that apply to students in the College (see
above).
The Faculty also adopted the following rules:
I. All students of the School of Engineering and Architecture
shall be present on the opening day of the term.
2. In the future all lists of candidates for athletic contests shall
be submitted to the Secretary of the Faculty of the School of Engineer-
ing and Architecture.
3. All reports shall be handed to the dean not later than Monday
noon following the examination periods.
November 7, 1905. The Faculty voted that the presence of in-
structors in the School of Engineering and Architecture be requested
at the following Faculty meetings: Second meeting of the first term;
first meeting of the second term; last meeting of the second term.

WORK OF THE DEPARTMENTS.
[The following records cover only such work of the University as gives
occasion, by its novelty or other reasons, for report at this time.]
ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING.
The 5-h.p. two-phase induction motor built by Messrs. Kargau
and Rehm, of the class of 1905, as a thesis project, gave excellent
results under test, and is now permanently installed as a part of the
laboratory equipment.
The laboratory facilities have also been increased during the year
by the addition of two 1/2-h.p. series-wound motors and a direct-
connected motor-generator set of 6-kw. capacity, as well as by thirteen
Weston ammeters and voltmeters of various ranges. A room in the
basement of Cupples Hall No. 2 is being fitted up for the rapid and
convenient calibration of instruments.
The Wagner Electric Mfg. Co. of St. Louis has kindly loaned to
the Department one of its new type alternating-current single-phase
elevator motors. Mr. E. Ballman of the senior class will make a
complete experimental study of the motor as his graduating thesis.
GERMAN.
In October, a German comedy was performed in Cupples Theatre
by students of the Undergraduate Department.
The German Language and Literature section of the University
Library is to be known hereafter as the Emil Preetorius Memorial
Library, in honor of the late distinguished German-American leader.
This department of the library has been greatly enriched during the
past year through the generosity of a number of public-spirited German
citizens. In June, 1905, the surplus of the Schiller Centennial Cele-
bration by the United German Societies of St. Louis, amounting to
nearly $900, was presented to the German Library Fund. At the
same time the Treasurer of the celebration, Mr. Ben. Altheimer, turned
into the University treasury the additional amount of $1250, contributed
by about a dozen friends of the German Library, including himself.
In February, Mr. Edward L. Preetorius donated the sum of $1000 for
the same purpose. The like amount ($1000) has been donated by Mr.
Adolphus Busch, so that the total collection now has, in books and
cash, a value of about $6500. It may now be confidently expected that


## p. 188 (#196) ############################################

188
THE BULLETIN OF
the collection of books for the study of the German language and
literature will in the near future be fully adequate, not only for the
needs of the undergraduates, but also of Germanists in this part of the
country.
Under the auspices of the German Department and for the benefit
of its library, Ludwig Fulda, the celebrated poet-dramatist, gave
readings from his own works in Memorial Hall, on the evening of
March 23d, before a large city audience. After the lecture a recep-
tion was tendered the distinguished guest in the galleries of the
Museum of Fine Arts. A handsome surplus was cleared for the
German Library Fund.
MECHANICAL ENGINEERING.
In the line of original investigations undertaken by this depart-
ment during the current year, that relating to the cost of operating
the University power plant is probably most important.
The details of this work are being carried out by Mr. Vose, In-
structor in Mechanical Engineering, and the investigation, when com-
pleted, will furnish valuable data for determining the cost of heating,
ventilating, and lighting buildings of the type erected on the Uni-
versity grounds.
Other investigations are being made into special features of gas
engine and suction gas-producer operations.
Through the kindness of Mr. Richardson the Department has been
presented with a "Richardson Automatic Sight-Feed Oil Pump" for
installation in the steam engineering laboratory.
THE LIBRARY.
The real library of Washington University may be said to date
from the removal of the Undergraduate Department to the new site
From the inauguration of the University in 1857 until the occupancy
of the new buildings in February, 1905, no attempt was made to
gather a general library. The location on Washington Avenue was
within easy reach of the Mercantile and Public Libraries, and in the
former the University owned a large number of memberships for the
use of students, and the latter was free to all. The financial condition
of the institution did not allow of expenditures for books beyond those
actually needed in the courses of instruction and a few necessary
periodicals.
The Library never received any gifts or donations of value until


## p. 189 (#197) ############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
189
recent years, with the exception of the collection of Mr. Joseph
Coolidge, of Boston, amounting to about 3000 volumes, especially rich
in Italian and French authors. In 1891 the University received a
bequest from the late Stephen Ridgley amounting to $60,000. Under
his will this fund was to be retained until, with accumulated interest,
it was sufficient to erect a fire-proof library building. A part of this
money was used in building the present library building. The building
is absolutely fire-proof and has an ultimate capacity of 500,000 volumes.
It is well equipped with a splendid steel stack of two tiers, capable of
holding 40,000 volumes, and a large handsomely furnished reading
room.
The Library is designed to be, as far as possible, a library for
special study, and no attempt is made to supply popular books of the
day.
For the last few years about $6000 has been spent annually in the
purchase of books under the direction of the heads of the several
departments. The greater number of these are now well supplied
with the most important works on their subjects, including valuable
files of periodicals.
A special appropriation was made to enlarge the reference library,
which is now very completely equipped with all essential works of
reference.
One hundred and ninety-three serial publications are taken by the
Library.
The work of cataloguing the books has been progressing steadily.
With the small force of assistants it is necessarily slow. The decimal
system of classification has been adopted, and an effort is being made
to make the catalogue as complete and valuable as possible, by the use
of many cross references.
The Library is open, not only to members of the University, but
also to other students and investigators who wish to make use of its
collections.
LAW SCHOOL.
The Law Department of the University (St. Louis Law School)
has been removed from 1417 Locust Street to the corner of Twenty-
ninth and Locust Streets. It is now installed in the building formerly
occupied by the St. Louis Club. The new library room is a special
feature, being entirely fire-proof and well lighted. It is eighty-eight


## p. 190 (#198) ############################################

190
THE BULLETIN OF
feet long by thirty-six feet wide, and has shelf capacity on the walls,
without the use of alcoves, for more than twelve thousand volumes.
Five smaller rooms are also used for library purposes, partly for book-
stacks and partly as study rooms. For lectures and recitations there
are four large, well-lighted rooms or halls. Five rooms are set apart
for offices. Four other rooms serve as sitting-rooms and students'
fraternity rooms. The alterations and additions to this building for
the purposes of the school make it one of the best equipped law school
buildings in the United States. The recent act of the Board of
Directors of the University in providing for the appointment of one
more professor who is to devote all his time to the Law School is in
keeping with the general progress of the school.

COMMENCEMENT, 1905.
To those who have watched the gradual growth of Washington
University for many years, Commencement Day of 1905 was an occa-
sion for heartfelt congratulation.
It was one of Missouri's best midsummer days, bright, clear, and
hot, with just sufficient breeze to render reasonably comfortable the
great marquee that had been erected on the campus between Cupples
No. 2 and the Library-Physics wing.
The buildings and grounds had never looked so well, with their
spread of green lawn and newly-made walks. From its staff on the


## p. 192 (#200) ############################################

192
THE BULLETIN OF
southeast turret of the main tower floated the national flag. The other
flag-staff was vacant, waiting for the ceremony that should fling to
the summer breeze, for the first time, the official myrtle and maroon
colors of the University.
This ceremony was the initial item of the long day's program.
Gathered on the broad terrace in front of University Hall were
members of the Board and the Faculties, students, and friends. The
great banner attached to its halyards lay in disordered folds upon the
lawn as Miss Lillie R. Ernst, for the women graduates and under-
graduates, made the presentation. In part, Miss Ernst's address was
as follows:
1
"When the formal inauguration of Washington University as a
teaching body took place on April 23, 1857, in the hall on Seventeenth
Street and Washington Avenue, the patient, devoted little group of
men sanely determined to plan only for the foundations of a great
institution; they must needs leave the completion of the work to those
who were to come. And not one of the men named in the charter or
concerned in the inauguration is here in the flesh to rejoice along with
us who are the beneficiaries of their consecration, over this second step
in the growth of their great idea. But their spirit, their faith, their
ideals, are the real foundations upon which our school has been built;
their high purpose and unflinching sacrifice, their noble sincerity and
the simple unselfishness of their devotion are the vital principles of
our traditions, and are our dominant ideal.
"And now I say that by more than fifty years of growth Washing-
ton University has earned the right to her magnificent housing. She
has earned the right to fly her flag-not as an empty sign, but as her
emblem, full of thrilling meaning to each one of us who are bound
to her by cords that reach the inmost heart-full of inspiration and
promise to all who reach for the highest in man's possibility and God's
greatness.
"Many times in the history of the world's events has it been the
part of the women to prepare the banners that have celebrated the
achievements of heroes, and in this great event we make no exception.
The women now give to the University this flag that shall through all
time stand for disinterested patriotism and consecrated purpose;
reverence for the best that the culture and experience of the past has
offered; strength of intellect and soul; and abiding faith in the power
and greatness of almighty love.
"It is with reverent heart and joyous hope that I loose the folds
to the winds of heaven.


## p. 193 (#201) ############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
193
"Wave over our beloved school in benediction and proclaim to
the wide world her message: PER VERITATEM VIS - through Truth
alone comes Power."
Chancellor Chaplin in accepting the flag tendered the thanks of the
University.
Immediately after this event the various parts of the Commence-
ment procession assembled in the rooms and corridors assigned to
them, whence they marched to form the main body of the procession in
front of the Library. Headed by a brass band the column moved
slowly around the first quadrangle and then over to the big tent. The
order of march was as follows:
Band.
Division I-The Undergraduates.
Division II-Board of Directors, candidates for honorary degrees,
invited guests, Deans, officers of the Alumni Association.
Division III-Professors, Assistant Professors and Instructors in
the Undergraduate Department; Professors and other members of
the teaching staff in the Law School, the Medical Department, and
the Dental College.
Division IV-Candidates for degrees.
Division V-Alumni and Alumnæ.
Among the guests who formed part of the second section were
representatives of many educational institutions of the country. The
following institutions were represented:
Amherst College, Boston University, Butler College, Central
College, Christian Brothers' College, College of the City of New York,
Colorado College, Colorado School of Mines, Columbia University,
Cornell University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Missouri
Valley College, Northwestern University, Oberlin College, Ottawa
University, St. Louis University, Shurtleff College, State University
of Iowa, Swarthmore College, University of Missouri, University of
Vermont, Western Reserve University, Westminster College, Yale

The seating capacity of the tent, about 3000, was hardly sufficient
for the great audience that had gathered to witness the conferring of
degrees and the inauguration of the new buildings.
The proceedings, which were very simple but impressive, were
begun with a prayer by the Rev. S. J. Niccolls, D.D. The addresses

For lack of space extracts only of such addresses as have been

MR. BROOKINGS: "I have been told to limit my remarks to five
minutes, and I think the time is all-sufficient for what is left to be said
about the University after the Chancellor and Governor Francis have
each devoted more than half an hour to that subject. First I wish to
say that I am deeply sensible of the sentiments so beautifully ex-
pressed by Miss Ernst in her flag-presentation address this morning.
There is not an alumnus of the University who has more reverence for
its past than have I and the other members of the Board of Directors.
It was this honorable past which attracted the recent support that makes
its future so promising. While our limited facilities and means have
confined our service to the city and the demands upon that service in
numbers have not been large, the instruction required has covered liberal
courses in both arts and engineering, and that the work done was
earnest and effective is evidenced by the standing of our alumni, sev-
eral of whom it has been our privilege and pleasure to honor today.
The Chancellor has explained to you something of the details of our
development during the past seven or eight years. We have during
this time increased our property account (plant and endowment) to
an aggregate of more than $7,500,000. We feel that the strength of
our teaching staff, the scope of instruction offered in the different
departments, our buildings, equipment, and residential attractions,
coupled with an adequate endowment for their proper care, all entitle
us to rank among the universities of the first class.
"While our numbers in the past have not been large, the student
body in the Undergraduate Department has nearly doubled within the
last four years, and as our city high school system has shown the
phenomenal development of more than doubling its numbers within
the same period of time (this growth being largely in the lower classes
and hence not as yet felt to any extent by the University), I am con-
vinced that from this source alone we may expect a large increase in
our numbers of undergraduates in the near future. Yet both our city
and its high school system are still in their infancy. We have not only
the facilities to take care of this city increase, however large it may
be, but are prepared to take our position as the university of the
metropolis, for just as surely as the city of St. Louis is the undisputed
metropolis of the great Southwest, just so surely is Washington
University, in my humble judgment, destined to be the seat of learn-
ing for that vast section of the country. Not that the state universities


## p. 196 (#204) ############################################

196
THE BULLETIN OF
and other local institutions will render any less service in the future
than in the past, but we shall supplement their work by a service which
only the city university can supply. The impossibility of developing
the professional schools of medicine and law to their maximum oppor-
tunities in any other environment than that of a large city is too well
understood for discussion, while it is equally unquestioned that the
city is practically one great laboratory for a school of engineering
and architecture; and in the judgment of many educators the mental
activities and opportunities for culture in the city are equally important
for the development of the best college or academic work. I had
hoped that President Butler, of Columbia University, would have been
with us today and given us a talk, such as only he can give, on the
subject of a city university. As the commencement exercises of
Columbia, however, were held yesterday, it was impossible for him
to be with us. In one of his recent addresses he said: 'It is my earnest
conviction that the great universities of this country will, like those on
the continent, find their future homes in the large cities. The city does
not consist merely of population or of large buildings or of wealth,
but of the opportunities for culture and refinement which all of these
draw to themselves.' He quoted Cardinal Newman's saying that every
city is in itself a natural university. He argued that a scholar, filled
with the impulse of service and eager to secure all the information his
fellows could contribute, would certainly seek his training in the city,
and concluded with the poet's evidence by quoting Longfellow's lines :
'Where shall the scholar live-
In solitude or in society,
In the green silence of the country,
Where he can hear the heart of Nature beat,
Or in the dark gray city,
Where he feels and hears the throbbing heart of man?
I make answer for him and say:
In the dark gray city.'
"I believe that Washington University is destined to be one of
the great city universities, and will conclude by urging that we, the
Faculty, the Alumni, the Board of Directors, and the citizens of St.
Louis generally-that we, here on this dedication day, earnestly dedicate
ourselves to the fulfillment of the work which has only just begun.
MR. RUTLEDGE: "This is a happy day for us. It is true that a
brand new set of traditions will have to be built up around this new
campus, and that the old traditions, so dear to us who grew up on the
old campus, in the tunnel, in the cellar, in the splendid halls and stair-
cases, and particularly in the attic and on the roof, when the art

students used to inhabit these regions, will soon be mere memories that
will never again be lived over by new freshmen, and only by us in our

"It is a great thing to have our dreams come true. And even

freshmen and succeeding classes of freshmen got to dreaming the

Go on, Mr. President and Directors, and dream some more dreams.

great dreamer of dreams of old.

"As our first class graduated only forty-three years ago we are

than the present holders of that title.
"So I now take great pleasure in introducing Mr. William R.

East; we have our Francis, our Flad, Krum, Crunden, Holman, Burnett,
and Wixford here. To the modest and retiring Wixford the city of St.
Louis should erect a statue of crystal to typify the bright water which
he has evolved from the turbid stream that flows by us, as though
with the alembics of the old alchemists.
"With all this, it strikes us old fellows that the sense of propor-
tion between the mental and the physical standards is being lost. It
would seem almost that the modern college exists for the education of
the muscle and not the brain. That gladiators and not scholars are
most to be desired. We all crave popular recognition. It is a common
failing of humanity. It is a poor recompense for the diligent, thought-
ful student, at the end of a laborious course, who has graduated
maxima cum laude, if you please, to be postponed in popular esti-
mation to some big-thewed and sinewy sprinter, or half-back, or
hammer thrower, whose future career consists in that of pitcher on
the nine of the Bumtown league. In medio tutissimus ibis. Let the
dust of the arena and the smell of the musty tomes mingle in at least
equal proportions. Let the college be known by its brain product;
not by its brawn and muscle.
"Let me not ignore the gentler part of the university graduates,
these young women who, laying aside the attractions of society, qualify
themselves for higher things in taking a university education. The
retentive memory and inexhaustible application of the woman make
the sterner sex 'sit up' and look to its laurels in the class room. The
world has better women, better mothers, and better children for their
self-denial.
"We stand 'at gaze' in the presence of these university dignitaries
and representatives who today honor us with their presence. We are
their rivals in a sense, but we all work to a common end in the gen-
erous rivalry for the uplifting of the standard of the true, the beautiful,
and the good.
"I know that in the struggle for enlightenment against ignorance
and prejudice Washington University will stand in the forefront of the
battle.
"Ein Hoch der Washington-Universität!"

MISS ERNST: "Unlike the gentlemen who have preceded me, I
have my paper in my hand. It is not under my napkin-nor is it in my
pocket with everything on it transferred into my head for extempor-
aneous use. I hold it and mean to use it. I have just a few things to
say, but do not want to leave any of them out, and, being a woman,
of course I want to be brief. No, I refuse to acknowledge the intent
of your demonstrations, for you know as well as I do that it is the
men's tongues that are like disordered clocks that keep right on strik-
ing, not to tell us the time o' day, but just because there is something
wrong in their insides. But to my points.
"To begin with I want to register a protest against a phrase.
Several times in the last year have I heard the phrase 'the new Wash-
ington University.' This is not a new university-it is our good old
school set in a new physical environment; that is all. Let them add all
the development possible, add all the modern methods, customs and
embellishments, but hold fast to what the school has stood for from
the first simplicity of life, steady, honest work, and democracy of
spirit, the cult of the fair and square. If they have these in this
gorgeous new home, we have our old University here; if they have
them not, I, for one, shall be quite willing to give this new school a
new name.
"But I am sure that the future is quite safe. So I shall confine
myself to acknowledging to a few large debts for the Alumni and
very especially for my own account.
"First, I am grateful that Washington University opened her doors
to women as early as she did, and I can wish to the women in the co-
educational institutions of the future no better opportunities than
Washington University offered us; equal rights with the men, equal
chances, and equal encouragement. When I think back to my own
experience and recall the cordial good-fellowship that existed between
the men and women of my time, the mutual appreciation and non-
interference, and the individual independence that I saw develop under
those conditions, I am strengthened in my hope that co-education may
continue at Washington University, undisturbed by even the cry of the
weakling: 'Deliver us, O ye who rule, from the threatening seminary!'
As the number of the alumnæ increases, and I welcome today's addi-
tion, I have great faith that we shall be able to repay in part the debt
that we are so glad to owe.
"Second point. Now that we are well past the dawn of the day
of the specialist, and the chairs are filled with specialists in this and
that and the other line, and well filled, too, for we all believe in this

modern development, -I do want to speak most reverently and appre-
ciatingly for the all-round kind of scholar that used to fill our chairs.

THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION.
During the past year the Alumni Association has devoted much
attention to increasing the interest in the University among the Alumni
and prospective students. The June reception was made more elaborate
than usual, and the attendance of non-resident alumni was unusually
large.
To attract the attention of students in the Southwest to Wash-
ington University, the Alumni Association offered one cash prize of
$200 and one of $100 to those young men resident in Texas passing
the best entrance examination to the College or the School of Engineer-
ing and Architecture. The first prize was awarded to Mr. King Townes
Coffey, of Sulphur Springs, Texas. The plan was deemed so successful
that at the annual meeting in January it was voted to make it a per-
manent policy of the Association, and to offer the same prizes for the
year 1906, under the same conditions.
It was also decided that a special effort be made to induce the
students in the secondary schools to visit the University, and the
President was instructed to name a special committee to make arrange-
ments for such visits.
The President was also instructed to name a committee of three
to consider the matter of a University hymn, and to offer a prize of
$25 to the author of an acceptable composition.
The following officers were elected: Grant Beebe, '88, President;
Richard McCulloch, '91, Vice-President; Thomas G. Rutledge, '92,
Director; Everett Paul Griffin, 'or, Secretary; Chas. P. Pettus, '99,
Corresponding Secretary; A. L. Langsdorf, '98, Treasurer.
THE ANNUAL BANQUET OF THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION.
The annual banquet of the Alumni Association was held Saturday,
February 24th, at the Planters' Hotel. About seventy alumni were
present, and a telegram was received from the alumni holding their
annual dinner in New York City.
The guests of honor were Professor Francis E. Nipher and
Mr. Robert S. Brookings, President of the Board of Directors, who
were greeted most cordially by all present. The following is the
program of toasts:

The President, Mr. Beebe, gave the opening address, as follows:
"A year ago tonight we congratulated ourselves that Washington
University had at last come into her own, and that the removal to
the new buildings had taken place. Tonight I think we have equal
cause for congratulation in the fact that the first year under the new
conditions has been an unqualified success. Not only has the Fresh-
man class been the largest in the history of the institution, but the
Law School has been moved into better and more commodious quarters,
important additions have been made to the Engineering and other
laboratories, and the two secondary schools of the University that had
been left in the heart of the city, Smith Academy and the Manual
Training School, have been moved to new buildings that are not
surpassed anywhere.
"During the year the Alumni Association has devoted itself to an
endeavor to let some people know that there is such a place as Wash-
ington University. These people live in Texas, but I want to say that
there are people in St. Louis today who do not realize that they have
a first-class institution, the equal of any in the West, at their very
doors. These people must be enlightened. The University is a good
thing and we want to let in all our friends. The officers of the Asso-
ciation are anxious that the Alumni themselves shall visit the University
and see it under working conditions, that they may be able to describe
its merits from actual observation.
"When I was ready for college I was free to go anywhere. I
chose Washington University and I have never regretted my choice.
I believe that a Western man should go to a Western school if he
would be in sympathy with the West. Wise men from time im-
memorial come out of the East, but I believe that the West has a
breadth of thought and an openness of mind that are not found else-
where. For these reasons I have no hesitation in urging a young
man to attend Washington University, and I think every member of
this Association should do likewise. Let us all work together to
increase the influence of the University in this community.


## p. 204 (#212) ############################################

"We have lately heard of the simple life, the strenuous life,
and various other kinds of lives. I urge you to live the altruistic life
in university matters. It is a life that knows no failures, for he that
expects nothing will never be disappointed. Disinterested effort is
needed if the University is to attain the place it deserves to occupy.
When the day comes that only those take an interest in university
affairs who expect directly or indirectly to get something out of it,
that day the end will be in sight, and even the millions of a Rocke-
feller will not save the university from oblivion.
"I hold that a great university should offer to every man accord-
ing to his needs, and should take from every man according to his
ability. It is a mutual affair and both parties are equally interested.
I believe that every great institution succeeds or fails as this principle
of mutual obligation is lived up to or not. I think that the Alumni
have been loyal to the University in the past, and I trust there will be
no decrease of that quality as the years go by. The future students
will come to the University either because they are attracted by the
reputation of the institution and its professors, or because they are
led to select the University by the Alumni. It is, therefore, necessary
that the work of the University shall be kept up to the highest standard
by teachers and students, in order that it may be conscientiously
endorsed by the Alumni and the public. For, after all, the great
essential in any human enterprise is men, and this is particularly
true in a school where men are to be trained for life, and where example
is so much more powerful than precept.
"If those who give instruction are men of breadth of thought, of
depth of intellect and independence of action, the graduates of the
institution will have those qualities, which are the most needed in
our strenuous American life.
"The University has been fortunate in having among its pro-
fessors such men as I speak of. Every day that I live I am glad
that I came under their influence and had the benefit of their instruc-
tion. We have one with us tonight. He needs no introduction; he is
known at home and abroad; he has ever maintained that high standard
of scholarship that has made the reputation of the University; he has
taken a kindly interest in every student that ever came into his classes;
he is that always welcome individual, a gentleman and a scholar,
Professor F. E. Nipher."

The next event of the evening was the speech by the President of
the Board of Directors, who responded to the toast, "The Future."
Mr. Brookings said:
"In responding to your toast, 'The Future,' I must incidentally
touch, in a general way, upon university work in the West and South-
west, as our future is closely connected with those sections of the
country.
"Aside from my official, and your family, connections, our in-
terests, as citizens of St. Louis, are primarily centered in Washington
University. We are next, as citizens of Missouri, proud of the great
success of our State University, and finally, we rejoice in the strides
made by higher education generally throughout the West and South.
This development has affected alike the State Universities, located
as a rule in some small central town, and private institutions, like the
Northwestern University, the University of Chicago, and Washington
University.
"While the city and state universities necessarily compete to some
extent, their natural trend will, I believe, lead into distinct fields of
usefulness. Assuming that both will offer liberal courses in the arts
and those subjects forming a basis for what is commonly called a
liberal education, the strongest trend of state work would seem to
be in the direction of agriculture, forestry, and their kindred branches,
while that of the city university will naturally be along the lines which
will utilize the city's educational facilities; i.e., engineering, architecture,
medicine, and law.
"The potential strength of the city university, its influence upon
the city and the city's influence upon it, is rapidly developing the same
educational conditions in this country that prevail on the European con-
tinent. The city university confers its greatest boon upon the largest
number at the least expense. It is safe to say that many of the students
of Washington University would never have enjoyed the benefits of
higher education had they been compelled to leave the city. The ability
to live at home, at little or no cost, with the city opportunities for finan-
cial self-help during the years of study, coupled with the preparatory
advantages of the best system of public schools, make it impossible to
conceive of any large city without its university.
"Many of the richest in mental development are the poorest in
pocket, and it would be a distinct loss to the state were they deprived
of the opportunity to develop. It is this class of students, free from
the distractions of wealth and under the pressure of financial neces-
sity, who become the most useful citizens. One third of the entire

undergraduate body of Washington University receive, through

"As the city grows and the university grows, the city university

In answering to the toast, "The University in the Community,"
Mr. R. E. Cave, '99, made the following response:
"The one and only true aim and end of a university, which alone
can justify its existence as a university, is the uplifting and develop-
ing of man by a complete and generous education, which, as Milton
says, 'fits him to perform justly, skillfully, and magnanimously all the
offices, both private and public, of peace and war.' And this de-
velopment, to be full and complete, must be two-fold: It must tend
to the perfection of man, not only as a means or instrument of utility,
but to the perfection also of man as an end unto himself. The con-
ditions of society demand that an individual must be useful, must
have the means of living, and these means he must procure; he must
reduce himself to an instrument an instrument of utility to others,
and to that end he must master some trade, calling or profession.
That is the call of the community. And in answer to this utilitarian
demand of society, the university, if it wishes well and truly to play its
part in the community, must develop men as such means. It must
make of them creatures of invention, origination, and production. It
must foster and conserve, cultivate and refine in man those powers
and faculties which tend to such usefulness, and must raise them
to the highest possible degree of productivity and attainment. It
must mold man into the highest possible form of productive mechanism,


## p. 208 (#216) ############################################

208
THE BULLETIN OF
and to do this, and thus fully answer the call of this utilitarian demand,
it must not only provide opportunities for the many seeking that form
of education productive of quick returns, but must also provide oppor-
tunities for the few searching for deeper knowledge. The opportunities
for seeking knowledge afforded by the university can not be too large
or too far-reaching.
"It is true that in an age such as this, when the spirit of com-
mercialism is abroad in the land and when most men seeking to carve
out their own fortunes devote themselves early to the practical affairs
of life, few can pursue their studies up to, still less beyond, the age of
manhood. But these few should be the object of the especial care of
the. university and every opportunity should be afforded them. As
Professor Huxley well and wisely says, 'it is of vital importance to the
welfare of the community that those who are relieved from the need
of making a livelihood, and still more, those who are stirred by the
divine impulse of intellectual thirst or artistic genius, should be enabled
to devote themselves to the higher service of their kind, as centers of
intelligence, interpreters of Nature, or creators of new forms of
beauty.' The accomplishments of men such as these, who seek know-
ledge neither for financial profit nor in search of the bubble reputation,
but out of the pure and unadulterated love of knowledge itself, while
less quick of result than the accomplishments of others, are yet, even
for the purposes of usefulness, far greater and much farther reaching.
And the university, if it wishes to fully and truly answer even the
utilitarian call of the community, must lend unto these men also every
aid and opportunity in working out their great ends.
"Be useful to me or away with you! So says the community to
the university. And what has been the reply of our dear Alma Mater?
Right well and nobly, as you all know, has she responded. She
has sent forth her lawyers, to be chosen by the people to enact the
laws, others to sit as judges in the enforcement of the law, and yet
still others as most able and eminent advocates of the law. She has
produced her doctors, to lay the healing hand of science upon the
heated brow and alleviate and assuage the pain and suffering of the
sick and miserable. She has sent forth her merchants and her brokers,
who have put their shoulders to the wheel of progress and bent every
nerve and energy to the uplifting and upbuilding and advancement and
growth of this grand old city and to the spreading of her name afar.
She has furnished the foremost engineers, mechanical, electrical, and
civil. From her halls have come men who have given their lives to
the search for knowledge for the love of knowledge. She has provided


## p. 209 (#217) ############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
209
chemists who by leaps and bounds have hastened the progress of
their science and discovered means of purifying and clarifying the
water supply of their native city. And when the occasion called she
was able to furnish the material for the Presidency of the World's
greatest International Exposition. Thus she has answered the call
of the community. And well and truly have all these men played their
respective parts in life. And just in so far as they have been instru-
ments of usefulness in the community, just in so far as they have
fulfilled the true end and purpose of their lives, just in so far has
our dear old Alma Mater fulfilled its mission in the development of
man as an instrument of usefulness or productiveness in the com-
munity, just in so far has she aided in the steady gain of man.
"Such has been the work of this University and she should receive
the full measure of the credit therefor; yet, before passing from this
subject, I would call attention to the fact that the university, under the
existing conditions, has not received, and does not, and will not,
receive that credit. Our University has educated and sent forth into
the community lawyers who have risen to such eminent heights that
they might well cast back the reflex of their glory upon their Alma
Mater, and doctors who have scaled the walls of prominence and become
standards of authority in their profession. But what credit or benefit
has the University as a whole received therefrom? Practically none.
We hear that this man graduated from the St. Louis Law School or
that man graduated from the St. Louis Medical College. But who
knows that he is a graduate of Washington University? There is
not the proper closeness of affiliation between the respective depart-
ments of our University. The accomplishments of each and every
department should redound to the credit of all. And that they do not
is to a certain extent the fault of this Association. If a man is not
eligible to membership in the Alumni Association of a university,
if he is an outcast therefrom, you can hardly expect that man to
attempt to reflect any credit for his success upon that university. There
was a time when even the mechanical, electrical, and civil engineers,
graduates of Washington University, were not eligible to membership
in this Association, and the doctors and lawyers are still outcasts.
That is something which should be remedied. There should be an
Alumni Association of Washington University which should be in-
clusive of all graduates of all departments. And until that, somehow
in some way, is brought about, the University, as a whole, will continue
to lose a certain portion of the benefit and credit which is clearly her
meet and due.

THE BULLETIN OF
"As I have already intimated, in addition to this development of
man as an instrument or means, the university should strive to ac-
complish its higher and nobler purpose in the development of man as
an end unto himself. That is, the university should strive to aid man
in the cultivation of himself, for it is only in the accomplishment of his
own perfection that man, as a creature, can truly manifest the glory of
his Creator. His own perfection constitutes the goal of activity to
which he tends and ought to tend. And it should be the sphere of the
university to enable him to make everything subordinate to that full
and harmonious development of his individual faculties which alone
can raise him to the full measure of the true stature of manhood, with
powers of introspection and self-knowledge, in which his full per-
fection and his true happiness consist. That should be the ultimate aim
and object of all education, cultivation, and refinement of man. It is
productive of little that may be measured in the form of immediate or
patent effects, but its action upon the future generations of the com-
munity and nation will be widespread, and that effect upon the future
generations must ever be kept in mind. For as the eye of prophecy
looks down the avenue of the future it may behold pages of wondrous
glory unfolding for this community and nation. But there is a con-
dition which underlies and is absolutely essential to it all-and that
condition is the intellectual clearness and moral worth of the individual
citizen. And this condition can only be fulfilled by the aid and activity
of the universities. They always have been and ought to be the true
fortress of the higher life of the nation."

UNIVERSITY NECROLOGY.
ELISHA HALL GREGORY.
Elisha Hall Gregory, M.D., for over fifty years Professor of
Surgery and Anatomy in the St. Louis Medical College, one of the
two schools now merged in the Medical Department of Washington
University, died on February 11, 1906, in his eighty-second year.
Dr. Gregory came to St. Louis in 1848 and, beginning the practice of
medicine in the following year, was engaged in that profession till
his death.
During his lifetime he was honored with many public trusts. He
served as a member of the Board of Health of St. Louis; as President
of the State Board of Health; as President of the State Medical Asso-
ciation of Missouri; and twice as President of the St. Louis Medical
Society. In 1886 he was elected President of the American Medical
Association. At the time of his death he was President of the St. Louis
Surgical Society, and Chairman of the Board of Overseers of the
Medical Department of Washington University. Dr. Gregory had been
in St. Louis but a short time when he connected himself with the St.
Louis Mullanphy Hospital. Until a few years ago he was surgeon-
in-chief at that institution, and at the time of his death was still so
regarded, although he had given up active work in that capacity.
In the death of Dr. Gregory the University loses an efficient and
devoted member and one who commanded not only local but national
respect among the profession. It is a consolation to his surviving co-
workers to know that appreciation and reward came to this faithful
servant of the community in his own lifetime to encourage and crown
his labors.
GEORGE W. TAUSSIG.
Mr. George W. Taussig, the youngest member of the class of
1870, died at his home in Kirkwood on November 28, 1905. Mr.
Taussig was distinctly a product of Washington University. He was
graduated from what is now called Smith Academy in 1866; received
his bachelor's degree from the University in 1870; and was awarded
the degree LL.B. by the Law School of the University in 1872, thus
pursuing his studies at one institution uninterruptedly for nine years.
He continued the studious habits of his youth through life. He
had a remarkable facility in languages, speaking several modern


## p. 212 (#220) ############################################

212
THE BULLETIN OF
tongues with fluency, also keeping up and increasing the collegian's
familiarity with Latin and Greek. His wide and varied reading did
not culminate in mere formal acquisition. His alert mind, in which a
well regulated artistic temperament was noticeable, appropriated what-
ever was noble and beautiful, and made it part of his own being.
Not only literature, but music and painting as well, found in
him an ardent student. In all these pursuits he was eminent in our
community for his knowledge and taste. For many years he was
actively engaged in the Choral Symphony Society; he was the leader
of a literary society that made a careful study of Browning; and his
friends knew that his acquaintance with the Bible went beyond that
of most laymen.
He was active as a lawyer at St. Louis until two years before his
death. For the last two years of his life he was an invalid.
JULIUS BAIER.
On May 8, 1905, occurred the death of Mr. Julius Baier (C.E.,
'85), an alumnus whose work has brought honor to himself and to
the University. Mr. Baier will be remembered, not only for his
thoroughness in his own profession, but for his remarkable versatility.
In addition to his work upon several of the large buildings in St. Louis
(notably the Coliseum and the Century Theatre) he devoted himself
to other pursuits-mastering and demonstrating his ability in the prac-
tical details of mining, mechanical, and electrical engineering; inter-
esting himself actively in the organization of the library of the
Engineers' Club of St. Louis; investigating the matter of wind-pressures
and preparing a paper upon that subject for which he was awarded
the Norman Gold Medal in 1897; concerning himself actively in the
affairs of the Alumni Association of the University, and in other ways
showing an exceptional breadth of interest. Mr. Baier was one of the
Alumni selected by the University to receive an honorary degree at
the Commencement Exercises in June, 1905, a distinction which the
University was prevented from awarding by his untimely death.
EDWIN HARRISON.
In the death of Mr. Edwin Harrison, who passed away on May 13,
1905, the University was deprived of one of its best friends and loyal
supporters. Mr. Harrison's interest in the University was directed
specifically toward the development of the Manual Training School;


## p. 213 (#221) ############################################

THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
213
and although he was for years a member of the Board of Directors
of the University, it is as an enthusiastic donor to the Department of
Manual Training and as the chairman of its managing board that he is
best remembered.
It was in 1878 that Mr. Harrison first interested himself in that
work by contributing thirteen hundred dollars to make possible the
purchase of new appliances and to meet the current expenses for that
year. In the following year Mr. Harrison agreed to put up a suitable
building for the department, and the structure was erected at his
expense. At the same time, the managing board was organized and
Mr. Harrison became its first chairman, a position which he held until
his death.
From the date of his appointment, June 17, 1879, until the day
of his death, a period of almost twenty-six years, he was an ardent
believer in the school which he had helped to found, and was ever
ready in his quiet, modest way to bestow upon it not only his bene-
factions but his own personal attention.
CHARLES PARSONS.
Mr. Charles Parsons, a member of the Board of Directors, died at
Wequetonsing, Michigan, September 15, 1906, in his eighty-second
year. He left his collection of works of art to the University, with
the sum of $75,000 for their care and for purchase of pictures. By
Mr. Parsons's will it is provided that the collection may be retained,
during his lifetime, by his nephew, Mr. Charles Parsons Pettus, the
Librarian of the University, who is made residuary legatee of the
estate. Mr. Parsons's connection with the Board of Directors of the
University was of brief duration, less than three years and a half, his
election dating from April 4, 1902. But he had long served faithfully
on the Board of the School and Museum of Fine Arts, and had shown
in many ways a care for the interests of art and art education in
St. Louis.

The Association
THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION is an organ-
ization of officers, graduates, and friends of Washington
University devoted to the furtherance of the University's work
and the extension of its usefulness and influence throughout
the community. Its principal activity is the maintenance of a
series of public lectures and lecture courses; to these lectures
members of the Association are admitted free. Eligible to
membership are all officers, graduates, and former students
of any department of the University, and other persons
who may be nominated by the Executive Council of the
Association. The annual membership fee is three dollars.
THE BULLETIN of the Washington University Association
is designed to provide a medium for the publication of a
selection of lectures from the Association's courses and for
the occasional publication of other papers of a special local
or educational interest; to record the corporate interests of
the University and its scholarly activities; and to serve as an
organ for the interests of the Alumni. The Association is
hot responsible for opinions expressed by lecturers and con-
tributors. THE BULLETIN is, for the present, published
annually, on the University anniversary. Each member of
the Association is entitled to receive one copy; others may
obtain copies at fifty cents, postpaid, by addressing the Secre-
tary of The Washington University Association, St. Louis, Mo.

The Bulletin of the
