NUMBER FIVE
APRIL 23, 1907
EDITORIAL
The anniversary-keeping habit shows signs of becoming a
fixed trait of the American character. It is a poor date on the
calendar that had not some eminent person-
age born, or some more or less interesting
transaction achieved upon it, at a period ante-
cedent to any given year by one or another
of those distances of time to which our deci-
The
Commemorative
Habit.
mal number-system leads the modern imagination to attach a
species of mystical import-a lustrum, a decade, a century, or
some fraction or multiple thereof. And since none of these
occasions is permitted to pass unhonored and unsung, we seem
to be almost perpetually in the act of 'keeping' something. The
custom, even though it grows a trifle hackneyed, has manifest
advantages. It notably simplifies the labors of magazine edi-
tors, since a mere consultation of the almanac now suffices to
determine to what topics a large part of any particular issue
shall be devoted. It lends even to ancient history a vicarious
contemporaneousness and a plausible appearance of 'news
value,' and thus lures to the reading of historical, critical
and reminiscential matter many of a newspaper-reading
generation who would never condescend to such outworn themes
were they in a less journalistic disguise. And, for its best com-
mendation, the fashion doubtless does something to foster a
desirable piety, a sense of the continuity of things, and a whole-
some gratitude to that past without whose labors and loyalties
we heirs of the ages should have a sorry enough patrimony.


## p. 6 (#232) ##############################################

6
THE BULLETIN OF THE
Perhaps the only just objections that can be made to the prac-
tice of commemoration are that, if too frequently resorted to,
it leads to a certain overstraining both of the retrospective gaze
and of the prophetic vision; and that an excess of it may, in
time, even involve us in an embarrassment like that of Sterne's
hero, who, resolved to devote his declining years to setting down
a faithful narrative of his earlier life, found that each past day's
history took two days in the recording.
Since Washington University has two birthdays within as
many months-the anniversaries of the granting of its charter
and of the beginning of its actual life as an
The University's institution-and since the events connected
Semi-Centenary. with those days took place only four years
apart-there may, perhaps, seem to be a spe-
cial temptation here to an over-development of the commemora-
tive habit. The semi-centenary of the earlier of these occasions
was duly observed by the University in 1903, as recorded in
the BULLETIN of that year, and again, in a belated manner, in
1905. But it may be permitted us to observe that the true day
we celebrate is the day marked by the appearance of the present
issue of this annual-that Washington University's real semi-
centennial anniversary comes at the end, not of fifty years of
existence as a legal entity, but fifty years of continuous service
to the community. In spite of previous celebrations, therefore,
it is fitting to invite to the mood and the reflections appropriate
to such an anniversary those who have not hitherto given way
to them-and, with the Latin poet, to invite those who have, to
do so now the more. For, if we are to keep anniversaries, here
is one that we, at least, cannot help regarding seriously, one
that, however unmarked by the larger world, brings with it
fruitful matter for consideration among neighbors. The occa-
sion is not only naturally dear to the graduates and members
of the University; it should be of significance to the entire edu-
cated part of the community to the satisfaction of whose higher
needs the University was perpetually dedicated, on the April
day in 1857 when the best citizens of the town, with the famous


## p. 7 (#233) ##############################################

WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
7
orator from Massachusetts, met to announce becomingly to the
West the birth of what the not infelicitous fashion of the time
called a new seminary of learning.
Anniversaries can, perhaps, not be better utilized than by
taking advantage of them to revitalize an earlier inspiration,
and to recapture the enthusiasm that attached
to an ideal when it was new and unfamiliar.
And for this purpose it is worth while to remind
ourselves how relatively novel and original a
Washington
University's
Originality.
thing in its day was the institution which the
founders of Washington University brought into being. That
group of high-minded and public-spirited men of affairs, in-
spired largely by the ideals and personality of one man of rare
powers of moral leadership and educational statesmanship.
formed the conception of a university to be distinguished by
three characteristics: (1) it should be independent both of
church and state, and forever removed from any danger of sub-
servience to either sect or party; (2) it should be definitely
and irrevocably dedicated to complete liberty of thought and
teaching; (3) it should not be hidden away in some inaccessi-
ble abode of supposed rural innocence, but should be situated
in, and closely in touch with the life of, a great city. Any of
these characteristics was assuredly a rather bold rarity in
1857.
Taken together they give to Washington University
much of the distinction of an educational pioneer. Other insti-
tutions in other places have since adopted one or another
of these characteristics, though there are even yet but few
thoroughly and unequivocally committed to all three. But
Washington University is identified with them by an older
bond than almost any other; and they are, and must remain,
of the very essence of its traditions and its ideals. The
University claims the support of all those who believe that it is
upon these principles that a university (or at the least, a pre-
eminent and indispensable type of university) can best be based,
and those who at any time are temporarily charged with the
management of the University's policies and affairs have it pri-


## p. 8 (#234) ##############################################

8
THE BULLETIN OF THE
marily as their task to give the fullest possible expression, in
each generation, to all that is implied by these characteristics.
And behind these specific features that distinguished Wash-
ington University at its beginning, lay, plainly enough, a spirit
-more general and less easily definable of educational origin-
ality, of aggressiveness, of individuality. This university was,
as Dr. Eliot early intimated, not there merely to offer routine
instruction to such random youth as might seek, or be sent to,
its halls; it was to "educate the leaders," it was to insist upon
quality and distinction first of all, and it was itself to be a
leader in shaping the mind and influencing the direction of
educational development in all this Middle Western country.
"Such an institution," said Dr. Eliot, when he appealed in New
England for support for the still very young and small college,
"may be to the whole Mississippi Valley what Harvard is to
New England." And like expectations were widely enter-
tained, both East and West. It was in such a temper, with
such principles and such hopes, that the University began its
work.
It is profitable, then, to improve the occasion by reminding
ourselves of these ideals and hopes and by honestly inquiring
Past
and Present.
how far in the present circumstances of the
University they are realized. In its half-cen-
tury the University has had its periods both of
maximum and minimum vitality, times when its
original afflatus inspired it with full or with diminished force.
And since the University is, in the last analysis, a charge upon
the community, these vicissitudes have been due as often to ex-
ternal as to internal causes-to an increase or a decrease in pub-
lic spirit, in the higher civic pride, in the vividness with which
the leaders of the life of the city and the surrounding country
have realized that a society does not live by business alone. Upon
the whole-high as have been the University's standards, great
as has been its usefulness, and encouraging as have been the
developments of the last few years-it must be said that the
University is still far from a full realization of its early promise
or a full expression under contemporary conditions of the whole


## p. 9 (#235) ##############################################

WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
9
import of its early ideals. It has not yet come to be "to the
whole Mississippi Valley what Harvard is to New England,"
either in magnitude (which is the thing of least consequence)
or in influence or in educational leadership-though its relation
to the metropolitan city of the Valley, and its age, as well as its
independent character and its central position, might not unrea-
sonably make that seem its natural destiny. It is still capable
of a greater infusion of that spirit of originality and distinctive
individuality that marked its origins. And it has not yet so
strongly touched the intellectual and moral life, so informed the
mind and transformed the current standards of success, in the
great commercial city at its doors, as it must be no small part
of its eventual function to do. In many ways, the University
does not mean so much to the city, nor the city to the University,
as a not unduly sanguine prophet would have been likely to
predict fifty years ago. The two still need to be brought into
closer relations. The support of the work of the University
should rest upon a broader base of general interest and sym-
pathy, and should be less dependent upon the special enthusiasm
and the liberality of a relatively small number. To rest satisfied
with the present hold that the University has upon the popular
regard, or with its material endowment, or with the intensity
of the intellectual vitality within it, or the range of its intellec-
tual influence without, or with the present total of its public
usefulness, would be to confess that the present generation of
this community has more meagre ideas upon such matters, and
a less whole-hearted devotion to the fulfillment of the Univer-
sity's ideals and of its normal destiny, than had the generation
that first conceived and established it.
Meanwhile, in the history of this half-century of useful work
and in recent progress, there is abundant occasion for retro-
spective pride and for the sense of achievement.
But the principal fruit of our anniversary-keep-
ing may well be to stimulate a more just appre-
hension of the needs of the present and of the possibilities re-
maining unfulfilled, and to revivify, in all who are in any degree
Future.


## p. 10 (#236) #############################################

10
BULLETIN OF THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY ASSOCIATION
now responsible for the well-being of the University, the zeal,
the courage, and the breadth of view of the founders. If this
result follows, so much of indulgence in the commemorative
impulse may yield not only a renewed appreciation of the Uni-
versity's past, but also a pledge that its future will not be
unworthy of its beginning.


## p. 11 (#237) #############################################

ENGLISH SPELLING *
HENRY CAPLES PENN
Professor of English in Washington University
The question of reform or simplification of English spelling
has interested many people of late. To the present writer it
has appealed in a very practical way. For several months a
little girl, seven years old, has been bringing home from school
lists of six to ten words that she must learn to spell; and the
daily drill is an exercise so full of seemingly unnecessary
torture, that it is often hard to refrain from interposing. To
insist that a child shall simply commit to memory form after
form in which there is neither rhyme nor reason, in which rule
is defied and analogy disregarded, where there is no "therefore"
to satisfy the natural "why" of the child's mind, seems for the
moment and afterward-little less than criminal. The pro-
cess in the case of many words is not educative; it is a mere
puzzle, utterly irrational, without even suggestion of system or
meaning. It does not discipline but taxes the memory, does
not strengthen but burdens it. As for the power of reasoning,
it seems at times as if that could not fail to be perplexed to un-
certainty, wearied to stupidity, even reduced to impotence.
It is probable that only a few even of those that have shown
interest in the question have realized the inconsistencies, from
the learner's point of view, of English spelling. The attitude
of most of those opposing the movement is possible, I suspect,
because the matter has not been brought home to them; it would
affect them differently if they had now to pass through the
agony. It is hard for the question to get a hearing.
* Lecture delivered before the Washington University Association, November 20, 1906.


## p. 12 (#238) #############################################

12
HENRY CAPLES PENN
But there must be two sides. It has been repeatedly pointed
out that authority is pretty much on the minority side. The
advocates of reform include the students of the language, men
who are accepted throughout the scholastic world as masters
in English linguistics; such are Professors Skeat and Sweet in
England, Jesperson in Denmark, Lounsbury of Yale. And the
movement is endorsed by philological societies in England and
America, and by the National Educational Association of the
United States. On the other hand, in much that has been
written against it there has been shown a lamentable ignorance
of the history of the language, and a spirit of mere abuse that
can not fill the place of argument. When people say that
"spelling reform is a pestilent heresy," its advocates "cranks of
high and low degree," its highest sponsor not "phonetically
safe and sane," simplified spelling itself a "grotesque misspell-
ing," soon to be among "outworn fads and follies," we hear
neither exposition nor argument.
This does not mean that the opponents of spelling reform
are in the wrong nor that its advocates are in the right; but,
with linguistic scholarship generally on the one side and lin-
guistic ignorance generally on the other, scholarship can not
be wholly wrong. There is ground for argument.
Among the facts that explain the almost universal oppo-
sition to reform are these:
(1) General ignorance of the language in any but its pres-
ent stage of sounds and signs. Few people conceive of any
other dress as possible, or have any knowledge of how present
fashions came about.
(2) People receive their impressions through the eye, and
are guided by it rather than by the ear. They learned spelling
at a time when they were too young to rebel against the
tyranny of it; and having long ago accustomed the eye to pres-
ent spellings, they are naturally irritated by having the un-


## p. 13 (#239) #############################################

ENGLISH SPELLING
13
familiar now thrust before them.
The uneasiness reform
brings to them blinds them to the relief that it might bring to
their children, and their children's children to the third and
fourth and nth generations.
It is true that spelling addresses itself to the eye, but sound
is the thing to be suggested; and this comes with less expense
to the reader, especially to the child learning to read, if the
signs have some consistent relation to the sounds.
(3) A third reason why people oppose spelling reform is
that some reformers are too thorough; and these give the im-
pression that every reform movement has as its goal phonetic
spelling. The misconception grows partly out of hasty, care-
less, stupid, or willful misunderstanding. In every popular
discussion of the work of the Simplified Spelling Board it is
assumed that the Board is aiming at the introduction of
phonetic spelling. The President has been caricatured as ad-
vocating it. The view misrepresents his order, and, un-
doubtedly, the creed of almost all the thousands that have
joined in the movement. A very few are ready to break away
from the anchorage of fixed spelling, and drift with the tides
upon the unstable element of sound. For them one should
adapt the words of Tennyson:
O thou that after toil and storm
Mayst seem to have reach'd a purer air,
Whose faith has centre everywhere,
Nor cares to fix itself to form,
Leave thou thy sister when she prays,
Her early heaven, her happy views.
The present outcry against simplified spelling is without
ground in so far as it is an outcry against phonetic spelling.
Granting, then, that spelling reform is something more than
a preposterous dream of mad idealists, it is at least worthy of
consideration. The movement may take-in fact, is taking-


## p. 14 (#240) #############################################

14
HENRY CAPLES PENN
two directions: the introduction of phonetic spelling, and the
simplification of present conventional spelling.
The former is for general use impracticable. The printing
press has established and will maintain and ought to maintain
a conventional spelling until some sublimation of the telephone
and the phonograph makes the printed page and the manu-
script useless. When newspapers, other periodicals, and books,
when letters and records committed to manuscript, addressed
to the eye, cease to be, the spelling of words may become
secondary, the sound of words the all in all.
But phonetic spelling has its uses, important though limited.
The adoption of an international phonetic alphabet seems pos-
sible. In 1904 the linguistic associations of America (with the
National Educational Association) arrived at practical agree-
ment in the matter. The alphabet of the International Phonetic
Association of France, which numbers among its membership
linguistic students of other countries, is extending rapidly and
is now well-nigh dominant among continental phoneticians.
The creation of an international scientific alphabet should not
be long delayed.
There is great need for an accurate phonetic alphabet in all
scientific linguistic work. A means of that kind has already
been adopted in two great dictionaries, to indicate pronun-
ciation-the New English Dictionary in England, and the
Standard Dictionary in America; it ought to be in universal
use for this practical purpose. Some have even dreamed of a
gradual education of the civilized world to the acceptance of
such a common alphabet. They have argued that, with it used
in all dictionaries and spelling books alongside the conventional
spelling, all school children would become familiar with it; in
two or three generations every educated person would know
and be able to use the phonetic signs, and would prefer them
because of their clearness and accuracy. But the dream leaves


## p. 15 (#241) #############################################

ENGLISH SPELLING
15
out of account the constant shifting of sound values, the im-
possibility of petrifying pronunciation; a phonetic spelling
would be as unstable as the sounds it represented.
There are still other obstacles in the way of committing to
phonetic signs the sounds that make up English speech. One
is the constant variation of quality in every word, and
every syllable of every word, consequent upon the syntax
of the word, upon its neighboring sounds, and the mood
of the speaker. If the phonetic spelling represented, as
it must, the sounds of the word when spoken fully, distinctly,
apart, then every reader and speaker would make that spell-
ing nugatory at every breath. The spelling would represent
not words as actually used, but words learned in the spelling
class; it would have to be, in some degree, a conventional, un-
phonetic spelling. Another obstacle is the divergence of pro-
nunciation, even among the best educated people of different
sections of the country. The objection is of special force in
America, for here divergences are wide. To make phonetic
spellings practicable for general use it is necessary to set up a
standard pronunciation, and then to make that pronunciation
permanent. The first is improbable, the second impossible of
accomplishment. A phonetic alphabet could at best become a
vehicle for communication only among scientific people; three
or four letters from it might in course of time be added to the
present conventional alphabet.
Simplification of spelling is quite another thing. Its advo-
cates recognize that a large number of present spellings are ex-
ceptional-that is, so far from the general practices of the lan-
guage that they must each simply be memorized, like Chinese
characters.
Two main sources of anomalous spelling are these:
(1) At the introduction of printing spelling was chaotic.
Out of the mass of current forms printers from the beginning


## p. 16 (#242) #############################################

16
HENRY CAPLES PENN
chose rather those that were already archaic, thus perpetuating
consonants that were already silent, and fixing vowel signs
already defective or misleading. Other simpler spellings were
in constant use, freely in manuscripts and frequently in print;
but the weight of tradition told in favor of the inapt forms sur-
viving from older usage or adopted bodily from a foreign
source. (2) From time to time arbitrary, unhistorical spell-
ings were foisted upon the language, through incompetence,
carelessness or error of scribe or printer, and through the zeal
or pedantry of mistaken etymologists. In a few cases the alien
form has drawn pronunciation to its bosom and so made itself
secure; but in most, spelling and pronunciation remain diver-
gent.
Now, a simplified spelling or simplified speller-proposes
to go back to the time when printing fixed the spelling, and
make a more rational choice. It can be done now, because we
realize how imperfectly it was done then, and because we have,
further, a knowledge of the language, its processes of evolution
in broad lines and in details, that has been gained only within
the last generation. We can now choose spellings more in
harmony with the genius of the language, more satisfying to
reason, and easier to learn, than was then possible, or possible
even to the best scholarship of the first half of the nineteenth
century. And it will be an easy task to remove the errors of
false etymology and false analogy.
The chief difficulty lies in winning the many who do not
know to accept the lead of those who do know. It is striking,
but not strange, that people who in any other science yield to
the authority of specialists, in matters of language set up their
Having by constant contact with it got practical use of
English as it is today, they assume to know all about it. They
would not dictate to the engineer what quality or quantity or
form of material he shall use in a bridge, nor to the painter
own.


## p. 17 (#243) #############################################

ENGLISH SPELLING
17
how he shall mix his colors; they leave to these men the decision
as to the what and the how. They accept the opinion of scien-
tists in every science but that of linguistics. The geologist has
authority as the historian of the earth; the philologist none
as the historian of language.
In support of their position, spelling reformers represented
by the Simplified Spelling Board urge:
(1) That the simplification of spelling would lighten the
task of learning to spell, and with less effort make better
spellers.
(2) That it would make the process of learning to spell a
means of mental discipline, and not, as to a grievous extent it
is now, of taxing the memory with inconsistent and meaning-
less forms.
(3) That simplification would purify some words of alien
elements, rid some of encumbrances with which time has clogged
them, restore some to a simplicity perfectly in harmony with the
past history and the present spirit of the language.
(4) That it would measurably reduce the cost of publica-
tion in print and manuscript, inasmuch as it would save space.
This is a matter of mere calculation, and easily demonstrable;
some regard it as trivial, although careful estimates make it
about $40,000,000 a year.
(5) It would lighten the task of the foreigner who learns
the language.
In what has been said in opposition, a great deal has been
expression, in terms more or less civil, of personal feeling. The
less civil exhibitions it is needless to notice; they express a
temper, and generally an ignorance, impervious to reason. But
against any change in spelling there is a good deal of sincere
protest arising from the fact that the new forms are offensive
to the eye; and this (as a writer in a recent number of the Fort-
nightly has said) is merely because they are unfamiliar. It can

not be that there is any inherent ugliness in the simpler spell-

perhaps might be improved?
Neglecting the personal equation, for that will solve itself
in a generation, we have two main questions to consider: a
possible gain for the child learning to spell, and a possible loss
in the historical flavor of certain words.
Opponents of the movement deny that it would be of peda-
gogic advantage. A university professor of English, writing to
The Nation, says that bad spellers among the freshmen are put
into a "pity sakes" class and taught to spell. He finds that the
words they miss are not among the famous three hundred; that
by the end of the freshman year only one per cent remain poor
spellers. His conclusion is that more thorough drill and more
rational drill would make practically all of us good spellers.
But some of the words that freshmen fail on might be found in
the final list submitted by the Simplified Spelling Board; the
three hundred are samples. And for all one can know, students
fail on the simpler words because the anomalous forms have
been as lions in the path-the larger terrors of spelling may
have exhausted their strength or put to flight their valor; some
spellings are monstrous enough to discourage both teacher and
pupils. While it is true that more rational methods of teach-
ing spelling, application in the task of a knowledge of the
phonetic devices in the present system, and a study of phonetics
along with spelling, so far as the unphonetic character of
spelling will allow, will all make for quicker and completer

mastery of the difficulties, the gain becomes the greater as the

fellows.
Another serious paper makes out a case in some respects
strong; it is a psychologist's "protest against simplified spell-
ing." But however convincing this paper is on the side of the
psychology of spelling, a student of the language can agree
with only part of it. The writer emphasizes, in paragraphs
that every one interested in the public schools should read, the
radical defect in American elementary education, namely, the
lack of thorough drill and efficient discipline. Every layman
in psychology will agree in this. But, admitting all that is
urged in this direction, there is still the promise that a sim-
plified spelling in addition to more efficient training in the
schools would bring about better results in the spelling class
than the latter alone; and the fact justifies reform unless the
opponent of reform offers valid reasons against it.
Not all the reasons that the psychologist urges seem valid.
One, indeed, strikes the non-psychologist as odd. "Give us,"
the argument runs, "as many optical hints for the discrimina-
tion of words as possible." The anomalous spellings, the pres-
ence of silent letters, of signs strikingly divergent from the
normal representations of sounds, are really of advantage, in
that they fix the words more firmly in the memory. But is not
this the result of the special attention that the exceptional
form exacts? These strange words that we seize so firmly cost
more to get. If they do not, why not make spelling easier
by marking more words in that way? The end of the logic is
Chinese: every word to be learned as a whole, and apart from
every other word. If the reductio ad absurdum is unfair, tell
us what proportion of words, and just what words, should

and eye, and by ear first; and English spelling must be a com-

what suggests most readily to the mind the sound with which
the ear is familiar.
But the Simplified Spelling Board expresses the opinion
that reform would make English easier for a foreigner to

with the conjugation, nothing is easier than to learn that the
ending -ed indicates the participle. Nothing, perhaps, gives
the eye of the foreign reader such a feeling of safety. That is
now gone. The poor boy will now have simply to learn by

sadly, 'Exceptions from the rule of -ed are addrest, affixt, blest,

The case is not so bad as this. A linguist would say: There
are neither new or old exceptions in the way of the student that
has had proper instruction in the grammar and phonetics of his
own language. In these English dental preterits and par-
ticiples, inflectional -d in some words becomes -t in accordance
with the phonetic law of assimilation. The "exceptions," new
and old, arrange themselves under a law of language and offer
themselves to the German student of English not as freaks of
language but as normal features, such as he recognizes in his
own speech, delightful and easy to learn because he knows them

not as mechanical devices to mark tense, but as rational, physi-

The most thrilling day in the experience of a student of
language is the day when he realizes that his "mother tongue"
is not an article of manufacture, mechanically fitted by various
lifeless devices to express more or less imperfectly his thought,
but is a growth, a living thing, capable of responding, as every-
thing else in the world of life about him, to his own emotion, and
gathering unto itself the life of all that have gone before him.
And like pleasure and widening of vision, and stimulation of
imagination, come to him on the day when he recognizes that
other languages, too, are alive, developing under the same vital
influences as his own. If the student of his own or of foreign
speech can feel the natural law in the spiritual world of lan-
guage, words and the forms of words will plant themselves in
his mind.

What has been said with regard to the loss of the -ed identi-
fication of preterits and participles applies to the latter part of
this quotation. It is better for the foreign student not to rest
with the impression that the English language is freakish; he
will understand-will master-the language more readily if he
recognizes the normality of its phenomena, even at slightly
greater tax upon his memory. But simplified spelling would
increase the chance of confusing homonyms to what degree
would depend upon the simplifying, how far it went toward
making moat over into mote or the reverse. The extent of the
harm may be exaggerated. In English the word order gives the
clew; their context distinguishes words that are alike to the ear,
and will do the same for those alike to the eye. It is true that
the foreigner does not find it easy (unless favored with the
presence of a teacher) to take hold by sentences; but to make
any progress at all he must from the beginning get at the sense.
Before he has run across many homonyms he will, indeed must,
have become able to gather from the context their meaning.
The absence of inflections may trouble him, not the presence of
homonyms.
But still it may be doubtful whether simplified spelling
would help the foreign student of English, unless he studies it
in England or America. For the multitudes that come to Amer-
ica, learn the language here, and use it here, spelling reform
would lighten the task as it would for native learners. For the
foreigner-at least the adult and isolated student-who remains
a foreigner it may promise little. That, however, is not of great
force against the movement.
Simplified spelling may not

anglicise the world against its will. One may recognize the

spelling is good for English people, it is desirable, even if it
adds a straw to the load of the foreign student of the language.
English for the English.
But that does not mean American for the Americans.
Americanism that flaunts itself before English eyes just to prove
that it is American is lamentably narrow. The American
should claim as an Englishman his right in the language and
literature that a common ancestry has handed down. Ameri-
cans-native and adopted-should rally, as many of them think
they have done, to the defense of "our mother tongue" from
mutilation at the hands of spelling reformers.
The writer above quoted asks: "Shall we destroy the his-
torical flavor of words?" And the correspondent of The Nation
closes with the sentence: "If the time, money and energy now
given to the simplified spelling movement were used to secure
a wiser method of teaching orthography, the results would be

A constant objection to simplifying spelling is that it will
do "violence to the history and genealogy of our mother tongue."
The contrary is the case. The etymology argument has been


## p. 24 (#250) #############################################

24
HENRY CAPLES PENN
repeatedly shown to be without foundation. Revision of spell-
ing would in many cases bring words nearer to their true
source; it would remove many false and arbitrarily imposed
etymological marks; in a few cases it might at worst take off
the label merely-no loss to any intelligent visitor to the
museum.
Here are five words with beautiful etymological spellings:
hough, through, though, tough, plough. They furnish a philol-
ogist interesting material for a lecture; a bone from the fore-
leg of a cat would do as much for the anatomist. Nobody else
has use for either; any other spelling or bone would serve the
layman just as well. In these words the combination -ough
stands for five individual sounds. In only one is the vowel
really ou; in two the gh represents nothing; in one it stands for
k, and in one for f. A simpler spelling is current in America
for two of the words, hock and plow, the former also long in
England. Why not choose like simple forms for the others?
"It obscures the etymology of words and destroys their histori-
cal significance." Does it do this for hock and plow?
Now, these spellings are historical. They were once
phonetic. Every sign was meant to represent a sound that was
heard; but if that is sufficient reason for preserving the letters,
the same reason holds good for going back another stage or two,
and adopting the earlier forms hoh, thruh, thoh, toh, ploh. The
first two of these suggest the present sounds more readily than
the accepted spellings; the third does so equally as well; the
other two are unphonetic, but no more so than the ough forms;
and all are strictly etymological.
But admitting these spellings, on etymological ground as
urged, what about modern spellings that are not historical-
that perpetuate the errors of scribes of five hundred years ago,
the choice of uneducated printers three hundred years ago, the
mistakes of incompetent etymologists two hundred years ago?

the main entrance to one's own house. Only on extraordinary
occasions would one need the information.
And sometimes the information is misleading.

English from Anglo-Norman, a dialect of which the "reduction

but o and ou came also into use, the former a device of French
and Norman scribes to distinguish the vowel where (for ex-
ample, alongside morn) u would not be clear to the eye, the
latter a sign in general use among French and Norman scribes
for short as well as long u. By the time of Chaucer the sign
ou had come into general use, but honor is also historical and
legitimate, and honur historical but long obsolete.

Simplification might blot out the obvious marks of
parentage in many words that have come direct from Latin or
Greek, or the later French, or from other foreign sources. The
Old French, especially the Norman dialect, is hardly foreign;
blood came with the language, and so long ago that both were
thoroughly absorbed in the Middle English period and became

words that are in some degree foreign, a change to purely
English spelling might quite alter the face.
It is not my understanding that simplified spelling proposes
to do that. Nothing that has been proposed robs any foreign
word of its looks so far as to denationalize it. The spelling
remains close enough to the original to suggest at once that
original to any one for whom the original has any meaning.
The mere foreign look of the word is worth little.
But words gather meaning. Each word carries for each
reader a set of suggestions, some or all of which may fade away
with a change of spelling. "When fantom is written like a kind
of fan, and prolog like a kind of log, do not most of the over-
tones disappear?" Gost and gastly lose their terror, deign its
proud bearing, sovereign its regal pomp.
It is here that simplified spelling will lose us most; some
compromise may be politic. In any case, however, the loss is
not total. Many such words may rightly claim an English
dress and air. Nearly all of the words in -logue were in Eng-
lish use before they took the French spelling. Dialog takes the
English reader back to 1200; Wyclif is authority for decalog;
catalog is older than catalogue; even prolog is historical. An
English reader may feel in a return to these earlier and English
forms some compensation for the loss of the French. That is
especially so when simplification takes us back to Milton and
his sovran, perhaps even to Chaucer and his fein (the pedantic
Gower spells it feign). The loss in pomposity and even in
dignity is balanced by the gain in sincerity and genuineness.
Still the student of language, along with others, is sensible
of a loss. The spelling deign brings before him the formality
of the court, disdain the freer use of the people. It is worth
while to "ake" with a-c-h-e if that will make the grotesque and
impressive figure of Dr. Samuel Johnson rise before the
imagination. A linguist can enjoy toying with the ety-

mological hints treasured up in l-a-u-g-h even more than other
adult mortals, though children find it no joke. Is this æsthetic
enjoyment worth the cost?
Any one, in short, who knows enough about English to
recognize etymology where it stares from the face of the word
and to nod a familiar return, has no need of the obvious marks
that simplification of the spelling would remove; any one at
home in the foreign source of a word could as vividly realize
that source in the simpler form; but for all, in the case of a few
words, there would be some loss of suggestion not wholly made
up by the different content of the new or new-old form. The
loss would not be overwhelming, for it would affect only pres-
ent-day æsthetic values; much of the Elizabethan content of
words is already lost to the average reader (simplification
might help to restore it), and much of Milton, and even of
eighteenth century authors. When, in the works of these old
authors, our present-day spellings carry our present-day mean-
ings, they bury from us half of the earlier sense and three-
fourths of the poetry. Nor need the loss be permanent. As
the eye, once familiar with new forms, would not find them
offensive, so the æsthetic sense could in a measure accommodate
itself to the change. Familiarity is all.
But the present paper, so far, has neither favored nor
opposed any specific reform. It makes no defense of the three
hundred words around which a battle is raging, nor does it
marshal the whole army and munitions of war that the Sim-
plified Spelling Board may have assembled in its secret camps
and arsenals. There is, indeed, too much divergence of opinion
among the reformers themselves to write a platform upon
which they can stand, a creed to which they will subscribe.

grievously irrational, nor that there have been gross misunder-

## p. 29 (#255) #############################################

ENGLISH SPELLING
29
from the Simplified Spelling Board and gained the approval
of President Roosevelt. The answer is easy to much of the
clatter. Why doesn't the President reform his own name? the
shallow cry. For the same reason that he does not write it
with a little "r." Proper names have and ought to have an
individuality beyond that needful for other names; their indi-
vidual spellings neither demand more attention nor give them
more prominence than they deserve. Where this is not the
case, peculiarities in proper names may be justly ridiculed, as
any inexcusable peculiarity of dress may be.
Some valuable criticism of the work of the Carnegie Board
has appeared. Mr. William Archer, in the October Fort-
nightly, after expressing sympathy with a movement to sim-
plify but not to phonetize English spelling, questions the wis-
dom of the plan of simplifying. It is his opinion that a system
of reform ought to be carefully worked out by a competent,
representative, and authoritative body, and then put into effect
at once; the piecemeal reform would keep us in confusion the
while it lasted. He feels, too, that the fact that the further
plans of the Board are withheld in detail helps to create dis-
trust. But the work of the Board, especially the action of the
President, has served the good purpose of arousing public
attention and creating interest. It may be possible now, where
it was not before, to carry out the further suggestion, that is,
for an authoritative body to formulate the scheme, adopt the
principles, and work out the details, of the changes to be recom-
mended.
A review of the history of the language, especially with
reference to its spelling, will give results that can perhaps be
of service in the task. It will, in general, show that-
(1) The English vowels are very unstable, more so since
the introduction of printing than before. Phonetic spelling
must constantly shift to keep up with their whirl. It is better


## p. 30 (#256) #############################################

30
HENRY CAPLES PENN
to hold to the signs now in use, except in the case of individual
changes that do not involve a general shifting of signs. But
consonants are relatively stable; signs fixed now will stand for
generations.
(2) At the time printing was introduced there were cur-
rent in good use numerous spellings and generally more than
one pronunciation for each word, the varied forms having their
source in shiftings of quantity and quality that make up the
natural development of language, in dialectal divergences, in
current foreign forms beside the native, and in a great mass of
archaic spellings in accumulated manuscripts.
(3) Printers chose wilfully, but in the main from archaic
traditional spellings of older, rather than from the living pho-
netic spelling of contemporary manuscripts-letters, journals,
accounts, diaries-not intended for publication; and further,
they made no pretense of following the manuscript that authors
put before them. We do not know how Shakspere spelled; the
chances are that his spelling was as free as his sovereign's, and
that was free to the point of phoneticism. In five autographs
he spells his name in three ways.
(4) Present spellings are a selection from the earlier
already archaic sixteenth and seventeenth century printers'
spellings, the selection being made by eighteenth century editors
who worked with no historical nor linguistic knowledge of the
language, and whose decisions, therefore, could not always be
in harmony with the spirit and genius of the language.
(5) Nevertheless, English spelling is for the mass of words
reasonably satisfactory. It can not be much changed without
radical revision of the whole body of words, on the phonetic
basis; and this is not desirable. A review of the history of
English spelling shows principles applied from time to time
that can still be applied to simplify the anomalous forms in a
degree that will put them into the main categories of English


## p. 31 (#257) #############################################

ENGLISH SPELLING
31
spelling. Such are the principles of indicating quantity by
doubling the vowel sign, or the following consonant, or by the
use of mute e. Signs like o and ou (ow) for etymological u,
introduced for clearness in manuscript, need not be kept up in
print that makes the u distinct, except where the value is diph-
thongal, as in house, now. Middle English long vowels, now
become short, no longer need the double sign, such as ea in head.
Past practices of the language warrant the dropping of silent
consonants except where clearness of meaning suffers. Com-
promises must be allowed.
A review of the processes by which our spelling came about
should cure extravagant worship of the established letter, and
ought to undermine much of the reverence in vogue for some of
the spellings that afflict the dictionary. One in touch with the
language all through its history can feel no special attachment
for some details of its modern dress.
The movement toward simplification should be planned by
and for Englishmen and Americans together. The committee
or board undertaking the work should be dominated by English
linguists-men familiar with every detail of the language in all
its stages; familiar with its literature, and with the atmosphere
that each word (and each spelling) has collected around itself
during the eight centuries or less that the word has lived in
uninfiected form. These men should see that every change
recommended is in harmony with past practices and usages.
They should approach the task with eyes fixed not on the excep-
tional forms only, the anomalies of English spelling, but upon
the main lines of development and the principles and direction
of growth that these reveal.
Associated with them should be men familiar with the
psychology of language, and also men of affairs-editors, pub-
lishers, business men, familiar with the public and its practical
needs, and with the practical matter of winning public sym-


## p. 32 (#258) #############################################

32
HENRY CAPLES PENN
pathy and approval. These latter may offset a natural tendency
in the philologists, and the psychologists, toward a revision that
might not prove practical nor practicable. Useful advice, too,
might come from men familiar with the difficulties that beset
the teacher of spelling in the primary and secondary schools,
and also from teachers in business schools and from competent
stenographers. But to put on the committee representatives of
every class from which valuable suggestion might come, would
make an unwieldy body. The needful thing is that the com-
mittee should command the respect of intelligent public opinion,
that it should respect the best-informed public opinion, and that
it should move in no direction not approved by English lin-
guistic scholarship.
After all is done the scheme formulated, the principles
adopted, and the methods of applying them determined upon-
it may become evident that reform can not be accomplished.
But there is hope that the results of competent revision of
English spelling will commend themselves to the people who
make public opinion.
Professor Skeat, in a paper read last year before the British
Academy on the problem of spelling reform, says with reference
to the conditions in England: "There was at that date [1881]
a slight hope of success, but whatever chance it had was
promptly howled down by writers for the daily and weekly
press, who did not understand so much as the rudiments of the
problem, and had neither sympathy with nor mercy upon any
one who was capable of instructing them. The same unsus-
pected ignorance prevails still, and is as noisy and contempt-
uous as ever. The only hope obviously lies in the possibility
that a suspicion of their own ignorance may some day dawn
upon writers who, after all, are unaware of their prejudice and.
are only unintentionally dishonest.

should come to pass that a real Spelling Reform should pre-

ARCHITECTURE AND CIVIC PROGRESS
FREDERICK M. MANN
Professor of Architecture in Washington University
Civic
Architecture is the art of building beautifully.
progress I would define as the outward expression in better
laws, finer institutions and greater civic beauty of a growing
state of enlightenment among the people. Beautiful buildings
with their settings and the setting must be considered as an
integral part of every architectural work-are not only the
material evidences of good taste, but also a potent stimulus to
better taste; and good taste is an attribute of cultured and
refined sensibilities, without which the existence of a high
degree of enlightenment is inconceivable.
There is, of course, no such thing as a uniform state of
culture among the people of a community. The highly cul-
tured, the less cultured, and the barbarian (as to refinement)
must dwell together. The highly cultured feels that he must
not only bend his best efforts to protect himself from that which
is unpleasant or shocking to his own sensibilities, but he
desires to bring broadening influences into the lives of the less
fortunate of his own community particularly. No one will
gainsay, I think, that ugliness is degrading and beauty elevat-
ing. This is as true with the cultured as with the uncultured.
To displace ugliness and enthrone beauty is then vitally our
common interest. Not one of us would be willing to say that
he has not some elements of the barbarian within himself-we
all need elevating influences about us.
Aside from pure religion and patriotism, I can think of
nothing in a man or in a community of men more elevating or


## p. 35 (#261) #############################################

ARCHITECTURE AND CIVIC PROGRESS
35
more inspiring than civic pride. The service of every element
that will develop and foster it is needed. Civic beauty-
beauty in the material city-is undoubtedly the most effective
single instrument that can be made use of toward this end.
Our people are, for the most part, absorbed each in his own
narrow affairs. They do not, as a rule, seem to find them-
selves able to devote sufficient time and study to the govern-
ment and the working institutions of the city to understand
and come into close touch with them, even though many desire
to do so. On the other hand the exterior aspect of the city
forces itself upon them at all times, in all places, when idle
and when at work. Now, however oblivious we may imagine
ourselves to be of our surroundings, they have their effect upon
us whether we are conscious of it or not. The eye of the
worker wanders for a moment, and an aspect of ugliness or
beauty has left its impression; and when he leaves his absorb-
ing task and enters the public thoroughfares of the city, no
exertion in study or in thought is necessary for the physical
aspect of the streets to force itself upon him. He is compelled
to become familiar with it. Either its ugliness casts a blight
upon him, or its beauty uplifts and stimulates him and makes
him proud to feel himself a part of it. What an uplift the
Greek must have felt as he approached the Acropolis ! and how
pride of citizenship must have stirred within the Roman as he
passed through the public places of the Eternal City and
entered the Great Forum with all its wonders of architecture !
The part architecture may play in civic progress is, then, not
only toward the cultivation of public taste, but the develop-
ment and stimulation of civic pride.
The art of architecture seems to-day to be passing through
a chaotic phase. We are, however, undoubtedly in a period of
growth and development. There seems to me to exist a con-
dition of awakening. The question is, how can we take advan-


## p. 36 (#262) #############################################

36
FREDERICK M. MANN
tage of this condition and press architecture into full service
as an agent for civic progress. How can we raise it from a
passive position as a follower of material prosperity, where its
growth must necessarily be erratic, if not slow, to the status
of a positive instrument for civic advancement ? In answer
to this question, I would name two or three directions in which
improvement is possible: first, in the architects; second, in the
individual builder; and third, in improved building regula-
tions. Architects must all seek proper training; the individual
who has control of building enterprises must seek a broadly
intelligent conception of the public nature of works of archi-
tecture; finally, carefully considered regulations must be
enacted, not only governing architectural design in individual
buildings, but, what is more important, the relation of build-
ings to each other.
A consideration of the first point, the training of the archi-
tect, discloses some unsatisfactory aspects of this question and
partially explains the existence of architectural monstrosities
along some of the streets of our cities. While high training
of the architect would seem to be a foregone conclusion, the law
of demand and supply is the regulating influence in the profes-
sion of architecture as in all other callings. While clients are
satisfied with mediocrity, or even ugliness, there is little in-
centive to the young architect to spend costly years in arduous
training. This forms the most serious complication in the
architectural situation of to-day. Our architects' offices are
filled with young men whose education has ended in the com-
mon schools. After a few years there, with knowledge cover-
ing not much more than a few simple methods of construction,
they begin the farce of architectural practice, possessing neither
the elements of a liberal education, nor even an awakened taste,
and in almost absolute ignorance of architecture as one of the
noblest of the fine arts. To go into this important matter more


## p. 37 (#263) #############################################

ARCHITECTURE AND CIVIC PROGRESS
37
in detail, there are in the United States, according to a count
which I have made in a business directory, about five thousand
practitioners calling themselves architects. Perhaps three
thousand of these have begun practice within the last decade.
American schools of architecture are now graduating about one
hundred men each year. Since the number has been so large
only during the past three or four years, it would be a safe
assumption, I think, to say that the total number of graduates
in the whole decade has not exceeded seven hundred and fifty.
While many of these eventually found their way into other
callings, the total number has probably been maintained by the
incoming of foreign trained men. Among the architects who
began practice more than ten years ago the proportion of
schooled men is yet smaller. It will, therefore, be a conserva-
tive statement to say that of all the architects of the country
at most only seven hundred and fifty in three thousand, or one
in four, have had a systematic training for the profession they
are practicing.
While no one would contend that all the
schooled men do creditable work, nor that all unschooled men
do uniformly poor work, it is clear that too large a proportion
of the men who design buildings to beautify or to mar our
cities are men who have had little or no opportunity to gain a
liberal education, to learn the theory of architecture or to train
systematically the artistic gifts with which nature endowed
them. There are, however, signs of improvement, for, keeping
pace with the existing growth of taste and appreciation of
architecture, there is a perceptibly increasing number of edu-
cated and liberally trained men in the ranks of the profession,
and there is also an active campaign among the more en-
lightened of the profession for the better training of the younger
generation. Although these are hopeful conditions, the public
should provide a much more vigorous accelerating impulse


## p. 38 (#264) #############################################

38
FREDERICK M. MANN
than it does at present, by constantly demanding better and yet
better design in all classes of buildings.
This leads to the consideration of the position in the ad-
vancement of architecture of those who have control of building
enterprises. The exclusive right of the individual to control
his building operations ends with the building's interior
arrangement and its utilitarian function; in its exterior ex-
pression of beauty or of ugliness-the public has a rightful
share. Each work of architecture is a lasting monument and
a public one, in the sense that one of its functions is to adorn
a public thoroughfare. It is destined to become a perpetual
elevating influence if beautiful, a constant debasing influence
and menace to public taste if ugly. Hence in his building enter-
prise the individual incurs a grave responsibility to the public,
and one demanding serious consideration, not only by the indi-
vidual himself but by the public as well, that it may safeguard
good taste and stimulate the pride of the people in their city.
The third point for consideration is the public regulation of
architecture. Architecture in the sense of beautiful building
is a matter in which, as I have pointed out, the public is deeply
concerned. In no other art or calling is this so true. Paint-
ings and sculpture are hidden from public view, and familiarity
with them is a matter of individual choice. Music is also for
the few and under the control of the individual. In the prac-
tice of medicine or the practice of law each separate case affects
scarcely more than the individuals concerned; but the work of
the architect is enduring, and none can escape its influence.
A wise regulation of architectural productions would then seem
desirable, extending as far as it can be made effective. Laws
regulating the height of buildings are to be found even in the
Roman Code. The requirement of a uniform height and a
fixed cornice line for contiguous buildings, such as is in force in
the city of Paris to-day, is even better. In the less crowded


## p. 39 (#265) #############################################

ARCHITECTURE AND CIVIC PROGRESS
39
residence sections a fixed building line is nearly always de-
sirable.
The question of architectural design is, however, a matter
so indefinite and so intangible that there seem to be few regula-
tions concerning it that can be clearly defined by law. The
impossibility of direct control by definite laws should bring
about the establishment of a properly qualified commission,
somewhat similar to those in two or three of our cities, notably
New York; and such a commission should be a recognized
institution in every municipality. Their powers should, by all
means, include authority to pass upon the design of every pro-
posed building, without exception. Cities already regulate the
safety and sanitation of all buildings; their design as well
should be a matter of careful regulation. The fancy of the
uncultured individual certainly should not be allowed riotous
caprice in this direction.
On the other hand, the man of cultured taste, being less
confident of the competence of his own judgment, would recog-
nize at once the possibilities inherent in this fully qualified and
wisely chosen body, whose powers should extend to embrace not
only individual designs but the more momentous question of
the larger relations of buildings to each other and the formula-
tion of general and sectional schemes of architectural treat-
ment.
Under the head of public regulations comes the question of
licensing architects, about which much discussion has gone on
within the ranks of the profession. Safety and sanitation of
buildings, as I have said, are already safeguarded by law with
fair efficiency. The improvement of design, therefore, becomes
the main consideration affected by such a system as this. The
more efficient method of dealing with architectural design
would seem to be the direct control of the design rather than
control of the designer. Even were it possible, in the practice


## p. 40 (#266) #############################################

40
FREDERICK M. MANN
of a fine art, to set up a standard by which the diverse person-
alities and temperaments of art workers could be measured (and
therein lies the great difficulty of this system), individual
caprice would still be left to run riot; and if we are to bring a
sense of unity, of dignity and impressiveness into the streets of
our cities, we must not thus continue to allow the parts to
govern the whole. This is not a good principle of art produc-
tion and has never yet resulted in any worthy work of art either
small or large. If, however, we can not at once bring about the
competent control of design directly-and I admit this to be
difficult at present-we may at least bend our efforts towards
assuring the possession of proper qualifications by the designer.
I therefore believe in the licensing system at the present time
and under present conditions.
A paper on architecture and civic progress would not be
complete without some reference to the encouraging, hopeful
and widespread movement for civic improvement. Not only
do these hopeful signs show themselves in such well known
examples as Washington, Cleveland, Buffalo and other large
cities, but also in many smaller cities throughout the land. It is
a splendid movement indicative of growing taste, growing civic
ideals and civic pride. Let the beauty of the civic center be
extended to embrace a beautiful city. The elevating influences
that reflect from the beautiful city will infallibly contribute to
build up within the citizens a human life more orderly, more
harmonious and more beautiful.

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW *
PAUL ELMER MORE, '87
The position of Longfellow is somewhat curious. He was,
and I suppose still is, the most beloved poet of the past century,
and this not only among the ignorant and half-educated, but
among people of the finest culture. Men as different in tem-
perament as Kipling and J. H. Shorthouse gave credit to his
wonderful knowledge of the sea, and to Shorthouse, at least, he
was always "very dear." He was also one of the favorite poets
of so cunning a magician in words as Lafcadio Hearn; and to
such names one might add indefinitely. Yet it remains true
that Longfellow has never been quite accepted by the professed
critics, that they have spoken of him commonly with reserva-
tion, sometimes even with contempt. Not many, indeed, have
adopted just the insolent tone of Mr. Francis Gribble-who-
ever that hypercritical gentleman may be in Putnam's and
the Fortnightly, to whom Longfellow was merely a "prig," with
no characteristic habit except that of "decorating his person,"
a "poet of the obvious and the hum-drum," a man "equally
devoid of humor and of passion," whose "intellectual outfit
consists of a 'store suit' from a theological emporium." We
have a right to be incensed at any magazine for printing so
scurrilous a diatribe. But, waiving this foolishness of conceit,
we must still acknowledge that there has been a distinct under-
current of protest against the poet's easy popularity. Not his
the felicity he attributed to the greatest name of all, thinking,
no doubt, of the cavilling he himself endured even during his
life: "O happy poet, by no critic vext!"
[*Read at the St. Louis Wednesday Club, February 27, 1907. A small part of
the paper, in different form, has been printed in The Nation.]


## p. 42 (#268) #############################################

42
PAUL ELMER MORE
And this contrast between the love of so many readers for
Longfellow and the hesitation of his critics is perfectly com-
prehensible. The critics are mainly right. Let us not blunt
or pervert our taste by ignoring distinctions. In the first
place, no one who has stored his mind with the work of the
great poets can read Longfellow without stumbling continually
over reminiscences that do not fall exactly under the head of
plagiarism, but that have the effect of reducing what has been
nobly and individually written to a kind of smooth common-
place. I might from my own recollection almost fill the hour
with these dulled echoes of a finer music. Let me illustrate
by a few examples. Longfellow, we are told by his biographer,
wrote but a single love poem (and I, for one, am ready to honor
him for this reserve), that sonnet to "My morning and my
evening star of love! My best and gentlest lady!" 'Tis a
pretty, and, among poets, rare compliment to his wife; but
somehow the taste of it grows flat, and that best and gentlest
lady drops to something resembling the merely respectable,
when we recall the most perfect of all Greek epigrams, Plato's
᾿Αστὴρ πρὶν μὲν ἔλαμπες, which came to Longfellow, no doubt, through
Shelley's version :
Thou wert the morning star among the living,
Ere thy fair light had fled;—
Now, having died, thou art as Hesperus, giving
New splendor to the dead.
It is not, observe, that our Longfellow has taken the pre-
cise thought of the original; there is here no charge of stealing.
It is rather that his image suggests the same image used dif-
ferently and more poetically by another. In the same way
his complaint beginning, "Half of my life is gone, and I have let
The years slip from me," inevitably forces a comparison with
Milton's more resonant note: "When I consider how my light
is spent Ere half my days."


## p. 43 (#269) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
43
Again Longfellow writes:
God sent his Singers upon earth
With songs of sadness and of mirth,
That they might touch the hearts of men,
And bring them back to heaven again-
and we remember Keats:
Bards of Passion and of Mirth,
Ye have left your souls on earth!
Have ye souls in heaven, too,
Double-lived in regions new?
Longfellow writes of the unseen dwellers in "Haunted Houses":
We meet them at the doorway, on the stair,
Along the passages they come and go,
Impalpable impressions on the air,
A sense of something moving to and fro
and the memory goes back to Thomas Hood's lines in the most
ghostly of English poems :
Those dreary stairs, where with the sounding stress
Of ev'ry step so many echoes blended,
The mind, with dark misgivings, fear'd to guess
How many feet ascended.
O'er all there hung the shadow of a fear,
A sense of mystery the spirit daunted,
And said, as plain as whisper in the ear,
The place is Haunted!
But it would be tedious to multiply examples. The point,
as I have said, is not that Longfellow was a plagiarist or
lacked originality-greater poets than he have taken their own
where they found it with a more royally predatory hand-but
that these rather vague resemblances of language and meta-
phor so often draw our attention to the lower plane upon which
his imagination moves. And here I would beg for a little
indulgence. This distinction between the higher and lower
planes of the imagination goes so near to the very roots of taste


## p. 44 (#270) #############################################

44
PAUL ELMER MORE
and criticism; it is a matter so elusive withal, that I would run
the risk of an insistence which may seem like the proverbial
breaking of a butterfly upon a wheel. The question turns upon
that dualism, or duplicity, in human nature, often misunder-
stood and today more often ignored, the perception of which
does yet in some way mark the degree of a poet's or a philos-
opher's initiation into the mysteries of experience. To make
the point clearer, let me compare two poems which are known
by heart to all, and whose effect can be tested by the impres-
sions of memory. One is Longfellow's "Weariness," of which
I will quote the first and last stanzas:
O little feet! that such long years
Must wander on through hopes and fears,
Must ache and bleed beneath your load;
I, nearer to the wayside inn
Where toil shall cease and rest begin,
Am weary, thinking of your road!
O little souls! as pure and white
And crystalline as rays of light
Direct from heaven, their source divine;
Refracted through the mist of years,
How red my setting sun appears,
How lurid looks this soul of mine!
The other is Heine's even more familiar lyric on a somewhat
similar theme : Du bist wie eine Blume, which in my trans-
lation will at least be less trite, however much of its charm may
have evaporated:
So fair and fresh and pure
Even as a flower thou art;
I look on thee, and sadness
Glideth into my heart.
'Tis as tho' my hands were resting
Upon thy head in prayer,
Asking that God might keep thee
So pure and fresh and fair.


## p. 45 (#271) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
45
Now, both of these poems have the power of touching the
heart, and both have attained the noble distinction of living in
the mouths of men; yet it would be uncritical to say that the
impression from them is quite the same, or that their reputation
is quite equal. I would not seem to be insensible to the ten-
derness of Longfellow's lines, but something, one feels, is still
lacking to give them that peculiar subtlety of appeal which
belongs to Heine's even simpler song. And I think that, if we
look into this difference, it will appear to depend most of all
upon the greater and lesser depth of that sense of dualism which
the two poets have felt and put into language. There is in
Longfellow's poem the contrast of innocent childhood and old
age wearied of the world; but this contrast springs from the
cumulative effect, so to speak, of time, the refracting mist of
years, and beyond this the idea scarcely goes. The emotion
conveyed is barely, if at all, distinguishable from the senti-
mental pathos of daily, commonplace life. Whereas in Heine
something different and, it must be said, higher, enters. It is
not easy, as it never is in the case of true poetry, to define pre-
cisely where this added touch comes in-whether in the imagery
of the prayer, the lingering cadence of the repeated epithets, or
in some haunting vagueness of romantic irony-but one
instinctively thinks more of the symbolical power of the poem
than of any personal incident or emotion; and this contrast
between the loveliness of youth and the satiety of age becomes
a sign of a conflict inherent in the poet's own heart, nay, if you
will, of the enigmatical dualism, the pathetic or terrible sense
of transiency, that runs through the heart of the world.
Well, let us accept this lower position for the greater part-
but not for all, as I shall attempt to show of Longfellow's
poetry. Let us admit that his peculiar popularity is due to the
fact that he does not require of us any violent readjustment of
our ordinary moods, that he sets our own daily thoughts and


## p. 46 (#272) #############################################

46
PAUL ELMER MORE
emotions to music. Is he not to be prized, and praised, for this?
Like Whittier, he is the poet of the hearth and home, yet with a
curious difference.
It is in accordance with the well-known
tricks of poetic inspiration that the Quaker poet, who was never
married and in his earlier years of manhood had no settled
abode, should have written much of the peace and protection
of the home; whereas Longfellow, who knew all the intimate
joys of the family, should have dwelt more on the forebodings
and memories of loss. We think of Whittier's "Snow-Bound,"
with its snug comforts of the hearth in a New England winter,
or of his "Pennsylvania Pilgrim," that blandest of pastoral
poems. Even his fancies of the future life took on this ideal of
the home, as I have pointed out in another essay. But these
are not the notes of Longfellow. He, rather, in a hundred
various keys sings of the parting of friends; of resignation for
the "one vacant chair"-
The air is full of farewells to the dying,
And mournings for the dead;
of the cry of David in the Chamber over the Gate for Absalom
his son. Even in his child poems there often lurks a shadow
of anxiety:
I said unto myself, if I were dead,
What would befall these children? what would be
Their fate, who now are looking up to me
For help and furtherance? Their lives, I said,
Would be a volume wherein I have read
But the first chapters, and no longer see
To read the rest of their dear history,
So full of beauty and so full of dread.
It is the treatment of these, and other such themes as these,
that has made him the one poet whom you will find in almost
every household, the poet who is really read and enjoyed by the
people; for it is just this sentiment of facile pathos that marks
the real popularity. And here, also, we discover his true part


## p. 47 (#273) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
47
in the Teutonizing and romanticizing-if the word may be
passed-of New England culture. From sources of German
metaphysics, whether directly or indirectly from Fichte and
Schelling and Schleiermacher, Emerson brought in his tran-
scendental philosophy; from the same romantic school came the
impulse that strengthened Hawthorne in his love of the weird
and the subterranean, as also his peculiar sense of solitude in
the world; there Thoreau got his mystic nature cult-always, it
need not be added, with differences caused by other surround-
ings and traditions. Longfellow brought from Germany the
ideal of a world literature which should absorb the best of all
lands; but more than that, he imported into Cambridge the
sentimental note that runs through German letters. He gave
to our poetry the romantic Empfindsamkeit, refined and
qualified indeed by the purity and sweetness and strength of his
own nature.
For there is about his muse, I know not what, a certain
gracious sweetness, which has the power, as was said when he
received his degree at Cambridge, England, "to solace the ills
of life and draw men from its low cares ad excelsiora"-an
allusion which was caught and applauded by the captious under-
graduates. One might analyze the elements of this charm in
part, if it were profitable. He had in the first place the rare
gift of rhythm; his lines sing themselves inevitably, and there
is never, except in some of his hexameters and his blank verse,
any doubt about the cadence, or any feeling that the cadence
does not fit the thought. Lowell was thinking of this easy
rhythmical quality when he wrote of Longfellow on his
sixtieth birthday:
I need not praise the sweetness of his song,
Where limpid verse to limpid verse succeeds
Smooth as our Charles, when, fearing lest he wrong
The new moon's mirrored skiff, he glides along,
Full without noise, and whispers in his reeds.


## p. 48 (#274) #############################################

48
PAUL ELMER MORE
And then Longfellow has the second, and still rarer, gift of
interest, the power of catching the reader's attention with the
first word and holding it to the end. Personally I am not par-
ticularly fond of "Evangeline" and the other longer poems, with
the exception of some of the "Tales of a Wayside Inn" and "The
Golden Legend;" I think his virtue lies elsewhere. But all, or
nearly all, of them have at least the trick of arousing interest.
So the fancy is stirred by those first words of "Evangeline,"
"This is the forest primeval," and kept awake by the shifting
scenes of nature and the sentimental appeal until the very close:
While from its rocky caverns the deep-voiced neighboring ocean
Speaks, and in accents disconsolate answers the wail of the forest.
(Hexameters, by the way, as sonorous and rhythmical as any in
the language.) Not all the great poets have this gift of in-
terest; it is not conspicuous in Milton or Virgil or Wordsworth;
it even goes at times with very inferior qualities; but always it
is an immense aid in enforcing whatever other powers a writer
may possess. It would not be easy to say in just what this
faculty of interest resides. In Longfellow it, perhaps, depends
mainly on his power of making the reader feel at once that
here are his own ideas, almost his own language. Nor are the
artifices of rhetoric wanting. Especially, like Lowell, our poet
had a wonderful gift of metaphor. You would be surprised if
you went through Longfellow and marked the copiousness, the
variety, and the ingenuity of these figures. Even from memory
one might bring together a long list of metaphors and similes
transforming a single group of appearances, such, for example,
as the phenomena of night. One might begin with the first
words of the poem that follows the prelude of his first volume
of collected verse:
I heard the trailing garments of the Night
Sweep through her marble halls.


## p. 49 (#275) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
49
How miraculously that too familiar image expresses the gradual
hushing of the earth as twilight descends! Or, to pass from
sound to vision, there is the even better known stanza :
and the darkness
Falls from the wings of Night,
As a feather is wafted downward
From an eagle in his flight.
Less subtle and less familiar are a dozen other metaphors of the
night that might be quoted, such as the lines in "Hiawatha":
Where into the empty spaces
Sinks the sun, as the flamingo
Drops into her nest at nightfall
In the melancholy marshes ;—
or this more trivial comparison:
In broad daylight, and at noon,
Yesterday I saw the moon
Sailing high, but faint and white,
As a schoolboy's paper kite ;-
or this more aerial fancy:
As a pale phantom with a lamp
Ascends some ruin's haunted stair,
So glides the moon along the damp
Mysterious chambers of the air.
These are but a few of the metaphors I might from my own
memory bring together on a single theme. Most wonderful of
all, perhaps, is that comparison whose beauty has grown dim to
us through too much repetition:
And the cares, that infest the day,
Shall fold their tents, like the Arabs,
And as silently steal away.
(And here again his art is helped by his delicate rhythmical
sense. As an example of the force of little things, let the stanza
4
