be read without the word "as" in the last line, and see how flat
it seems in comparison.)
But
Now metaphors, I know, are a dangerous rhetorical weapon,
and as a rule they are used with extreme parsimony by the
greatest poets; you will find a score of them in Longfellow to
one in Homer. Their tendency is to substitute the amusement
of fancy for the more tenacious vision of the imagination; they
distract the mind ordinarily from its intense preoccupation and
so lessen, while diversifying, our intellectual emotion.
they are peculiarly appropriate to such a talent as Longfellow's,
as they are to Lowell's, and to them is largely due the con-
tinuance and ease of the reader's interest. And apparently
they flowed into Longfellow's mind entirely unbidden. There
is in his published verse nothing better in its way than this
simile jotted down in his diary, January 29th, 1849 :
Another of Emerson's wonderful lectures. The subject "Inspira-
tion;" the lecture itself an illustration of the theme. Emerson is like
a beautiful portico, in a lovely scene of nature. We stand expectant,
waiting for the High Priest to come forth; and lo, there comes a gentle
wind from the portal, swelling and subsiding; and the blossoms and
the vine leaves shake, and far away down the green fields the grasses
bend and wave; and we ask, "When will the High Priest come forth
and reveal to us the truth?" and the disciples say, "He has already
gone forth, and is yonder in the meadows." "And the truth he was to
reveal?" "It is Nature; nothing more."
These are the qualities of thought and manner that have at
once made Longfellow the most beloved of poets and kept him
from full acceptance among the critical.
But there is still
another aspect of his work, which is sometimes overlooked. The
weakness in his genius, as in that of the New England school
generally to which he belonged, was an absence of resistance.
There is a significant entry in his diary, under the date March
22, 1848: "He (Lowell) says he means never to write any
more poetry-at least for many years; he 'cannot write slowly


## p. 51 (#277) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
51
enough." One feels this lack of the inward check in much of
Longfellow; the lines flow from him too smoothly and fluently;
they have not been held back long enough to be steeped in the
deeper and more obstinate emotions of the breast. When the
proper resistance came to him, it was commonly the result of
some check imposed by the difficulties of form, rather than of
his own artistic inhibition. Thus of all his poems, the dramas
in blank verse are about the flattest, and as a rule his power
increases with the intricacy of the rhymes employed. The rule
is, of course, not without exceptions. To some readers the easy
flow of the trochees in "Hiawatha" have the charm of a singing
brook that bubbles over its pebbles all a summer's day. And
occasionally in those free quatrains, whose secret he learned
from Heine, and which seem so easy, but are really so difficult,
he strikes a note that is rare enough in English. So, one sleep-
less night, he makes this entry in his diary: "Nahant, Septem-
ber 8, 1880, four o'clock in the morning," and then turns the
memorandum into verse:
Four by the clock! and yet not day;
But the great world rolls and wheels away,
With its cities on land, and its ships at sea,
Into the dawn that is to be!
Only the lamp in the anchored bark
Sends its glimmer across the dark,
And the heavy breathing of the sea
Is the only sound that comes to me.
When reading these lines, it is easy to understand why Kipling
reckoned Longfellow among the few poets who really knew the
sea. No one who has spent much of his time on some quiet
harbor of our Atlantic coast can fail to be struck by the magic
evocation of that second stanza-the night-bound shore, the
single light low on the water, the sleepy wash of the waves. Or,


## p. 52 (#278) #############################################

52
PAUL ELMER MORE
take this stanza from the poem of meditations before the flames
of a driftwood fire:
And, as their splendor flashed and failed,
We thought of wrecks upon the main,
Of ships dismasted, that were hailed
And sent no answer back again.
Has ever any poet, in a few quiet words, expressed more per-
fectly the awe and mystery of the sea, the sense of that vastness
where so much may happen unseen and unknown of the world?
Such triumphs Longfellow wins now and then in the least
resistant metres, but his greater work, that on which his artistic
fame will depend, is in the more elaborate forms, particularly
in the sonnet. Professor C. E. Norton, who speaks of Long-
fellow with the authority of a friend and a critic, has just pub-
lished a sketch of Longfellow's life, with a selection of his auto-
biographic poems. It is an excellent book for the occasion, but
one could wish that he had, instead, brought together all the
sonnets, with a study of Longfellow as an artist. For ripeness
of style and imagery such a volume would stand easily at the
head of American poetry, and it would show an aspect of Long-
fellow's genius which is obscured by the bulk of his more popu-
lar work. It would place him as a peer among the great
sonnet writers of England. We should have but a slender
volume-there are altogether only sixty-three of the original
sonnets-but of what richness and variety of scope! Here in
brief compass are all the interests of his life. His long
acquaintance with books speaks in those six magnificent sonnets
prefixed to the translation of "The Divine Comedy," and in the
separate sonnets on Dante and Milton and Keats. Was ever
poet more splendidly celebrated than in this sonnet to Chaucer?
An old man in a lodge within a park;
The chamber walls depicted all around
With portraitures of huntsman, hawk, and hound,
And the hurt deer. He listeneth to the lark,


## p. 53 (#279) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
53
Whose song comes with the sunshine through the dark
Of painted glass in leaden lattice bound;
He listeneth and he laugheth at the sound,
Then writeth in a book like any clerk.
He is the poet of the dawn, who wrote
The Canterbury Tales, and his old age
Made beautiful with song; and as I read
I hear the crowing cock, I hear the note
Of lark and linnet, and from every page
Rise odors of ploughed field or flowery mead.
And then by the side of this set the contrasted picture of Shakes-

A vision as of crowded city streets,
With human life in endless overflow;
Thunder of thoroughfares; trumpets that blow
To battle; clamor, in obscure retreats,
Of sailors landed from their anchored fleets;
Tolling of bells in turrets, and below
Voices of children, and bright flowers that throw
O'er garden walls their intermingled sweets!
To write like this is to combine at once the function of the
critic and the poet. Wordsworth has surpassed him, perhaps,
in this use of the sonnet; but no other, I think, has equalled him.
But the literary flavor in this little book of ours would be no
stronger than the other interests we associate with him. Here
in the sonnets to Agassiz and Felton and Sumner, the friend-
ships that made so large a part of his life would find expression;
his tender solicitude for children speaks in "A Shadow" and
"To-Morrow;" his love of nature and the sea finds here its fullest
utterance; his reserved, yet earnest, part in the abolition
movement and the war gives pathetic dignity to "A Nameless
Grave," which Mr. Howells has signalized for its perfect grace
and ease; his reminiscences of travel, which did so much to
overcome our provincialism, give color to "Venice," "The River
Rhone," and half a dozen other sonnets; the sad fortitude of

his old age, as all old age is sad, breathes in this last sonnet he
was to write, his farewell inscribed to "My Books:"
Sadly, as some old mediæval knight
Gazed at the arms he could no longer wield,
The sword two-handed and the shining shield
Suspended in the hall, and full in sight,
While secret longings for the lost delight
Of tourney or adventure in the field
Came over him, and tears but half-concealed
Trembled and fell upon his beard of white,
So I behold these books upon their shelf,
My ornaments and arms of other days;
Not wholly useless, though no longer used,
For they remind me of my former self,
Younger and stronger, and the pleasant ways
In which I walked, now clouded and confused.
These are but glimpses of the infinite riches in little room
that a book of Longfellow's sonnets would offer. They would
set forth to unbelievers an artist of rare tact and power, and
they would be the best commemoration of the sweetest character
that ever revealed itself in rhymes. I know that some have
professed to find a certain solemn self-complacency in Long-
fellow's character. They turn to the selections from his diary
in the life published by his brother, and point with a kind of
patronizing smile at such an entry as this:
December 6, [1838. He was then in his thirty-second year.] A
beautiful holy morning within me. I was softly excited, I knew not
why; and wrote with peace in my heart and not without tears in my
eyes, "The Reaper and the Flowers, a Psalm of Death."
This man takes himself too seriously, they say; he has no
humor. And what then? Why, most of the great poets of the
world were without humor, and have they been any the less
accepted for that? Humor is well in its place, but there is no
reason why we should make a fetich of it, as most of us do in


## p. 55 (#281) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
55
these days. And as for taking his moods and inspiration over-
seriously, there is nothing in Longfellow's diary that in any
way approaches the stupendous solemnity of Wordsworth's in-
troductory notes to his own poems. But the best refutation
of such churlish criticism is in the poems of Longfellow, and
especially in the sonnet form, which from the time of Petrarch,
and of Shakespeare in English, has been the chosen vehicle for
poetic confession.
Turn again to that desired book of sonnets if you wish to
see the mellow sweetness and the strength of Longfellow's char-
acter. I have already referred to his single love-poem, the
sonnet to "My morning and my evening star," which, like most
of such effusions to a man's wife, rings rather flat; but not so
that other sonnet of commemoration. The story of Mrs. Long-
fellow's terrible death by fire and of her husband's efforts to
save her, is too well known to bear repeating, as may seem also
the lines which he wrote eighteen years afterwards, and which
were found in his portfolio, unpublished, after his own death:
In the long, sleepless watches of the night,
A gentle face-the face of one long dead-
Looks at me from the wall, where round its head
The nightlamp casts a halo of pale light.
Here in this room she died; and soul more white
Never through martyrdom of fire was led
To its repose; nor can in books be read
The legend of a life more benedight.
There is a mountain in the distant West
That, sun-defying, in its deep ravines
Displays a cross of snow upon its side.
Such is the cross I wear upon my breast
These eighteen years, through all the changing scenes
And seasons, changeless since the day she died.
I think we need have no fear of the slurs of shallowness and
foppery cast upon a man who carried his suffering so deep in
his heart that the world was unaware of its existence. And it

is pleasant to hear that the woman so honored was worthy
to be a poet's wife. She is described as having "great beauty,
and a presence of dignity and distinction, the true image of a
beautiful nature." Everybody knows the home over which she
presided, the Craigie House, in Cambridge, that looks out from
Brattle Street over what is now a park, named after the poet,
to the river Charles, celebrated by him in so many songs. It
had been Washington's headquarters when he was in command
of the army about Boston, and Longfellow felt the ghostly
presence of his great predecessor:
Once, ah, once, within these walls,
One whom memory oft recalls,
The Father of his Country, dwelt,
And yonder meadows broad and damp
The fires of the besieging camp
Encircled with a burning belt.
Up and down these echoing stairs,
Sounded his majestic tread;
Yes, within this very room
Sat he in those hours of gloom,
Weary both in heart and head.
But there were other memories attached to the old mansion,
which Longfellow did not put into verse. The lady who owned
the house and with whom Longfellow lodged before it came into
his own possession, was a personage that caused a good deal of
wonder and some consternation among the good people of Cam-
bridge. There are probably people still living who can recall
her figure as she sat at the window reading-reading that arch-
mocker, Voltaire, in the original French, it was believed. One
of the legends about her is to the effect that she sturdily refused
to allow the caterpillars on her elm trees to be burned. "Leave
them alone," she would cry; "what are we ourselves but miser-
able worms!"-which would seem to be as much Scriptural as
Voltairean.


## p. 57 (#283) #############################################

57
Here Longfellow lived a large and bountiful life, befitting
one to whom fame and honor and prosperity came hand in
hand, neither reluctantly nor singly. It is mainly in recog-
nition of his character as a man and poet that his centenary
has been turned all over the country into a kind of agape; but
it is partly also because, even better than Lowell, he represents
a beautiful society now passed away and almost forgotten. I
was interested the other day in looking through a pamphlet just
published, which contains the proceedings of the Cambridge
Historical Society-an association of gentlemen and ladies
formed a couple of years ago to gather and preserve local tra-
ditions. The papers are filled with memories of the little
college town to which Longfellow came as a young teacher,
steeped in the literatures of Europe. It would be pleasant to
quote at length from the recollections of Colonel Higginson
and Professor Norton; they give almost a better picture of the
quaint life of the day than Lowell's essay on "Cambridge Thirty
Years Ago." Says Professor Norton in his opening address:
So great are the changes in the town since my childhood that the
aspects and conditions of those days seem more than a lifetime away.
I have the happiness of passing my old age in the house in which I
was born. It has always been my home; but when I was a boy, it was
in the country-now it is suburban and in the heart of a city. Kirk-
land Street was a country road with not a single house on its southern
side, but with a wide stretch quite over to Harvard Street of marsh
land and huckleberry pasture, with channels running through the
thick growth of shrubs, often frozen in the winter, and on which we
boys used to skate over the very site of the building in which we have
met tonight. Down as far as to Inman Square the region was solitary,
while beyond Inman Square, toward Boston, was an extensive wood
of pines with a dense underbrush, the haunt, as we boys used to
believe, of gamblers and other bad characters from the neighboring
city, and to be swiftly hurried by if nightfall caught us near it. The
whole region round my father's house was, indeed, so thinly settled
that it preserved its original rural character. It was rich in wild
growth, and well known to botanists as the habitat of many rare wild


## p. 58 (#284) #############################################

58
PAUL ELMER MORE
flowers; the marshes were fragrant in spring with azalia and the
clethra; and through spring, summer and autumn there was a profuse
procession of the familiar flowers of New England.. It was a favorite
resort of birds, but there is now little left of it fit for their homes,
though many of them still revisit in their migrations the noisy locality
where their predecessors enjoyed a peaceful and retired abode.
But even a greater change than that from country village to subur-
ban town has taken place here in Old Cambridge in the last seventy
years. The people have changed. In my boyhood the population was
practically all of New England origin, and in large proportion Cam-
bridge born, and inheritors of Old Cambridge traditions. The fruitful
invasion of barbarians had not begun. The foreign-born people could
be counted upon the fingers. There was Rule, the excellent Scotch
gardener, who was not without points of resemblance to Andrew
Fairservice; there was Sweetman, the one Irish day laborer, faithful
and intelligent, trained as a boy in one of the "hedge-schools" of his
native Ireland, and ready to lean on his spade and put the troublesome
schoolboy to a test on the Odes of Horace, or even on the Arma
virumque cano; and at the heart of the village was the hair cutter,
Marcus Reamie, from some unknown foreign land, with his shop
full, in a boy's eyes, of treasures, some of his own collecting, some
of them brought from distant romantic parts of the world by his
sailor son. There were doubtless other foreigners, but I do not recall
them, except a few teachers of languages in the College, of whom
three filled in these and later years an important place in the life
of the town-Dr. Beck, Dr. Follen and Mr. Sales. But the inter-
mixture of foreign elements was so small as not to affect the character
of the town; in fact, everybody knew not only everybody else in per-
son, but also much of everybody's tradition, connections and mode of
life. It has been a pathetic experience for me to live all my life in
one community and to find myself gradually becoming a stranger to it.
And what society was gathered together in this village
among the fields and fens! Read the poems written by Long-
fellow on the death of his friends-on Hawthorne, Dana, Sum-
ner, Agassiz, Felton, and I know not how many others. Or,
which of our cities today can show any gathering of men equal
to the weekly meetings of Longfellow and Lowell and Professor
Norton to discuss the translation of Dante? We may, if we


## p. 59 (#285) #############################################

THE CENTENARY OF LONGFELLOW
59
choose, look back upon that life as in many ways provincial;
but how much of the strain and inconsequence of our would-be
cosmopolitan society it lacked. One need not be a New Eng-
lander, or a Harvard man, to join heartily in honoring the poet
who represents the highest and most homogeneous culture this
country has yet produced.
And it is wholesome for us to read and praise Longfellow.
It is not necessary to place his work as a whole beside that of
the greatest poets, or to overlook his shortcomings; but I think
even those shortcomings have their special value at the present
hour. We are apt to take our poets rather solemnly, when we
read them at all, to search for deep and complex meanings;
and in the process we often lose the inward serenity and
unvexed faith which it is the mission of the poet to bestow.
Not the stress of our emotion or our intellectual perturbation
is the measure of our understanding, but rather the depth of our
response to that word of the exiled Dante, when, in the convent
court, he was questioned as to what he sought-La pace, peace.
And Longfellow knew the meaning of that word as Dante used
it. In the sorrow that fell upon him after his tragic bereave-
ment, he found solace, or at least strength, in the daily trans-
lation of the "Divine Comedy." Every lover of poetry knows
the first and finest of the sonnets he prefixed to that work:
Oft have I seen at some cathedral door
A laborer, pausing in the dust and heat,
Lay down his burden, and with reverent feet
Enter, and cross himself, and on the floor
Kneel to repeat his paternoster o'er;
Far off the noises of the world retreat;
The loud vociferations of the street
Become an undistinguishable roar.
So, as I enter here from day to day,
And leave my burden at this minster gate,
Kneeling in prayer, and not ashamed to pray,
The tumult of the time disconsolate
To inarticulate murmurs dies away,
While the eternal ages watch and wait.


## p. 60 (#286) #############################################

60
PAUL ELMER MORE
We need have no fear of paying homage to a poet who wrote
such lines as those. And he himself, if he did not, like Dante
and his peers, build at the great cathedral of song, did at least
add to it a fair and homely chapel, where also, to one who comes
humbly and reverently,
The tumult of the time disconsolate
To inarticulate murmurs dies away,
While the eternal ages watch and wait.


## p. 61 (#287) #############################################

THE SOCIAL EXCHANGE
ROGER N. BALDWIN
Instructor in Sociology in Washington University
It seems to be evident that a larger number of people to-day
than ever before are interesting themselves in the study and the
adjustment of social conditions.
Society seems to be becoming increasingly self-conscious in
all its parts-the awakened consciousness in each part seeking
an harmonious adjustment to all other parts, together with the
fullest expression of individuality. As evidence, we need only
note the growth of labor organizations, the modifications in the
church, and the gain in civic interest.
In our ordinary discussions of social questions, theories too
often get the better of facts. We hear on one side the contention
that classes do not exist, that in our democracy we are all one,-
and on the other side we hear that society is a composite of
classes, naturally and rigidly separated. That there are lines
of social division dependent on wealth, education, race and
family must be accepted as a social fact, without questioning
its justice or desirability. But the fact must be accepted with
the provision, so often omitted, that these class differences do
not affect the common human nature-behind all divisions,
whether natural or artificial. Too often are traits of character
and standards of conduct ascribed by the rich to the poor as a
class, and by the poor to the rich as a class, -standards out of
all keeping with the natural action of human nature, and which
originate in the distorted knowledge one end of the economic
scale possesses about the other. This lack of knowledge is per-
haps illustrated by the old phrase, "poor but honest," which


## p. 62 (#288) #############################################

62
ROGER N. BALDWIN
doubtless originated with the well-to-do on the assumption that
a poor man would normally be a bad man-whereas possibly
"rich but honest" would convey an implication more in accord
with the truth.
The difference in the characteristics of rich and poor
as classes are of course differences in proportion of quantity,
not quality of the same characters influenced by different
environments. The poor boy and the rich boy may experience
the same bad impulses at one period in life to lie, steal, cheat
-but environment will be the factor to determine whether these
impulses will be fostered or eradicated. And the chances are
not so favorable for the poor boy. In the matter of social dis-
crimination it is a surprise to well-to-do people, accustomed to
the somewhat rigid code of those of social pretensions, to find
the same attitude among the poor-the attitude which creates
the barrier to social intercourse between the factory-girl and
the saleslady, the office-force and the factory-force-discrimi-
nations often so minute as to elevate those of "society" to a
plane of social broad-mindedness!
And the realization of this truth is so far from most persons
discussing social conditions, that they seem to treat the whole
class of poor in the light of laboratory specimens, -a sort of
"homo vulgaris" a foreign species.
The attitudes manifested towards private efforts for social
betterment may be roughly divided, in the fashion of omnis
Gallia, into three parts:-first, the attitude of contented indif-
ference, which, while recognizing the defects of the social or-
der, does not question its validity; then that of critical disap-
proval, which, even after experimentation, sees no worth in so-
cial effort; and, finally, that of confident interest, which sees
the only hope for amelioration of social conditions in the di-
rected, persistent and concerted efforts of individuals as well
as of public institutions.


## p. 63 (#289) #############################################

THE SOCIAL EXCHANGE
63
Doubtless the greatest of conscious, active social forces are
those departments of the public service which deal with social
conditions-especially the police, the school and the official
agencies for preserving public health. But omitting these, and
the various public and private organizations for the care and
relief of the sick, paupers, insane, defectives and criminals, there
is a fast-growing field of social labor which aims by private
philanthropy to extend to people of limited means in their daily
lives those opportunities enjoyed by the economically more for-
tunate. It is in this realm that we find the social settlement,
the neighborhood house, the institutional work of churches, the
missions, fresh-air organizations, newsboys' clubs, friendly aid
societies, home libraries and a multitude of other organizations
with a general or special purpose. And it was in this field that
the public library, the public bath and the public playground
but recently sprang up; for only by private effort and experi-
ment is a community first impressed with the wisdom of public
action.
Into this field today are coming a great number of people,
some receiving compensation, more working as volunteers, all
led by a great diversity of motives-some influenced by an over-
done, mushy sentiment (the "dear, suffering, poor people" at-
titude), some by the seduction of the fad, some by an active
conscience, some by well-defined conviction. But behind all the
motives lies a well-grounded reason, to which all would willingly
assent, the recognition that certain standards, opportunities
and ideals should be universal, and that, if they naturally orig-
inate only in a portion of society, they should be artificially
transplanted to its other parts. Thus the spontaneous and nat-
ural products of education and wealth-cleanliness, healthy
mental and physical activity, cordial association, neighborli-
ness-are being carried by means of private organizations to
those portions of society where such products are not, ordi-


## p. 64 (#290) #############################################

64
ROGER N. BALDWIN
narily, spontaneous and natural, where instead grow filth,
license, ill-will, prejudice and ignorance of the finer arts of life.
The chief private organization today which performs the
multitude of activities connected with thus raising the stand-
ard of living and equalizing opportunity is the social settle-
ment, or neighborhood house. The same general work is being
done largely of late by churches and missions. The settlement
idea originated in the English universities between 1875 and
1885, and has since spread extensively throughout Great Brit-
ain and the United States. While the settlement performs a
tremendous variety of functions of an educational and social
sort, from filling gaps where the school system is deficient to
organizing recreative clubs of adults, its essential feature is
the neighborly contact of educated men and women with those
who have had fewer privileges of education and training. Al-
though settlements have already accomplished a very great,
though somewhat intangible, amount of good in the poorer dis-
tricts of cities, and although they have helped broaden the hori-
zon of the thinking world, the artificial feature of residence is
so often subjected to such abuse as to call forth severe criti-
cism on the whole movement. The neighborhood house, which
does not necessarily involve the feature of residence, is prob-
ably a more stable type of institution, for it leaves greater free-
dom for expression by the people for whom the house exists.
The ideal of such a house is that of a social centre a greatly
diversified club-where the naturally associated residents of
the neighborhood may unite for social intercourse, recreation,
education, and for the protection and promotion of neighbor-
hood interests, themselves governing and supporting the insti-
tution without aid. That such conditions of association could
obtain now in the raw, unorganized, constantly shifting, and
very diverse parts of American cities, where most settlements
and neighborhood houses exist, is hardly to be expected-and


## p. 65 (#291) #############################################

THE SOCIAL EXCHANGE
65
aid from educated, interested persons is a prime necessity. But
the ideal is the total elimination of all such aid, and the entire
self-dependence of each institution in its own neighborhood.
In order to approach this ideal, more and more people are
constantly in demand, for it is only by this process, in combina-
tion with the public service, that conditions can be raised to
that state in which a neighborhood can take care of itself.
The universities of this country and Great Britain furnish
every year a large part of the interested "social workers" in
these centres. The spirit of social service has gone so far in
one Eastern university that, quite outside of academic necessity,
over four hundred young men out of two thousand undergrad-
uates engaged in some form of active social work during the
past year. The activities embraced teaching adults in night
schools, entertaining in philanthropic institutions, and con-
ducting boys' clubs or some form of athletics in settlements or
neighborhood houses. The same is true of women's colleges-
where the opportunities include teaching in both children's and
adults' classes, organizing clubs, helping in the conduct of work-
ing-girls' associations, in friendly visiting, and in the work of
home-libraries. Every university which is privileged with a sit-
uation in or near a large city, has these opportunities. Wash-
ington University in this matter is indeed well favored.
It is an opportunity of inestimable value for young men and
women during their cumulative process of college life to better
fit themselves for active, intelligent citizenship. For it is only
by contact and a true understanding of the intimate conditions
of life of all classes of people, that the college man or woman
can attain a point of view comprehensive enough to pass a fair
judgment on social or political questions. Without contact and
understanding the point of view will be warped by a priori
theory and prejudice.

## p. 66 (#292) #############################################

66
ROGER N. BALDWIN
St. Louis is an untilled field, and the laborers are few. The
private philanthropies of the city are probably fewer and more
feebly supported than in any community approaching its size
or wealth in this country. This is due doubtless to the rather
exceptional conservatism of the city. The burden of most pub-
lic and semi-public activities falls upon a small group of citi-
zens.
The stolid apathy generally prevailing here in regard to
social conditions has also one evident reason behind it-St.
Louis slums do not obtrude. Even a noted student and re-
former recently declared that St. Louis has no slums. Perhaps
he meant that there were lacking here those greatly congested
districts of Eastern cities, characterized by huge, overcrowded,
filthy tenement structures. Bad social conditions, when dif-
fused, are not so conspicuous. St. Louis has not, it is true, the
concentrated essence of the slum. But with all its space, St.
Louis has slums, if slums are defined as districts where dwell
the poor and ignorant in filthy surroundings and in over-
crowded apartments. A car-ride north and south on Broad-
way or Ninth street is convincing evidence, and a short excur-
sion through an alley or two would clinch the evidence with a
more intimate knowledge.
The way to betterment in St. Louis, as elsewhere, lies in the
active interest of individuals, an interest which works toward
solution by demanding of the public service greater efficiency
and a larger usefulness and by supplementing municipal efforts
by those special and general private activities of which the
neighborhood centre is both the most diverse and most funda-
mental. Through it and through its interested friends and
through its neighbors, there naturally comes about an exchange
of ideas and ideals, a better understanding, a stimulus to social
and individual well-being, which in time will result in a social
harmony devoid of the necessity of such an exchange.


## p. 67 (#293) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
Instructor in Spanish and Italian, Washington University
The genius of Cervantes has indelibly impressed upon the
world's imagination the figure of the knight errant, ever com-
pelled to pursue the vain shadows of his overwrought fancy and
ever suffering defeat and humiliation because of his want of
adaptation to the hard realities of an unsympathetic milieu.
Don Quijote's extravagancies may provoke our mirth, but at
the same time we are forced to admire the splendid earnestness
of his misdirected zeal. The sympathy one feels with the great
soul of the man makes his adventures, often disastrous and
always futile, seem tragic rather than comic.
It will be pertinent to inquire how Cervantes was able to
make of a madman a character of such universal appeal. Is
the work not a great deal more than the history of a disordered
mind, creating for itself a world of fantasy in the midst of com-
monplace environment? Is not the madness of Don Quijote
really a type of the author's inmost feelings and, more than that,
of the genius of his race?
Of Cervantes' daily life not much is known, except what can
be divined from his works. We do know, however, that his was
an extraordinary genius which somehow failed to make itself
much felt among contemporaries. All his life long Cervantes
drifted from one obscure employment to another, and the mat-
ters about which we have most definite information are his
imprisonments and financial difficulties. A combatant in two
naval wars, a captive in Algiers, a public official holding in suc-
cession a number of petty posts in Castile and Andalusia, he
surely did not lack opportunities for making his way among his


## p. 68 (#294) #############################################

68
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
countrymen. That he failed to do so shows, it seems to me, that
there must have existed in him a fund of idealism quite incom-
patible with the practical concerns of life in other words, a
quixotic strain.
Now I believe that this peculiar quixotic temperament, this
incompatibility with the practical concerns of life, this intoler-
ance of the compromises which must so often be made between
the ideal and the actual, is the most salient trait of the Spanish
national character. If, then, Cervantes is the greatest of Span-
ish authors and Don Quijote the central work of all Spanish
literature, it is because, in a certain sense, Don Quijote is the
most representative Spaniard and the genius of Cervantes the
one best fitted to interpret him.
In the present article I shall endeavor to illustrate, not from
the tale of Don Quijote, but from the actual history of Spain
what I understand the quixotic temper of the Spaniard to be.
An adequate conception of this temper, which constitutes at
once the strength and the weakness of the national character, is
most essential to an understanding of the astounding vicissi-
tudes of the Spanish people.
Everyone is familiar with the traditional Castilian, a frown-
ing, cloaked figure, haughty, cruel and revengeful, inordinately
proud of his ancestral blood, sullen in the presence of his
superiors and tyrannical towards his inferiors, unbending only
in the sanguinary pastime of the bull ring. This picture, it is
needless to say, has been colored by foreign prejudice and
ignorance. The real Castilian is, rather, like the Knight of
La Mancha, a man of gentle feelings. If history shows only too
much evidence for the darker picture, it is because a character
naturally amiable and benevolent, bas been warped through
obsession by an unrealizable ideal.
The real Spaniard may be said to exhibit the chief traits of
the mystic, since he shares with the latter a remarkable power


## p. 69 (#295) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
69
of detachment from the everyday affairs of life, joined with a
peculiar liability to obsession by ideals. Indeed, Spain has
always been noted for its mystics; and a tendency towards mys-
ticism in the mental make-up of every Spaniard may well be
reckoned as a main factor in Spanish quixotism. In some cases,
of course, mysticism, even in its most pronounced forms, is not
incompatible with a rather practical turn of mind and an
effective grasp of ordinary concerns. A striking example of this
phase of mysticism is Saint Teresa de Jesús, one of the most
exalted of mystics and at the same time a woman of wonderful
ability for organization and leadership. The mystic tempera-
ment does not necessarily make its possessors inefficient and
unpractical, but, as it usually entails an unreasoning devotion
to an ideal object, remote from the immediate aims of life, it
follows that whenever there is any conflict between such an
ideal object and immediate concerns the latter are ruthlessly
sacrificed. The true Spaniard is above all an intransigeant;
he abhors expediency and compromise; utterly heedless of the
inevitable consequences, he is deterred by nothing when in pur-
suit of an ideal object.
The ideal objects which have called forth the Spaniard's
devotion are the usual ones of religion, patriotism, loyalty, per-
sonal honor. It will be shown how all of these ideals, right-
eous and beneficial in themselves, were perverted by the quix-
otic spirit, eventually becoming menaces rather than aids to
the growth of a healthy national life. In what follows, the
Spaniard will first be looked at as a patriot, then in his rela-
tions to religion, and finally in his relations as an individual in
society. This arrangement is chosen partly for chronological
reasons: the illustrations of Spanish patriotism are drawn
from the whole field of Peninsular history; those of religion
embrace principally the period of the Catholic Revival; those
of social relations are based mainly on the writer's own obser-
vation.


## p. 70 (#296) #############################################

70
WINTHROP Holt CheNERY
As a patriot the Spaniard has shown a sublime capacity for
devotion and self-sacrifice, but this only in the great crises of
national life, when his soul has been stirred by the appeal of
a lofty ideal. The small but constant sacrifices of individual
preference and comfort which are so necessary to create an
organized and prosperous commonwealth, he is unwilling or
unable to make; but he can, in moments of national peril, rise
to unparalleled heights of self-sacrifice. From Saguntum and
Numantia to Santiago de Cuba, twenty-one centuries, there is
a long succession of battles and defenses in which the combat-
ants did not count the cost. That "discretion is the better
part of valor" is not a Spanish proverb. The same man who
sullenly conceals himself to escape being called upon to per-
form some trivial public duty, and who on election day can not
be dragged to the voting urns, will, if the patriotic impulse be
thoroughly aroused by a great emergency, sacrifice himself or
his dear ones without a qualm. Extravagant tales of the de-
votion of vassals to their liege have a large place in Spanish
literature; a typical one is that of Guzmán el Bueno, the grue-
some story of a commander who, rather than consent to sur-
render a stronghold to the king's traitorous brother, lets his only
son be dismembered alive in his sight. Such a tale, even if it
be not a relation of sober fact, at least illustrates the temper
of the people who applaud it-it has been taken as the theme
of a modern play-and the sort of patriotism which appeals to
their imagination.
Who has not been stirred by the recital of the great
deeds of the Peninsular War, when the Spaniards, with the aid
of the British, expelled the hosts of the mighty Napoleon? A
country disorganized, impoverished, brutalized by every
species of misrule, headed by pusillanimous sycophants who
licked the feet of the usurper, roused itself and repulsed the
master of Europe; bands of undisciplined volunteers, famished


## p. 71 (#297) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
71
and ragged, withstood the veterans who had conquered on a
hundred battlefields. It was the triumph of quixotism, of the
Spanish spirit of unquestioning devotion to an ideal. What
mattered it if every Spaniard perished, if only the sacred soil
of the fatherland might be freed from the defilement of the in-
truders? A less glorious example of the same spirit is still
fresh in the memory of all. Sacrifices, made to recover the
native soil from the usurper, we can applaud, but the blood tax
of the futile Cuban War appalls. Admiral Cervera, steaming
out of Santiago harbor to face the inevitable annihilation of
his fleet, is doubtless a heroic figure but also eminently quix-
otic. Such a fruitless and uncalled-for exhibition of valor re-
minds us not so much of Thermopylæ as of the genial hidalgo
tilting at the windmills.
In the intense mind of the Spaniard, love of country often
assumes, as might be expected, the form of an uncompromis-
ing sectionalism. Regional feuds, quickened by the intransigent
quixotic temper, outlive the conditions from which they sprang
and engender long periods of internecine strife most fatal to
national progress. Lost causes are not disposed of once for
all, but linger on and on as the ideal of a certain section or
class. It is safe to say that there are today in the northern
provinces of Spain thousands of men who, once thoroughly
roused, would cheerfully sacrifice their lives and their all to
seat on the throne of St. Ferdinand the fat and lazy reaction-
ary who on any pleasant day may be seen navigating the canals
of Venice in his electric launch. To his quixotic partisans
this obese and ill-favored old gentleman is no other than the
sacrosanct person of his most Catholic Majesty, Don Carlos
VI, by Divine right absolute monarch of Spain and the Indies.
The intensely localized patriotism of the Spaniard has
curiously affected his religion. The inhabitant of a given section
inherits and cherishes an extravagant devotion for some local-


## p. 72 (#298) #############################################

72
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
ized cult (advocation is the technical word) of a saint, usually
the Virgin Mary. On migrating to another section of the
country, the devout Spaniard does not transfer his worship to
the advocations of the new habitat, but with quixotic obstinacy
clings to his original cult, transmitting it to his children. Thus
the Aragonese everywhere worships the Virgin Mother under
the advocation of the Pillar, in memory of the wonder-working
image of Our Lady on a marble column in the basilica at Sara-
gossa. In any well-ordered family of Aragonese extraction one
daughter will be named Pilar. I mention these localized cults
not to discredit the religious feelings of the Spaniard, which are
apt to be very real, but merely as a further illustration of the
disintegrating effects of a sectional spirit which is absolutely
uncompromising.
The foregoing prepares the way for a more general discus-
sion of the Spaniard's relation to religion, which was to form
the second division of my subject. In Spain, until very recent
times at least, patriotism has been merged in religion; the
natural springs of love for the native land have been forced into
unusual channels by religious appeal. For several centuries
Spain has been pre-eminently the Catholic nation, the particular
champion of the Catholic religion, the chief bulwark of Catholic
orthodoxy. And going further back to the earlier centuries of
christianized Spain, before the Mohammedan invasions, we dis-
cover the same devotion to an ideal of uncompromising ortho-
doxy. At the Council of Nicæa, the first general assembly of
the Christian church, the forces of reaction which defeated the
liberal party were led by a Spaniard, Osius, Bishop of Cordoba.
In Spain, too, we hear of the first persecutions of Christians by
each other on account of differences of interpretation in matters
of faith. Such persecutions were rife already in the fourth cen-
tury. Again in the sixth and seventh centuries under the later
Visigothic monarchs, when the native elements became once


## p. 73 (#299) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
73
more predominant and overthrew most of the institutions intro-
duced by the Germanic conquerors, there was a recrudescence of
religious intolerance. The monarchy became a sort of theoc-
racy, absolutely dominated by ecclesiastics. Fanaticism was
rampant and the unbridled persecutions of the Jews which took
place at that time seem to have been a determining cause of the
invasion of the Arabs and Moors, an event of transcendent im-
portance which for several centuries all but obliterated Chris-
tianity in the greater part of the peninsula.
The heroic struggle of the Reconquest affords a sublime
example of the indefatigable perseverance of the Spaniard
when a great ideal object is involved. A handful of half-savage
mountaineers in a remote corner of Spain bid defiance to the
organized power of the Caliphate. Fomented by religious zeal,
the revolt grows and spreads until all Spain is recovered for
the Cross, and Christian zeal lays the foundations of a world
power. Individual leaders like the Cid (Rodrigo Diaz de Bivar,
A. D. 1040-1099) doubtless were often shifty and sordid in the
extreme, utterly careless of the interests of holy faith when
material stakes were in jeopardy; but I think it must be ad-
mitted that it was the ideal of the re-christianization of Spain
which infused the heterogeneous elements with a single pur-
pose and made a nation possible where everything else tended to
disintegration.
The religious zeal which created a nation, had it always been
directed into such channels, could excite nothing but admira-
tion. In the history of Spain, however, the good that comes of
great movements is generally neutralized by the baneful action
of quixotism-which in religion assumes the form of that arch-
enemy of progress-fanaticism. Scarcely had the Catholic
Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, achieved the union of Cas-
tile and Aragon under their joint rule, when they gave them-
selves unreservedly to the ideal of universal conformity in mat-


## p. 74 (#300) #############################################

74
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
ters of faith, and to this end instituted the Spanish Inquisition.
The Roman Inquisition was already an old and tried institu-
tion when it was brought into Castile. In other countries it had
been generally employed to meet peculiar circumstances or to
aid in the carrying out of a definite political policy. But in
Spain, from this time on, it was to be applied in all its rigor
as an engine for the preservation and purification of the faith.
No one was to be exempt from its action; nothing was to be com-
promised; it was to be the final expression of Spanish intransi-
gence. Grandees and archbishops were haled before its tri-
bunals, and no influence, however potent, saved them from ex-
periencing its rigors. Even the monarch himself seemed power-
less to intervene when matters of faith were involved.
The founders of the Spanish Inquisition have been charged
with the most sordid motives; not the extirpation of heresy,
but the wealth to be gotten from the confiscated estates of
heretics, has been represented as their real object. It is doubt-
less true that economic considerations played a large part in.
the persecution of the converted Jews. The greater number of
these conversos, with characteristic thrift taking advantage of
their new religious bonds to gain power and wealth, naturally
aroused the envy and hatred of their less clever, but more ortho-
dox, Old-Christian neighbors. The confiscated estates of
wealthy Judaizers, in addition to maintaining a host of
officials, helped to replenish the chronically depleted treasury
of the crown. Nevertheless, recent studies of the inner work-
ings of the Inquisition, based on hitherto unpublished or in-
accessible documents, have shown pretty clearly that, after all,
what gave such immense and lasting power to the Holy Office
was neither cupidity nor race hatred, but the Spanish zeal for
an ideal. If we may judge from numerous recently published
letters, the chief concern of even so grasping a monarch as
Ferdinand the Catholic was, primarily, not easily-gotten
wealth but the unification of religious belief and practice.


## p. 75 (#301) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
75
Another example of the Spaniard's intolerance of com-
promise is seen in the expulsion of the Jews. This took place
under conditions of unparalleled injustice and hardship in the
reign of the Catholic Monarchs, after the Jews had dwelt for
centuries in the peninsula. Here again, economic motives
were not lacking to prepare the way for this momentous step.
The consolidation of power in the hands of the Catholic
Monarchs was followed by a rapid development of industry,
due to the cessation of civil wars and the efficient policing of
the country by the Santa Hermandad, a sort of militia created
by Queen Isabella. The Jews, who were almost the only money-
lenders in the country, naturally played an important role
in the launching of industrial enterprises. and by shrewd
deals earned for themselves more riches than good-will.
It was pointed out that the new political organization of the
country brought obloquy upon the conversos, because of their
too great prominence in the new order of things; similarly, the
new industrial development led to the expulsion of the uncon-
verted Jews. But in the latter case, as well, the religious
motive was predominant. It alone can explain the forcible
deportation of a whole people, the greater number of them
humble laborers and artisans whose meagre subsistence would
not have aroused the envy of the poorest. It was but another
example of the ruthless intransigence of the Spaniard-quixot-
ism turned to fanaticism.
That the determining motive in these matters was religious
rather than economic is well illustrated by the fate of the
Moriscos (i. e., descendants of converted Mohammedans) who
were permitted to remain in the Kingdom of Valencia until
1610. The presence of these people was not a menace to the
economic prosperity of any large class of Spaniards. Like the
Jews, they were exceedingly industrious, but unlike them they
had no penchant for amassing usurious wealth. A race skilled


## p. 76 (#302) #############################################

76
WINTHROP Holt ChENERY
in agriculture, they transformed the plains of Valencia into the
garden of the peninsula-the huerta, as it is still called. Their
expulsion meant ruin to the Old-Christian landowners of
Valencia and great economic loss to the country at large, but
their tainted blood rendered them all suspect in the faith and,
in consequence, there was no longer room for them in Catholic
Spain.
More than a hundred thousand souls were cruelly
driven from their native land amid the rejoicing of their fellow-
countrymen, who hailed in this barbarous act the realization
of a great ideal-unitedly orthodox Spain.
Probably the most distinctively Spanish outgrowth of the
fanatic spirit which characterized the Catholic revival in Spain,
and something, moreover, which could hardly be paralleled
elsewhere, save in the caste institutions of Hindustan, is the
extravagant prejudice against Jewish blood-a prejudice which
acquired legal force in the remarkable statutes concerning
limpieza. In the Middle Ages there had been a good deal of
intermarriage between Jews and Moors, on the one hand, and
Christians on the other, but with the growth of the Catholic
sentiment there arose a predilection for unmixed Christian
blood, fostered, no doubt, by the fact that the nobility, as the
representatives of the conquerors, came mainly from the north
where there had been little or no admixture of non-Christian
blood. These Cristianos Vicjos arrogated to themselves
great moral superiority on account of their limpieza (unmixed
blood). When, in the fifteenth century, the conversos
acquired power and influence, there was still greater inter-
mingling, so that a constantly increasing value came to be put
upon the possession of limpieza. Very early in the organi-
zation of the Spanish Inquisition it was made a rule that no one
could serve the Holy Office in any capacity who was not of
unmixed Old-Christian descent. This was done, no doubt, in
fear that collusion between Judaizers and officials with con-


## p. 77 (#303) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
77
verso connections might subvert the principal object of the
tribunal, namely, the punishment and suppression of Judaizing
heresies. Prudential reasons, however, soon dropped out of
sight, and limpieza became just another quixotic ideal. It was
exacted not merely.of the servants of the Holy Office, but of
aspirants for almost any sort of preferment; it was made a
condition of membership in the military orders; it was soon
required for nearly every public office. Its terms were defined
with extreme rigor; the discovery of a single Jewish ancestor
later than A. D. 1391 disqualified one from occupying any post
of honor. A sentence from the Inquisition transmitted to pos-
terity the same taint as Israelitish blood. It did not matter
whether the offense were grave or trivial; the taint was in-
delible and the inherited infamy perpetual. A careless word
could brand with infamy not merely the utterer of it, but also
his remotest descendants, debarring them all from advance-
ment of any sort. In later times, when Judaizers had become
all but extinct in Spain, the looking-up of genealogies became
almost the chief business of the Holy Office; certificates of
limpieza continued to be issued until the final suppression of
the Inquisition in 1820. Even as late as 1859 limpieza was a
prerequisite for a commission in the army, and I believe that it
is still necessary for entrance into the military orders.
Having discussed the effects of quixotism in the Spanish
ideals of patriotism and religion, it remains to take up the
third and last division of the subject: quixotism as it influences
the lives and characters of individuals in their ordinary social
relations. We saw the Spaniard's religious ideal, pursued
with ultra-quixotic recklessness, was orthodoxy-an ideal
which would have made for national solidarity, had the means
employed to advance it been more rational. The social ideal
of the Spaniard, on the other hand, is personal honor (or inde-
pendence), an ideal good in itself; but when allied with the


## p. 78 (#304) #############################################

78
WINTHROP Holt CHENERY
quixotic temper it becomes a disorganizing and de-socializing
force.
The exaggerated sentiment of personal honor, so common
among Europeans, is a legacy of the society of the feudal
period. In those barbarous days when petty warfare was a
regular business and the physical courage and endurance of a
handful of men-at-arms might win or lose a city, there grew up
among the warrior class an overweening sense of individual
importance; the individual knight felt himself to be not a
servant of the body politic, but its master-all things must be
subservient to him. As a Christian he owed certain obligations
to society, it is true, but nothing should stand in the way of
the general recognition of his personal valor and worth. Amid
the confusion of the Reconquest the chivalrous ideal had abun-
dant opportunity to grow and spread. The Castilian conquerors
constituted a superior caste, and it was not long before all
Spanish Christians felt themselves to be a peculiar people-a
race of knights errant. An immoderate cult of personal valor
and independence took its place by the side of religious fanati-
cism as another quixotic ideal.
In some respects the social effects of the new ideal were
distinctly good. An exalted notion of personal dignity begat
courtesy; every man was expected to approach the standard of
the caballero. The generalization of a high ideal of courtesy
makes for social equality. Probably in no other European
country do people of all classes meet and converse on such
a democratic footing as in Spain. Where everybody is polite,
those in the higher walks of life have no need to raise about
themselves bulwarks of reserve and hauteur in order to defend
and preserve their dignity.
In other respects, however, an excessive sense of personal
dignity acts as an obstacle to social and economic progress. A
nobleman can not engage in business, the former prominence

remains locked up in unproductive ancestral domains, while
foreign capital comes in to exploit, for the benefit of foreign

forbid that the ancient names of Spain's aristocrats should be
smirched by contact with such base concerns! They will
rather, like the Duke of Veragua, lineal descendant of Colum-

Coming down to that larger class of people who, having
inherited no lands, are in consequence compelled to work, a
similar spirit is found to prevail among them also. Trade and
labor are ungentlemanly necessities; but being one's own em-
ployer removes the worst of the stigma. As a natural conse-
quence of this individual sentiment, petty shops and factories
multiply, perpetuating primitive conditions elsewhere obsolete
-conditions, moreover, which bring quite as much hardship
and loss to employers and employed as inconvenience to the
general public.
Another evil effect of the excessive accentuation of personal
dignity, and one from which all classes of society suffer, is an
inordinate passion for the outward and material signs of per-
sonal distinction. To be able to drive out every afternoon in a
handsomely appointed carriage seems to be for many Spanish.
families the sum and end of existence. To appear in public
faultlessly dressed is more important than to be well nourished.
A fastidious pulchritude in person and dress is not regarded as
a luxury for the wealthy, but a duty and necessity in every self-
respecting person. Decayed cities, with whole quarters literally
falling in ruin, display on the main streets a dazzling array of


## p. 80 (#306) #############################################

80
WINTHROP Holt CheNERY
shops devoted to articles-de-luxe for the toilet. Laborers earn-
ing twenty cents a day, on festivals manage to show themselves
in exquisitely fitting custom-made clothes; and the very beggar
in the street conceals his patches under an ample capa, which
he drapes about him with dignity worthy of a grandee.
The general lack of thrift which one observes in Spain is a
phenomenon closely connected with the desire for personal dis-
play. The great majority of Spaniards are curiously indifferent
to riches, except as they minister to the needs just mentioned.
To walk when one might drive, to go without fashionable clothes
merely to put by money in the form of savings-these are things
which find no place in the average mind. An exalted sentiment
of personal honor, especially when it is joined to remarkable
indifference in money matters, results in a high standard of
common honesty. In no other country of Europe do travelers
habitually leave their rooms open and their valuables lying
about. In many of the smaller inns, not frequented by for-
eigners, there are neither locks nor bolts; need of them has never
made itself felt. But while the exaggerated self-respect of the
Spaniard begets the most punctilious honesty in private deal-
ings, in positions of public trust, on the other hand, he is apt to
feel little or no responsibility. "Grafts" of every sort go on
practically unchecked, and the most shameless "grafters" are
not always upstart politicasters, but often gentlemen of exqui-
site culture, some of them even littérateurs of distinction.
Honor is thought of merely as a relation between individuals.
The dominance of a quixotic individualism has made all but
impossible the ideal of a well-ordered commonwealth.
The study of the effects of the quixotic temper might be car-
ried into other fields. Abundant illustration of the immoderate
idealism of Spaniards might be adduced from literature and the
fine arts; another division would be devoted to the national
pastimes the theater, the bull ring and gambling. I think,


## p. 81 (#307) #############################################

THE QUIXOTISM OF SPAIN
81
however, that the peculiar bent of the Spanish mind has been
made sufficiently apparent. It will be enough to conclude with
a few words concerning the probable causes of quixotism and
its general relation to other mental states.
It is commonly a thankless and unprofitable task to attempt
to discover and correlate causes of psychic and social phe-
nomena. Even in the most carefully prepared generalizations,
so many factors must be abstracted, or, at best, left indefinite,
that the results are vague and unconvincing. The elements of
heredity and environment which enter into the evolution of the
Spaniard are peculiarly heterogeneous. Equally diverse, also,
are the numerous theories advanced to explain the national
character; the climate, the topography, the blending of races-
everything, in short, has been laid under contribution. Not
seldom, effects are confused with causes; the Spaniard's bigotry,
for example, is represented as a result of his religion, whereas,
viewed from the ethnologic standpoint, his religious intoler-
ance is but the reflection of innate propensities.
In view of the persistence of quixotism throughout the whole
historical period of Spain, it seems safe to assert that it is not a
product of recent environment, but an indelible racial charac-
teristic. The nearest parallels to the unpractical, quixotic tem-
perament we find not in Europe, but in Asia and Africa, espe-
cially among the Mohammedan peoples. In spite of seventeen
centuries of Christian training, the Spaniard, like all of these
peoples, is at heart a fatalist; when not inspired by a quixotic
ideal he is a pessimist as well. Everything seems to indicate
that the Spaniard is more closely related to the white peoples
of Northern Africa than he is to the trans-Pyrenean stocks; he
is probably to be regarded as the purest European representa-
tive of that Mediterranean race which, according to the teach-
ings of recent anthropologists, peopled Southern Europe from
Africa long before the appearance of the Indo-Europeans.

SOME SOURCES OF DISTURBANCE IN THE
MENTAL DEVELOPMENT OF CHILDREN
EDGAR JAMES SWIFT
Professor of Psychology and Pedagogy in Washington University
The changes which the nervous system of children under-
goes after seven or eight years of age are essentially develop-
mental. The brain has now attained ninety per cent, or more,
of its maximum weight, and, though measurements show
further enlargement, this increase is comparatively slight and
wholly inadequate to account for the amazing expansion in
mental capacity which begins at about this time of life. The
length of time required for perfection of function varies for
different organs. Those that are concerned with vital processes
must, of course, mature very early, and with them comes the
organization of the spinal nervous centres essential to their
control. The growth of the complex structures of the cortex,
in which the physiological processes that underlie the higher
mental functions occur, and the differentiation of these func-
tions, belong to the formative period of childhood, and the higher
an animal stands in the evolutional series, the greater the length
of time needed to complete this development. This is required
by the increasing uncertainty of the environment. Animals
that are born fully developed are incapable of sudden adaptive
changes. Their nervous systems are built to explode in definite
ways and the appropriate stimulus is the spark that sets it off.
A ready-made nervous system ceases to be efficient the moment
the environment becomes changeable or the production of
offspring drops below the point of compensatory supply. Nerv-
ous structure must keep pace with growing complexity of


## p. 83 (#309) #############################################

DISTURBANCE IN THE MENTAL DEVELOPMENT OF CHILDREN 83
surrounding conditions; and, as man was born amid the throes
of climatic convulsions, a nervous system with fixed reactions
could not meet his needs. The higher nervous structures--
those which appeared latest in the evolutional process are the
last of all the organs of the body to become functionally per-
fected, and somewhere, hidden within their recesses, lies that
which marks the difference between man and the highest ani-
mals below him.
The incomparable difference in mental capacity between the
child of seven, when the brain has so nearly reached its maxi-
mum size and weight, and the adult, indicates corresponding
neural changes, though our knowledge of the nature of tissue-
anabolism during the growth process is at present exceedingly
meagre. Rudimentary cells must develop and become capable
of functional activity and the labyrinthine system of intercellu-
lar fibers association paths-must be organized. All this
requires time, and it is because of its long period of immaturity
that the nervous system is so sensitive to its environment. The
heads of children living in tenement houses, for example, are
smaller than those of children in healthier surroundings. No
organ while developing is able to offer much resistance to dis-
Continual change in chemical and molecular structure
makes its derangement easy. Its tissues have not yet acquired
the firmness that, a little later, will enable it to hold its own
against the strain which now so easily breaks it down. The
constituents of the nerve cell are in a condition of unstable
equilibrium. Its superabundant energy is over-prone to dis-
charge, and this disruptive tendency makes the inroad of bad
heredity easy, and exposes it, defenseless, to the onslaught of
disturbances incident to growth and development.
ease.
Education is not merely the training of cell-structures
through the inertia of their inherited qualities. The develop-
ment of each individual brain is as truly an evolution as is that

EDGAR JAMES SWIFT
of the race. Investigation has shown that instincts do not
appear until called out by the appropriate stimulus. If the
stimulus is delayed beyond their nascent period these instincts
may never appear. Hodge has found that the "untamable"
ruffed grouse can be domesticated. His investigations prove
beyond question "that a grouse chick hatched in an incubator
or under a hen, from an egg taken from a nest in the woods, is
every whit as 'tame' as a chick of the domestic fowl; and it
remains so until it experiences something to make it 'wild."
Clearly, education, in a large sense, has much to do with the
actualization of qualities and characteristics, even when they
have behind them the impelling force of racial heredity. Unde.
veloped nerve cells are always found in human brains, and
probably no one will venture to assert that they were all predes-
tined to remain half formed and useless. The inference that
their growth was checked by poverty of stimuli or by derange-
ment through nervous disturbances is not unreasonable, espe-
cially when it is remembered that the same condition of arrested
development, only exaggerated, is found in the centres for sense
organs whose use was lost in early life. It is probable that each
area of the cortex has its own time for developing, determined,
in turn, by need for functional activity, though our knowledge
of the manner and time of growth in different parts is still very
inadequate. The critical period, when growth to functional
perfection may be interrupted by nervous disturbances, is, of
course, greatly extended by this prolongation of development.
Any disturbance at this time is disastrous, not alone in arresting
growth, but also in opening paths of nervous disorder. As
nervous energy, like other forces, tends to take lines of least
resistance, these erratic impulses easily become habitual. Func-
tional derangement often continues for no other reason than
because it began. A large part of a physician's work consists

in helping organs to function rightly until the old habit has
been broken and a new one acquired. A better way is not to
let them acquire diseased habits.
"Chorea is essentially a disease of childhood."* "The vast
majority of cases develop between five and sixteen years of
age."† In the great majority of cases, the first attack occurs
between five and ten years of age, and after this, although
second attacks are not uncommon, primary attacks are rare.
Chorea is believed to be an infectious disease of bacterial origin.
If this is true, the disease cannot be inherited in any other way
than as a neuropathic predisposition. There may be a bacterial
invasion of the central nervous system, or even of the cortex,
but these cases are probably infrequent. The disease is believed
to be usually caused by bacterial inroad into some other part
of the organism. As in all other infectious diseases, lowered
vitality, lessening, as it does, resistance, renders the subject
especially susceptible to attack. For this reason the disease
often follows in the wake of measles, chicken-pox, rheumatism,
and diphtheria.
The first beginnings of chorea in children are frequently
misunderstood and thought to be the result of perverseness. A
child, when in school, is seen to be restless and to move nerv-
ously from side to side in his seat. If observed more closely,
the muscles of the fingers or hands may be seen to twitch, and
the child is likely to drop his pencil or slate or any other light ob-
ject which he may be holding. In addition, indications of mental
disturbance may be detected, either before or at about the same
time as the muscular irregularities appear. "These symptoms
consist of a slight loss of memory, and inability of the patients
to apply themselves to their studies as well and continuously
as formerly. Children who were previously of an obedient and

in the corners of the mouth, and in the lips. In more severe
cases the strangest distortions may be seen. "At one moment

The first symptom of chorea to attract attention may be inco-
ordination of voluntary movements. This is most noticeable
in the lack of precision of the hand and forearm. At this stage
of the disease there is always evidence of more or less insuffi-
ciency of muscular control. The child has difficulty in innervat-
ing the required muscles, and when, with a supreme effort, he
finally succeeds, the movement is intermittent and accompanied
by other useless innervations, showing a purposeless diffusion
of nervous energy. Sometimes only one side is affected and the
movement on the normal side of the body is accompanied by a
similar one on the abnormal side.
The arm movements of choreic children are often made with
a flourish. If told to shake hands, instead of putting the hand
straight out, as a normal child does, it is first waved around a
trifle. If the child sits in a chair, with his hands resting flat
on his knees, and counts ten aloud, the fingers will be seen to
twitch, even after he has been cautioned to hold them still. If
told to put out his tongue, it is usually darted out, and, while
out, it often writhes and squirms in a characteristic manner.
When told to put it back, the child withdraws it quickly and
closes the mouth abruptly.
Some slight deflection from the normal disposition is often
the first indication of approaching nervous disturbance. Fre-
quently the change betrays itself only during the excitement of

Case 1.-Girl, age ten years. The child was bright and well-
advanced in school, when without any discoverable reason she
suddenly began to be listless and emotional. The change came
so gradually as not at first to attract unusual attention, espe-
cially as, at first, the remonstrances of her teachers and parents
seemed to have good effect. Later, however, when scolded, she
became so excited that she was removed from school. By this
time her lethargy had caused her parents to consult a physician,
and he found that her left arm and leg were becoming weak.
Within a short time choreic movements developed in the left
side. This proved to be a tedious case of chorea, from which,
however, the patient finally entirely recovered.
Case 2.-Boy, age ten years. Choreic movements began in
the right hand, and soon the entire right side of the body was
affected. Later, his right hand became weak and he dropped
articles which he was holding. His tongue also showed the
characteristic choreic movements. He was taken from school
and recovered, under treatment, in three weeks.
Case 3.-Girl, age nine years. The child had never been
sick before. Her attack began with twitching of her fingers,
and muscular weakness and lack of co-ordination caused her

Frequently, it is the bright, precocious children who show
choreic symptoms. Their nervousness is often a feature of their
brightness. They are able to accomplish a good deal in a short
time, and so their teachers are apt to urge them on, though they
are just the ones who should be restrained in their mental devel-
opment.
Case 7.-Girl, age eight years. For a month, or more, the
child had complained of aching "all over," but the pain was
especially severe in her ankles and knees. Her parents thought
that she had growing pains, and a physician, who was consulted,
prescribed a tonic. She continued to attend school and her
teacher remarked that she was very bright in her studies. Mean-
while she was observed to open and shut her eyes so nervously
that she was taken to an oculist, who at once recognized chorea,
and advised that an alienist be consulted. Three weeks passed,
during which time the eye movements grew worse and, in addi-
tion, general restlessness became noticeable. When she was
finally taken to the alienist, choreic movements were general.
On his advice she was at once removed from school, but, up to
the time of leaving, her school work was of an unusually high
grade and her deportment entirely satisfactory.
Case 8.-Boy, age thirteen years. This boy greatly annoyed
his parents and teachers by a sort of snorting and sniffing. He
was often chided, but without effect. Finally, however, it be-
came so annoying that the boy was taken to an alienist, who at
once detected chorea. During all this time the lad was distinctly
bright in his school work.
At times the emotional side of the malady is prominent, and
the manifestation of the disease may then follow a compara-
tively slight shock.
Case 9.-Boy, age thirteen years.. The attack followed the
extraction of a tooth. Choreic movements were evident in both
sides of the body.
Case 10.-Boy, age twelve years. The first noticeable peculi-
arity was a pharyngeal click. His parents and teachers thought

it nothing more than a vicious habit, and they tried to make
him stop it, but without success. Meanwhile, things did not go
right at school. The boy was nervous and fidgety, and wholly
incapable of concentrating his attention. The most trivial
annoyance would cause him to burst into tears. When seen by
the physician, choreic symptoms were easily recognized.
Case 11.-Boy, age eleven years. This boy had always borne

involved in three or four fights with his schoolmates. Investi-

These misdemeanors were leniently dealt with because of his

however, another exceedingly vicious attack upon a classmate
would have caused his expulsion had not his father asked the
privilege of quietly withdrawing him. In his home, also, the
boy had begun to show capricious irritability and emotionalism,
crying at the least provocation. This case well illustrates the
fact that emotional symptoms of the disease may precede the
characteristic movements. Not infrequently, in school children,
chorea is preceded by a condition of irritability, which is quite
commonly misinterpreted, and, as a result, mental derangement
is liable to be more firmly established.
Case 12.-Girl, age sixteen years. This girl was exception-
ally healthy looking, and intelligent and bright as well, as is so
likely to be true of choreic children. Shortly before the time
of which we are speaking her teacher noticed, with surprise,
that she was falling behind in her work. Her mother, also, had
observed that she was losing her wonted vivacity and becoming
indifferent to her work. Meanwhile, though protesting that she
was perfectly well, the girl began without cause to exhibit emo.
tional outbreaks. For no observable reason she would burst
into tears, and about this time choreic movements began to
appear. At first the motor disturbances occurred only during
her emotional attacks, but soon they became constant, and then
the cause of her trouble was apparent. Removal from school,
with out-of-door life, effected a cure in about two months.

Case 13.-Boy, age six and a half years. This child was in
the kindergarten, and had always been well-behaved at home

would become gentle and tractable. This condition continued
for more than two weeks before choreic movements were pro-

his recovery was complete.
The cases cited above were taken from the records of alien-
ists, and for that reason may be thought to have been uninten-
tionally colored by the physicians' interest in nervous diseases.
Unfortunately, such cases are not uncommon. One physician,
in a letter to the writer, says, "I frequently see choreic children
on the streets and in the street cars. In some instances the man-
ifestations are not very pronounced, but they are readily de-
tected by the practiced eye. There is considerable variety in
these movements, both in their location and intensity. The
disease may be first manifested by slight grimaces, often by gen-
eral restlessness, which make it impossible for the child to
subside into a restful position. In the vast majority of instances,
the presence of choreic movements should be the signal for
removing the child from school."
Conversation with any thoughtful teacher will show that
the condition has not been exaggerated. The following cases,
taken from the writer's note book, were described to him by
teachers:
Case 1.-Girl, age eighteen years. "This girl," says the
teacher, "has been under my observation from the age of thir-

teen to eighteen. During this time nervousness was manifested

Case 4.-Girl, age twelve years. The teacher was unable

The involuntary movements characteristic of these choreic
cases may be caused by bacterial irritation in the sensori-motor
areas of the cortex, though, as Förster* has pointed out, they
are sometimes reflexively produced by peripheral affections.
