In its acute form, chorea readily yields to treatment, pro-
vided the patient is placed under right conditions. The first
requisite, however, is that the nervous system be given complete
rest, and so the child should at once be removed from school.
"I know of many cases," says Weir Mitchell,* "which get well
when they cease to study, and relapse at every new effort to do
school work." It is because of the danger in delay that it is so
important for parents and teachers to be acquainted with its
usual symptoms. "The state of disordered action, whatever be
the essential cause, is sometimes ineradicably impressed upon
the nerve elements, and chronic chorea results."†
Among the diseases of the nervous system are certain ones
for which no pathological alteration in the neural apparatus
has been discovered. While it is probable that neural changes
of some sort also underlie these nervous disturbances, which
improvement in the means for their investigation may yet dis-
close, so far as present knowledge goes they seem to be the
manifestation of derangement of functional control. To this
class of nervous affections belong tics, or habit spasms.
Simple tic, according to Taylor, is a frequent disorder of
childhood, and occurs most commonly between five and ten
years of age, while eighty per cent of the cases fall between the
ages of five and fifteen.
The origin of this motor affection is usually a movement
voluntarily started for the relief of pain, or for some other
good reason. Later, when the irritation which caused the act
has disappeared, the movement, now purposeless, continues,
involuntarily, as a tic.

"Over and over again," writes Dr. Weir Mitchell,* "some
anxious mother will ask you to notice her child on account of
some little trick or gesture in which the child indulges. Then
you will see that it is winking rapidly, or pursing up the mouth,
or drawing it to one side, or, perhaps, that the brow is lifted
at intervals, or a shoulder shrugged, or some forward movement
of the jaw or head is repeated over and over, at varying inter-
vals." Whatever may be the movement, it is likely in time to
disappear and be replaced by another. The child may resist
the inclination, but continued resistance brings discomfort,
while yielding gives at least momentary relief. The trouble is
aggravated by attracting the child's attention to the defect, or
by deterioration in health.
The motor phenomena of tics are the outward manifestations
of a central functional process, and, for this reason, imitation,
to which the young are especially prone, plays an important
part in the propagation of the disorder. If, to this tendency to
imitate, there be added a highly nervous temperament, the most
favorable combination is furnished for the development of the
malady. On this account it is of great importance that children
who exhibit this neurosis be removed from school, so as to pre-
vent the spread of the disease through imitation, for, among
predisposed children, nothing is more contagious. It is not
necessary that the movement be continually present to start
the imitation. Seeing it only once may suffice, since the novelty
of a movement often fascinates children and, by holding their
attention, gives the cue to the imitative tendency.
Home surroundings, as Meige and Feindel have shown,† are
often active exciting factors. Vacillating parents, in whom
inexcusable submission to capricious entreaties alternates with
unreasonable prohibitions, who are tender or harsh, patient or

Case 1.-Boy, age eight years. For nearly a year before the
conference with the physician, this lad had been in the habit
of moving the left half of his face, and it was noticed that when
he was fatigued the spasm was more severe. Upon the advice
of the alienist he was taken from school and sent into the coun-

the movements had practically ceased, though they still occur,
in a slight degree, if, for any reason, his health deteriorates.
Case 2.-Girl, age eighteen years. Until eight years of age
she was strong and well. At this time, however, she became

movements of the body were noticed, with sudden elevation of

the beginning of the disorder, the fingers of her left hand were
in constant motion, the left shoulder was frequently elevated
and rotated inward, her mouth was puckered at irregular inter-

marked the date of her cure. During this interval she also
practiced gymnastics and spent much of her time out of doors.

Migraine frequently first manifests itself in childhood,
though it is not so common as chorea and tic. According to
Gowers, one-third of all the cases begin between five and ten
years of age, while two-fifths occur between ten and twenty. Its
beginning is often preceded by slight pains and spasms, or by
some ill-defined distress in the stomach, which the child is unable
to describe, but which may lead to erratic acts. Not infrequently
the malady is first disclosed by obscured vision, which super-
venes in such a manner as to confuse the child. One physician
reports that two children recently came under his care who,
for a few minutes at a time, were unable to see writing or
figures on the blackboard, but a little later saw them clearly.
Their teachers, not understanding the conditions, thought that
the children were shamming.
The following case illustrates in how strange a manner the
attack may be ushered in:
A girl, ten years of age, and bright in her studies, suddenly
began, one day, to belch and to produce a gurgling sound. She
was reprimanded by her teacher, but insisted that she could
not help it. Within a day or two the same act was repeated,
and this time her teacher was convinced that it was done from
mischievousness. A few days later a similar attack was pro-
longed, and as the child was evidently in distress she was sent
home with a note asking her mother for an interview. Before
the mother visited the teacher the girl had suffered two attacks
at home, and, as in the second of these she was in great distress,

Heredity is undoubtedly an important predisposing factor
in causing migraine, but it is no less certain that, in many in-
stances, the onslaught of the disease is due to exhausting nerv-
ous strain. This may be a partial explanation of the prevalence
of the disease among precocious children. Recurring emotional
excitement, fatigue, or excessive school work, especially when
attended by anxiety and worry, make fertile soil for renewing
the growth of morbid hereditary tendencies.
Authorities disagree regarding the frequency of hysteria in
childhood, but it is probably more common than has generally
been admitted. Clarke* says that the disorder is not infre-
quent in children and, according to Gowers,† one-half of the
cases occur during the second decade of life, while Raneyi
states that a very large proportion of the cases occur at the age
of puberty. Agreement is general that, in cases of juvenile
hysteria, the excess of females, found among adults, does not
occur. The influence of surroundings is seen in the partiality
of the disorder for the only child, as well as in the frequency
with which imitation spreads its symptoms among school chil-
dren. Fear of failure in school work, in the case of timid
children, and continued ridicule by playmates, are important
exciting causes, especially with those predisposed to nervous
instability, and precocious children are particularly prone to
the disorder. Though quiet, retiring, children are not free from
hysteria, it is much more likely to occur in the highly emotional,
because excitable, volatile, natures indicate lack of inhibitory

Inquiry concerning the nature of the disorder does not bring
an answer that is altogether satisfactory. No pathological
change in any part of the brain, has, as yet, been discovered, and
many of its phenomena seem to justify the view that its origin
must be sought in purely psychical conditions. The mental
states which exist in hysteria appear, many times, to be sep-
arated from the regular stream of consciousness; they have
their own groups of associations which cannot be connected
with any of the ideas that constitute the normal consciousness
of the individual. This break in consciousness makes it difficult,
if not impossible, to influence the diseased ideas in the usual
way, and renders the disorder peculiarly responsive to sugges-
tive treatment.

Epilepsy is the most serious of all developmental neuroses,
because of the nervous deterioration to which it usually points.
Clouston puts it next to insanity, in gravity, and adds that


## p. 102 (#328) ############################################

102
EDGAR JAMES SWIFT
"almost all cases of true epilepsy first arise during the growth
and development of the brain."* Spratling's studies† show that
the greatest number of cases occur before five years of age, and
that the next, and almost equally dangerous period, is from
ten to fourteen. After the age of nineteen the disease decreases
rapidly in frequency. Periods of rapid brain growth, and of
physiological change the approach of puberty-are evidently
the dangerous ages for this dread disease.
The small importance which some writers attach to heredity
in the etiology of the malady is probably due to the fact that
their statistics must, necessarily, be based on cases in which
the ancestry was conspicuously bad, and this becomes evident
when one sees that their conclusions are derived from patients,
one or both of whose parents had some clearly-defined disease
of the nervous system. If, in this instance, however, we mean
by inheritance predisposition to serious nervous derangements,
then it is probable that all epileptics inherit the disease. But
the question of greatest importance here is not whether in a
given case it is possible to find hereditary characters by which
the occurrence of epilepsy, or other neuroses of development,
may be explained, but it is rather whether, under such circum-
stances, the disease must appear. Positive assertions on this
point are perilous, but the effect of open air treatment on the
insane, resulting, not infrequently, in their complete cure, cer-
tainly indicate that we have hardly begun to avail ourselves of
the possibilities for thwarting defective heredity, especially in
the young, when recuperative forces are so strong.
The function of the cortical cells is the conservation of
energy generated by the nutritive processes. This nervous en-
ergy, when accumulated in the cell, is available for the further-
ance of the physiological changes which underlie organic and
physical activities, and, evidently, the most important office
*Neuroses of Development, p. 97.
Epilepsy and Its Treatment, p. 50.


## p. 103 (#329) ############################################

of nerve centres, next to storing energy, is its economic
utilization. This is the weak point in the nervous system of
children. Inhibitory centres mature slowly. Action is the first
requisite, and, for this reason, motor centres must develop early,
and energy, uncontrolled, is diffused aimlessly through the
nervous channels, influenced by only one purpose-motion-
for it is by movement that the young come to a realization of
their power.
With the development of inhibition, nervous action is no
longer directed toward mere movement, and now sudden, unreg-
ulated discharges suggest a state of central instability which
may easily become pathological. Epilepsy is characterized by
explosive liberation of nervous energy, without adequate stimu-
lus. As the usual manifestations of the disease are generally
known, it has been thought best to cite only one case, which is
of special interest because of its peculiarities.
A little girl, eight years of age, while standing in line with
her classmates during a recitation, suddenly broke away from
the others and ran around in a circle three or four times, then,
for a moment, looked confused, giggled a little, and became
quiet. When reprimanded by her teacher she insisted that she
did not know what had happened. Although unable to explain
this behavior, her teacher was convinced that the child was tell-
ing the truth. At another time, when school was being dis-
missed, the girl behaved in exactly the same manner. As her
teacher thought that she detected a momentary dazed condition,
she reported the incident to the girl's mother. Soon after the
same act was repeated at home, and has since happened fre-
quently, and become more prolonged and intense, and, on two
occasions the child sank to the floor before the attack was over.
It is now evident that she was suffering from epilepsy. The
alienist, who reported the case to the writer, says that he has
known of several similar instances among school children, and
each time the automatic movements were regarded by the
teacher as evidence of willfulness.


## p. 104 (#330) ############################################

104
EDGAR JAMES SWIFT
The nervous disorders considered in this paper belong to
the group of neuroses which are classed as developmental be-
cause, if they occur at all, they make their appearance during
the period of growth. Half an hour's observation of pupils at
their school work will convince one skilled in interpreting nerve
signs that these maladies have become so common as to menace
our national health, and the significance of this for education
has been too generally ignored. It is in the stress of growth,
when organic processes make the heaviest demand upon the
nervous energy accumulated by nerve-cells, that disorders of
development are especially liable to occur. Before seven years
of age all available energy is needed for brain growth, and, after
that, the adjustment of neural functions makes its claim. Soon,
also, the emotions are rampant and movements are settling
down to volitional control.
Nervous energy is not inexhaustible, and, if it is drawn upon
too largely by the intellect, the bill must be paid from the de-
posit which should remain to the credit of physiological develop-
ment. Happily, racial indolence often refuses to be coerced,
but it is unfortunate that instincts are so frequently the child's
only defense against the errors of intelligence.
One of the most important contributions of physiology to
education is the discovery that the organization of nervous
structures, in the different parts of the brain, occurs at widely
separated periods. Some areas mature very early, while others
are slow in attaining full development; and precocity, instead
of being a source of pride to parents, should be regarded with
suspicion and carefully watched. Growth, whether physical
or mental, is always in danger of arrest, and brain nutrition,
and the establishment of nervous stability, ought to have the
first place in education. During childhood, nervous centres
discharge spontaneously, and there is danger lest the habit of
overflowing be fixed, and hereditary tendencies be converted
into actual disease.

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
Professor of Philosophy in Washington University
An educational system (by which I mean much more than
a school system) is to be judged by its fruits; and a scheme of
secondary education is therefore to be judged by the mental
furnishings and intellectual efficiency of young men and
women at the age at which they leave the high schools. It does
not seem unreasonable to expect that at least that picked part
of the graduates of our secondary schools who enter college
should come provided with the ability to write their own lan-
guage with some correctness as regards spelling, grammar and
the rhetorical proprieties; that they should have acquired some
power of enjoying good literature and some disposition to read
it voluntarily; that they should have some acquaintance with
the commonly accepted standards of literary value; that they
should be familiar with the biblical and classical stories and
legends which constitute the presupposition and background of
English poetry and of a large part of English speech; that they
should have some accurate knowledge of the history of their
own country and of England; that they should have some inter-
est in the more important events and more momentous contro-
versies of their time, and the habit of following the course of
current affairs and of reading more than the sporting, "society"
and crime columns in the newspapers; that they should even
have some personal tastes, youthful hobbies, social or political
or literary or scientific enthusiasms of their own. A good deal
more than this is expected, and is pretty commonly found, in
German or French or Russian students at eighteen years of age.


## p. 106 (#332) ############################################

106
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
If not even these things are to be found in any considerable num-
ber of our college freshmen, it is necessary to conclude that, for
some reason or other, our young men and women are, in general
knowledge, in intellectual interests, and in mental discipline,
from two to three years behind students of corresponding age
in the countries mentioned.
That this is indeed the case that our educational processes
suffer from some such mysterious and unfortunate retardation
-has been emphatically asserted of late by more than one
leader in American education. But these assertions have not
always been accepted at their face value by the optimistic lay-
man or the complacent officials of our schools. The college
professor is often supposed to be as naturally and inevitably
prone to grumble about his students as the sailor is to grumble
about his food; and the complaints of both are likely to be dis-
counted by the outsider. It seems desirable, therefore, that
some inquest into the actual mental equipment of the average
freshman in our colleges should be made, in order to ascertain
how far the now fast multiplying criticisms upon the concrete
results of elementary and secondary education in America are
justified by the facts. Such an inquest, covering the greater
part of the last two freshman classes in Washington University,
is here reported. The examinations to which these freshmen
were subjected were not, for the most part, designed to test
their retention of the specific contents of the text-books they
had recently studied in the high schools; as they had all been
admitted to college, either upon examination or (more usually)
upon certification from schools of good standing, they could all
presumably have reproduced with some fidelity a considerable
part of this text-book material. The tests here recorded were
intended merely to show whether, as a result of the whole edu-
cational process through which they had gone, these young men
and women of an average age of eighteen had acquired in gen-


## p. 107 (#333) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
107
eral anything that could be called the beginnings of an educa-
tion; whether they possessed those fundamental and minimal
attainments which, as I have said, it seems not unreasonable to
expect; whether, in particular, they had acquired any elemen-
tary proficiency in using their own minds and in handling the
materials of expression in English, any measure of healthy
intellectual curiosity, or any spontaneous and intelligent inter-
est in either literature or the world's affairs.*
Since the students in these classes came, for the most part,
from schools in or about St. Louis, one remark ought in fair-
ness to be prefixed to the display of youthful erudition which is
to follow. The situation which this report shows is not a local
situation; it is very nearly a national situation. I have a fairly
intimate acquaintance with several other colleges, scattered
from Massachusetts to California; there is reason to believe
that the entering students in most of them would make no
better showing than those whose efforts are here set forth. And
so far as this section of the country is concerned, the group of
freshmen who received the present tests, it should be understood,
were not the average of their species; they were distinctly a
corps d'élite. For they came from schools which, whatever their
limitations, are confessedly above the prevailing average in the
Middle West; and they had been admitted to a college which
maintains entrance requirements that are understood to be
higher than those of the greater number of its neighbors. More-
over, many of these students came from the families of
professional men or well-to-do or wealthy city business men, and
must therefore be supposed to have enjoyed some intellectual
opportunities in their homes. A similar examination of the
whole number of college freshmen in, say, Missouri and Illinois,
would, I am confident, show results far more remarkable.

The first test was one which has already been applied to
students at other colleges-first, I believe, by President Thwing
at Western Reserve. The results here reported therefore
merely confirm the conclusion indicated by the earlier investi-
gations: that a great proportion of our American students enter
college having only the dimmest and most inaccurate knowledge
even of those narratives and those symbolic types in the biblical
literature which constitute the most recurrent commonplaces of
literary allusion-which, indeed, furnish a large part of the very
substance of the language for all its more elevated or poetic
uses.
It would be superfluous to insist upon the indispensa-
bility of an acquaintance with the English Bible as a pre-
requisite, not only to any study of our literature, but even to any
pleasurable reading of the English classics and to any appre-
ciation of the characteristic values of certain types of English
style.
In the present case, a number of familiar passages, mostly
from English poets, were either slowly dictated to the students
or placed before them on the blackboard, and they were required
to identify and explain the allusions. The test was given to
both the College and the Engineering School freshmen classes
entering in September, 1905-the former class numbering 34
students, the latter 55. The first three of these passages were
also put before one college freshman English class of September,
1906, numbering 28 students. Here are the results:

To be noted in many of the answers is not merely a lack of

3. "Being without influence or following, he was made the
scape-goat for the whole band of conspirators."
It was this biblical metaphor which gave the impulse to the
most wonderful and bewilderingly diversified flights of the
imagination. Very few gave up the question without an
attempt at an answer; but very few, on the other hand, really
knew what the scape-goat was; and the result was an admirable
array of misinformation and wild guesses. It is, of course, not
unnatural that a detail-even though an especially celebrated
and picturesque detail-of the Jewish ritual should be less
familiar than the narrative parts of the Old Testament. Yet
surely nearly every one professing to possess an elementary
education might be expected to have some general knowledge
of the meaning and source of a metaphor so familiar in English
speech. But thirty-four out of sixty-two-or about half of the
answers in the two College classes were considered failures, and
forty-two-or nearly three-quarters in the Engineering class;
and of the remainder, many were rather less than half right. I

There is one large group of answers which proved particu-

of the Higher Criticism. In spite of a great range of variation
in detail, all of this group showed such a degree of unity in the
essentials of their error that any historical critic would infer,
with pretty complete confidence, that they were all variants

some reference to children driven out as a means of getting rid

although in it, too, we are still among the goats: "Scape-goat
has something to do with a marriage ceremony. Two goats were
sent out." Next comes a somewhat fuller explanation, which

single relatively coherent version: "Among the Israelites it
was the custom at a wedding to send two children away from
the house to take away the evil." And when, at length, the fol-
lowing was reached, the Higher Criticism concluded that it had
come upon something closely approximating the original type-
form: "During Biblical times at Hebrew marriage feasts it
was customary to have one or two children who should go into
the woods when the feast began and take all the bad luck from
the bride and groom with them. These were the original scape-
goats." Here, then, was the material for a very neat and con-
vincing piece of critical reasoning based upon internal evi-
dences; but could any external evidence be found for the con-
clusions reached? What was the common source of this series
of kindred erroneous answers? The learned reader will rejoice
to hear that the source was discovered and the Higher Criticism

II.
For a test of their general knowledge of contemporary
literature and of literary standards, the twenty-eight members of
an entering College class in English were asked to name those
whom they believed to be the six greatest living writers of
English (whether of poetry or prose). Fifteen of the class
were unable to name so many as six living writers, one giving
only one name, one giving two, two giving three, five giving
four, and five giving five-while one student, perhaps from a
contempt for the moderns, seemed not to be acquainted with a
single living author. The class as a whole found forty-three
contemporaries who could be regarded as having claims to a
place upon this roll of honor-though five of these 'living'
writers chance to have been dead for periods ranging from two
years to half a century. One or two really eminent names figure
in about half the lists; but even in the better papers sufficiently
surprising associates are promoted into the company of these
celebrities. Here, for example, is a selection that begins well
(it is the only one mentioning Mr. Swinburne), but hardly holds
out to the end: "Swinburne, Howells, Kipling, Doyle, London,
Loomis." Fairly representative lists are the two following:
"Kipling, Chambers, George Aide, H. Smith, Ernest Seaton
Tompson;" "Jack London, Winston Churchill, James Whit-
comb Riley, McCutchen." Taking all the lists together, and
grouping the authors mentioned by the number of votes each
received for a place among the six greatest living English
writers, we get the following accurate representation of the
knowledge of contemporary letters to be found in a College

III.
A student's voluntary reading, in books other than school
text-books, is not only the best index of his taste and literary
judgment, but also, perhaps, the more important source of his
real education. In order, therefore, to discover what American
students of eighteen years-graduates of the best high schools
and academies in this part of the West-read, and how they
estimate what they read, each of the twenty-eight members of
a College Freshman class in English was asked to name, and
give some account of, "the most interesting and valuable" of
the books (other than text-books) that he had read during the

their genre. Of the literary character of some of the others it
is difficult to speak with propriety. It is, then, upon such food
that our young eagles feed.
IV.
The possibility here naturally suggests itself that our mod-
ern youth, if they are weak in biblical lore and in literary knowl-
edge and taste, may compensate for these limitations by a more
lively interest in, a more intimate acquaintance with, the con-
crete facts of history and the social and political issues of
modern life; that if they read newspapers rather than reputable
books, they may after all thereby come to be the more at home in


## p. 123 (#349) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
123
current history and in the movements and controversies of their
own time. In order to ascertain how far this possibility corre-
sponded to the facts, an examination covering chiefly a few com-
monplaces of English and American history, current events and
modern celebrities was set a freshman class of thirty-eight, a
few days after their entering the College, in September, 1906.
I give the questions and a report on the answers:
1. (a) What was the Magna Charta? (b) The Bill of
Rights?
(a) Seven were unable to answer this question; four
answered it incorrectly; twenty-seven answers were considered
correct. To make up this last number, all answers were counted
upon the credit side that showed any approximate general
knowledge of the subject, even though that knowledge were
abundantly mixed with error. Here, for example, are two
answers that passed muster: "The Magna Charta was a treaty
that King John of England granted to the Commons;" "The
Magna Carta was a book of laws drawn up by King John to
satisfy the land-owners." The following paradox, also, was
considered to show an ignorance rather of the language than of
history: "The Magna Charta....changed the government of
England from an absolute monarchy to an autocracy." Among
the incorrect answers, the following gives, perhaps, the most
interesting view of the subject: "The Magna Charta was a
charter given to a company of English people granting them
certain lands and the privilege of living upon it, that is, in
America."
(b) The Bill of Rights was known only to seven (though
English history is, I believe, usually taught in the high schools);
the remaining thirty-one were either unable to answer (19), or
answered incorrectly (12).


## p. 124 (#350) ############################################

124
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
2. (a) Who was Oliver Cromwell?
This was answered not altogether incorrectly by twenty-
seven; it was missed by eleven. In the former category were
placed such answers as these: "Oliver Cromwell helped the
army of England in a number of ways. He taught the soldiers
to sing anthems and hymns on their way to battle. Then too,

when the people had chased James to France." Several of the
students answering incorrectly confused Oliver with that
Thomas whom Wolsey charged to fling away ambition.
(b) Who was Benjamin Disraeli?
Twenty-six knew nothing at all about Disraeli; two iden-
tified him wrongly; ten knew at least that "he was an English
statesman;" though of these, few knew much more, and only one
mentioned his title.
(c) Who was William Morris?
Twenty-two knew nothing of this writer; seven gave some
correct information about him; the remaining nine confused
him with other persons-four, with the financier of the
American Revolution; one, with "the inventor of the cable."
Only one or two knew of his relation to socialism; his immor-
tality appears chiefly to be associated with furniture.
(d) Who was Garibaldi?
The Italian liberator was unknown to thirty-one; seven had
heard of him as having something to do with the history of
Italy.

12. Give the causes and results of the Russo-Japanese War.
Twenty-nine only appear to have attempted to answer this

"Why, that I cannot tell," said he,
"But 'twas a famous victory."

V.
After recording sympathetically his impressions of the arch-
itectural splendors and the outward stir and bustle of academic
life in three or four of our universities, Mr. H. G. Wells, in his
uncommonly thought-provoking book on America, courteously
raises a more searching question in the form of a confession of
ignorance: "I have," he says, "been unable to get any concep-
tion how far these tens of thousands of students in these insti-
tutions are really alive intellectually, are really inquiring, dis-
cussing, reading and criticising." Upon this, the main issue,
the foregoing materials throw, perhaps, only a somewhat
indirect illumination. Yet some ray of light they do indubitably
throw, since intellectual vitality, in the sense that Mr. Wells
indicates, seems scarcely compatible with so extreme a poverty
of elementary information, with so exaggerated an innocence
of literary standards and criteria, and with so great an impo-
tence in the use of the simpler apparatus of thought, and of the
English tongue. But it is worth while to add, upon this point,
a little more direct, if less objective, evidence, drawn, not from
formal written tests, but from fairly extensive observation; and
here I do not confine my generalizations to freshmen. The "tens
of thousands of students," of all undergraduate classes in our
colleges seem, as a rule, not to be engaged, with much zeal or
youthful intensity, in "inquiring, discussing, reading and criti-
cising." Their lack of intellectual curiosity-of the mere nat-
ural love of "finding things out," of the capacity for taking a
lively pleasure in the exercise of the powers of the mind is a
perennial matter of astonishment to many of those who have to
do with large masses of undergraduates. Above all, one singu-
larly misses in the greater number of them (and the exceptions
are as often young women as young men) that which is the
natural and appropriate manifestation of intellectual vitality in


## p. 129 (#355) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
129
youth-enthusiasm for causes, passion for ideas, the riding
of hobbies, the reverencing of self-chosen leaders and heroes
of the intellect. Mr. Lang has somewhere spoken of Oxford as
a place where young men "fall in love with the Absolute." That,
perhaps, is hardly to be expected of our more practical and less
metaphysically-minded youth; and there are those who would
even question whether devotion to that object is, in the long
run, very profitable. But over social issues and the great his-
toric controversies of this most stirring of periods one might
surely expect to find the imaginations of nearly all liberally-
instructed young persons kindled, their feelings impassioned,
their capacity for enthusiasm roused. Yet one finds, but for
very rare and welcome exceptions, a singular phlegm and calm-
ness prevailing, in the presence of these issues and controversies.
Neither jubilant iconoclasts nor ardent reactionaries in religion
testify, in any appreciable numbers, to the prosecution of seri-
ous and whole-hearted, even if immature, reflection among our
students on the ultimate human questions. Hot young Social-
ists are sadly to seek. For though doctrinaire Socialism, or any
other such hopeful and hasty scheme for remaking society and
ending the woes of men, is doubtless a blunder and an illusion,
it is an illusion singularly fitting and amiable in youth;-so
much so that the lack, at a certain age, of any tincture of it is
almost an indecency, a mark of ungenerous meagreness of sym-
pathy and imagination. The absence of this spontaneous
interest in the great contemporary issues-an interest that
should normally express itself in the enthusiastic adoption of
some conviction or other-shows itself (and here I am not
giving impressions, but calling attention to an obvious fact)
quite curiously in the methods of our student debating societies,
and especially in the phenomenon of intercollegiate debate in
America. In the debating societies current questions are, after
a manner, discussed. But there is an entire lack of spontaneity,
9


## p. 130 (#356) ############################################

130
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
both in the selection of questions and in the apportionment of
the sides to be taken by the several members having part in
one of these exercises. If the fact were less familiar it would,
I suppose, appear incredible that young men of university train.
ing should be so indifferent on such questions that their choice
of sides must needs be determined by lot, or by arbitrary nomi-
nation. One might naturally expect that any member of such
an organization would so well know his own view, would care
for it so much, and would have so extreme a repugnance to even
seeming to defend any other, that the debates would simply be
carried on by the successive appearance of voluntary and en-
thusiastic champions of one or the other side. But I suppose
every one knows how little this corresponds to the reality, as
one usually finds it in those stiff, galvanized and essentially
insincere performances called debates. In intercollegiate debat-
ing we have a still more remarkable spectacle. In these con-
tests, enthusiasm for the 'glory' of an institution has entirely
taken the place of enthusiasm for causes; young men, often
of considerable talents, appear before large audiences and, as
representatives of their university, argue with all the plausi-
bility and simulated zeal they can muster, for causes in which,
I suppose, in about half the cases, they have no real belief, or
for which, at all events, they usually have no genuine concern.
It is probably better that we should have even this sort of
serious discussion than none at all; but, at any rate, I
fear that it cannot be said that our system of debating is an
encouraging piece of evidence for the presence among our under-
graduates of a true intellectual vitality or of real intellectual
seriousness. Nor do I think we shall find that evidence, upon
such a scale as we ought to look for, anywhere else.
*
In the main, it has been the purpose of this paper to set
down certain facts for the consideration of those whom they


## p. 131 (#357) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
131
may concern. But it may now be permitted the writer to append
his own haec fabula docet. The burden of this academic jere-
miad certainly is not the degeneracy of our youth; it is that
there must be some serious cause of leakage or of retardation
somewhere in our system of education-especially of pre-univer-
sity education. The students in our colleges-and in particular,
I am sure, those to whom these written tests were given-are,
after all, very excellent educable material; in the main, an
eminently healthy, vivacious, well-meaning and, in many prac-
tical matters, sensible lot of young people, with intellectual
abilities assuredly not below the average, and with all the nor-
mal capacity for intellectual curiosity, for the enjoyment of
the use of their own powers, for sensibility to the infinite inter-
estingness of ideas, and for generous moral enthusiasm. How
comes it, then, that in nearly two-thirds of the number we have
failed to develop these capacities to such a degree as might
legitimately be expected at their age-as, in fact, is a good deal
more commonly found at their age in other communities not
ostensibly more devoted to the education of the young than
are we?
It ought to be said in the first place, I think, that we are in
some danger of being deceived by the extraordinary increase
in college attendance in this country. We are likely to suppose
that this increase means a corresponding increase in the gross
sum of knowledge and 'culture' to be found in our population.
But such an expectation would be unreasonable. The greater
part of his or her preparation for college a boy or girl must get
at home-from the influence of parents, from 'tumbling in a
library' of good old-fashioned books, from stimulating table-
talk, from all sorts of intellectually invigorating conditions in
the domestic environment. Now the increase in college attend-
ance probably means, in most places, that more and more young
people who have not had the benefit of these conditions are


## p. 132 (#358) ############################################

132
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
entering college. A generation or two ago, I suppose, the greater
part of American college students either came from the families
of professional, and therefore more or less cultivated and
bookish, men-lawyers, doctors, ministers, teachers, bankers-
or else were themselves young people of exceptional talents and
ambitions, who had made especial efforts and sacrifices to secure
an education. Now there is a broad and beaten highway, with
little or no charge for tolls, through high school and college to
the bachelor's degree; and many there be that go in thereat,
from all classes of our population. This is a result at which
everyone with any democratic spirit must, on the whole, rejoice.
But the fact remains that, since school and college cannot (or,
at least, have not yet learned how to) give any very intensive
education to boys and girls who get no education at all outside
of school and college, we cannot expect, and shall not get, such
results as might be looked for with a smaller and selected body
of students. To some appreciable degree, in short, the univer-
sities' increase in popularity and in number of intrants doubt-
less is accompanied by a general lowering (not, indeed, of the
nominal requirements), but of the actual standards of knowl-
edge and cultivation and intellectual proficiency presupposed
by graduation.
But, for three quite definite reasons, I do not think that this
consideration goes very far towards accounting for the results
-or lack of results that this paper has set forth. For, in the
first place, the privileges of the higher education are diffused
in only a little less broad and democratic fashion in Scotland,
France and Germany; yet the results obtained in those coun-
tries seem to be much more nearly satisfactory. In the second
place, Washington University, in which these tests and obser-
vations were made, should be exceptionally little affected by
the tendency mentioned. The University has a relatively small
undergraduate body; it maintains a tuition-fee higher than that


## p. 133 (#359) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
133
of any other college west of the Alleghenies, while it also has
an extensive provision of scholarships; so that its students
should be chiefly either the exceptionally gifted and ambitious,
or the exceptionally privileged in domestic surroundings. And,
finally, some of the most impossible papers, in these examina-
tions, were handed in by young people whose home advantages
were, or should have been, unusually great. We cannot, there-
fore, explain the undue intellectual immaturity of the average
of our students by a reference merely to the relative increase
of those whose early education in the family has been defective.
There has, indeed, I believe, taken place a deplorable lowering
of the educational efficiency (both in intellectual and moral
education) of the American family; but this change runs
(though not equally nor proportionally) through all classes
of the population and the families of men of all professions.
This general change is, I suspect, one of the real and important
causes of the results under consideration. It is itself due to
a variety of ulterior causes, partly social and economic, such
as the greater intensity of commercial and professional life,
and the extreme preoccupation of the heads of families in
business affairs. Even the notable increase in gentleness and
tenderness towards children, that new pædolatry that has been
so characteristic a phenomenon of the last half century, has
contributed somewhat, I am afraid, both to the intellectual and
moral undoing of the generation that has been reared under it.
As a result, a larger share of the business of educating the
young (both their minds and morals) appears to devolve upon
the school. The business is one which cannot go by default;
and it is therefore necessary for the school-in other words, for
the educational profession-to face consciously the additional
demands and responsibilities resulting from this weakened
efficiency of the family, and to make definite provision for
meeting them. One of the first means for doing this must, no


## p. 134 (#360) ############################################

134
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
doubt, be in educationally rehabilitating the family itself, by
educating the parents; by organizing, that is to say, a much
more effective, constant and definite coöperation between
parents and teachers than is as yet generally found.
But after all these causes in which the family is implicated
are duly allowed for, there seems to remain a large balance of
deficiency in our educational results, which must be charged to
the schools. There is space to refer only briefly and rather dog-
matically to two features of the situation in our schools which
seem to be most to blame for the singular intellectual backward-
ness of the average freshman.
The first is the fact that the school work has very generally
been overgrown with certain accretions and incidental concerns
that take up the greater part of the pupil's spare time, energy,
enthusiasm and inspiration. The chief of these side-issues is
athletics. The real fault with American school and college
athletics is not that in the actual games young men occasionally
injure their bodies, but that in devoting most of their time to
thinking, talking, speculating and scheming over these games
they stunt and enfeeble their minds. It is what a student does
with his mind outside of the time devoted to the direct work
of the class-room and to physical exercise, that gives the mind
force and fibre and pleasure in its own activity. Class work
in a high school should be merely the starting point for addi-
tional and independent reading and inquiry and discussion, the
stimulus to new and more spontaneous and personal interests.
But how can intellectual interests be expected in young persons
whom we permit, or even encourage, to conceive that the most
significant and engrossing thing in the whole life of their school
is the defeating of a rival establishment in one or another of the
succession of sports that fills the year? The mental energy of
the human animal is, after all, limited in quantity. How can a
youth whose imagination, when left to itself, is given over


## p. 135 (#361) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
135
largely to meditation upon "the prospects of the team," have
much left for the enjoyment of great literature? How can one
whose enthusiasm is spent without measure or restraint in
"rooting for the school" have much surplus ardor to bestow
upon public causes or intellectual hobbies? How can one whose
fixed objects of reverence are football captains and other athletic
celebrities, be capable of a mind-enlarging hero-worship of the
great figures of history or literature? All this predominance of
athletic interests is natural and healthy enough in a boy at
ten or twelve years of age; it is neither natural nor healthy at
eighteen, for it signifies arrested mental development. Athletics
do not, of course, constitute the only time-consuming and
thought-absorbing distraction in the schools; with them go
school politics, an excess of social diversions, "class spirit,"
school fraternities (where school authorities are weak enough
to permit their existence) and other unprofitable preoccupa-
tions. Taken together, these things seem so to fill the leisure and
consume the energies of the majority of the students as to crowd
out nearly all more serious concerns and more significant activi-
ties. One great cause, in short, of retardation in the mental
development of our young people seems to lie in the hypertrophy
of side-issues in the schools.
But the facts exemplified above also point to serious weak-
ness in the actual teaching, the class-room work, of our second-
ary and lower schools. The questions put to these groups of
freshmen covered, it is true, chiefly matters not ordinarily the
subjects of text-book instruction. But it is, of course, a truism
that the more important result of education is not the retention
of certain information, but the acquisition of certain forms of
power and skill and discipline. And a reading of the examina-
tion papers of these freshmen shows an astonishing failure in
the schools to produce this kind of result. Some two-thirds of
these students neither know much of anything, nor (so far as


## p. 136 (#362) ############################################

136
ARTHUR O. LOVEJOY
thought and expression go) can do anything skillfully or neatly.
They can not spell, nor punctuate, nor construct well-knit sen-
tences, nor logically dispose their material in paragraphs. They
have no ability to discriminate between reputable English words
and colloquialisms or vulgarisms. What facts they remember
they remember in a confused, muddled, unorganized fashion.
They are particularly deficient in powers of analysis, and in
ability to keep in mind any even slightly complex scheme of
relations or of interdependence between the parts of a subject.
Where they have learned certain rules or principles, they are
still unable to apply them in practice; so that college instruc-
tors in English, though they find a considerable number of
freshmen who can glibly repeat rules of grammar or punctua-
tion or paragraphing, are still compelled to devote half a year
to drilling these young men and women of eighteen in the very
rudiments of English composition. In short, the majority of
our college intrants, though they may have quick, adaptable
and active minds, certainly have entirely undisciplined minds.
Their methods of thinking and of writing can only be character-
ized as sloppy. They show no signs of ever even having heard
of such a thing as a qualitative standard in intellectual work-
of neatness and precision and order, to say nothing of what the
mathematicians signify by 'elegance.' And all this betrays a
serious vice in the methods of teaching in the schools. It is
manifest that qualitative standards of accuracy and form are
not sufficiently insisted upon in the pupils' work, and that there
is not enough persistent, exacting, rigorous drill in doing things
'just so,' and in getting things 'just right,'-in the constant
application of principles and rules to particular cases, in think-
ing straight and in expressing thought precisely. This prelim-
inary work of drill and discipline ought to be all accomplished
by the time the student comes to the university; for it is the
characteristic function of the schools, while it is not appropriate


## p. 137 (#363) ############################################

THE MIND OF THE FRESHMAN
137
either to the special functions of the university or to the subject-
matter of the greater part of the university studies. But in
point of fact a year or two must be devoted in the college course,
not to making students acquainted with subjects, but to train-
ing them in methods, -in the art of using the simpler faculties
of their own minds, of expressing themselves decently in their
own language, and of doing all their work with some care for
accuracy, form and thoroughness.
It seems, then, a fair conclusion from effect to cause, that
the secondary and middle schools are, as a rule, in this day
and generation, far too easy-going, too tolerant of slipshod work,
too often forgetful of the prime essential in the intellectual edu-
cation of the young-that they shall not only know at least a
few things well, but also have learned to do a few things well.
Though our fitting schools do not seem inordinately successful
even in providing the minds of a large fraction of their students
with the requisite mental contents, it would still appear that
they pay so much attention to content as to neglect training in
right mental processes.
But it is not, after all, to a consideration of theories about
the causes of the situation presented in the early part of this
paper, that I desire chiefly to invite the reader's attention;
rather to a consideration of that situation itself.
It is, at all
events, not a necessary or unavoidable situation. There is no
reason, physiological or psychological, why healthy young per-
sons of eighteen, after twelve long years of subjection to highly-
elaborated educational processes in a civilized modern commu-
nity, should have so little to show for it all. If this, at least, be
generally recognized, we may hope that those in charge of our
schools will have the wisdom to devise the proper remedies and
the courage (for it will need courage) and the persistency to
apply those remedies.


## p. 138 (#364) ############################################

SOCIALISM*
E. BENJAMIN ANDREWS
Chancellor of the University of Nebraska
If I have any special qualification for discussing socialism
it is that of sympathetic opposition. I was once as near being
a disciple of Rodbertus as I could come without baptism into
the church. I thought I saw in Rodbertian socialism, socialism
scientifically wrought out and applied, a remedy for the most
glaring social evils.
In time and upon study, however, the system which had
seemed to me so desirable grew to look quite otherwise, the
difficulties connected with it assuming vaster and vaster propor-
tions, until in my thought they towered above and outnumbered
those necessarily bound up with the present order. I was thus
converted to the opinion that society has greater hope of reform
on the general basis of individualism than by flying to the un-
known though inevitable ills accompanying a socialistic régime.
None the less I retain for the manner of thinking which so
long engaged me a respect which most of its opponents do not
have. I can not condemn socialists as is commonly done. Not
only are the majority of them true philanthropists at heart, but
their ideas and ideals are worthy the most careful thought.
Indeed, one not versed in Marx's reasonings can hardly be
called fit to discuss any leading social theme. I rejoice in
socialistic study and agitation; vast net good must issue from it.
Few can help going far with the socialists in their indict-
ment of present industry. Much wealth without merit, much
poverty without demerit, cross purposes in production inducing
* Abstract of a lecture delivered before the Washington University Association,
December 6, 1906.


## p. 139 (#365) ############################################

SOCIALISM
139
glut, scarcity, waste and injustice; idle wealth that might be
supporting industry, but is not; enforced idleness and poverty;
fraud in trade, and the tyranny and menace of corporate power;
these and other such evils exist, and they are grave. Usually,
socialists do not overmagnify them. If such distresses are
curable, all wish to know how.
Most wise people, whatever their style of social thinking,
sympathize with socialism in wishing the public power, when
necessary, to extend more or less its economic function. Now
and then, of course, some one still denounces it as dangerous
per se, regardless of place or circumstance, e. g., the municipal
ownership of street railways. It is hard to see why this is more
a peril than the owning of schools or of water or gas works by
cities. There is nothing alarming, either, in the proposal that
government should purchase and work mines. Public owner-
ship of mines is in continental Europe the regular thing, as is
the public ownership of railways.
If the question were merely whether or not it is desirable for
government to possess and administer certain indispensable
public utilities, it would not be worth discussion. The thought-
ful people are few, however opposed to socialism, who do not
believe that government will in time take over a great many of
the productive agencies now in private hands. Government
might go a long way in this without even an approach to social-
ism. Socialism would not be reached until all material instru-
mentalities for the production of wealth had passed into the
state's hands, or at least so many of them that individual initia-
tive in its present and historic form had ceased its functions.
Nor need anti-socialists have any radical quarrel with social-
ists over Fabianism. Call the Fabians socialists, if you will,
they are of a very innocuous stripe. The three great tenets of
orthodox socialism, that economic conditions absolutely deter-
mine social, moral and political ones; that profits are always


## p. 140 (#366) ############################################

140
E. BENJAMIN ANDREWS
and inevitably iniquitous; and that therefore all productive
property and occupations without exception ought to be in state
hands, Fabianism denies. What is unfortunate in Fabianism is
that it seems to look upon state economic activity as rather the
normal order, to be departed from or not insisted on only when
personal initiative is clearly better. I should urge just the
reverse that individualism ought to be the standing presump-
tion, to be resolutely trenched on when it fails, provided public
functioning is certain to do better, but always to be preserved
and acted upon as the normal. I deem this difference in points
of view rather important; but public ownership has not yet gone
so far that a Fabianist policy and a rational individualism need
at present clash.
The Socialist Millenium. Here, at least, I fear I, for one,
must part company with socialism, that mode of thought in its
orthodox form seeming to me to proceed upon presuppositions
wholly unscientific.
One of these is the assumption that the estate of the human
species on this earth can be radically bettered-made over, per-
fected-so that sin and misery shall in effect disappear. This
I judge to be faith only and not reasoned conviction. In com-
mon with all healthy men I share such faith, but I can not exalt
it to the level of dogma or of scientific prediction. Its basis is
primarily religious, though it derives more or less support also
from the progress which humanity seems to have made in the
past. Each of these grounds is worthy of recognition. The belief
in question is, therefore, not to be ranked as mere credulity. It
can not, however, on the other hand, be accepted as a scientific
premise. We hope for a city of God, to be established right here
in this actual earth; but if you ask for a demonstration that it
will come, I can give you nothing of the kind, and no one can.
On the contrary, also, the scientific data all seem to point
the other way. There is a sadly convincing induction, familiar


## p. 141 (#367) ############################################

SOCIALISM
141
to students of social history, that whenever material betterment
comes to the ignorant poor, as through a rise of wages or the
cheapening of bread, it is speedily checked by increase in popu-
lation. The principal consideration that forbade me to find in
socialism a panacea was the insight that, granting to socialism
as a purely economic resort all that is claimed for it, which was
further than I could go; supposing socialism to bring to pass
economically all that Rodbertus, Marx or any apostle ever
claimed, the community would soon be again suffering from its
old-fashioned ills through the irrational multiplication of the
species. However great economic prosperity may come through
socialism or otherwise, the sort of humanity we have had to deal
with thus far, the only kind of men we know, will use such
prosperity to multiply perniciously, to develop a submerged
tenth, an ignorant and vicious proletariat, whose woes will be
so great as again and very soon to lower the average weal well
toward zero.
I am not forgetting what socialists say against this. Marx
would have us believe that economic welfare inevitably begets
intellectual and moral sanity. I could never see any proof of
this. It is another bland and thoughtless assumption. Innumer-
able cases of physical plenty could be cited, taken from all the
historic centuries and from the most diverse conditions of race,
climate and society, which are not followed by mental or moral
uplift. I instance the good-for-naught Anglo-Saxon men in the
most prosperous parts of this country-without large families,
rarely sick, able to command good wages if willing to work, yet
forever in rags, without a cent's worth of property or credit;
e. g., Joe Beal, in Sam Walter Foss' poem, "He'd Had No
Show:"

If, therefore, we wish to go upon a basis of fact and not upon

phant, any permanent deliverance from the principal woes that
are upon us.
Two Types of Socialism.-Permit me now to distinguish be-
tween two types of socialism, scientific and popular, for, to some
extent, what I have still to say can be made more relevant by
treating them apart.


## p. 143 (#369) ############################################

SOCIALISM
143
Socialism of the reasoned sort, as worked out by Rodbertus
and in part by Marx, is at first sight very attractive. It meets
many objections on which the more popular doctrine has no
word. Thus, it is anti-communistic, not proposing that all
men's services shall be rewarded alike irrespective of ability and
fidelity, but aiming to mete out rewards in an equitable manner.
By the device of labor-time money, essaying to make costs and
prices exactly agree, it proposes that any person shall command
for a day's toil products costing the community precisely the
amount of time-toil units to which he has been subjected in
the day's work. Not "to all men alike;" but, "to every man
according as his work shall be." This system, patiently elab-
orated by Rodbertus, is so perfect and workable at many points
that it tempts one to hail it as a real herald of the bliss for
which we sigh. I have elsewhere analyzed this scheme, finding,
to my regret, that in practice it must after all either utterly
break down or else produce its little benefit at the cost of
greater ills than it removes.
Much more interesting is everyday socialism, the type now
disturbing modern politics by ominously gaining converts daily.
I may dub it "loose socialism," "state socialism," or "the social-
ism of the man in the street." Increasing hosts of intelligent
men and women who never heard of Rodbertus, impressed by
the working of trusts, of the postoffice and of public ownership
in this country and elsewhere, jump to the conclusion that the
complete generalization of such ownership would usher in a
millennium. Their cry is "only substitute Uncle Sam for Uncle
John Rockefeller, Uncle Pierpont Morgan and all such, and the
thing is done." Rodbertus' careful planning for equity they
ignore as superfluous labor.
I can not help regarding such people as under a complete
hallucination. There is much history to prove how enticing
and ideal a plan may look when viewed in the block, yet fail


## p. 144 (#370) ############################################

144
E. BENJAMIN ANDREWS
hopelessly under the searching test of experience. Compare the
expected with the actually realized, (a) in the freeing of the
Spanish-American republics from Spain; (b) in the introduc-
tion of free trade in Great Britain, and (c) in the abolition of
slavery in our South.
Results of Socialism. -The best substitute for trial by fire is
an analysis of fire and of the bodies which are consumed or puri-
fied thereby. Can we not, by a parallel process, analyzing the
system and also the nature of the human subjects on whom it is
proposed to try it, ascertain what the result would be were the
state made employer of all, and popular socialism actually put
to the test? Let us attempt this.
Frankly, socialism, as popularly advocated, would be likely
to promote reform in a few not unimportant particulars. It
would perhaps at points act more happily than any less drastic
change.
The abolition of business corporations would, of course, end
gambling in domestic stocks; but there would still be Canadian,
Mexican and European stocks and bonds, and also for a long
time our own government bonds, which last would be likely
to fluctuate under the proposed regime as never before.
Produce gambling would also be left to flourish. In a word,
the gambling which connects itself with speculation would be
little affected by socialism of the rough and ready sort.
Under such socialism the evils of scarcity and glut might be
obviated by the careful gathering of statistics telling supply
and demand. It is to be remarked, however, that, owing to
diversity of seasons and weather and to people's changing tastes
and wants, the evils referred to can at best be only a little
diminished, while what can be done in this way trusts are now
rapidly bringing about.
Where Socialism Fails. The proposed socialism would not
prevent crises. Crops may fail or immense conflagrations or


## p. 145 (#371) ############################################

SOCIALISM
145
epidemics occur as now. Ups and downs in the value of money
may also take place. Any improvement in these respects is
as likely without socialism as with. Strikes and lockouts will
also still be possible. Friction between capital and labor is
in nowise certain to be abolished by making the public the
sole employer. The form of the boss system must continue
under socialism. At present wage scales are rarely drawn
up by the actual owners of properties. Agents, managers,
superintendents, do this. Such functionaries would still be
required, even under socialism, and one of them and the
workers under him might disagree upon wages as now. The
general public, owning all things, would likely enough insist on
high wages, but then as now, a special group of laborers may
demand remuneration which can not be conceded. giving rise to
a strike on the one hand or a lockout on the other. The strife
may then spread from establishment to establishment, enforced
idleness, under-production and want ensuing, as is so unfor-
tunately the case at present. I can not see how socialism is to
assure any appreciable improvement in matters of this sort.
State socialists assume that their establishment of society
would annul profits, interest and rent. It would not, unless
private property of every kind and degree were done away with;
it is not proposed to go so far as that. The fee of consumable
property, residences and their furniture, pleasure grounds, per-
sonal libraries, kits of tools, clothing, and so on-the fee, in a
word, of all property which is no longer capital, but has been
passed over to consumers for consumption purposes-the fee of
all such property is to remain in private hands.
But as surely as this is so, loaning and economic rent will
to some extent continue. Savings banks will, of course, be
owned by government, but is there to be no inducement for peo-
ple to deposit in them, no rate per cent? And if, residence land
or even houses being privately owned, the fashion shows favor

for certain wards, streets or corners, I should like to know what

Profits, too, would stay. Suppose that by some art or device
you or I can sell given products cheaper than the state mills,

In the main, no doubt, profit-taking under that name will
cease, but if industry is to go on strongly, the same or similar
winnings must be permitted in the form of salaries. Supervis-
