BOOK REVIEWS
STUDIES IN MODERN GERMAN LITERATURE.
STUDIES IN MODERN GERMAN LITERATURE: By Otto Heller
Ph.D. Ginn & Co., 1905.
The scope and quality of Germany's contribution to litera-
ture in the second half of the nineteenth century are strikingly
out of proportion to the scant attention paid to it by American
critics. In no other European country has the realistic impulse
shown in the theory and practice of Zola, Ibsen and Björnson
received such interesting and consistent application to the
drama as in Germany. Yet the attempts of criticism in this
country to understand and evaluate these realistic experiments
of our continental cousins have hitherto been largely confined
to book reviews, on the one hand, and to general treatises upon
German literature, on the other. Such discussion has suffered,
therefore, either from the fugitive nature of its appearance or
from its subordination to the purpose of more extensive ex-
position. Mr. Heller's Studies in Modern German Literature
are a successful attempt to supply in part the lack just noted.
By confining his attention to three main topics, Sudermann,
Hauptmann, and Women Writers of the Nineteenth Century,
the author has space for a fruitful and suggestive discussion of
essential features of latter-day German literature.
Recognizing the dangers that beset the would-be applier of
the historical method to the tasks of literary exposition and
estimate, Mr. Heller confesses in his preface to the deliberate
use of a more frankly impressionistic form of criticism. While
this may occasionally challenge objection by its subjectivism,
it certainly escapes the more serious faults of barren theorizing
and of the obscurity, for the general reader, involved in all
adequate discussion of the sociological springs from which
literary movements flow.
The author's main purpose is informational. He attempts
to make clear to the foreign reader the substance, aim and


## p. 189 (#415) ############################################

STUDIES IN MODERN GERMAN LITERATURE
189
artistic form of representative works, chosen from each of the
three fields mentioned.
In Sudermann and Hauptmann we are asked to recognize a
supplementary duality, like that easily traceable in the ninth,
thirteenth and eighteenth centuries in the Heliand and Otfrid's
Evangelienbuch, in the Nibelungenlied and Gudrun, in Wol-
fram von Eschenbach and Gottfried von Strassburg, in Klop-
stock and Lessing, Goethe and Schiller. Even in the nineteenth
century our critic associates in a similar sense such names as
Kleist and Körner, Uhland and Hauff, Heine and Lenau,
Grillparzer and Hebbell, Reuter and Scheffel, and others.
While this grouping is subjective and perhaps fairly open to
doubt in detail, it is in the main quite in harmony with German
literary facts.
Hermann Sudermann seems to our critic the masculine,
resourceful, and persistent member of the literary duumvirate,
whose other partner, Gerhart Hauptmann, is a highstrung,
exquisitely sensitive and essentially feminine nature, that
readily responds to every passing impression. Sudermann, we
are told, is first and foremost a satirist. Like satirists of all
climes and in all ages, he is always frankly subjective. He
cares not to show us the world as it appears to his senses, but
to draw a convincing likeness of that which things suggest to
his inner experience. Sudermann is, therefore, though often
called modern from top to toe, no thorough-going naturalist;
for he takes no pains to keep himself or his philosophy out of
his work. He is a catholic-minded cosmopolitan, who is also
at bottom a good German, city-bred, sagacious, sophisticated, -
a man impelled to criticize men's motives, especially the stereo-
typed moral notions unthinkingly accepted from each genera-
tion by its successor. His chief purpose is to construct an
effective criticism of the basis of current morality. His chief
tenet is that morality, like anything else of real value, must
be earned, not inherited. He is firmly convinced of the exist-
ence of latent moral forces, whose free development would raise
human nature far above the second-hand morality of our present
every-day life. His work as a dramatist is addressed primarily
to the liberation of these forces. This didacticism is always


## p. 190 (#416) ############################################

IGO
BOOK REVIEWS
apparent. While it is usually subordinated to the purpose of
the dramatic artist, it occasionally becomes painfully evident,
when mere theatricalities take the place of organic and con-
sistent dramatic development. Mr. Heller denies that Suder-
mann is a poseur; critics have commonly called him such,
through mistaking his artistic limitations for a vain display
of his own ego. In each of the poet's works we hear an in-
variably sincere and more or less vigorous sermon. The poet
believes, therefore, in the efficacy of teaching. An examination
of works like Frau Sorge and Es war convinces the critic that
in the opinion of Sudermann a strong will may come out
victorious in the fight with the threatening consequences of
heredity or of past error. The author of Es war approves the
active, forceful and impelling characters in human society, and
for the weak, the passive, the drifting creatures, who are victim-
ized by the strong and masterful, he has only sympathy, pity,
blame or contempt. In this we see, of course, a reflection of
the superman ethics of Nietzsche.
Recognizing the insularity of social groups and the natural
friction and irreconcilable differences between them, Suder-
mann favors the efforts of individuals to develop to the utmost
their natural gifts, even at the risk of breaking utterly with
the class in which they were born. The struggle of the indi-
vidual thus circumstanced becomes the subject of numerous
dramas like Die Ehre, Heimat, and Sodom's Ende. Mr. Heller
rightly sees in Die Heimat (Magda) an even clearer embodi-
ment and justification of Sudermann's ethical views than in
Die Ehre. For the individual here achieves the right to develop
beyond the narrow pale of the convictions and prejudices of
her class at the cost of a complete rupture with her father.
The slight motivation of Magda's return to her father's house,
which precipitates the sequel, is rather unduly emphasized by
Mr. Heller; for the real motivation of the sequel lies farther
back in the girl's development of her native talent beyond
what her class regards as permissible. The subsequent details
are relatively insignificant. Here, as in all the later works of
Sudermann, salvation for the individual who breaks with the
class assigned him by birth, lies, not in sterile repentance and


## p. 191 (#417) ############################################

STUDIES IN MODERN GERMAN LITERATURE
191
return to the old home, but in resolutely facing and meeting
the new situation after frankly avowing one's own past and
present attitude to life. It means an out-and-out abandonment
of the conscience and moral standards of the social group to
which the individual had hitherto belonged. Even Das Glück
im Winkel, with its resignation of the heroine to a humdrum
existence in the company of her elderly, unattractive, though
generous-hearted husband, which seems at first blush a distinct
turn of Sudermann in favor of the accepted morality of society,
proves upon closer inspection to be quite in line with the views
just outlined; for Elizabeth's dismal choice and lot are clearly
the result of her own weakness and failure to belong to the
heroic type of exceptional individuals, whose superman morality
Sudermann frankly approves. Here perhaps more strikingly
than elsewhere the dramatist maintains the thesis that freedom
belongs by right to the strong and bondage to the weak.
After a clear and suggestive consideration of Sudermann's
chief works-his Johannes, Die drei Reiherfedern, Johannis-
feuer, Das Ewigmännliche, Es lebe das Leben, Der Katzensteg,
-Mr. Heller finds the art of the East Elbian simple, direct,
vital and quite devoid of all truckling to the dominant literary
taste of the hour. He is not at all blind to the weaknesses of
the poet-his so-called theatricalities. He concedes the dra-
matist's love of highly colored settings that occasionally serve
no good purpose in the economy of his work. He regards as
inartistic the injection of the author's views into the run of the
plot through the mouth of some representative, like Count
Trask in Die Ehre. He also regrets an excess of speech-making
and other declamation. But he is quite right in saying that
were Sudermann posing as a "naturalist," these defects would
have a significance for the critic wholly lacking in case of a
writer who is frankly not a follower of the cult.
Now, we have seen that Sudermann is a preacher. He is
quite out of concert with the world as it now is. The eternal con-
flict between the views, beliefs, customs, ideals, and institutions
of yesterday and the imperious claims of the life of the present
generation is the general theme of all his work. He is no
pessimist. He believes society capable of regeneration under


## p. 192 (#418) ############################################

192
BOOK REVIEWS
the leadership of the strong individual. Hence, his insistence
upon the claims of the superman's views of social obligation.
Mr. Heller traces a progress in the art of Sudermann, from the
class conflict as in Die Ehre through the self-assertive struggle
of the individual, as in Die Heimat, to a third phase as in Es
lebe das Leben, where the strength of the individual is mani-
fested primarily through self-abnegation and only secondarily
through self-assertion. Sudermann's criticism of life is, on
the whole, constructive. Only in Sodom's Ende and in Der
Sturmgeselle Sokrates does Sudermann ply the lash of reckless
destructive satire. He is prevented from this by a gift of genial
humor that mellows his views of life and art.
In Gerhart Hauptmann, Mr. Heller recognizes a powerful
writer, whose genius is essentially lyric. Hauptmann's leader-
ship in the so-called "naturalistic" movement and his persistent
use of dramatic form have led many critics in Germany and
elsewhere to overlook the fundamental feature of his natural
endowment, and to pronounce him the greatest living dramatist.
The present writer shares Mr. Heller's view as to this point.
Equally satisfactory is his formulation of the abiding service
of naturalism to the higher realism, into which it is now merged,
as the "accomplished reunion of dramatic art with actual life
after a long and disastrous period of separation."* Then fol-
lows an allusion to the essential tenets of "naturalism," includ-
ing the use of dialect and jargon, environment through the
epic detail of expanded stage directions, etc. The difficulty
encountered by a peculiarly lyric temperament, like Haupt-
mann, in adjusting itself to the tenets of this new art code is
clear. Furthermore, Mr. Heller finds in Hauptmann an
essentially feminine nature, highly sensitive to impressions,
gifted with a subtle yet sterile receptivity, prone to brooding
pensiveness, and handicapped by a certain debility of the will,
which leaves the poet in doubt on major questions of life and
art. In other words, Hauptmann, unlike Sudermann, has no
definite and consistent philosophy of life which he cares to lay
before the world in his books. And the bewildering variety
*Cf. Martin Schütze: The Services of Naturalism in Life and Literature. Sewance Review, ΧΙ
(1903), pp. 425-443.


## p. 193 (#419) ############################################

STUDIES IN MODERN GERMAN LITERATURE
193
of artistic methods which he has employed first and last, is good
proof of the contention that his apprenticeship to "naturalism"
was rather a matter of chance than of conviction. His aс-
quaintance with Arno Holz and Johannes Schlaf, whose real-
istic sketches impressed the poet as the "acme of consistent nat-
uralism," doubtless did much to determine the crassly natural-
istic form of Hauptmann's first drama, Vor Sonnenaufgang
(1889).
Our attention is called to three conspicuous defects in
Hauptmann's dramas. First, the characters are stationary,
i. e., they seem incapable of any real development. They appear
in very realistic guise at the outset; but our interest in them
soon flags through their sameness. Second, these characters
show in the course of the play little capacity for developing
ideas beyond the original scant stock with which they begin.
This they turn and turn again until it seems like the proverbial
fixed idea that proves their undoing. Mr. Heller regards this
poverty as the reflection of a similar lack in their author. The
attentive student of Hauptmann's art is readier to assent to
these strictures than to the third, urged by our critic, who
reproaches the poet with failure to exhaust the dramatic possi-
bilities of his chosen material. To demand inevitable causal
connection between the succeeding parts of the picture of life
presented by a convert to "naturalism" is to expect him to
violate the fundamental postulates of naturalism itself. For
the "naturalistic" artist is concerned, not with cause and effect,
but with sequences. Mr. Heller's criticism seems, therefore,
directed not against Hauptmann's art, but against "naturalism"
as a theory of art. It is, of course, legitimate to pick flaws in
the theory of extreme "naturalism;" it seems, at the same time,
but just to discriminate between the man and the theory. It is,
for instance, indubitably true that Hauptmann's plots are
weak. This may be the result of incapacity for constructive
work of this sort; it may, however, be the result of the artist's
strict adherence to the "naturalistic" theory of dramatic art.
For a dramatic plot implies a deliberate selection of parts, not
found by the "naturalists" in nature and, therefore, not
tolerated by them in art.
13

BOOK REVIEWS
Mr. Heller urges that Hauptmann's alternation of method
from naturalistic to symbolic and back again since the com-
pletion of his six early realistic plays, makes the curve of his
future development problematic. He supports this view by an
exposition and discussion of all the numerous works of the
poet, "naturalistic" and symbolic, from 1889 to the present.
Lack of space forbids more than a passing word emphasizing
the thoughtful and stimulating work in these pages. He be-
lieves Hauptmann, as a natural lyrist, to be at his best in the
fairy play (Märchendrama) because here the mood counts far
more than the plot. He points out that the really great passages
of all his dramas are lyric. He omits to call attention to
Hauptmann's resemblance to Goethe in this particular. While
admitting the atmospheric strength of Hauptmann's historical
plays Die Weber and Florian Geyer, he finds both plays weak
in action and unskillful in the use of masses of men. He cer-
tainly falls far short of the standard set by Schiller in Wallen-
stein and Tell. He regards Die versunkene Glocke as the high-
water mark of Hauptmann's efforts hitherto. Without dwelling
much upon the symbolism of the piece, Mr. Heller praises the
wonderful beauty and naturalness of the lyric passages in
which it abounds. Here, too, he finds proof of the poet's real
strength and of his limitations. In all his attempts to vivify
nature, to endow her with life and soul, Hauptmann shows
wonderful mastery; he is not equally successful in using the
symbols of nature to tell a story of human life. He sees nature
in her entirety, whereas human life appears to him in fragments
which he has never yet succeeded in fitting together into an
even fairly consistent whole. We share our critic's generous
praise of this lover of nature, alive to all her charms and calls.
We recognize wonderingly and admiringly in the author of
Die versunkene Glocke the highly gifted lyric poet, filled with
a subtle appreciation of nature's relation to man and to art,
and the musician, whose mastery of that marvelous instrument
his German mother tongue is unrivalled by that of any other
modern writer. Such wondrous outbursts of delicate fancy
and pure melody in verse have scarcely been heard in the work
of any other dramatist since Shakespeare.'

In concluding this brief notice of Mr. Heller's book, we must
omit all mention of his third essay, entitled, "Women Writers
of the Nineteenth Century." It must suffice to say of it that it
is the product of the same serious and intensive study of the
subject-matter as that whose fruit we have in the author's dis-
cussion of Sudermann and Hauptmann. The three essays are
felicitously expressed in idiomatic English that would do credit
to a native writer. They are pervaded by an atmosphere of
genuine humor that adds a distinct charm to the book. The
whole is a critical performance of great merit and a substantial
contribution to American scholarship.

STARR WILLARD CUTTING.
UNDER PONTIUS PILATE.
UNDER PONTIUS PILATE: Being part of a correspondence
between Caius Claudius Proculus in Judea and Lucius
Domitius Ahenobarbus at Athens, in the years 28 and 29
A. D. Translated and edited by William Schuyler [W. U.
1874]. Funk & Wagnalls Company, New York, 1906.
Mr. Schuyler throws down the gauntlet to Dr. Osler, and
celebrates his advent into the ranks of the grandfathers by
writing a novel; nor does it seem likely that the reputation won
by his former works will be diminished by his latest perform-
ance. Already reviews of a highly appreciative sort have
appeared in local and other newspapers and periodicals, and
perhaps no recent book has attracted more attention in the
city. There is no doubt that the popularity of the author has
much to do with this, but the book itself is likely to entertain
the general reader and to prick the attention of a reviewer.
The book is hardly to be classed as a novel. It describes in
epistolary form some of the chief events in the narrative of the
gospels as they became known by report or by personal knowl-
edge to an officer on the staff of the Roman procurator. Of the
twenty-four letters, which form as many chapters, all but one
are supposed to have been written from Judea. The eleventh
alone was sent from Athens by the Stoic friend, Domitius. The


## p. 196 (#422) ############################################

196
BOOK REVIEWS
fiction that a Roman is writing for a Roman is fairly well
maintained; strict accuracy in this regard is not to be required,
but at times it seems a little strange that the absent corre-
spondent should be expected to know so much about angels,
devils and the Passover. The atmosphere of the Roman prov-
ince is created by a banquet scene and by gladiatorial games,
but the author does not dwell upon these, thinking, perhaps,
that our interest in such things has been dulled by recent
fiction. After the great popular success of Ben Hur and Quo
Vadis, it would be unwise for a novelist to try either a chariot
race or a banquet scene.
In a familiar correspondence we do not expect a book style,
and the author has warned us in his preface that the language
will be colloquial. We are led to suspect, however, that the
prefatory note was not written after the book was finished, as
it should have been, but before. At any rate, it does not square
with what the author has actually done, for he is not always
modern in his dialogue, nor consistent in his treatment of the
Scriptures. Such expressions as "I would speak with you"
(p. 36), and "She whom you seek is not here" (p. 35), are not
the modern colloquialisms we were promised. Again, when he
says, "This night thy soul shall be required of thee" (p. 59),
we have the antiquated style of the King James version. We
are glad, however, to emphasize the fact that we prefer Mr.
Schuyler's practice to his promises in the preface; it is de-
cidedly better that he did not do as he intended. The force of
the thought is greatly decreased if taken out of its biblical
form.
While speaking of style, it is timely to point out the dif-
ficulty of being colloquial without being commonplace. It was
the claim of Wordsworth that the language of poetry should be
the language of common life, and in this he taught a significant
lesson. His poetry, which at first reading seems to be so
unlike our daily speech, is, on closer examination, found to con-
sist of the most familiar words, while familiar collocations are
avoided. The truth is that few words are so condemned to
vulgar use as not to be redeemable for literary purposes; but
there are many invariable sentence forms that, in a serious


## p. 197 (#423) ############################################

UNDER PONTIUS PILATE
197
context, fall like a discord upon the ear. Mr. Schuyler offends
occasionally. We can not help feeling a twinge of protest
when he says: "The Nazarene completely bewitches the women;
they all lose their wits over him." (p. 156). Again, "John the
Baptist?" I asked Herod: 'Is that the prophet who made such a
sensation last year at the fords of the Jordan?"" It sounds a
little tame when Proculus goes up to Jesus at the trial and
says, "I will do all I can for you." This is, perhaps, a matter
of taste; and we throw the responsibility of deciding it upon
the instinct of cultured readers.
With regard to the translations from the Latin, we are
inclined to think that the author could have done better him-
self. Some are neatly rendered, but several are indifferently
done, and one, on page 203, is rendered quite senseless by the
introduction of a foreign idea. For a barbarous spelling,
focmina (p. 156), and for a slip in the Latin, Mater mala, filia
deteriora (p. 185), we must, presumably, blame the author.
Minor inaccuracies occur that do not greatly impair the
literary value of a book of this sort, but may be interesting to
those who are curious on the question of historical truth. The
imposing and ceremonious address at the beginning of the
letters was not customary among intimate friends, who said
simply, for example, "Cicero to Atticus, greeting." A patri-
cian like Claudius would hardly have been found upon the
staff of a petty procurator like Pilate. The cognomen Proculus
was not used by the historical Claudians. The incident of the
fifth letter could not have occurred in Alexandria, as there
were no propraetors in Egypt, and noble Romans were for-
bidden the country; it was directly under the Emperor and
governed by a prefect. Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus-the
name of Mr. Schuyler's hero-happens to have been the name
of the Emperor Nero before he was designated as the heir of
the Cæsars; the Domitian family was for generations noted for
cruelty and vice, and it seems a little strange to find a member
of it represented as a pious Stoic recluse. The Cyrenaic
Aristippus would hardly have enjoyed himself in such good
Stoic company as we find him in (p. 173). The use of the
emetic, twice mentioned as if it were a commonplace of Roman


## p. 198 (#424) ############################################

198
BOOK REVIEWS
life (pp. 59, 61), is no more typical of Rome than the orgies of
a New York reprobate are of America.
The most striking feature of Mr. Schuyler's book, when com-
pared with recent fiction of the same class, such as Diomede
the Centurion, or Silanus the Christian, is its extremely ortho-
dox tone. It seems as if its treatment of the Scriptures would
be equally satisfactory to a Roman Catholic and a Christian
Scientist, while other authors have taken one side or another
upon the questions of the higher criticism. One who knew
nothing of the author might well imagine our book to have
been written by one who had not heard of the results of modern
scholarship; by internal evidences it would be hard to guess
whether it was a work of the seventeenth or the twentieth
century. It seems that Mr. Schuyler has chosen to reserve the
best of his knowledge, and simply tell the old story in new form.
It is to be remarked that Epicureanism is no more represented
from its intellectual side than is Christianity. Proculus is an
Epicurean only as any pleasure-seeker may be called by the
same name. Had he been a philosopher as well, we might have
found the miracles discussed in relation to the physical theories
of Democritus, or God's providence in the light of the Epi-
curean doctrine of the indifference of the gods. From the
point of view of the more thoughtful reader, the letter of the
Stoic is the most interesting of all.
N. W. D.

THE WORK OF THE ASSOCIATION.
On the whole the work of the Association has been conducted
this year on much the same lines as in 1905-06. The activities
of the Association have however been hampered during the year
by the early resignation of the President, Mr. I. H. Lionberger,
and later in the year by the resignation of the Secretary, Mr. R.
S. Starbird, who was compelled in January, on account of ill
health, to relinquish his work in the Association, to which he
had devoted much time and enthusiasm. Mr. Lionberger's place
was filled by the election of Professor W. W. Keysor, and Mr.
Starbird's by the election of Professor J. F. Abbott.
The experience of last year in holding lectures at the Uni-
versity buildings, together with the fact that the previously
poor street-car service has during the year degenerated to a
point which apparently marks the lowest stage of car-service
inefficiency, has led to the plan of holding nearly all the course
lectures in one place, the Academy of Science building. That
this has been a good move is evident from the fact that the
attendance at the course lectures has increased remarkably
from the beginning to the end of the season, in some cases tax-
ing the capacity of the lecture room.
The single public lectures
have as usual been held at various places in the city, and in
spite of the eminence of the speakers and the high character of
their addresses, have been attended by lamentably small
audiences. Convinced that no better lectures have been offered
to the St. Louis public, either this year or previously, the Sec-
retary is at a loss to understand the apathy of the members of
the Association, or to offer suggestions for improvement.
The coming of Professor Eugen Kühnemann, Kaiser Wil-
helm exchange-professor in Harvard University, for a course of
lectures on German Literature, was the occasion of a reception
tendered him by the Association in the galleries of Memorial
Hall, on the evening of February fourth. The very inclement

weather no doubt kept away many members of the Association
who otherwise would have attended. Arrangements were made
whereby members of the Association were admitted to all of
Professor Kühnemann's lectures.

MCMILLAN HALL.
Notable among the events of the University year was the
laying of the corner-stone of McMillan Hall, the University's
first dormitory for women, on October 20, 1906. A large com-
pany of graduates and friends of the University assembled for
the occasion. Prayer was offered by the Rev. Dr. McKittrick,
Chancellor Chaplin made brief remarks, and Mr. W. K. Bixby
gave the principal address. After the stone had been duly laid,
a reception was given by the Alumnæ Association in the British
Pavilion, in honor of an event so significant in the history of
the higher education of women in the West. Mr. Bixby's
address was as follows:
"The name to be borne by the structure of which we lay the
corner-stone today means so much to me, so many memories
cluster about it, so much of the inspiration of my life is asso-
ciated with it, that I may be pardoned if the personal note
dominates in what I have to say.
"This building is designed to crown with completion a plan
left unfinished by the death of William McMillan. The im-
mediate donor is here, carrying on with cheerful devotion and
simple modesty the work of helpfulness which she has set her-


## p. 209 (#435) ############################################

MCMILLAN HALL
209
self to do.
The burdens she has lightened, the sorrows she has
assuaged, the joys she has brought to joyless hearths, the lives
she has broadened and the ambitions she has made possible of
realization-these things may be known some day when she can
no longer prohibit it. This hall is erected by her in behalf of
one whose memory is to her the dearest of all earthly possess-
ions, and to the fulfillment of whose purposes her own life is
consecrated.
"William McMillan was an unusual man. He was a devoted
husband and father, and the most loyal of friends.
He was
known in the business world as a man of large affairs, possessed
of great ability, sterling integrity and dominating force of
character. His name rarely appeared in the public prints, and
never with his consent. Forceful and gifted with marvelous
foresight in business, he was in private modest and retiring,
with a peculiar horror of anything which seemed like heralding
his own good deeds. It was a cause of regret to him that it was
not possible to withhold from public knowledge his generous
gift to Mary Institute, and many were the devices to which he
resorted to hide, even from those nearest to him, his many deeds
of charity. How great was the number of these, and how well
planned, will never be known. They are engraven deep upon
the hearts and held sacred in the memories of those whom he
befriended. The large fortune which Mr. McMillan acquired
he did not especially value for himself. He loved work for its
own sake. He liked to deal with great enterprises, and his
ability to handle them grew with their magnitude. But wealth
came to him as an incident. His greatest pleasure came from
doing for others, and, although he helped wherever help was
needed, yet the cause of the higher education of women seemed
especially to appeal to him. The reason assigned by him to me
for making no charitable bequests in his will was that it was
his intention to devote most of his time for several years to
come to careful, systematic investigation of the ways in which
he could do the most permanent good, especially along educa-
tional lines; and only his death prevented him from carrying
out his plans. He was early to foresee the significance for
women of the changing social and economic conditions of our
14


## p. 210 (#436) ############################################

210
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
age, and was eager to assist in opening for them the door to
their newer and broader life. Masterful as he was among men,
there was much that was beautifully feminine in his nature.
Early in his career, and as he was able, he contributed to the
education of women. His benevolences of this character mul-
tiplied with his means. He gave largely, quietly, and where
possible, secretly, to institutions for the education and advance-
ment of women. He himself defrayed the cost of the academic
and collegiate schooling of young women in growing numbers as
the years went on and his wealth increased. They are to be
counted by scores. Some of them he had never seen. He fol-
lowed their training with solicitude, aided them with helpful
counsel, and watched their subsequent careers with pride.
Among the greatest pleasures of his later years was the reali-
zation that by his assistance horizons had been enlarged and
intellects enriched, and a way to independence opened. Be-
ginning thus, it was inevitable that Mr. McMillan's work in this
direction should grow. He wanted to do something for the
community in which his active life had been spent, and to which
he owed so much. His gift to Mary Institute followed. And
now Mrs. McMillan extends that work, and the two plans com-
prehend the whole field of scholastic instruction, beginning with
the child and ending with the well-rounded, mentally disciplined
woman.
Here, then, is the plant. Here are gathered the materials
for the working out of these lofty purposes. It is a memorable
day for the University. It is a memorable day for the
community. It is no time to discuss co-education. What
may be the precise method employed in working to the sought-
for end is of minor import. All over the land woman has come
into her own. As she has seized her opportunity, so will she use
it, and fashion to her own best needs the methods to be employed.
She has come into the economic and intellectual activities of
the world by a pathway which she herself has aided in building.
In the long run she will for herself very largely compel the
methods which shall be employed for the equipment of her
younger sisters for the world's struggle, and there the matter
may confidently be allowed to rest. Mistakes there have been


## p. 211 (#437) ############################################

MCMILLAN HALL
211
and will be, but the path ever tends toward the goal. We hear
much of a lack in young women of the tender bloom of feminin-
ity which charmed us in their mothers years ago. We stand con-
victed of the seeming decay of chivalric delicacy in men. These
things may or may not be altogether true, but, if true, they are
of the day and hour. They are a malodor blown hither by the
breeze, and which the breeze will waft away. But this we
know-the atmosphere of business life is clearer, purer, and its
manners better, for woman's participation in it, and the home
certainly becomes no less dear when the wife is the clear-headed
and valued counselor, or the sister a helpful comrade. We
should protest against the flippancy which would assail this as a
materialistic age. Every age has been and will be materialistic
in so far as it must supply material needs, but this age is fully
as much spiritual as material. Look about you! There is not
a building in this majestic group whose name is not associated
with the name of some man supposedly given up to material
things. As never before in the world's history, wealth realizes
its responsibility and looks upon itself as a stewardship, to be
administered for the building up of the race. In this realiz-
ation lies something of the hope and promise of a happier and
better future, and toward that future we may look in buoyant
assurance that from this high plane humanity will never with-
draw."
The new McMillan dormitory will probably be completed in
time for occupancy at the beginning of the next college year. It
contains rooms for about one hundred and ten students, besides
dining rooms, reception rooms, and a gymnasium. The gym-
nasium will be used by all the woman students of the Depart-
ment of Arts and Sciences, and the dining room will be open to
students who live in the city and wish to lunch there. Tempo-
rarily, some of the rooms will be occupied by certain of the
married professors. The University will not furnish the new
dormitory, but leave each occupant of a room to furnish it for
herself.
The cost will be approximately $300,000, all of which is
given by Mrs. William McMillan. The style of the architecture
of the building is the same as that of the other buildings of the


## p. 212 (#438) ############################################

212
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
University, a form of Tudor-Gothic, and the materials will be
the same as formerly used. The body of the walls is of rough
Missouri granite with cut trimmings of Bedford stone. The
building is thoroughly fire-proof. In the main, it will be two
stories high, but there will be a small number of rooms on the
third floor.

THE WORK OF THE DEPARTMENTS.
The following reports are intended to cover only such features in
the work of any of the departments of the University as, by reason of
their novelty or their general interest, give especial occasion for some
statement concerning them at this time.
APPLIED MATHEMATICS AND MECHANICS.
In consequence of the increased attendance in the School of
Engineering and Architecture, Professor Woodward has been
given assistance in Applied Mechanics. Dr. James, who is the
author of a work on Theoretical Mechanics, gives instruction
in what is known as "Mechanics I."
As a compromise in changing to the new course of study,
"Mechanics V," for the current term becomes Applied Mechan-
ics for ten weeks and Differential Equations for ten weeks.
Henceforth differential equations will be required of electrical
engineers, and offered as an elective to all others. Professor
Woodward maks a specialty this term of the theory of inertia
ellipses, antipoles, antipolars, and cores as applied to eccentric
loads, and the principle of "Least Work," as applied to a dis-
cussion of the elastic arch.
ARCHITECTURE.
The vacancy in the instructing force of this department,
caused by the resignation of Mr. McGoodwin, was filled by the
appointment of Mr. Louis C. Spiering and Mr. Wilbur T. True-
blood, each to give partial time to the work. The instruction
scheme of the Department was changed to place the work in
Design under Mr. Spiering, who studied this subject for a num-

215
ber of years in Paris under Lambert, one of the most eminent
French architects, a professor in the French Academy of Fine
Arts, from which Mr. Spiering graduated.
CHEMISTRY.
Dr. L. McMaster, of Johns Hopkins University, was
appointed to the position of instructor in chemistry, formerly
held by Mr. Sherman Leavitt, the latter having resigned to
accept a position in the Bureau of Chemistry, Department of
Agriculture, Washington, D. C. Miss Ione Hudson, A. B.,
Washington University, has also been appointed to an instruc-
torship in chemistry.
The equipment of the chemical laboratory has received the
following additions, provided for by the fund given by Mr.
Adolphus Busch: five new analytical balances, a motor gener-
ator for electrolytic work, apparatus for conductivity experi-
ments. Mr. Edward Mallinckrodt, Sr., has given a collection of
824 chemical specimens to be used on the lecture table to illus-
trate the lectures.
The following researches are now being carried on: (1)
"Careful Analytical Examination of Instances of Multiple Pro-
portions," Professor Keiser, Dr. McMaster and Mr. Graf. (2)
"Isolation and Analysis of the Acid Carbonates of the Alkaline
Earth Metals," Dr. Keiser and Dr. McMaster. (3) "The Action
of Chlorine upon Portland Cement," Dr. Keiser and Mr. G. C.
Stevens. (4) "The Interaction of Acetylene and Cyanogen in
the Presence of Finely Divided Platinum," Dr. McMaster and
Professor Keiser.
CIVIL ENGINEERING.
The Civil Engineering Museum has been enriched by the
installation of eight models illustrating methods of river im-
provement, the excellence of which is unequaled anywhere.
Many important and valuable photographs of engineering works
have been received and hung on the walls of the Department;
among which are about thirty such photographs given by the
American Bridge Co.
The equipment of instruments has been increased by the pur-
chase of several transits and levels and of a complete Base Line
Measuring Apparatus of the most approved pattern.

{
The research work involving the development of the law of
the fatigue of concrete, which has been under way in this
Department for four years, has now been completed and the
results published. The results are considered to show that
concrete is subject to this phenomenon as definitely as was
proved for steel by the historic tests of forty years ago, made
under the direction of the Prussian Government.
The investigation of actual stresses in bridge members,
begun as thesis work a year ago (notice of which was printed
in the Railway Age of January 11, 1907), is to be continued this
spring.
The investigation made last year to determine for concrete
beams the correctness or incorrectness of proportionality
of strains during loading period proved such usual assumption
not strictly correct; this thesis work has been reviewed by the
Engineering World in its issue of February 15, 1907.
ENGLISH.
An additional instructorship in English was established by
the Board of Directors in May, 1906. For 1906-7 Mr. Walter
Leighton, A. M. (Harvard), was appointed to the position.
A course in Argumentation and Debate (English 3) was
conducted during the first term of 1906-7 by Mr. Leighton. This
work, hitherto not attempted, is now, it is hoped, an established
part of the English composition instruction. It may not only
serve as an effective educational course, but may contribute to
the success of students in local and intercollegiate debates.
ECONOMICS.
In the Department of Economics this year, for the first time,
a course is offered for training in research. It is open only to
students who have studied Economics two years. The topics
for investigation are chosen from subjects dealt with in previous
courses.
Mr. G. Lippincott, a graduate student in Economics, has
been authorized to prepare for the Carnegie Institution, under
the supervision of the head of the department, a history of
manufactures in the Central Mississippi Valley. The mono-
graph will be issued in the publications of the Institution.

ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING.
The resignation of Mr. E. L. Barber, who succeeded Mr. A.
F. Krippner as instructor in Electrical Engineering, was fol-
lowed by the appointment of Mr. J. H. Hunt, a graduate of the
University of Michigan, class of 1905. From the time of his

with the Western Electric Co. of Chicago in the capacity of
designer of direct current machinery.
The equipment of the Department has been increased by

Professor Langsdorf is at present engaged in an experi-
mental investigation of the distorting effect of hysteresis on
alternating current waves.
GERMAN.
In place of Dr. Paul Reiff, who resigned at the end of 1905-6,
Mr. Philipp Seiberth was appointed instructor in German. Mr.
Seiberth received his first and second degrees in Arts from the
University of Indiana, and came to Washington University
from Columbia University in New York, where he had held a
similar position. Professor Heller has received an invitation
from the oldest German university (that of Prague) to act as
director of the memorial edition of the works of Charles Seals-
field (Karl Postl). The edition, which is to appear as a separate
division of the "Deutsch-Böhmische Bibliothek," will com-
prise sixteen volumes, including Sealsfield's biography. Among
Professor Heller's collaborators are to be Professor August
Sauer, of the University of Prague, Professor A. B. Faust of
Cornell University, who is the real pioneer in Sealsfield lore,
and several other scholars on both sides of the Atlantic. It is
expected that this work when completed will throw much new
light on the literary relations between Germany and the United
States. As a side issue involved in the subject, Professor
Heller expects to make a careful comparative study of Balzac
and his European and American contemporaries. A large por-
tion of this work is to be done in Europe.

PHYSICS.
Two papers by Professor Nipher have appeared during the
year, giving the results of his work in the Physical Laboratory
on the measuring of pressures in a fluid stream. One was pub-
lished by the American Philosophical Society, and was read by
him at the Franklin Bicentennial Celebration. The other was
published by the Academy of Science of St. Louis.


## p. 220 (#446) ############################################

220
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
The first paper dealt with the elimination of velocity effects.
This becomes necessary in such measurements as the determi-
nation of wind pressures against buildings, and in the study of
the flow of gases through pipes. It is capable of use in the study
of the discharge of natural gas. The effect of friction due to the
sides of the conduit has been studied, as well as the distortion
of the lines of flow due to bends in pipes.
The writer of these papers has published a series of papers
on this subject during the last ten years. The work had its
origin in a law case where the frictional effect of trains of cars
on the air was involved. The Supreme Court of Missouri de-
cided in that case that there was no such thing as air friction,
with its resulting shearing of layers of air on each other, but
this view does not seem to have been generally adopted.
In the study of such problems, there are two methods by
which velocity effects may be separated from the pressures to
which velocities are due, each being separately measured. Both
of these methods were devised and perfected by Professor
Nipher.
The first method requires that the tube which is to collect
the pressure at any point shall terminate in a disk to which
another disk is clamped, these disks being sandwiched with
disks of wire cloth which are of larger diameter. This wire
cloth layer serves as an approach to the mouth of the tube, pre-
venting the effect of air currents across the mouth of the tube.
It also prevents compressions and rarefactions due to the tube
itself from affecting the pressure to be measured. Such tube
collectors are now mounted upon the Physics Building for the
determination of wind pressures on its walls.
The Pitot tube has long been used for measuring velocities
by a direct determination of pressures due to a current blowing
into its open end. The equation of Sir Isaac Newton is used
in computing velocity from the pressure thus collected.
Professor Nipher's investigation has shown that if the open
end of the tube is so directed that it makes an angle of sixty
degrees with the stream lines of the air, the pressure due to
velocity is exactly zero. The Pitot tube has heretofore been
constructed on the theory that the two collecting tubes should


## p. 221 (#447) ############################################

THE WORK OF THE DEPARTMENTS.
221
be at an angle of ninety degrees with each other, although it
was known that the results thus obtained were incorrect. The
present results were obtained from experiments on a railway
train, a special car having been fitted for the purpose by direc-
tion of President Fish of the Illinois Central R. R.
The paper in the Transactions of the Academy of Science of
St. Louis gives a method of checking Newton's equation, by
experimental means, two methods having been used. This
paper also contains a mathematical discussion of the effect of
rotation on the pressure within a closed tube containing a
column of air. This discussion leads to interesting results in
connection with the action of fan blowers.
Incidentally, it
reveals the fact that rotation methods heretofore used in cali-
brating anemometers and other devices for measuring pressures
in and velocities of a current of air, should be looked upon with
great suspicion. The result of all the experiments made dur-
ing ten years, shows that the method discussed in a former
paper gives the most reliable check on Newton's equation. This
method is the one used on a train of cars moving with a meas-
ured velocity. This velocity was pushed to sixty miles per
hour. The only objection thus far urged against this method,
was in the decision of the Supreme Court of Missouri. In this
decision the results were determined to be wholly without foun-
dation.
SOCIOLOGY.
The Department of Sociology was established in the fall of
1906 by the announcement of one full course in practical
sociology. The course was designed to cover in a very general
way the whole field of social phenomena, very little attention
being given to sociological theory-a treatment based upon the
conviction that a systematic study of actual human contacts is
the best possible preparation for intelligent citizenship. And
intelligent citizenship, in its fullest sense, is certainly the prac-
tical object of all sociological inquiry. As the Department is a
new one, and as the mere term "Sociology" has no well fixed
meaning, some outline is here given of the work undertaken.
In order to get a comprehensive point of view, the class is first


## p. 222 (#448) ############################################

222
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
introduced to Spencer's Doctrine of the Unknowable, and is
rapidly advanced via the nebular theory and the theory of evo-
lution to man. The physical man once evolved, his probable psy-
chical and social development is traced, up to the appearance of
a well-ordered society. From this point on the inquiry is anatom-
ical-taking up in order of units of aggregation; -the family,
the State, the Church, economic organizations and the school.
Each unit is studied from an evolutionary point of view, and
the problems connected with each in modern life are discussed
both socially and ethically. The significance of each problem
throughout the world today is brought out, but the main dis-
cussion centers about conditions in the United States, Mr.
Carroll D. Wright's "Outline of Practical Sociology" being the
text-book in constant use. The first half-year ends with the
study of the liquor problem, and its influences on social organ-
izations.
From an examination into the "anatomy" of society, it is
a very natural step to its "physiology." Thus, the second half-
year's work opens with a study of movements of population.
This involves a study of immigration, the consequent race prob-
lems, internal migrations and the movement from country to
city. After a general study of urban conditions and tendencies,
there naturally follows, as a final topic, an inquiry into the
treatment of that residue of the population-the defective, de-
linquent and dependent classes.
The course is conducted by lectures, discussions, reading
and reports. By far the most valuable part of the course is
the individual report, based on personal research and observa-
tion. Most of the material for these reports is gathered from
local sources, - St. Louis furnishing an almost unworked and ex-
ceptionally fertile field in this line of investigation. The "field
work" is supplemented by a few excursions, in which the whole
class participates.
The Department has been greatly aided in building up its
library by the kindness of Mr. M. B. Greensfelder, a member of
the class, who donated a generous sum toward the purchase of
necessary reference books.


## p. 223 (#449) ############################################

ZOOLOGY.
Beginning with the fall semester, 1907-8, a course in Gen-
eral Entomology is to be given by the Department of Zoology.
The increased interest in both the economic and the purely
scientific side of this study, together with the fewness of the
places in America where it may be satisfactorily pursued, makes
it highly desirable that a beginning should be made here at
Washington University, with the hope that in the course of
time it may grow into a department, or at least be under the
direction of an entomological specialist. The convenience of
access to the Missouri Botanical Garden, and the assurance that
every facility possible will be provided for economic or biologic
research there, should give opportunity for entomological in-
vestigation not equaled elsewhere. The importance of the study
of insects in connection with nature study in the schools makes
it essential also that those in the teaching profession should
have an opportunity for pursuing this branch. The insect col-
lections number about 6,000 authentically identified species of
coleoptera and about 2,500 named species in the other groups.
It is the intention to build up a working library as soon as
possible. The following subjects of research are being under-
taken in the Zoological laboratory:
1. Investigation of the galvanotropic response in bacteria.
2. Reversal of tropisms and its relation to metabolism in
bacteria and in paramecium.
3.
Variation in lachnosterna.
4. The intuition of developmental stimuli in the fowl
through enzymes in the yolk.
THE CORRESPONDENCE SCHOOL.
The work of the Correspondence School, during the past
year, has naturally been devoted largely to organization and to
working out of details. But although comparatively little
effort has been made to secure enrolments beyond advertising
in a few teachers' publications, yet so well established and so
popular is this method of instruction that inquiries have come
from every State in the Union, the Philippine Islands, and


## p. 224 (#450) ############################################

224
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
Puerto Rico, and students are now enrolled from eighteen
States.
An analysis of the inquiries received for several months
shows a strong demand for instruction along three lines:
courses that will enable graduates of the smaller high schools
to complete their preparation for entering college without
being compelled to leave home; college instruction for secondary
teachers who have had little or no opportunity for higher
work; advanced and normal instruction for both elementary
and secondary teachers who have had no special normal train-
ing.
Substantial progress has been made for meeting these needs.
In secondary and elementary instruction eighty-five courses are
now offered, covering all the work given in the best second-
ary schools, and fitting students to enter any of the leading
colleges of the Middle West. Arrangements are partially com-
pleted by which certificates of admission to Washington Uni-
versity will also be accepted by many other colleges. The State
Examiner for the city dental and medical colleges has indicated
his willingness to accept these certificates for admission to the
institutions for which he acts.
Courses are now being given from the college in the depart-
ments of mathematics, history, English, chemistry, and educa-
tion. For the work in the sciences, apparatus, chemicals and
other supplies are furnished, and for all other courses requiring
the need of reference books not accessible to the student,
arrangements have been made whereby books, when not in use,
may be loaned from the library. This offers opportunities to
the teachers and others in the smaller cities and towns where
library and laboratory facilities are meager, to pursue advanced
work very profitably. A superintendent of one of the larger
city schools, in expressing his delight with a course he is taking,
adds that he shall continue his studies by correspondence as
long as he is in school work.
Undoubtedly the most fruitful field, and one in which the
greatest good can be accomplished, lies in what may be termed
normal instruction. With the thousands of teachers in every
State who have had no normal training and who can not afford


## p. 225 (#451) ############################################

THE CORRESPONDENCE SCHOOL
225
the time or money to attend normal schools, it shows consider-
able lack of enterprise and of realization of the crying need of
this great body of teachers, that no systematic effort has been
made by the State Normal Schools to reach out and help these
young people by correspondence instruction. Some work has
been done in the East, and results reported are extremely grati-
fying, but in the West no effort has yet been made. The sum-
mer schools are practically valueless for giving this training,
because of the short term and because of the amount of ground
to be covered in this limited period. Furthermore, the teachers
are exhausted by the winter's work and are in no condition to
study during the heat of the summer.
The editors of several teachers' magazines have written this
department, speaking of this fact, and urging that such in-
struction be offered by correspondence.
In accordance with these demands, extensive plans have
been formulated in collaboration with the Department of Edu-
cation, by which instruction of this nature may be given. It is
expected that by next September courses will be offered in both
elementary and secondary subjects adapted particularly to the
needs of teachers, with parallel courses in special methods for
each subject. In addition to this, instruction will be offered in
psychology, history of education, philosophy of education,
primary methods, nature study, general methods, and many
courses of collegiate grade especially helpful to teachers who
wish more advanced work in the subjects they are teaching.
In its relation to the University, the Correspondence School
is supplying one element, the lack of which seriously handicaps
the University in extending its influence beyond a very narrow
field. There are very few alumni or former students engaged
in teaching. No one factor extends the influence of a university
more widely or draws students more generally than a body of
former students scattered among the public schools of the
country. About ninety per cent of the correspondence students
are engaged in teaching, many of them at the head of city and
village schools. Their enthusiasm is even greater for the Uni-
versity than is that of the average student in residence. They
are more mature and serious minded; they have reached the age
15


## p. 226 (#452) ############################################

226
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
when they appreciate the value of college training and of the
opportunities offered in correspondence instruction; and in
proportion to their enthusiasm for this work do they sing the
praises of the University which has given them these privileges.
An incident, occurring shortly after the Missouri State Uni-
versity-Washington University football game, last fall, illus-
trates this point. A correspondence student, principal of one
of the smaller high schools of the State, sent in the following
comment, written at the end of his lesson: "M. S. U., 0; Wash-
ington U., 12. Hurrah! Glorious!"
Furthermore, the work is making the University known in
districts where otherwise its reputation would never penetrate.
Students are now pursuing courses with the intention of com-
pleting their work in the University from as far east as New
York and West Virginia, and as far west as Washington. Many
inquiries are also coming from distant places, due either to in-
formation given by correspondence students or to advertising
matter relating to the Correspondence Department.
THE UNIVERSITY CHAPEL.
A change has this year been made in the conduct of the
daily chapel exercises which has resulted in a material and
gratifying increase in attendance. These exercises, conducted
five mornings in the week by clergymen of the city, have hitherto
been held during the fifteen minutes preceding the first lecture-
hour of the morning-that is to say, from ten minutes before to
five minutes after nine. The attendance, of Faculty or
students, has usually been small; and at times has dwindled to
so scant a handful as to justify doubts whether the Uni-
versity was warranted in asking clergymen to come out to
address so extensive an array of empty benches. It has been
the opinion of some of the Faculty who believed in the attrac-
tiveness, as well as the value, of chapel exercises, that this poor
attendance was not due to indifference so much as to the in-
convenience of the hour. Those students and instructors who
do not have work at nine o'clock do not, as a rule, come to the
University buildings until later in the morning. The chapel-


## p. 227 (#453) ############################################

to speak briefly. As a result, the average attendance has been
at least quadrupled. Following is a list of the chaplains

THE ALUMNI
THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION.
The Alumni Association of Washington University has just
passed through a most successful year. All the meetings of the
Alumni were largely attended and characterized by an enthu-
siastic spirit.
THE JUNE DINNER.
On June 21, 1906, the annual June dinner and reunion of the
Alumni took place at the British Pavilion on the new Washing-
ton University grounds, immediately after the Commencement
exercises. A committee of the Alumnæ had tastily arranged
and decorated the long tables at which the Alumni, the Alumnæ,
the Faculty and members of the Board of Directors, were seated.
There were present at the luncheon in all about one hundred
and fifty, including graduates of the College and Engineering
Department, the members of the class of 1906, who were the
guests of the Alumni Association on this occasion, almost all
the members of the Faculty, with their wives and several
members of the Board of Directors. After the very acceptable
luncheon, President Grant Beebe, of the Association, delivered
a brief address, and short and appropriate speeches were also
made by Hon. Charles Nagel, a member of the Board of Direc-
tors; Professor A. O. Lovejoy, a member of the Faculty; Miss
Sophie Roever, on behalf of the Alumnæ, and Oscar J. Winter-
mann, on behalf of the class of 1906. After these addresses,
which were greatly enjoyed by all present, the members of the
Association and others present, visited the various buildings
of the University.
ANNUAL BANQUET.
The annual banquet of the Alumni Association was held
on Saturday evening, February 23, 1907, at 7:30 P. M., at the
Planters' Hotel. Dinners were also held on the same evening
by the branch associations in New York and Chicago. The St.
Louis banquet was very successful, there being present the
largest attendance in the history of the Association. More


## p. 251 (#477) ############################################

THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION
251
enthusiasm and college spirit was delivered at this banquet
than on any other previous occasion. The meeting was presided
over by President Richard McCulloch, of the Class of '91. The
following toasts were responded to by the following speakers:

Between the various speeches, well-known college songs were

Six Years Old," "Good Old W. U.," "Co-Ca-Che-Lunk," "Vive
L'Amour," "He's a Jolly Good Fellow," "Here's to W. U.,"
"Auld Lang Syne," and ending with the Washington Univer-
sity yell.
An innovation was introduced this year in the form of a
so-called insurgent programme. This resulted from a conspir-
acy between Campbell Cummings, Daniel N. Kirby, Wm. II.
Bryan and Thomas G. Rutledge. Mr. Wm. H. Bryan acted as
toastmaster of the insurgent programme and each insurgent
when called upon responded to the toast prescribed for the
regular speakers. Mr. Campbell Cummings, in starting the
insurgent, revolt, stated that he and his associates were dissatis-
fied because they had not been given a place on the programme,
and had, therefore, arranged a programme of their own. Mr.
Wm. H. Bryan acted as insurgent toastmaster. Daniel N.
Kirby responded to the toast of "We Lawyers;" Wm. Schuyler
responded to the toast of "We Profs;" "We Engineers" was
responded to by Edgar Flad; "Athletics from the Faculty View-
point" by Thomas G. Rutledge; "Us Babies" by W. G. Drosten,
and "We Grandfathers" by Wm. S. Curtis. After the insurgent
programme the regular programme was rendered, which was

ALUMNI NECROLOGY.
WILLIAM DUNHAM HUDSON.
WILLIAM DUNHAM HUDSON was born at Pittsfield, Mass.,
September 28, 1871. He died December 2, 1906, at Wawautosa
Sanitarium, Milwaukee, Wis.
At Washington University Mr. Hudson pursued the course
in Arts, graduating in 1893. He completed his law school
courses in 1895. During his undergraduate life, Mr. Hudson
was editor and also business manager of Student Life. He was a
member of the Glee Club, the Washington University Dramatic
Club, the Texta Club, a local fraternity, and of the fraternity
of Phi Delta Theta.
Mr. Hudson's participation in athletics was confined to
tennis. For two seasons he was champion of St. Louis County,
and another season won the championship of St. Louis on the
courts of the Triple A, in Forest Park.
Following his graduation from the University, Mr. Hudson
was repeatedly a director of the Washington University Alumni
Association, and served as secretary of the Association for sev-
eral years. He was also president of the Phi Delta Theta
Alumni Association.
These activities of Mr. Hudson's in his career as an under-
graduate and as an alumnus, show his popularity with his
fellows and the trust that they felt could be reposed in him.


## p. 254 (#480) ############################################

254
THE ALUMNI
To those who knew Mr. Hudson, it is idle to add that these
honors came unsought. It is nearer the truth to say that they
sought him out and were forced upon him, in spite of his habit-
ual reserve and a modesty that always made him diffident of his
fitness for an office.
Mr. Hudson's business associates recognized his possession
of qualities peculiarly suited to his profession, that insured a
successful career for him at the bar; those who had merely
social acquaintance with him were able to judge correctly of
his manliness, his sincerity and the loftiness of his personal
standards. It was, however, vouchsafed to his intimates alone
to know how fine were the issues of William Hudson's life. It
was of a greater, but not of a better man, that it was written,
"Should any record leap to light, he would not be ashamed."
P. S. S.
PAUL F. COSTE.
Paul Felix Coste was born in St. Louis July 18, 1856, re-
ceived his education in the public schools of St. Louis and
graduated from Washington University in 1875, and from its
law department-the St. Louis Law School-in 1877. Born,
reared, educated and passing his whole life in this city, he
became a well-known and prominent citizen, and his death at a
time when he was still in the prime of life, terminated a career
of great private and public worth.
His interest in Washington University was constant and
keen. He was an active member of the Alumni Association
and once its President. For many years he was a lecturer in
its law department.
As a lawyer Mr. Coste was known for his industry and
ability, and he early became a prominent member of the St.
Louis bar. Among his fellow lawyers he was particularly
known for his absolute fairness and directness, and no trickery
or sharp practice was ever charged against him. He enjoyed
a large and responsible practice. In 1904 he was appointed a
delegate to the Universal Congress of Lawyers and Jurists at
the Louisiana Purchase Exposition.
Throughout his life much of his time and energy was devoted
to public-spirited enterprises. He was a member of the Board


## p. 255 (#481) ############################################

ALUMNI NECROLOGY
255
of Commissioners of the Mullanphy Emigrant Relief Fund and
twice President of that Board. When the Board of Education
of the City of St. Louis was taken out of politics, Mr. Coste was
one of the first members of the reorganized Board. He took a
leading part in bringing public school affairs out of chaos and
mismanagement, and in inaugurating the present admirable and
business-like administration. He served as a member of this
Board from 1897 to 1901, and was twice its President. When
he retired from this office, to which he had been elected by the
people of the city, the rule of non-partisanship as to politics in
school matters had been demonstrated to the people as a dis-
tinct improvement in school administration. Mr. Coste lived to
see the fruits of his labors and those of his colleagues recognized
in the universal admiration now accorded to the St. Louis pub-
lic school system, its school buildings and instruction. He was
also a member of the Civil Service Reform Association.
Mr. Coste's death occurred in St. Louis on the 26th day of
June, 1906. He is survived by his widow, two daughters and
T. F. C.
one son.
WILLIAM CARR GLASGOW.
Dr. William Carr Glasgow died at his home in this city,
March 22, 1907. He was born in Saint Louis January 16, 1845,
and was the son of William Glasgow, Jr., and Sarah Lane, the
daughter of Dr. William Carr Lane. Dr. Lane was the first
Mayor of Saint Louis, and for many years one of the leading
physicians of the town. Dr. Glasgow received his early educa-
tion in private schools, and, principally, at a certain school that
afterwards became the preparatory department of Washington
University. During the Civil War his family went abroad, and
for the three years that they remained in Europe young Glasgow
was a pupil at the Real-Gymnasium in Wiesbaden.
Upon his return to this country Glasgow was entered as
an undergraduate at this university, and in due course obtained
the degree of Bachelor of Arts. Immediately thereafter he
commenced the study of medicine, and was graduated from the
Saint Louis Medical College in 1869.
The next several years were occupied in graduate work both
here and abroad, but the greater part of this period was spent


## p. 256 (#482) ############################################

256
THE ALUMNI
in the clinics at Vienna, where he gave especial attention to
laryngology and diseases of the chest, branches of medicine to
which he devoted himself almost exclusively after taking up his
practice here in 1872.
In 1872 Dr. Glasgow was appointed Lecturer on Physical
Diagnosis in the Saint Louis Medical College; in 1885 he was
made Adjunct Professor of the Practice of Medicine in the same
institution; and in 1890 he was made Professor of Diseases of
the Chest and Laryngology in the Saint Louis Post-Graduate
Medical School. Subsequently he joined the Faculty of the
Missouri Medical College, with which institution he continued
as an active and acceptable teacher until it became, with the
Saint Louis Medical College, the medical department of the
Washington University. In this new Faculty he was again
made Professor of Medicine and Laryngology, which chair he
held until his death, although for the past year he had been
obliged by ill-health to relinquish the active duties of the
position.
Dr. Glasgow was one of the founders of the American Laryn-
gological Society, and its president in 1890; he was also a
member of the American Climatological Society. At the meet-
ing of the Congress of Arts and Sciences, held during the
World's Fair, he was honored with the chairmanship of the
Section of Laryngology.
Although not a voluminous writer, Dr. Glasgow made some
very notable contributions to the medical press. Probably his
most important and original work was a very able study of
influenza as affecting the lungs and throat. The various papers
he wrote on this subject contained observations of great scien-
tific and practical value.
As a medical practitioner, Dr. Glasgow was a skillful diag-
nostician and therapeutist, conservative in his judgments, cling-
ing to old things if good, but willing to accept new methods and
ideas if they could be proved better.
Personally, Dr. Glasgow was a kind and absolutely sincere
man, who tried faithfully to do his duty in this life.
W. A. H.


## p. 257 (#483) ############################################

ALUMNI NECROLOGY
257
JOHN W. SPARGO.
John Webster Spargo was born in Pittsburg, Pa., May
27, 1852, and died in St. Louis, Mo., Jan. 11, 1907.
He entered the University in January 1871, then in his
twentieth year, as a member of the Freshman class somewhat
in advance of his class. By hard work during the remainder
of the year and the following vacation, he was able upon
examination to enter the Junior class in September, and was
graduated in 1873 with the honor of Salutatorian in the class
with Dean Curtis of the Law School and Principal Bryan of
the Central High School. After some years in business, Mr.
Spargo entered the Manual Training School as a teacher, and
later the Central High School, where he remained until his
recent sudden and untimely death.
He was a man of energy and a faithful teacher, whose loss
is keenly felt by all who knew him. He left a wife and four
children, two sons and two daughters, one of whom is a mem-
ber of the present sophomore class in the Department of Arts
and Sciences.
The Editors regret that through the loss of the manuscript
during the printing, it is impossible to include in this year's
Bulletin Mr. Fay's memorial of Mr. A. H. Zeller, '92.
