FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN
NOVELLE
PHILIP SEIBERTH
Instructor in German, Washington University
The Novelle is probably the best and most specifically
German product of German literature in the nineteenth
century. It is the descendant, of course, of the old novella
of Bocaccio, Cervantes and their schools, but much changed
in spirit and form. The classical novella was what the
word itself means, a story of some interesting new event,
calculated to entertain, and to gratify curiosity. It was a
favorite pastime of the Italians of medieval and renaissance
times to tell such stories, often to illustrate some general
observation concerning mankind, and always with a pre-
ference for extraordinary, sensational cases. This continues
to be the character of the novella and its nearest relative,
the poetic tale, until the beginning of the nineteenth century.
As early as the fifteenth century there existed in Germany
many collections of tales, their purpose expressed in their
titles; e. g., Rollwagenbüchlein, Wegkürzer, etc., all belonging
to the variety known as "snippet-stories," and being, in a
large majority, importations or adaptations of the Italian
species. In the eighteenth century, Lafontaine, Sturz,
Merck, Haken, Engel, cultivated the genre, still with an eye
on French and Italian models; their conception of the
Novelle was, essentially, also that of the great German
classic poets and the older romanticists. A. W. Schlegel
expresses himself to this effect, that "the Novelle ought
in every point of its nature and heart to be new and strik-
ing." Goethe conceives it to be "a new unheard-of event."
Of modern story-writers it is Paul Heyse who clings to the


## p. 46 (#534) #############################################

46
PHILIP SEIBERTH
original definition and practice. Hence the surprising,
sudden turns in most of his Novellen. The English "short-
story" and the French "conte" conform very largely to
the older notion of the short narrative. It was for the
Germans of the last century to strike out in a new direction,
to carry the development of the form farther, to deepen and
widen its possibilities. In this new form it is the most
elastic and catholic of all forms, admitting of any subject
or mood whatever. It may be epic, lyric, or dramatic, or
all of these at once. With this large scope it is really more
closely related to the ballad than to its prose ancestors.
Still, however wide the range of the Novelle, it is nevertheless
susceptible of demarcation, both in its inner and outward
form. Storm, one of the masters to be discussed later,
claims definite structure and technique for it. He says,
"The Novelle is the strictest and most compact form of
prose-fiction, the sister of the drama, and it rests with the
author to make it express the highest in poetry." Many
attempts at an exact definition of the Novelle have been
made in recent years, some of them rather foolish. The
fundamental facts are simple enough, and can be stated as
follows: The Novelle or short-story must have for its
subject a plot which calls for treatment on the short-story
scale. It is not a compressed or condensed novel, but a
story of simple proportions though fully developed. It has
unity of plot and, naturally, does not tolerate much episode,
or digression. The treatment ought to be concise and
essential. One need not go beyond these obvious funda-
mentals. Too much theorizing or even legislation is out of
place in any form of poetry, but most of all in this.
In its beginnings in the hands of the romanticists, the
new German Novelle does not at once have this clear
physiognomy; matters were, for the Novelle, in transition.
To be sure, the romanticists had a strong preference for
short tales, and handled the species in the freest and
easiest way imaginable. They lacked patience, and per-


## p. 47 (#535) #############################################

FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN NOVELLE 47
haps power for sustained composition in the larger, difficult
forms, and it was this temper which inclined them towards
the lyric and the fairy-tale. In their Novellen they told
their weird, phantastical, humorous, skittish fancies, always
caring more for mood and quaintness than for form. The
charming Märchennovelle is their own special creation.
The best and most popular of them are: Tieck's Volks-
märchen, Fouqué's Undine, Eichendorff's Taugenichts, and
Chamisso's Peter Schlemihl.
The forerunner of the poetic realists to whom the century
owes the remarkable burst of Novellen is the great dramat-
ist, Heinrich von Kleist, with his unique story of Michael
Kohlhaas. Here the new Novelle is established, with all
the "concentration, compression, ingenuity and originality"
that any theorist of short-story-writing would wish to have.
It is an entirely objective account of the authentic case of
the horse-dealer Kohlhaas, who defends his outraged rights
against the injustice and corruption of laws until he is
changed from a sane, peaceful and honest man into a demon
of revenge. It should be read first, as the classic of the
Novelle, exercising great influence upon all subsequent
realistic story-writing. In this connection, it will be well
to call attention, briefly, to a few writers, mainly of the
first half of the century, who, without being primarily
story-writers, have contributed some masterpieces to the
short narrative. Such are: Mörike: Mozart auf der Reise
nach Prag; Grillparzer: Der arme Spielmann, and Das
Kloster bei Sendomir; Ludwig: Zwischen Himmel und Erde;
Annette v. Droste-Hülshoff: Die Judenbuche; Immermann:
Der Oberhof; Wildenbruch, with many of his Novellen.
Now to turn, after these preliminaries, to the main
purpose of this paper, which is to present the four con-
spicuous masters of the Novelle, Keller, Storm, Meyer
and Heyse, for a concise characterization of their personality
and art. The first three, notably, are men who have a large
outlook upon life. Because they think, understand and


## p. 48 (#536) #############################################

48
PHILIP SEIBERTH
feel deeply and sympathetically, they are philosophers,
poets and teachers of their people. There is in them not
a trace of that insincerity and lack of seriousness found in
those who make writing a mere sport or an industry. Art
for art's sake, narrow artistic doctrine and other similar
vices and moonshine as they are absent from all great
art, so are they foreign to theirs.
I.
We are very fortunate in having a biography of Gottfried
Keller by his countryman, Jacob Bächtold, which deserves
to become a classic in biography; for there is in Keller the
same intimate, inseparable relation of life and works, as in
Goethe and so many Germans. The main facts stand out
boldly: a solitary imaginative youth, unjustly expelled
from school at fifteen; a misguided attempt at painting;
dogged persistence in writing, though without any success
or hope; in the background the poor mother and sister.
At last, after many hardships, he was appointed to a
highly gratifying Government position. The story of the
years of suffering and failure is told in his first work, Der
grüne Heinrich, as remarkable a book of human experience
as has ever been written-truth told as fiction. Experience
and observation underlie everything that Keller has done.
Die Leute von Seldwyla, a cycle of Novellen, soon followed
the novel; and, barring two volumes of verse, Keller re-
mained true to the short story. In the Novellen it was
Keller's intention from the first to give pictures from life
characterizations showing the direct action of character
upon character, and of circumstance upon circumstance.
During his fifteen years of office, Keller's writing was
suspended, and his resignation was chiefly due to his desire
to complete what had been planned or begun years ago.
A few things originated entirely in this late period.
The complete cycle of Seldwyler Geschichten is unique
in conception and form. In the introduction Seldwyla is


## p. 49 (#537) #############################################

FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN NOVELLE 49
described as a quiet old sunny town somewhere, but really
nowhere, and therefore everywhere, in Switzerland. The
citizens of this town are a queer lot; they are enterprising
and promising in youth, but later begin to speculate, and
in due time fail in business; whereupon they either go out
into the world, to return as wise men taught abroad by
experience, or they stay at home at some modest useful
occupation. The women are usually saner and more
practical than the men, and often have to take husbands
and affairs into their own hands for better management.
At all times the Seldwylians are ready for a good time, or any
undertaking that promises a sensational experience. Practi-
cal joking, drinking, occasionally a little revolution to help
business along, and various original devices for eventful
living-that is what they indulge in to relieve the monotony
of life. At bottom they are a good-natured sort of people.
It is easy to see that Keller intended to give a humorous,
but true, picture of his countrymen as they used to be in
old days before modern industrialism spoiled poetry and
put an end to the amiable follies of this good folk. Keller
had in himself a good share of Seldwyle nature. There are
Seldwylians out of Switzerland, too; "Spiessbürgertum"
is found all the world over, and so the stories have a general
appeal and typical value in the bargain. The style, in all
of Keller's tales, is surprisingly original; a refreshing new
idiom and vocabulary take the place of conventional
phraseology and usage. There is astonishing invention
and much humorous detail in many odd characters and
their doings. Still, despite all humorous by-play, one feels
that here are types, who, if they are often foolish, are
therefore all the more human. Besides, German humor is
very different from the English or French. English
novelists are very prone to caricature, ridicule, overdraw
and satirize, until too often no sympathy or dignity is left.
German humor is entirely consistent with love and respect,
-in fact, it springs from a sympathetic feeling. That is
4


## p. 50 (#538) #############################################

50
PHILIP SEIBERTH
the nature of Keller's humor. Upon occasion, when it
becomes necessary to punish meanness or hypocrisy,
Keller knows very well that the whip is the only adequate
instrument to use. Without being a moralist like Thackeray,
he is a pedagogue of the people, his teaching growing
spontaneously out of the story, entirely without sermoni-
zing. If serious art is to have a purpose, what else can it be
than the interpretation of life with a view toward the im-
provement of it. The best stories of the first round are
probably: Romeo und Julie auf dem Dorfe, Kleider machen
Leute, Die gerechten Kammacher, and Dietegen.
The Züricher Novellen, drawn from memorable epochs
of Keller's native canton and city of Zurich, have very much
the same good qualities. Intimate acquaintance with the
past, coupled with the purpose of getting at the real life of
the past, make these tales prominent classics of historical
fiction. It is not historical narrative of the common sort,
history in novelistic dress, but a resurrection of the past;
Swiss life shown in intimate human perspective. The
best of these pieces are: Der Landvogt von Greifensee and
Das Fähnlein der sieben Aufrechten.
The subtle psychology of modern love and marriage is
the theme of Das Sinngedicht, -a round of five Novellen,
set in the connecting framework of a sixth. The delicate
touch and sympathetic penetration called for by such a
subject, together with an undercurrent of precious humor,
show Keller at his best as a consummate artist. But most
admirable is the exquisite finesse of the Sieben Legenden,
in which Keller seems entirely to depart from his usual
Here certainly is something absolutely unique
in the world's literature: legends from early Christianity
and of the Virgin Mary turned into human stories, without
profanation and without loss of their naive legendary
charm: Eugenia, Dorotheas Blumenkorbchen, das Tanzlegend-
chen. Keller's last work, Martin Salander, is a somewhat
unpleasant book on the rottenness of the modern business
manner.


## p. 51 (#539) #############################################

FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN NOVELLE 51
spirit. The old champion of honesty and decency is grimly
hostile towards the swindling practices of the latter-day
Swiss money-makers.
Keller is now fully recognized as the greatest personality
in German literature since Goethe. Outside of Germany,
the French know him and seem to like him, while England
and America have, characteristically enough, remained
complacently and blissfully ignorant of him. As an antidote
against the silliness and insincerity into which the American
novel too often runs, Keller would prove invaluable.
II.
The extreme north has given Germany another story-
writer and poet, who is as much identified with his native
Schleswig-Holstein as Keller with Zurich-Theodor Storm.
He represents the best ethical temper and artistic genius
of the low-German countries, and is so thoroughly German
and unspoiled by foreign influence that if any foreigner
were to ask, "What is specifically German?" we could say,
"Read all of Storm, then you will know." Storm's art is
very deeply rooted in the northern German lowlands. The
strange fascination of the heath and marsh, in their various
moods and seasons, has found its poet in Storm, their
gloomy, uncanny aspects, when the night and mists are
upon them, and their beauty on a summer day with flowers,
bees and solitude. Nor is there lacking the spell of the
ocean in "sea-girt Schleswig-Holstein." When Danish rule
drove the German patriot, Storm, from home, and com-
pelled him to live in Prussia and Saxony eleven years, this
landscape and the memory of his youth and happiness
there haunted him constantly. It was this sadly reminis-
cent mood out of which grew his first poems and Novellen.
They are all the more poetical for that. For, after all,
memory and imagination, calling up the past and idealizing
it in the retrospect, is what the poetic process consists of.
Storm is a lyrical nature of quick sensibility and delicate


## p. 52 (#540) #############################################

52
PHILIP SEIBERTH
feeling. His narrative is sometimes suggested and entirely
dominated by a song; and, again, the mood of the story is
condensed into songs in the course, or at the end, of a tale.
Yet, in spite of all the pervading lyrical sentiment, there is
no vagueness, but a solid basis of character and incident.
Storm's remark, "When I am deeply moved, I turn to
verse," may be taken as a key to his art. The plots of his
early stories are natural and simple. They are the ever-
returning basic experiences, the simple facts of human life,
as in the Volkslied, undistorted by subjective reflections
or whimsical fancies. Later, and particularly after his
return to his home country, a harder and more energetic
tone begins to assert itself. In place of soft outlines and
melancholy resignation, we now find a growing preference
for stories of tragic life. We are more reminded of the
intensity, stern though subdued, of the northern ballad.
The element of fate and tragedy gives to many of the later
Novellen a distinctly dramatic character. This, together
with the strict economy of style and essentiality of content,
quite coincides with Storm's conception of the Novelle as
"the sister of drama." There is no doubt that here a
climax of the poetic possibilities of the Novelle is reached.
There is not one weak story in the fifty odd pieces of his
making. Storm, as well as Keller and Meyer, is an author
who must be read entirely, because he is good all through.
Some of the best of his stories are: Unter dem Tannenbaum,
Ein grünes Blatt, Auf der Universität, Veronika, Viola
tricolor, Pole Poppenspäler, Waldwinkel, Ekenhof, Zur
Chronik von Grieshuus, Aquis submersus, Psyche, Hans und
Heinz Kirch, Ein Fest auf Haderslevhuus.
III.
A writer not so specifically German in theme, but en-
tirely so in conception, is Conrad Ferdinand Meyer, a
fellow townsman of Keller. While he resembles Keller in
soundness of ethical sense and finely didactic import, he


## p. 53 (#541) #############################################

FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN NOVELLE 53
represents an entirely different class of Swiss society.
Keller was a man of the people, anything but an aristocrat
in the ordinary connotation; often a declared enemy of
esthetic refinement and the circumstance of gentility.
Meyer was a patrician by birth and education. Besides,
he was of a very retiring disposition, which, during adoles-
cence, grew dangerously pathological. But he succeeded
in throwing this temper off when he became a student at
Lausanne. He read widely and traveled in Italy and
France, until, at forty-five, he published his first work:
Huttens letzte Tage. He is from the first mature and
finished. Fontane, the greatest German novelist of the
century, was sixty when he wrote his first book, and
seventy when he wrote his best. In both cases, late pro-
duction carried with it the great advantage of abundant
study and experience. Meyer has read deeply into the
history of civilization and thought, and has perfect acquaint-
ance with the epochs from which he drew his Novellen.
To be entirely familiar, from the sources, with Renaissance
Italy, the age of Louis XIV, the Reformation and the
Thirty-Years' War, and then to turn this into narrative
and poetry, is no small matter. What Meyer did was to
look back upon these epochs, to see, with the eyes of the
psychologist and the reconstructive imagination of the
poet, the moving forces and human fates of these great
times. In one of his poems he represents Michael Angelo
among his statues, musing on their origin in his soul and
upon his attitude towards these children of his mind:
Ihr stellt des Leids Gebärde dar,
Ihr meine Kinder, ohne Leid!
So sieht der freigewordne Geist
Des Lebens überwundne Qual
Was martert die lebendge Brust,
Beseligt und ergötzt im Stein.
"You show the features of pain, you my children, with-
out pain. Thus the free mind looks upon life's torments


## p. 54 (#542) #############################################

54
PHILIP SEIBERTH
overcome. What tortures the living breast, delights and
pleases in stone." We may say that this is, in a very large
measure, Meyer's own attitude towards his subjects. Above
and besides philosophic aloofness and artistic objectivity,
there is warmth and feeling, and that most human of
instincts, to feel it your highest duty to understand sym-
pathetically, rather than to praise or blame. It has been
pointed out that Meyer is particularly fond of dwelling
upon critical moments, and that he is mainly attracted to
eventful periods with large, new possibilities, and to psycho-
logical trials of great men, who are tempted to forget their
higher purposes and destinies. Meyer is not so much in-
clined to show the march and development of things as
to present a panoramic view of one significant situation or
combination, splendidly portrayed. This great art of
painting brilliantly and in full costume and furniture is
notably seen in his Renaissancenovellen, magnificent times
and men, magnificently portrayed. A story of this nature,
from English History, is Der Heilige, the story of Thomas
Becket, that perplexing human puzzle. To show how
these things might have been, to make Becket intelligible,
is Meyer's purpose. If one would see how much more light
a free and bold use of the imagination can throw upon
history, than the anxious fear and trembling to go beyond
authenticated fact, one should compare this story with the
unconvincing, dull drama which Tennyson has made of the
same theme. Here, as in so many cases, poetic probabilities
bring us nearer to truth than any pedantic attempt to piece
the apparent incongruities and contradictions of history
together. In Die Hochzeit des Mönchs there is admirable
technique in the manner in which the story itself is mirrored
in the framework of another that is woven around it and
into it. The very way in which Dante the narrator is
introduced, and induced to tell the story, and the picture
of his exit after it is ended, are masterful detail. One
can learn skillful construction from Meyer; but it is not


## p. 55 (#543) #############################################

FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN NOVELLE 55
the technique of clever devices and contrivances which some
shallow theorists are so glad and quick to detect. Meyer's
technique consists in following the biological line of character
and event, which is indeed the only natural way. Meyer's
stories are not reading for the general public. A high degree
of humanistic culture is needed for the full understanding
of such "Kultur- und Kunstnovellen" as those from Re-
naissance Italy and the reign of the "Roi soleil." For that
matter you cannot read Goethe or George Meredith without
paying high admission. Meyer's style is clear, even and
classic. The quintessence of his personality and art is
concentrated and crystallized in his poems, which are
meditations, moods, pictures and reflections in lyrical
form-Gedankenlyrik-from the same elevated sphere of
idea and feeling in which his stories move. Similarly,
Hebbel, Keller and Storm have precipitated their inner
life, a world of feeling, in lyrical concentration.
IV.
Boccaccio, "the father of the Novelle," has one great,
true-begotten son among the modern German masters,
Paul Heyse. With him the Novelle once more becomes the
"remarkable event," which by means of some extraordinary
occurrence reveals a new side of human nature in clear
outline. According to Heyse's own dictum, the Novelle
must have "a strong, distinct silhouette." One can easily
see that this desire to find something new, and to accentuate
the striking features of the story, is very apt to take away
from the naturalness and inevitableness of the life repre-
sented. He has not the loving care for detail which the
others have, but instead, more form and machinery than is
good, and a corresponding minus of content. His style
is nothing if not elegant-so much that "too beautiful"
has, in many quarters, become a by-word in speaking of


## p. 56 (#544) #############################################

56
PHILIP SEIBERTH
him. Heyse's regard for form and his preference for sub-
jects from the cultivated sphere of life are inherent in his
nature and the circumstances of his education. Art and
culture surrounded him from childhood. He is so esthetic
that his aristocratic antipathy against the coarser facts of
life has really made him blind to the seamy side of things.
Still, it would be wrong to call him fastidious. He is always
human, and in his more than hundred Novellen-not to
speak of his novels and dramas-he offers a great variety
of human experience. In the last analysis, too, he is a
realist. His favorite theme is love, or, more specifically,
the natural right of a strong passion to maintain itself
against prejudices and obstacles. It really comes to this,
that Heyse, the artistic exponent of worldly esthetic
culture, postulates, and in his works practically uses, a
separate and freer code of morality for his favorite upper
ten thousand than the laws and traditions will allow to
common humanity.
It would be unfair to demand from an author as prolific
as Heyse that he should always be at his best. Only a very
great writer can, at all times, give the best of his nature and
art; or a conscientious minor poet who does only what he
can do well. If a selection of Heyse's best were made, he
would appear a finished poet, in the first rank, among novel-
ists and lyrists. Such pieces as L'Arrabiata, Das Mädchen
von Treppi, Die Stickerin von Treviso, Der letzte Centaur,
etc., are classics of great beauty and individuality.
Keller, Storm, Meyer and Heyse, together with some
of their predecessors, have established the Novelle as a great
new form of modern literature, and, in the opinion of many,
as the most remarkable branch of nineteenth century
literature in Germany, with the possible exception of the
lyric. It has since been taken up by nearly all of the best
writers, so that now we are in the midst of a veritable
millennium of the Novelle. One must never forget that
the German world, with its many tribal units, contains


## p. 57 (#545) #############################################

FOUR MASTERS OF THE MODERN GERMAN NOVELLE 57
greater variety of milieu and character than any other
nation of Europe; and some day the earth will be moved
to wonder, when the wealth of this life and soul comes to
be realized. The mere mention of Rosegger, Seidel, Raabe,
will suffice to convince one that the Kellers, Storms and
Meyers are not dead in the Germany of to-day.

HEREDITY*
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
Until recently Instructor in General Biology at Washington University, now Re-
search Assistant in the Carnegie Laboratory for Experimental Evolution, Cold
Spring Harbor, L. I.
Common experience teaches us that the son is not
exactly like his father, and that the daughter is not an
exact replica of her mother. Sometimes one sees an
unmistakable resemblance to an uncle, an aunt, a grand-
father, a grandmother or some more distant relative. In
a large family some of the children may have the features
and the physique of one of the parents and the mental
peculiarities of the other, or they may resemble very
remarkably some quite distant relative. Cases may be
found in which it is impossible to discern any close approxi-
mation to the features of any near kinsman. Observation
teaches us, however, that blood relatives are, on the whole,
similar; family resemblance is as much a matter of common
experience as individual diversity. At a reception or on the
street we frequently feel that a face seen for the first time is
nevertheless not unfamiliar, that it must belong with some
family group of our acquaintance.
This similarity of blood kinsfolk must be due either to
heredity or to environment; it must be referable to the
inherent likeness of the descendants of the same ancestor,
or to the fact that the members of the same family are
surrounded by comparable environmental conditions. Now
the conditions of environment are by no means sufficient
to account for the similarity which we see in members of
a family. Living under the same general climatic condi-
tions as their neighbors, blood relatives have only their
home environment peculiar to themselves. And even
this may differ almost as widely between members of a
*Abstract of three lectures delivered before the Washington University Associa-
tion, January 29, February 5 and February 12, 1907.


## p. 59 (#547) #############################################

HEREDITY
59
small family group as between them and their neighbors.
The home surroundings and the nurture of parents and
children, grandparents and grandchildren, or cousins, may
be antithetic, and yet this family resemblance in physical
and mental traits may persist in unmistakable clearness.
This similarity of kinsfolk we call heredity. We see
it everywhere, and respect it. In America we affect to
despise coats of arms, but we do not conceal the names
of ancestors, or their brothers or sisters or their wives'
cousins who have distinguished themselves. Blood tells,
we say if we can mention men prominent as writers,
fighters, educators or statesmen in our own family circle.
The fancier of dogs or the breeder of swine will not tolerate
an animal in his kennels or pens, unless he can show you its
family tree. The seedsman carefully weeds out every
individual of his choice pedigreed race which falls below his
ideal. A single ear of corn may sell for two hundred
dollars. These things are so because we realize that there
is a phenomenon called heredity. All this has been known
for a long time, and much has been written concerning it,
but in recent years scientists have taken a most important
step forward. They have realized that the amount of
similarity among relatives must be measured, and they
have developed methods whereby such calculation can
be made with precision.
This, then, is the problem which the scientific student of
heredity has before him: to determine quantitatively how
closely similar are parents and children, brothers and sisters,
uncles and nephews, cousins and cousins, and all other rela-
tives in respect to all characters for which we can obtain
any workable standard of measurement.¹
1 For the information of the professional student of heredity, I will say that I
have omitted all discussion of Mendelian phenomena, and have confined my atten-
tion to the results obtained by the mathematical analysis of the data obtained
from large series of individuals. This is not because I am not in sympathy with
the other kind of work. Little has been published along Mendelian lines for the
human species, from which I have largely drawn my illustrations.


## p. 60 (#548) #############################################

60
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
Every comparison involves a contrast. To determine
the likeness of two objects, we note and classify the points
in which they differ. This is precisely the method which
must be employed in the investigation of heredity. The
amount of similarity must be measured in terms of devia-
tion from some standard value. The one selected as the
most satisfactory is the mean condition in the series of
objects, organs or individuals under consideration. If we
are working with the stature of a thousand men, we deter-
mine the average height of the men of this series, and then
the position of any individual or series of individuals with
reference to this standard.
If time were available, I might dwell long upon the
problem of variability. Variation is an almost universal
attribute of organisms. Of recent years it has been found
possible to treat this problem quantitatively, and some of
the most remarkable and important results of modern
biology have grown out of these studies.
As an introduction to variation in human characteristics,
I have selected a table (Table I) published by Francis
Galton, in his Natural Inheritance. Many other illustrations
as good as this, and some which are better, may be found,
but I choose to use this because it is taken from one of the
classics of modern biology. Indeed, the work which was
done on this table only a few years ago forms the corner-
stone of the quantitative sciences of variation and heredity.
In taking up the investigation of the problem of the
inheritance of stature, Mr. Galton was confronted by the
difficulty that the mean stature of women differs from that
of men. We must consider both father and mother in
dealing with the problem of inheritance, but how are we to
work with such different characters as the stature of men
and women? Mr. Galton overcame this difficulty by
transmuting all measurements on women into their male
equivalents by multiplying by 1.08, the factor necessary
to increase the average stature of women to the average

In the first column of this table will be seen the classes of
stature of the 205 mid-parents of 928 children. On the
opposite side of the table, to the right hand, will be seen
two columns, one giving the number of parents of each

stature from below 64.5 inches to over 72.5 inches, it
appears at once that there are only a single pair under 64.5
inches, and only five pairs above 72.5 inches, while there are
forty-nine couples with the more nearly average stature
of 68.5 inches.
The figures at the heads of the columns, ranging from
below 62.2 inches to above 73.2 inches, show the heights
of the adult children reared by each class of parents. The
transverse row of totals, next to the bottom line of the
table, shows the total number of children of each grade of
stature. We remember that the statures of daughters
have been reduced to the equivalent values for sons, so that
both may be entered together on the same table. Here
we are dealing with over four times as many adult children
as there were mid-parents, but there is a closely similar
arrangement of the individuals. Only five children fall
below 62.2 inches, and only fourteen are taller than 73.2
inches; but as many as one hundred and thirty-eight are
classed as 67.2 inches tall.
Both the mid-parents and their offspring show a con-
siderable variability. The 205 mid-parents are distributed
in eleven classes, and the largest number of individuals in
any class is forty-nine; the 928 children may be assorted
into fourteen classes, and the largest number in any class
is one hundred and thirty-eight. Not only are both mid-
parents and their children variable in stature, but this
variability exhibits a very pronounced regularity. In both


## p. 63 (#551) #############################################

HEREDITY
63
cases we see the extreme conditions represented by but a
few individuals, while the average condition is represented
by many. We remember that we measure variability by
determining the deviation of the individuals from the mean
value. Here we see that the frequency of individuals in
each class steadily decreases as the class deviates farther
and farther from the mean, either by becoming larger or
smaller. The distributions of the "variates," as the
statistical biologist calls them, seen here are very typical.
So regular are they that the mathematician can write the
formula for a curve which will express the results of these
measurements very well. Variation is not chaotic but
orderly, and this fact justifies the treatment of problems of
heredity by mathematical methods.
There are other points to be gained from an inspection
of our table. First we notice that all children of mid-
parents over 72.5 inches tall are 72.2 inches or over in
stature, while those of mid-parents less than 64.5 inches
tall are 69.2 inches or under in stature. Here it is per-
fectly clear that tall parents have taller children than short
parents, and this, we say, is due to heredity. The case of
the mid-parent less than 64.5 inches tall is particularly
interesting, for here we have a single pair who reared
fourteen adult children. An inspection of the data shows
that these children are on an average shorter than the
children of taller parents, say those of 69.3 inches, but it
also proves conclusively that they are not identical among
themselves, or with their mid-parent. The conclusions to
be drawn from these two conditions are that stature is
inherited from parent to child, but that inheritance is not
perfect. The statistical biologist would express this idea
by saying that the character of the offspring is not absolutely
determined by the type of the parent. The other arrays, as
the series of children produced by parents of any type are
called, all show the same phenomena, but since there is
more than a single pair in all the stature groups of mid-


## p. 64 (#552) #############################################

64
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
parents except this one, the results are not so conspic-
uous.
This conclusion is so important that it will bear re-
stating. In all cases, the offspring of mid-parents differing
from each other by less than an inch, vary among them-
selves through a range of several inches. These arrays
furnish an additional illustration of the law of variation
briefly indicated above. In all cases in which the number
of individuals is sufficiently large to yield smooth results,
the mean values are seen to be represented by the largest
number of individuals, while the frequency of individuals
decreases towards the extremes of the range of variation.
As the stature of the parents increases, the bulk of the
figures in the arrays shifts to the right, showing that the
children do, on the whole, inherit their parents' stature,
although inheritance is not perfect, as is shown by the
variability of the children from parents of the same type.
That the characteristics of the offspring are in part
determined by those of their parents may be shown in still
another way. In the last column to the right are given the
medians of the arrays of children produced by each parental
type from 64.5 to 72.5 inches in height. The median is the
value which divides a series of objects into two halves,
the one containing the smaller and the other the larger
individuals. In the present case it is practically equal
to the mean. The conclusions just drawn receive an un-
qualified substantiation in these medians. As the stature
of the parents increases, the average, or median, stature of
the children also increases, but within certain limits these
children form a variable array.
There are still other peculiarities of the laws of heredity
which are very well illustrated by this table. While the
median stature of children increases as the stature of their
mid-parents becomes greater, the rate at which the two
series increase is not identical. In fact, an examination
of the lowest and the highest grades of mid-parents for


## p. 65 (#553) #############################################

HEREDITY
65
which the numbers are trustworthy, shows that the stature of
children of the parents of the lowest grade is on an average
taller than that of their parents, while the stature of the
children of parents of the highest grade is on an average
shorter than that of their parents. These extreme cases are
not aberrations; the medians of the filial arrays reveal the
fact that the children are on an average taller than their
parents for all parentages up to and including those 67.5
inches tall, but shorter than their parents for parental
classes of 68.5 inches and more. Mid-parents 68.5 inches
in height are the most common, but the average or median
value for both the parental and the filial population is about
68.25. This is the point which divides the population of
mid-parents into two equal groups, one of which produces
children of less than their own stature, and the other of
which have children of more than their own stature.
It will be clear that in both of these cases the tendency
is for the stature of children to be intermediate between
that of their own parents and the average of the general
population. The children tend to be more mediocre than
their parents. This is Galton's law of regression to medioc-
rity. The children of parents who deviate from the mean
of the parental population deviate from the mean of the
filial population, and in the same direction as their parents,
but in a less degree. This is the law which confronts gifted
parents, when they hope that their children will be as gifted
as themselves. It is this law which may cheer the less than
mediocre parents with the hope that their children will
excel them and approach more nearly the mid-condition
of the race.
The examination of the figures in this table has taught
us some matters of fundamental importance concerning
inheritance. It would be most desirable, however, if the
relationship between parents and children could be ex-
pressed in a single term, if some mathematical coefficient
could be found for the strength of heredity which would
5


## p. 66 (#554) #############################################

66
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
enable us to compare likeness of parent and child, of
brothers, or of relatives of any degree of nearness whatever.
Such an expression has been found, and is one of the most
powerful tools of scientific investigation. It is known as the
coefficient of correlation.
This coefficient is calculated from the body of a cor-
relation table, as such an arrangement of data as that which
we have been considering is called, by a rather tedious but
not very difficult mathematical process, which need not
be explained here. The coefficient of correlation ranges
from 0 to 1. If, in a population in which the parents as a
class, and the children as a class, have the same mean, and
the same variability around the mean, the children of every
group of parents had the characteristic under consideration
developed in the same degree as their parents, correlation
would be perfect and would be expressed by the coefficient
1. If, on the other hand, it were to be found that the
children were no more like their own parents than they
were like other members of the community, there would
be no correlation, and the coefficient would take the value 0.
The degree of similarity of objects, relatives, or phe-
nomena of any kind whatever, is conveniently and quantita-
tively expressed by a value of the correlation coefficient
ranging from 0 to 1, and from 0 to -1. The condition of
equal means and variabilities has been assumed merely
for convenience of verbal definition; in actual work it is not
at all necessary for it to be fulfilled. Correlation is a
measure of the average similarity of associated individuals,
organs, objects or phenomena comprised in a series. It can-
not, therefore, be calculated for a single pair of relatives,
but only for a large number of pairs forming a sample of
the whole population. It is a general tool of research,
which may be applied to meteorological observations,
fertility of plant lice, inheritance of conscientiousness,
population and national debt, or any other relationship.
The exact meaning of this coefficient may be made clear


## p. 67 (#555) #############################################

by a few illustrations from relationships with which we are
so familiar as to have a very good general idea of what this
amount should be. The correlations for those selected are:
Right and left femur in man.

Any considerable difference in the lengths of the right and
left femur would be very noticeable in its effect on the
individual, but we rarely see deformities of this kind, and
naturally we expect an almost perfect correlation. We
find .96 instead of the upper possible limit of 1. The
relation between forearm and stature in the human species
is a much less intimate one, and we find it expressed by the
fairly low coefficient, .37. Men and women prefer to marry
those of an age not too different from their own, and as a
quantitative expression for this preference, we have the
rather high correlation coefficient of .76.

In the problems of heredity many difficulties are to be
encountered. Francis Galton long ago reminded us that
many pitfalls surround those who tread the paths of
statistics. But statistical methods "are the only tools by
which an opening can be cut through the formidable
thicket of difficulties that bar the path of those who pursue
the science of man." Caution in accepting results which
have not been verified by a large number of investigators
working independently, and with a wide variety of materials,
methods and conditions, we must always have. Neverthe-
less, I cannot but feel that these investigations are a great
milestone on the highway of science, from which we shall
measure progress for many years to come.
It is not necessary to confine investigation to parents


## p. 73 (#561) #############################################

HEREDITY
73
and children; intensity of hereditary resemblance may be
measured for any degree of kinship whatever. All that
is necessary is to secure a measure of the desired character
in all the individuals of a considerable series of the relatives,
and prepare a correlation table similar to the one above.
The practical difficulties in securing suitable material can
be realized only by those who have attempted some such
work. Some data are available for grandparents and
grandchildren in man, and several large series of records
for coat color have been worked over for pedigreed dogs,
horses and cattle. In the ancestral series, the parents have
by far the greatest weight in determining the character-
istics of their children, but the earlier ancestry cannot be
neglected. The correlation between grandparents and
grandchildren is considerably less than that between
parents and children; in fact, the contribution of the
ancestral generations seems to decrease in a geometrical
ratio.
Let us recur for a moment to the law of regression to
mediocrity explained in an earlier paragraph. Our figures
indicated that the children are more mediocre than their
parents, that they tend to be intermediate between their
parents and the average of the population. What can be
the explanation for such a phenomenon? Here a knowl-
edge of the earlier ancestry will serve us. A man has four
grandparents, eight great-grandparents, sixteen great-great-
grandparents, and so on. He inherits from all these, and
such a large number of individuals are very likely to be
merely an average, or mediocre, sample of the whole
population. It is this mediocre blood from earlier ancestors
which draws the son of the gifted man down towards the
mean of the race. It is this good average blood of the popu-
lation which lifts the son of a degenerate individual above
his father. It is important to have high-grade parents,
but it is better to have high-grade grandparents as well.
Selection of the ancestry earlier than the parents reduces


## p. 74 (#562) #############################################

74
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
the tendency to regression. Our present knowledge of
heredity indicates that, with judicious selection for two or
three generations, a strain may be greatly improved.
This conclusion applies not merely to the amelioration
of the race, but to its deterioration as well. Just as the
encouragement of marriage and parenthood among indi-
viduals above the mean will raise the character of the race,
so the free marriage and the unlimited fertility of those
below the average will keep down the physical and mental
standards of the future.
The many interesting problems of heredity, of which
we have given a few examples, might easily detain us at
the expense of the question of the practical utility of such
knowledge. Are not these results merely interesting in a
general way to the layman, and perhaps important to the
scientist with some particular theory of heredity or evolu-
tion, but of no real importance to the public at large?
What utilitarian justification can the statistical biologist
offer for the enormous expenditure of time and labor which
the obtaining of such results as these requires? These are
questions which will be asked by those of practical tastes.
Had it been possible for me to review comprehensively
the literature of statistical biology, I am sure that it would
have been unnecessary to emphasize the practical impor-
tance of much of the work. Here I have of necessity con-
fined myself to the most general explanations. The few
illustrations which could be introduced were drawn from
studies on man, not because evidence from other forms was
not at hand, or because these are particularly suited to
establish some cherished theory, but because they repre-
sent some of the most careful biological researches of modern
times, and because a human audience is likely to take the
most lively interest in the human species. There are two
ways in which a knowledge of heredity may be of practical
importance. The first is in the improvement of animals
and plants to better fit them to serve man's needs, and


## p. 75 (#563) #############################################

HEREDITY
75
the second is no less than the amelioration of the human
stock itself.
One of the problems for the future to solve is how to
provide food and raiment and shelter for a constantly in-
creasing population. In the year 2000, President Pritchett
tells us, the United States will be inhabited by over three
hundred and eighty millions of people. Assuredly all
possible forces must be harnessed, and all available re-
sources developed to their uttermost, if this mass of human-
ity is to have the necessaries of life and a little more. It
will not be sufficient in those days that two blades of grass
be made to grow where but one grew before; they must be
blades of better grass. There was a time when men con-
tented themselves with crab-apples and wild strawberries,
but their ideas are not the prevailing ones to-day. In the
future, the best that nature yields must be found, and its
utmost capacity for improvement realized. Plant and
animal breeding-by which is meant something very
different from plant and animal growing-are daily profit-
ing from the results of scientific investigation. It requires
no courage to-day to predict that in the future the most
important advances in agriculture will be due to the im-
provement of animals and plants to better fit them to meet
the quantitative and the qualitative requirements of man.
And remember that agriculture is not merely the means by
which some men make their living, but the source of the
food of all of us. Gratifying progress has already been
made towards the solution of some of the fundamental
biological problems of plant and animal breeding, and as
our grasp of the laws of variation and heredity becomes
more firm material results will not be lacking.
These are matters which can be only incidentally
touched in passing. Our illustrations have been drawn in
the main from the human species. Let us follow our
problem to the end. Aside from the economic importance
to be attached to the work of animal and plant breeding,


## p. 76 (#564) #############################################

76
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
has the science of heredity any significance for the welfare
of the human race? Some of the characters for which the
strength of heredity has been determined are apparently
of no great importance to the individual or to society.
Color of hair or eyes, or the curliness of hair, would seem to
be of little significance to a race, although it must be said
that there are differences in the mortality of individuals
with light and dark hair and eyes. But when we turn to
such characters as ability and conscientiousness and
health, and find that they are inherited in the same degree
as stature, color of hair, and dimension of head, I think that
there can be but one conclusion. Such results as these
show the immense influence which the physical and mental
characteristics of the parents have upon their offspring.
They speak eloquently of the great significance and respon-
sibility of parenthood.
Nor are these the only facts in support of the view that
a knowledge of heredity is of basal importance to the
philanthropic student of society who is anxious that his
work shall be enduring and not pass with the present. Let
us examine the inheritance of characteristics unquestion-
ably disadvantageous to both the individual and society.

society when he furnishes us with quantitative information
concerning these matters. Some may say that a knowledge
of evils does not remove them; but in many of these cases
it is not only in our power, but it is our duty to the genera-
tions which are to follow, to reduce the evils. The State
says that the pick of the physically fit must go to the front
to die defending their homes, or fighting for the aggrandize-
ment of their Government; why should it not rule that the
physically degenerate shall not pass the burden of their own
helplessness on future generations? The community decrees
that a man must educate his children; why should it not
say that if he is mentally defective he shall bring no weak-
minded children into the world? Public sentiment de-
clares that relatives of certain degrees of nearness shall not
marry; why should it not also turn its mighty forces against
those marriages which are to breed weaklings, whose bodies
are to be hotbeds for the germs of disease?
Opinions cannot, I think, differ as to the answers to
these questions; but all must recognize the immense practi-
cal difficulties to be overcome in approximating the ideal.
It is as easy to suggest remedies as it is to give advice to
a sick acquaintance. Now that public interest is being
aroused in these matters, the number of dilettante novelists
and playwrights who will give us the benefit of their in-
spiration on the subject may be expected to increase.
But let us always remember that our ignorance of the
normal and the pathological physiology of society is pro-
found, and that extreme measures might easily work more
harm than good.
Perhaps there are some lines along which an imme-
diate advance is possible. Do we detain the mentally
deficient, hereditarily insane and incurably criminal in
our institutions of charity for a time, and then, when they
seem outwardly improved, turn them loose upon society to
procreate others of their own kind? Are our families of
the greatest ability contributing their share to the popula-


## p. 78 (#566) #############################################

78
JAMES ARTHUR HARRIS
tion which is to follow, or are the parents of the coming
generation the mediocre, or even less than that? One
most competent to speak on these matters has said:
"Nations which breed freely only from their poorer stocks
will not be dominant factors in civilization by the end of the
century." In populations which have been investigated,
it has been found that about twenty-six per cent. of the
married population contributes about one-half of the next
generation. Is this twenty-six per cent. the best quarter
of those who might become parents? We often hear the
cry that our choice American stock is dying out. If this
be true, what is the reason for it-physical inferiority or
social conditions which need correction? Only about
fifty per cent. of our women university graduates marry at
all, and those who do are mothers of families too small to
maintain the race. What is wrong with our educational
system, and how can it be corrected? Such are the ques-
tions which press upon us for solution. Many of them can
be solved, I think, and conservative but effective measures
may be taken which will do much to raise the physical and
mental standards of the future.
These are matters which, if I mistake not, will soon be
widely discussed. Their colossal importance to the com-
munity and to the nation no one can deny. But let me
urge that in these matters enthusiasm and moderation
both be watchwords. Enthusiasm in research, because
we have vital matters with which to deal; moderation in
propaganda and action, because we are still woefully
ignorant. Let our methods be hygienic rather than surgical;
for we have only begun to study the body politic, and in
our eagerness to achieve great results we might slash an
artery in operating to remove a mole. Here I have ab-
stained from proposing means of securing desired results.
Many suggestions-some of them good and practical, and
some of them, I feel, useless and pernicious-are to be found
in the rapidly growing literature of Eugenics. All who


## p. 79 (#567) #############################################

HEREDITY
79
are sincerely interested in the welfare of the race, who
believe that sound bodies and vigorous minds should be the
heritage of the grandchildren of those now living, should
give thought to these matters. Let there be education of
the public to their significance. Above all, let us insist
that scientific investigation shall furnish us with the facts
which are essential in determining sane action on problems
such as these. Scientific research alone can lay a secure
foundation upon which an enduring system of statecraft
can be builded. Let us have the fullest sympathy with
those who are dressing the stone and preparing the mortar
for this foundation.

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII CENTURY*
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
Assistant Professor of Spanish and Italian, Washington University
It is a bold undertaking to discuss in a single lecture
the Spanish drama of the first half of the 17th century, -
the most important literary manifestation of the Spanish
genius. All that I shall attempt is a brief essay on the
drama as a product of the nation and epoch, avoiding, as
far as possible, the technicalities of literary history and
any accumulation of unfamiliar names.
I shall outline very briefly the political, social and
intellectual conditions of Spain in the 16th and 17th
centuries, with some notice of the vernacular literature
which preceded the literary drama, and a sketch of the
primitive Spanish stage. A short biography of Lope de
Vega, as the creator and chief representative of the Spanish
drama, will precede a brief discussion of his work, genius
and influence. The Spanish theatre at the time of its
greatest development will be reviewed, and I shall conclude
with a notice of Calderón, its last notable dramatist, and
the author of its most celebrated masterpieces.
In order that we may have clearly before us the milieu
in which the Spanish drama was produced, it will be well
briefly to survey the history of the period. It is note-
worthy that Spain's greatest achievements in literature
are not coincident with her greatest exaltation as a world-
power, but manifest themselves after the beginning of
political decay. The notable monuments of her modern
literature appear first in the last years of the 16th century,
while her period of national greatness begins something
more than a hundred years farther back.
The history of Spain as a European power begins with

the union of the crowns of Castile and Aragon, brought
about by the marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabel
of Castile, known to history as the Catholic Monarchs (Los
Reyes Católicos). The recognition of Isabel as Queen of
Castile put an end to a long period of civil strife, and
united the greater part of Spain under a firm rule. In
1479, ten years after his marriage with Isabel, Ferdinand
acceded to the crown of Aragon, a kingdom much smaller
than Castile, but important because of its considerable
appanages oustide of the peninsula, the chief of these being
the islands of Sicily and Sardinia. Under the strong rule
of the Catholic Monarchs, united Spain was rapidly trans-
formed into a powerful absolute monarchy; a regular
police stamped out lawlessness, and a regular soldiery kept
in subjection the turbulent nobility and communes who
were angered by the curtailment of their ancient privileges.
In the memorable year of 1492, Granada, the last remaining
possession of the Moors in Spain, fell into the hands of the
Catholic Monarchs, and Mohammedan rule ceased forever
in Western Europe. The same year also saw the discovery
of the New World under Spanish auspices, and the election
of a Spanish Pope.
In a few words I have tried to suggest how, in the reign
of the Catholic Monarchs, Spain emerged from medieval
conditions, and in the course of a single generation became
a world-power, ready on the one hand to appropriate the
newly-discovered wealth of the New World, and on the
other to use it for furthering her dynastic aims in all the
political quarrels of the Old World. But destiny held in
store for her yet greater opportunities. It would be
tedious to relate just how it came about that Charles I,
grandson of the Catholic Monarchs, inherited, in addition to
Spain and the Indies (with the important Italian appanages
of the Spanish crown), the Low Countries, Austria and
numerous holdings of the Hapsburgs in Germany and Italy,
-in short, the richest countries of Europe. Grandson of
