## p. 82 (#570) #############################################

82
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
the Emperor Maximilian, he was in 1519 elected Emperor
as Charles V, obtaining so the overlordship of all Italy and
Germany.
But not even the indomitable energy of Charles, nor the
zeal and bravery of his Spanish soldiery, could keep in order
an empire so vast and so heterogeneous, or stem the rising
tide of the Reformation. During the greater part of his
life, Charles, as the champion of Catholic unity, exhausted
the resources of his immense estates in a losing fight against
Protestantism in Germany and the Low Countries. In
1555, prematurely aged and discouraged, he withdrew to
the seclusion of a Spanish monastery, dividing his immense
realm between his son Philip and his brother Ferdinand.
The latter received Austria and the candidacy to the
imperial dignity; Philip succeeded to the crown of Spain
and the Indies, annexing to it the Low Countries.
Charles V waged incessant war on the Protestants in the
interests of a united empire; his son, Philip II, determined
to exterminate all heretics in his dominions in the spirit of
an inquisitor. His long reign, filling all the rest of the 16th
century, was most disastrous to Spain. His ruthless
Spanish soldiery drenched the soil of the Low Countries
with the blood of hundreds of thousands of Protestants,
and the result was the independence of Holland, while Spain
remained depopulated and impoverished by the drain of
continual foreign war.
I have recalled to you, in this brief outline, the external
history of Spain from the accession of Ferdinand the
Catholic until the death of Philip II, because the events of
these reigns determined very largely the character of
Spanish national life for the next two centuries, and created
the special conditions of the intellectual and literary milieu
which produced the Spanish drama.
First of all, Spain, as a result of the religious wars which
her monarchs waged, became the representative Catholic
nation. From the earliest times Christian Spain has stood


## p. 83 (#571) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
83
for united orthodoxy, and it was natural that her people
should have no toleration for the schism-begetting inno-
vations of Luther. The great part which Spaniards were
called upon to take in the religious wars of the 16th century
only inflamed their Catholic zeal. They stood ready to
immolate themselves and the prosperity of their country
at the bidding of their fanatical monarch whenever he
called them to fight for the Cross-in other words, the
unity of Catholic Christendom. In these days of divided
interests it is very difficult even vaguely to imagine the
extent to which 16th century Europe was dominated by
religious ideas. The more the zeal of Protestantism waxed
in Northern Europe, the more the flame of the Catholic
reaction glowed in Spain. Even sensuous and material-
istic Italy, overrun with Spanish priests and soldiers, was
compelled to abandon the scepticism of the humanists,
and put on the garb of immaculate orthodoxy. Some
notion of the religious obsession of Spain at this period may
be had from the numbers of people who took sacred orders
or entered religious congregations. When the whole popula-
tion of the country hardly numbered seven or eight millions,
it is estimated that there were some four hundred thousand
clerics and religious. In some large towns, as Valladolid,
for example, nearly one-half of the population dwelt in
religious houses or were directly attached to the service of
ecclesiastical establishments. Men of superior ability,
almost without exception, were to be found in the service of
the Church. There was nothing else that then seemed
worth while, and, for persons of plebeian birth, it was
almost the only path to posts of honor and distinction.
Men of pre-eminent genius, who in these times might have
been great statesmen, scientists or authors, became mystics
or preachers, or devoted their marvelous talents to founding
or reforming religious orders: as did, for example, Ignatius
Loyola, the founder of the Society of Jesus.
The 16th century, the period of Spain's political great-


## p. 84 (#572) #############################################

84
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
ness, when the unmatched valor and efficiency of her
soldiery made her rulers the arbiters of three continents,
was not productive of enduring Castilian literature. The
religious exaltation of the times evoked a large number of
mystic and religious writings. Two great names stand out
from the many-Fray Luis Ponce de Leon, and that most
remarkable woman, Saint Teresa of Avila. To these two
renowned mystics we owe the first developed modern
Castilian prose. Their writings, plain, direct, forceful, are
still models of prose style. In the 16th century they
restored to Castilian prose the vigor and naturalness which
it was losing through imitation of the latinizing artificialities
of contemporary Italian models.
While ecclesiastics and religious were writing volumin-
ous works for edification, courtiers and gentlemen of leisure
continued the old tradition of inditing verses, but the old
Spanish types of verse were neglected for the fashionable
Italian modes. Octaves, sonnets, and all the elaborate
canzone forms displaced the national romance, cuaderna vía,
quintilla, etc., these latter forms being henceforward rele-
gated to rustics and strolling singers, and to the stage,
where, as we shall have occasion to notice, a splendid de-
velopment awaited them.
Not only did the courtly poets of the 16th century
appropriate Italian verse forms, but Italian words and ideas
as well, so that their verse was merely a colorless imitation
of an exotic school. The soul-stirring events and crises of
16th century Spain found no great poet to sing them, nor
did any genius arise to emancipate Spanish poetry from the
yoke of foreign fashion.
But fortunately for the artistic future of the nation,
Spanish literature in the 16th century was not wholly con-
fined to works of religious exaltation or effusions of italian-
izing verse. To this period of Spain's literary development
belongs the creation of the modern novel in both of its
main types, the romantic and the realistic. In Spain and


## p. 85 (#573) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
85
Portugal the medieval tales of chivalry first took on the
form of a romantic novel, arranging the episodes of prowess
and adventure about a continuous love story. Amadis de
Gaula, of uncertain Portuguese authorship and translated
into Castilian in 1508, was the first, and its immense vogue
called forth many sequels and imitations, which throughout
the 16th century delighted successive generations of hyper-
imaginative Spaniards.
Far more interesting to the modern student, and also
far more important to the subsequent development of
Spanish literature (and other modern literatures as well),
is the second type of novel evolved in the 16th century, —
the picaresque, the prototype of the realistic novel. A
pícaro was originally a miserable, half-naked boy, employed
to turn the spit in medieval kitchens. Later the term
was generalized to mean any ragged young vagabond who
made a precarious livelihood by the exercise of native
cunning and guile. The pícaro makes his entrance into
literature in the story of Lazarillo de Tormes, a work of
disputed authorship, the earliest known editions of which
bear the date 1554. It is a most realistic account of the
wanderings and adventures of a pícaro, who, in the service
of successive eccentric and unlucky masters, eked out a
starved existence. He gets into all manner of "scrapes,"
but in the end makes a way for himself by rather shady
means, and becomes a respected citizen. The humor is
not always delicate. A thrashing or a broken head, visited
upon somebody through Lazarillo's machinations, is a stock
method of provoking merriment.
The real interest of Lazarillo de Tormes, however, does
not lie in the multifarious adventures of its hero. If that
were all, it would be merely a sort of Peck's Bad Boy. The
biography of the picaro is the vehicle for a marvelously keen
satire on the social and economic conditions of contemporary
Spain. Here there is no echo of the unmatched valor of
Spanish arms or of the world-embracing projects of the


## p. 86 (#574) #############################################

86
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
Catholic Monarchy by which all Europe was being thrown
into confusion, but instead, the frankest possible presenta-
tion of the vices which were opening the way for the pre-
mature decay of the nation, -the sloth and improvidence
of the nobility, the corruption of ecclesiastics and officials,
the widespread idleness and ignorance of the people, and the
portentous growth of parasitism and beggary. The wonder
of it is that royal censors and ecclesiastical inquisitors
allowed such plain speaking to pass unchallenged.
Naturally the success of Lazarillo de Tormes was imme-
diate, and it found many imitators, but to the genius of
Cervantes was reserved the artistic triumph of uniting in
a single work the realism and satire of the picaresque novel
with the fantasy and idealism of the romance of chivalry.
Published early in the 17th century, the Quijote may be
regarded as an epitome of all the literary movements of the
preceding century. Not only does it embody the literary
tradition of both the types of popular novel, but it shows
also the results of the Italian influence, including, as it does,
pastorals, novelle and many passages of latinizing prose.
I should like to say more about this incomparable work,
still read and enjoyed by all classes of people throughout
the civilized world, the greatest monument of Spanish
literature and one of the greatest in any literature, but as
it lies quite outside of my general subject, the drama, I may
only mention it as a landmark in the literature which pre-
ceded the great development of the theatre in the first half
of the 17th century.
I shall, however, call attention to the character of Don
Quixote in so far as it is typical of the Spanish character in
general. Spaniards have always been, and are still, emi-
nently quixotic. Like Don Quixote himself, they are prone
to pursue ideals impossible of realization, remaining blind
to actual conditions and pressing needs. From the self-
immolation of the inhabitants of Numantia in 133 в. с., to
the naval battle of Santiago de Cuba in 1898, the history


## p. 87 (#575) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
87
of Spanish warfare has been full of such examples of heroic
sacrifice and wasted valor, of going to battle without count-
ing the cost. And quixotism was never more rampant than
in the period which we are studying, when Spain exhausted
herself and precipitated her own ruin in the vain attempt to
impose religious unity upon Europe by force of arms.
With this I conclude my general survey of the literary
movements which preceded and made possible the develop-
ment of the 17th century drama, but before I take up that
subject it will be necessary to say a few words about the
stage in Spain before the 17th century. In Spain, as in
other European countries, the beginnings of the stage were
wholly ecclesiastical, the earliest attempts at drama being
merely additions to the liturgy on certain festivals, but long
before the 16th century the stage had largely freed itself
from the limitations imposed by liturgical conventions.
Mirth-provoking interludes of wholly secular character were
freely introduced into the dramatic representations of the
most sacred mysteries of the faith.
Already in the 16th century there were many troops of
strolling players who were employed to give religious plays
on the patronal feasts and other red-letter days, celebrated
with pomp and show by ecclesiastical establishments. In
addition to their sacred repertory, these bands of pro-
fessionals took care to be well provided with farces and
comic interludes in the taste of the day. In seasons when
the church play business was slack, these people gave plays
on their own account in public squares or yards of inns.
These performances were not for edification, being often
extremely indecent. They were the subject of constant
attack on the part of the clergy, and several times in the
course of the 16th century the acting of secular plays was
absolutely forbidden by royal decree. But shows were the
meat and drink of the idlers of the time, and the popular
stage was able to survive in spite of persecution.
In 1568 all shows in Madrid were put under the control


## p. 88 (#576) #############################################

88
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
of a religious association, which received a share of the
profits. Soon after, two regular theatres were licensed-
the Patio del Príncipe in 1579, and the Patio de la Cruz in
1583, these two houses having henceforward a monopoly of
the business in the capital. It is significant of the fixedness
of some things in Spain that two of the three high-class
theatres in Madrid to-day still stand on the sites of these
earliest playhouses, and one still bears the old name of
Teatro del Príncipe.
As the name patio implies, these first theatres were
merely open courtyards, with a stage erected at one end,
and seats in the narrow galleries running around the three
remaining sides. The main body of the audience stood up
in the uncovered court. And it should be noted that these
primitive arrangements persisted throughout the classical
period of the Spanish stage. All the accessories were of the
simplest possible sort, painted scenery, artificial lighting
and spectacular effects being reserved for the plays given
at royal court functions and never seen in the popular
theatres.
The plays, brought out by hundreds during the latter
half of the 16th century, were not regarded as literature,
and consequently very few samples of them have come
down to us; but these few help us to bear with equanimity
the loss of all the rest. Regarded as literature, they are
unspeakably crude.
The theatre of the 16th century, however, performed
an important service in creating a regular theatre-going
public, and in fixing the general conventions of the Spanish
stage. The long-continued success of the popular stage
made it impossible for literary theorists to force upon it
the strait-jacket of the classical unities, or the artificial
separation of tragedy and comedy. Several 16th century
Spanish writers composed tragedies on classical lines, and
even had them acted, but their attempts were not crowned
with success, and before the advent of the great playwrights


## p. 89 (#577) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
89
of the 17th century it was recognized that the Spanish
theatre must be left free to develop on national lines.
At the end of the 16th century we find the Spanish
comedia written in verse and divided into three acts, called
jornadas or days, although neither between nor within the
acts were any rigorous time-limits imposed. The place of
the action changes at the whim of the author, and in the
absence of scenery was generally indicated by allusions
in the dialogue of the play, a more artistic device than the
signboard which was displayed on the Elizabethan stage.
Besides the comedia, there were short farces in prose, called
entremeses, and the final development of the religious play,
the allegorical auto in one act in verse, ostensibly devoted
to the exposition of the mystery of the Blessed Sacrament.
The autos were mainly performed on the feast of Corpus
Christi, and during its octave nobles and prelates vied with
one another in the splendor of the performances which they
offered on stages erected before their palaces.
In the last years of the 16th century, while Cervantes
was writing the imperishable tale of Don Quixote, a man
fifteen years younger than he was enchanting the public
with his marvelous gifts as a dramatic author, and was pro-
ducing plays which were to transform the Spanish drama
from a coarse pastime of the vulgar into the chief literary
genre of Castilian.
Lope Felix de Vega Carpio, called more briefly Lope de
Vega, was born in Madrid in 1562. I shall present some
biographical details, as the career of Lope de Vega is in
many ways eminently characteristic of the lives of literary
men of his country and period. Born of well-to-do parents,
he received a careful education, first in a noted Jesuit school,
and later at the University of Alcalá, then, as it is still, the
foremost in Spain, but now transferred from Alcalá to
Madrid. In those days the road to learning was not as
long as it is now, and at the age of twenty we find him
through with college and enlisting in the expedition sent


## p. 90 (#578) #############################################

90
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
to subdue the Azores, in revolt against the Spanish annexa-
tion of the crown of Portugal, which Philip II had just
effected. Returning to Spain, he was attached to the
household of the Bishop of Avila. As the son of a gentle-
man he could not, of course, engage in any kind of business,
but to be a sort of gentleman groom or valet in the service
of a prelate or grandee was a most honorable occupation,
and, outside of the Army and the Church, almost the only
one that a young man of family could embrace. A little
later we find him in the household of the young Duke of
Alba, a grandson of the Duke so dreadly famous in the
bloody religious wars of the Low Countries. The de-
scendant of the terrible soldier employed Lope's facile pen,
not to chronicle his grandsire's mighty deeds, but to allegor-
ize his own amorous escapades in a tedious pastoral in the
current Italian manner.
In 1588 Lope took part in Philip's
unlucky expedition against England. Back in Spain, he
resumed his rather questionable position as poet chronicler
of the adventures of the Duke of Alba.
At this period, Lope, though already married, seems to
have had some adventures of his own. Fighting a duel with
a noble, he was for a while exiled to Valencia, where he first
became seriously interested in the drama, although he had
composed plays since his early youth. Before 1600 he
served in the households of two more grandees, and married
a second time.
From the year 1600 on, Lope de Vega held the first
place among Spanish men of letters, and the immense
number of plays which he produced yielded an income
which might have made him independent, and that in a
period when authors relied for support almost entirely
upon the patronage of the great. But Lope was a typical
Spaniard, vain and ostentatious, and, at the same time,
lavishly generous, not knowing how to refuse any appeal
that came to him. Although he now maintained his own
establishment in Madrid, and earned what were then


## p. 91 (#579) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
91
fabulous sums for an author, he was always in dire financial
straits, and sought relief by cultivating the good graces
of noble and wealthy patrons, just as any poor writer might
have done. In some matters, as we have already had
occasion to notice, Lope's moral standards were not of the
highest, so that it does not cause surprise to find that his
principal patron was the profligate young Duke of Sessa.
The latter employed the now middle-aged poet to compose
amatory letters and verses for his numerous intrigues.
Lope's own disorderly conduct probably hastened the
death of his second wife, which occured in 1612. Filled
with remorse, Lope, who had always been fervently religious
and a devoted Catholic, now turned to the Church, and two
years later was ordained priest. During the remaining
twenty-one years of his life, he continued to exercise his
sacerdotal functions with unremitting zeal and piety, but
as these were limited apparently to a daily mass in a privi-
leged oratory attached to his own house, there was no
diminution in his poetical and dramatical output, and he
even found time to continue the writing of amatory missives
for the Duke of Sessa. There has come down to us an
interesting correspondence upon this subject, in which Lope
tries to beg off, because his confessor, very properly scandal-
ized by such conduct on the part of a priest, has threatened
to withhold absolution if the thing continues.
As Lope de Vega lived, so lived most of the literary
lights of 17th century Spain, although few enjoyed his
worldly prosperity. Nearly all were by turns soldiers,
courtiers and ecclesiastics. All were dependent upon
wealthy patrons, who obtained for them official or ecclesi-
astical sinecures which left them leisure for the pursuit of
letters, and all were strict Catholics, although in most cases
the exercise of religion was not incompatible with a good
deal of looseness in private life. All of these conditions we
find accurately reflected in the works these men wrote.
And, in particular, to understand the strange ideals, the


## p. 92 (#580) #############################################

92
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
perverse blending of the exalted and the trivial, the con-
fusion of the moral and the immoral, which characterize
the Spanish drama, one must constantly bear in mind the
checkered careers of the writers and the anomalous con-
ditions of the decadent society of 17th century Spain.
The prodigious literary activity of Lope de Vega seemed
miraculous to his contemporaries, and for us it remains
totally inexplicable, something without any parallel in the
whole history of literature. I shall not discuss his mis-
cellaneous poetic works, published in twenty-one large
octavo volumes, and comprising numerous epics and
pastorals, thousands of lyrics and rhymed epistles, whole
volumes of sonnets and a great body of sacred poetry-
some of the latter very beautiful and still popular in Spain.
Neither shall I present a minute analysis of each one of
Lope's eighteen hundred three-act dramas and four hundred
autos. Nor will you exact it of me when I tell you that
there are preserved to us not over four hundred and fifty
comedias, just a fraction of the whole number.
What did this marvelous exhibition of literary fecundity
accomplish for the Spanish theatre? If Lope had been
a mere scribbler, like his French contemporary, Hardi,
the answer would be-Nothing. But Lope was a great deal
more than a facile improvisatore. He was a dramatic
genius, and his astounding facility of composition was only
one manifestation of his many-sided talents. He found
the Spanish theatre in the crude state which I have de-
scribed, and he left it a matured institution, endowed with
a splendid literature, a source of models and plots for
generations of Castilian and foreign dramatists.
In the first place, Lope was wise enough to recognize
the value of the national traditions, whereas all the men of
letters who had preceded him in attempts to write for the
stage had endeavored to impose the rules of Latin tragedies
and comedies, together with the difficult Italian versification.
Lope accepted the comedia as he found it, frankly recogni-


## p. 93 (#581) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
93
zing that no good could come of violently breaking with the
popular forms. He kept for the main portion of the dialogue
the easy and supple romance, an eight-syllabled verse with
assonance of vowels at the close of every second line. In
lyric passages the romance gives way to rhyming stanzas of
the national twelve-syllabled verse. Sonnets and other
forms of the Italian hendecasyllabic are sparingly intro-
duced where special effects are desired. The rehabilitation,
through the drama, of the inherited Spanish verse forms,
so much neglected by the italianizing poets of the 16th
century, is not the least of Lope's achievements.
The subject of Lope's comedias in their bewildering
variety defy classification. The only limitations were
those imposed by the censors of Church and Crown. Clas-
sical mythology, Greek and Roman history, Old Testament
history, patristic and medieval hagiography, Carolingian,
Arthurian and crusading chivalry, Spanish and Italian
history, literary tales and folk-lore, pastoral, allegory and
dogma, were all put under contribution.
Lope's great achievement, however, was not the dram-
atization of historical or literary material, but the presenta-
tion on the stage of contemporary society, the so-called
Comedia de capa y espada, or Cloak and Sword Play, the
name having reference merely to the usual dress of gentle-
men of the period. Before this, contemporary life had
been represented only in the comic farces and interludes,
and in these only the lowest strata of society figured. The
cloak and sword play centered about the doings of nobles
and bourgeois, and reflects the transformation of the theatre
from a pastime of street loafers to the regular diversion of
the upper classes.
The substitution of genteel for plebeian dramatis personæ
did not mean, however, the suppression of the popular
element. In the cloak and sword plays Lope always intro-
duced a few vulgar characters, usually as servants of the
principals. The dialogue of these menials retains much of


## p. 94 (#582) #############################################

94
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
the coarse humor and unbridled license that were character-
istic of the old 16th century farces. The clever hireling,
clownish and vulgar, but at the same time resourceful,
witty and pert to the verge of insolence, became hence-
forward a stock role in every comedia, receiving the name of
gracioso, or wag. Lope's adaptation, in the rôle of the
gracioso, of the comic elements of the popular farce to the
polite comedy was a master-stroke of genius, and a fact of
great significance in the subsequent history of the Continen-
tal theatre. The witty domestics who play such a large part
in the comedies of Molière are all direct descendants of the
gracioso.
But none of Lope's imitators showed such consummate
skill as he in the disposition of the comic material afforded
by the graciosos. In his plays the underlings carry on a
continuous travesty of the acts of the principals, a sort
of play within a play, the burlesque of the graciosos being
skillfully employed to heighten by contrast the effects of
the main dialogue. For instance, if two lovers are unfolding
to each other their undying passion, careful, of course, to
dress it up in the elaborate euphuisms then fashionable,
their polished dialogue is from time to time interrupted by
a burlesque flirtation between their attendants on the other
side of the stage, the latter often mimicking the very ex-
pressions of their superiors, but always in such a way as
to provoke mirth without making the action of the principals
seem unreal or ridiculous. You will recall a similarly
arranged double dialogue in Goethe's Faust, namely, the
garden scene where Faust makes love to Margarethe, while
Martha coquettes with Mephistopheles.
The simultaneous interweaving of two plots, one re-
garding the masters, the other the domestics, is only one
example of Lope's fondness for complexity of structure.
Although his plays must have been written with almost
stenographic haste, still the plot is always highly intricate
and is usually consistently worked out. The cloak and


## p. 95 (#583) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
95
sword play in particular, untrammeled by any historical
data, afforded Lope's fertile imagination a virgin field for
the production of novel and ingenious plots. Thence-
forward the enredo, as the intricate plot was called, became
a regular feature of Spanish plays, but as a matter of fact
very few entirely new plots were devised. The genius of
a single man left to posterity such a vast storehouse of
dramatic material that successive generations of play-
wrights were content merely to adapt or plagiarize his
inventions.
But Lope de Vega was far too great a dramatist to
depend for interest solely, or even mainly, upon the plot.
While minute studies of character, involving elaborate
psychological dissections, are not to be looked for in plays
written so rapidly, nevertheless the elemental passions
which are the kernel of all real drama are presented with
force and truth. And to the ordinary motives of drama,
love, hate, jealousy, envy, avarice, etc., there is added one
that is particularly Spanish-honor.
Personal honor in European society is a remarkable
survival of social relations which were most natural and
fitting in the days of continual feudal warfare. But the
history of survivals is always the same: what was a
real necessity survives as a mere convention, and what
was once done in earnest continues to be performed in a
symbolic and attenuated shape. In feudal times, for
example, when the upper classes maintained their position
by deeds of arms, and not by bank accounts, disparagement
of a man's valor could only be avenged in blood. Compare
with this the France of to-day, where insults are wiped out
by firing bullets into the air.
Nowhere did the ideal of personal honor take such deep
root as in Spain. I have already spoken of the impractical
and uncompromising idealism which is a mark of the
national character. We should not expect men who were
ready to put whole nations to the sword in the name of


## p. 96 (#584) #############################################

96
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
religion to be satisfied with purely conventional codes of
honor and symbolic reparations. On the contrary, the
true Spaniard did not hesitate to sacrifice his life nor the
lives and happiness of those nearest and dearest to him
if his notions of personal self-respect demanded it. Lope
de Vega's most powerful dramas hinge upon questions of
honor. Naturally, to our common-sense vision, the ideals
pursued seem exaggerated, and even grotesque, and the
suffering and sacrifice which they entail inhuman and
purposeless, but Lope, let us remember, was writing for
men with just such ideals and perhaps capable of just such
deeds.
It must be granted, however, that the tragic effect is
stupendous. In the Spanish drama honor, unswerving,
unassailable, pitiless, remorseless, baneful, directs or thwarts
human lives and visits grewsome, because unmerited,
punishments, being in everything a worthy artistic counter-
part of the ruthless nemesis of Greek tragedy.
Castilian honor, as a tragic motive, found admirers out-
side of Spain; witness Corneille's Cid, the best known of
all French tragedies, itself adapted from a play on the same
subject by Guillén de Castro, a contemporary of Lope de
Vega. Castro modeled his plot on that of an earlier play
by Lope on a different historical subject. L'honneur
castillan, you remember, is the sub-title as well as the
subject of Victor Hugo's most successful drama, Hernani.
From neither of these plays, however, can one form an
adequate idea of the handling of honor as a dramatic
motive by Castilian writers. In the French Cid the too
harsh consequences are mitigated in accord with the con-
ventions of the 17th century French stage, while Hernani
is too fantastic, too heavily charged with Hugo's romantic
coloring, faithfully to represent the real Castilian honor.
I have sought to give you some notion of Lope de
Vega's extraordinary talent, of the immense range of his
theatre, and of the far-reaching influence which he exerted


## p. 97 (#585) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
97
upon the drama. Yet, in spite of these facts, Lope de
Vega is not one of the world's greatest names. In his
lifetime he seemed a much greater man than his contem-
porary, William Shakespeare, and infinitely greater than
his humble countryman, Miguel de Cervantes; but Shakes-
peare and Cervantes are securely enthroned in the world's
literary pantheon, and Lope de Vega is not. Lope brought
forth no peerless masterpieces to remain forever the wonder
and delight of a universal public. Shakespeare, I imagine,
wrote for the Globe Theatre rather than for the world, but
masterpieces of universal scope were the necessary result
of his incomparable genius. Lope de Vega, on the other
hand, composed stately epics which he thought would
immortalize his name, while he regarded the drama as a
literary genre of inferior rank. He even neglected to collect
his plays for publication until numbers of them were
published by others with false attributions, and not more
than a quarter part of his plays were ever printed. As a
world poet, a creator of enduring epic, he failed; he had not
the genius of a Dante or a Milton. As a playwright he
succeeded beyond all measure with his contemporaries,
perhaps just because he wrote his plays for them and not
for posterity. His theatre throughout is intensely Spanish
and local, with powerful appeals to all the prejudices of his
age. Lope created the Spanish drama, but to endow it with
imperishable masterpieces was the work of another, the
immortal Calderón, of whom I shall speak in a few moments.
In the reign of Philip III, Spain, though still outwardly
powerful, found herself, after a century of misrule at home
and fruitless warfare abroad, in a state of rapid economic
and social dissolution. And, as often happens in decaying
states, the bankrupt people, to console themselves for their
flown prosperity, ran after shows. Spain went theatre-mad.
Theatres sprang up everywhere. Grandees, prelates and
officers of state regaled their friends with sumptuous private
performances. The sensuous and art-loving young king,
7


## p. 98 (#586) #############################################

98
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
Philip IV, who reigned from 1623, made the theatre the
chief amusement of the Court, and squeezed from his de-
pleted treasury huge sums for gorgeous stage shows. During
the whole of the long and disastrous reign of Philip IV the
theatre continued to flourish exceedingly, and the dramatic
output of this period is little short of fabulous.
The very success of the theatre, however, was its ruin.
Those were not times of three-hundred-night runs, but, on
the contrary, every company had to have each season a
score of new plays. The inventive genius of all Spain's
playwrights could not satisfy such demands, and so old
plots of forgotten successes of Lope de Vega's or Tirso de
Molina's were furbished up anew. As their number in-
creased, plays grew more and more conventional, so that
within thirty years of Lope's death the stage had abandoned
all claim to a place in literature. Drama had sunk to a
machine-made sort of melodrama, and nothing could hence-
forth save the national theatre from sharing in the general
decay which overtook every Spanish institution.
The great period of the Spanish stage does not extend
much beyond the middle of the 17th century, but in the
period between 1600 and 1660 there flourished a truly
remarkable number of talented dramatic authors. En-
couraged by Lope de Vega's phenomenal success, there
appeared, as if by magic, a host of writers possessing a
complete mastery of Lope's recently-invented technique,
and ready to produce comedias that should rival his.
Of the many notable dramatic names of this period,
perhaps only one is of international interest. To Fray
Gabriel Téllez, a monk who wrote for the stage over the
pseudonym of Tirso de Molina, belongs the first drama
dealing with the story of Don Juan, the sacrilegious roué
who invited to a banquet the statue of the man he had
wickedly killed. Few dramas can claim such a numerous
and cosmopolitan offspring as Tirso's El Burlador de Sevilla,
the original Don Juan.


## p. 99 (#587) #############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
99
I bring my paper to an end with a brief notice of Pedro
Calderón de la Barca Henao de la Barreda y Riaño, after
Lope de Vega, the greatest name of the Castilian theatre,
and the author of its most admired masterpieces. Calderón
was born in 1600, and died at the advanced age of eighty-
one; but his long life was rather uneventful, if compared
with that of other literary men of his time. In his youth
he served in the wars. We hear of his fighting only two
duels, and suffering but one imprisonment. In 1636, the
year after the death of Lope de Vega, Philip IV began to
employ him to write plays for the Court, endowing him with
a knighthood in the wealthy military order of Santiago.
In 1651 he was ordained to the priesthood, and henceforward
enjoyed the emoluments of several royal chaplaincies.
Calderón's theatre, published soon after his death, com-
prises about one hundred and twenty comedias and seventy
autos, a very modest number if compared with Lope de
Vega's production, and less than that of Tirso de Molina
and many others. Calderón's plays, for the most part, con-
tinue on the lines laid down by Lope de Vega. Subjects,
plots and motives remain as characteristically Spanish in
treatment, with an added tendency to overcharge every
means of dramatic effect. Situations and motives are
strained until they become unreal and even unthinkable,
while a stilted elevation of the language, on the one hand,
or a perverse complication of it, on the other, often deprives
the dialogue of naturalness and spontaneity. These defects
belong not so much to Calderón as to the period in which he
wrote, and are premonitions of the rapid and complete
decay which overtook the post-Calderonian drama.
That which raises Calderón above all his contemporaries,
and bears his name triumphantly down through the cen-
turies, is the sublime poetry with which he clothed his
dramas. Lyric passages of unsurpassed beauty abound.
While, as I have said, the emphase and preciosité peculiar to
the times tend to make much of Calderón's theatre seem


## p. 100 (#588) ############################################

100
WINTHROP HOLT CHENERY
artificial, yet, on the other hand, his exalted imagination
could clothe abstractions in such luminous verse that they
hold us spellbound. In the allegorical auto he knew no
rival, and although formal allegory is not present in his
greatest dramas, we feel, nevertheless, that the rôles are
more symbolic than real. At least two of Calderón's dramas
rise to the level of great poems, the dramatic interest being
wholly subordinate to the sustained grandeur of the poetic
motive which runs through them.
To me the most beautiful of Calderón's dramatic poems
is the play called La vida es sueño (Life is a Dream). This
splendid poem pictures the unreality of merely human
aspirations and achievements by means of the vicissitudes
of an ill-starred prince. Brought up in chains, ignorant
of his rank, he one day awakes to find himself in possession
of everything that belongs to him by birth. Yielding to
his untutored passions, he abuses his newly-found freedom
and power, thus fulfilling the evil prophecies which led to
his early imprisonment. Again cast into prison, he is
again returned to power by a discontented faction, but,
weary and disillusioned, he forsakes the unrealities of
worldly power for the verities of religion. But without
the majestic poetry which accompanies it, without the
sustained dream effect which envelops the whole drama,
the mere plot seems hardly worth relating. Even more
admired than La vida es sueño is El Mágico prodigioso (The
Wonder-working Magician), an adaptation of the Faust
saga.
More than any other Spanish poet, Calderón has been
admired and imitated by foreigners, especially by the
English and German romantic poets of the first half of the
19th century, and I venture to close my paper by reading
you a bit of Shelley's version of a scene in El Mágico pro-
digioso. The spirit of the Evil One, being asked who he is
and whence he comes, replies:


## p. 101 (#589) ############################################

SPANISH DRAMA IN THE XVII. CENTURY
101
"Since thou desirest, I will then unveil
Myself to thee;-for in myself I am
A world of happiness and misery;
This I have lost, and that I must lament
For ever. In my attributes I stood
So high and so heroically great,
In lineage so supreme, and with a genius
Which penetrated with a glance the world
Beneath my feet, that was by my high merit.
A King-whom I may call the King of kings,
Because all others tremble in their pride
Before the terrors of his countenance-
In his high palace roofed with brightest gems
Of living light-call them the stars of heaven-
Named me his counsellor. But the high praise
Stung me with pride and envy, and I rose
In mighty competition, to ascend
His seat, and place my foot triumphantly
Upon his subject thrones. Chastised, I know
The depth to which ambition falls: too mad
Was the attempt, and yet more mad were now
Repentance of the irrevocable deed;
Therefore I close this ruin with the glory
Of not to be subdued, before the shame
Of reconciling me with him who reigns
By coward cession. Nor was I alone,
Nor am I now, nor shall I be alone;
And there was hope, and there may still be hope
For many suffrages among his vassals
Hailed me their lord and king, and many still
Are mine, and many more shall be.
Thus vanquished, though in fact victorious,
I left his seat of empire."

THE FORMATION OF PUBLIC OPINION AS
EXEMPLIFIED BY THE STANDARD
OIL CASE
AMBROSE PARÉ WINSTON
Assistant Professor of Economics, Washington University.
The mass of books and other writings on the Standard
Oil Company has been too great for most busy people to
examine with any thoroughness. It is, however, extremely
important that the essential facts in that company's history
should be understood with some precision, since the whole
course of public sentiment and legislation regarding large
wealth will doubtless continue to be influenced powerfully
by the prevalent opinion regarding this most famous cor-
poration; the acts and effects attributed to it are taken as
representative of the whole wide class to which it belongs.
It may, therefore, be useful to present a compact resumé
of the chief accusations which have provoked so bitter
hostility towards the company, and a review of the evi-
dence upon which these accusations are based, -together
with a few comments as to the significance of that evidence.
As the body of economic facts here considered is typical
of much that is most important in our whole economic life,
so the discussion here reviewed may be taken as typical
of the process by which, in the United States, popular
sentiment on economic questions is given form. By the
test of this instance one may judge how far the public are
capable of forming opinions on such matters-how keenly
or inaccurately they observe facts, how steadily or how
hastily they reason. Three sources have supplied the
public with its information: (1) Books (especially Miss
Tarbell's History); (2) Proceedings in court (especially the
trial famous for the amount of the fine imposed by Judge


## p. 103 (#591) ############################################

PUBLIC OPINION AND THE STANDARD OIL COMPANY 103
Landis in Chicago); (3) Official investigations (chiefly the
report by the Commissioner of Corporations, Mr. Garfield,
on the Transportation of Petroleum). The History, the
case at law, and the Report just mentioned, will here be
taken as representative of all that mass of writings.
The chief counts in Miss Tarbell's indictment are the
following:
1. The Standard Oil Company got lower rates from the
railways by bribing the railway officials: "The oil-carrying
roads were bullied, persuaded or bribed into unjust dis-
criminations." (Vol. II, p. 227.)
In the entire work no support is offered for this half-
hearted accusation of bribery. It is apparently offered
under stress of rhetorical necessity near the end of the
second volume, when the reader may be supposed to have
forgotten that in Volume I, (p. 170), at the only point
where any such charge is set forth circumstantially even
in quotation, it is discredited and, by implication, denied.
We are told there that a rival of the Standard Oil Company
asserted that a share of rebates was paid to the officer of
the road granting them, but he repeatedly declared that he
had no proof. Yet "there were plenty of people to overlook
his explanation and assert that he had given proof."
"The belief spread," says Miss T., " and is met even to-day
in oil circles."
2. The Standard Oil Company was charged with corrupt
political influence, especially with bribing the Ohio Legisla-
ture to elect H. B. Payne to the United States Senate.
The connection of the Standard Oil Company with the
bribery, if bribery there was, is proved by the following facts
(Volume II, pp. 111 ff.): (a) This gentleman (rich enough
to do his own bribing if he had any such inclination), was
father of the Treasurer of the Standard Oil Company, who
was supported, in working for the father, by other employés
of the company. (b) "All over the State" the Standard
Oil Company was charged with the crime. (c) In the

Senate "the name of the Standard was freely used."
(d) Senator Payne voted against the Interstate Commerce
Act. (e) Finally, through all this, "the Standard Oil Com-

it not?)
In this connection it is added that the Standard Oil
Company was making itself master of state and national
legislation. "There had been many evidences of this,
satisfactory to the initiated." Then follow a page of

proof." (P. 112.) (Evidence, "more or less poor in
evidence," not supported in any one instance of the half-
dozen by satisfactory proof, yet as evidence "satisfactory
to the initiated!")

The points just discussed-the charge of corrupt political

case," it will be noticed, is referred to by the reviewer
in enumerating the "methods of the Standard," though
the book reviewed, besides making that charge, also shows
that it was false. A reviewer is not expected to read the
books he reviews, but it seems not unreasonable to ask
that by exception, when one quotes from a book a grave
accusation of attempted murder, say, or arson-he should
know whether the author quoted has really made and
upheld the accusation. If a University professor and a
writer of good reputation, enlightening the public through
a superior journal like the Dial, stumbles thus, what
accuracy can be hoped for in the opinions of the public
at large, reading on such matters without the profes-
sional student's advantages in training and leisure?

It is hard to understand why a writer should thus,

to make sport of her readers through a just confidence that
they would prove too lazy to recall on one page what was said
on another-or even the same-page. It is a more probable
explanation that the worst methods of newspaper reporting
have here been carried over-not for the first or last time-
into the monthly magazine field. The publishers announced
a work as thrilling as any fiction; the reporter fulfilled the
requirements of the assignment, after the slovenly irres-
ponsible manner in which some reporters wield the irres-
istible power of the press.

10. The Standard Oil Company shipped oil by rail at
rates less than those paid by other shippers. Various

For the early period of the oil business it can hardly be

with the Pennsylvania Railroad, was at first a shipping
company, and later engaged in the oil-refining business.
Another rival was the Pennsylvania Transportation Com-
pany, owned by Jay Gould, President of the Erie Railroad.
So long as any one of these rivals refused to observe what
were ostensibly the general rates, every other one of them
was compelled, under pain of destruction, to do likewise.
It may perhaps be argued that one would readily thus
commit suicide if his moral standards were exceptionally
high, but it cannot be said that one's standards are exceр-
tionally low if, in the presence of such an alternative, he
decides to live.
(b) Whatever force there may be in the opinion that one
should not do wrong because his rivals do, that opinion has
no force as a ground of harsh censure in this case, since the
acceptance of rebates during the seventies was a thing at
which the most conscientious man might have no hesitation.
Miss Tarbell asserts, as the public have since generally
assumed, that the same rate to the large and small shipper
is required by "the most obvious principles of justice."
(Vol. I, p. 102). One who declares that such a matter
is obvious thereby confesses a failure to see that economic
facts are complicated and hard to understand. The case in
hand will serve to illustrate admirably the absurdity of try-
ing to determine the effects of an economic policy upon the
general well-being by the application of handy ethical
formulas. A typical instance was that in which Rockefeller
received from the Lake Shore Railroad a rate of 35 cents per

barrel of crude oil from the oil region to Cleveland, and

of shipping sixty carloads per day and relieving the railroad

would give them a rate which would put them on an equality

except that the oil company agreed to furnish tank cars,
stations and switches, and to load and unload. The Rocke-

AMBROSE PARÉ WINSTON
feller Company is denounced for complicity in the railroad's

railroad of risks by fire and accident, and part of its ordinary
expense in handling oil, for thinking they ought not to pay

lower rate, or to decide whether it might not all be justified
by the expense for stations, switches, loading and unloading;
in the philosophy of the "obvious," calculation is a waste
of effort.
So far as the low rate in these cases is due to services
performed by the Standard (loading, etc.) not ordinarily
performed by shippers, the lower charge is evidently
proper. But it is not "obvious" that the "wholesale
principle," by which buyers of large amounts of commo-
dities pay lower prices, should be condemned when it
applies to the purchase of railroad transportation, but
allowed as to other commodities. It is not "obvious"
that this principle in this connection tends towards monopoly
more strongly than it does in the supply of dry goods on a
large scale. So far as I know, no one has troubled himself
to make this comparison the subject of study; yet all
classes of people, including the professional economists,
have jumped at the conclusion that low prices for trans-
portation in large amounts are wrong, while low prices for
other goods in large quantity are right. Once more, in
this field of study, there is need, no less than in Engineering,
Physics, or Chemistry, of basing all general propositions on
careful investigation; yet in Engineering, Chemistry or
Physics, no one would think of assuming as obvious so
uncertain a proposition as this one. Men who have gained
advantage over their rivals by buying raw materials or
stock in trade in large amounts are commended. Thus,
for example, Mr. Marshall Field's newspaper biographers


## p. 113 (#601) ############################################

PUBLIC OPINION AND THE STANDARD OIL COMPANY 113
told of his buying cheap by buying in great quantities,
even buying the entire output of certain factories. They
referred to the fact that he overshadowed all rivals in the
Chicago district, and candidly commended his methods;
condemning at the same time in contrast, the Standard Oil
men for beating their rivals by buying transportation as
Field bought cloth. Evidently one sort of inequality
tends to monoply no more than the other; the degree of
inequality is alone decisive; it has not been thought worth
while to make a comparison as to this.
Low rates to large shippers were justified by many
judges and writers on law, both in the United States and
England during the period in question. These men recog-
nized the difficulty of the question; to their minds it did
not commonly appear "obvious." The English Justices in
Ransome vs. Eastern Railway Company, speak of the diffi-
culty of deciding what is an "undue preference," whether,
for example, if one thousand tons can be carried for a lower
sum per mile than one hundred tons and the railway lowers
the rate, "would the lower rate so charged give an undue
preference;" and the justices, with impressive modesty,
well becoming their great office, exclaim that the questions
involved were of a very difficult and complicated character
-"such as we feel but little qualified to decide." The
Scofield, Shurmer and Teagle case, involving a contract
between the Lake Shore Railway and the Standard Oil
Company, was referred by the District Court in Ohio to
the Supreme Court on account of the difficulties involved.
In another English case, Nicholson vs. the Great Western
Railway Company (97 E. C. L. 766), a coal company had
been allowed a lower rate because its business was of large
amount, invariably full and regular trainloads. The Chief
Justice speaks of a principle which has been repeatedly
recognized, viz., that a railway may lawfully make a dif-
ference in their rate of charge in regard to a contract for a
large quantity of goods to be shipped with constant regu-

If one condemns low rates to large shippers as tending
toward monopoly, one is bound logically to condemn like-
wise any of the advantages in expense to the large business
establishments over the small, for any economy or cheap-
ening of production tends toward driving competitors out
of business. The purchase of raw materials in large
amounts at lower prices tends toward monopoly as truly
as the wholesale purchase of transportation. Thus, for
example, the officers of the American Tin-Plate Company
are criminals for getting the tin used in their business at
a reduction in price of two or three cents per pound because
of their large purchases (Industrial Commission, Vol. I,

mill to one kind of goods (Id., Vol. I, p. 193).

11. The Standard Oil men are condemned for crushing
rivals and thus consolidating the oil business-in Miss Tar-
bell's vivid phrase: "corralling the refining and marketing
of oil."
This writer has failed to see that our whole busi-
ness world is a field of conflict, in which to succeed
one must deny success to others; the very fact of com-
mercial success is proof that rivals have been defeated
or destroyed; wealth acquired commercially is no less evi-
dence of destruction than the bloody scalp in the hand of
the victorious red Indian. The obvious and well-known
facts of the case prove this to the least intelligent person
who will consider them at all. The demand for any com-
modity at prices which will pay for its production is always
a limited demand; those persons produce and sell who are
able to sell cheapest, or in other ways attract buyers. This
is true, even where the casual observer does not notice the
agony of defeat and sees only the honorable success, or
fails to connect the defeat with the victory. The conflict
of the battlefield or the jungle is hardly more remorseless
than the conflict of trade.
Everyone knows that competition is the prevailing fact
of our economic system-but many people grasp the prin-
ciple loosely; they assent to it as a feeble Christian gives
assent to the doctrine of the church, but they do not in
any positive, active sense believe that we live in a system
of cruel competition. The proof of that failure to realize
what one passively admits is shown by countless examples.
Thus Mr. Marshall Field, the Chicago merchant, was en-
thusiastically praised at his death recently because he had
gained his great wealth honorably (which was very prob-
ably true), but also because, as the Chicago Record-Herald,
a very superior newspaper, said, "He crushed no one"
(which was not true). The Field house, by careful manage-


## p. 120 (#608) ############################################

120
AMBROSE PARÉ WINSTON
ment, by large capital, offered goods at low prices which
other merchants could not meet. There were many failures
in the retail dry goods trade of Chicago and the wholesale
trade of the Mississippi Valley and the Northwest during
the last thirty-five years. These unfortunates would not
have failed if the power of the more fortunate had not fixed
the prices at a low level in the general market. One of the
eulogies of Mr. Field well described the wholesale dry goods

"were, after a fashion, his rivals." If newspaper statistics
of sales may be believed, this house occupied a position in
the Chicago wholesale dry goods trade scarcely less over-

firms which were, "after a fashion, its rivals," was almost
crowded to the wall. A rival in the retail trade became so
discouraged by unsuccessful business that he committed
suicide. What of other mercantile houses which failed to
maintain themselves, even in an inferior position? The
formula, "live and let live," as it is commonly used (meaning
that one engaged in trade should be solicitous of the welfare of
his competitors and avoid defeating them), shows again that
people no more understand the economic medium in which
we live than a fish knows that water is H₂O. Miss Tarbell,
in the same spirit, complains that the Standard Oil Company
"made it hard for its rivals to do business" (one ought to

Corbett to do business." However repugnant the com-
mercial struggle may be to one who engages in it, he cannot,
so long as he remains in business, avoid seeking to destroy.
There lie before him simply the alternative courses of giv-
ing up the field or driving others out. Even in agriculture
this is true the farmer on a New England hill sinks into


## p. 121 (#609) ############################################

PUBLIC OPINION AND THE STANDARD OIL COMPANY 121
poverty because a prairie farmer, by strenuous effort of a
strong body, by long hours, effective machinery and fertile
soil, lowering the price of wheat, struggling to live, is un-
able to "let live."
Not only is it absurd to condemn one who defeats a
rival by merely selling cheap, but it is likewise absurd to
condemn one who, in defeating his rival, lowers prices for a
time below cost at competitive points without equally
lowering them elsewhere. If one once clearly understands
and does not forget that one must destroy or be destroyed
-must, if he survive, lower his prices below those of his
competitors-two conclusions inevitably follow. First, where
competitors meet prices must fall, and fall indefinitely (not
merely to the point fixed by cost of production). The point
to which the cutting must be carried on either side is always
an appreciable degree below the cut by the opponent. This
process, if mutual, has no limit until competition terminates,
either by agreement or the withdrawal of one rival. It has
happened a thousand times that in competition excessively
intense, railways have given their services for less than cost,
and sugar or steel has been disposed of likewise at a loss;
usually cutting below cost is regarded as a misfortune, not a
crime. Price cutting by the Standard Oil Company has
been condemned as a result of the popular superstition
which regards that company as occupying a demoniac
superiority to all rivals, holding their fate at its mercy.
The fact that it, too, has had to struggle for its life is
shown by Miss Tarbell in detailed accounts of these
struggles, and shown again comprehensively in her calcu-
lation that it controlled a smaller proportion of the domestic
oil market at the close of the history than it had controlled
twenty-five years before."
It follows from the essential nature of competition not
only that prices must go down where competitors conflict,

but that, second, prices will be kept up where competition
has been absent or ceased. Commercial rivalry, vary-

plies local variations of price. As Chairman Knapp, of the
Interstate Commerce Commission, has said very wisely in
another connection: "Competition is simply discrimination
-simply the right of every man who has a piece of property
to sell to one man at one price and to another man for
another price, or to vary that price to the same person,
when he thinks best."
All this does not mean that fierce competition is a de-
sirable thing; it is beyond doubt unspeakably horrible.
The wish that men might "live and let live" is beyond ob-
jection, if it is offered as a desideratum to be attained
through some restraint upon competition; it is absurd only
if one demands that an individual in the midst of a com-
petitive system should, by himself and alone, voluntarily
refrain from defeating his antagonists, with no power to
make them stop trying to destroy him. If the evils of
competition-underselling and the rest of them are ever
to cease, the restraint must be applied by some concerted
policy, and it must have some really binding force. It
may be general as in the Socialist plan; or it may be
merely combination or agreement between a particular
group of competitors. Such an agreement is commonly
called a trust. If in some degree it keeps up prices, it
saves from destruction every person outside the combina-
tion who could not bear a depression of prices below that
point; the fact that, as Miss Tarbell tells us, the "inde-
pendent" refiners did a larger percentage of the country's
business in 1903 than they did twenty-five years before, is
quite possibly due to the fact that the Standard, in keeping up
prices, made it possible for some of these independents to
survive. In the absence of some concerted restraint on
competition a man in business is as helplessly forced into
the excesses of competition as a person in a plague-stricken

town succumbs to the epidemic. Miss Tarbell's complaint
of Mr. Rockefeller that he argued for a restraint of compe-

a physician because he argued for sanitary precautions
against yellow fever, but "did not hesitate" to have the
fever himself and to infect others.
The fact that a company is large and powerful does not
change the case; even the most powerful company must
be remorseless or it will cease to be powerful. The History
shows plainly that there was (a) an excess of capital in-
vested in refining, and an excessive production of oil, with
runious competition among refiners; (b) a sincere effort of
the Standard Oil men to remedy these evils by a general
combination; (c) a failure by most refiners to see that
their only salvation lay in a restraint on competition;&
(d) the admission to the combination of others willing to come
in on terms not ungenerous and even remarkably liberal.

Toledo, etc., would not "normally" permit this wide differ-

expectation, but railway men are like other men, bound by
no single principle; they might quite likely consider it
hopeless to offer, on comparatively small business in their
territory, the rates possible for the vast shipments of the
Standard Oil roads. Though the Standard paid a lower
rate on oil from its big refineries at Whiting than the "inde-
pendents" paid from Toledo and Cleveland, the Standard
paid the same rate as the independents from its small Lima
refinery to the Ohio River crossings, though Lima is nearer
the river than Toledo and Cleveland (p 189). This shows
that large cargoes, not Standard shipments, secure low rates.
The recent history of railway rates is full of cases in
which railways have refused, for whatever reason, to stimu-
late the industries in their own territories by meeting the
rates which prevail in rival districts. The fact that busi-

Greater difficulty is presented by the charge that the
railways have wilfully violated the law requiring a publica-
tion of rates and that the Standard Oil Company has as-
sisted in this concealment of rates. Few questions are
more difficult. The difficulty arises (1) from the nature of
the facts to be judged; (2) from the logical method which
must inevitably be employed. The railway freight busi-
ness is not an occult science, but it consists of a multitude
of usages, each shaped with reference to long experience.
One who has had no experience with the practices is not
prepared to judge their significance, and cannot, in view of
the complication of the business, readily provide himself,
if occasion arises, with the information necessary to judge.
Law, medicine, engineering, railway practice or any other
profession is to be understood only by prolonged training.
It is further a principle of very general force that whatever
is unfamiliar tends to excite suspicion. A complicated ar-
rangement of railway rates or an unexplained method of
book-keeping arouses in the mind a suspicion of a trick or
a trap.
Further difficulty arises from the fact that one's con-
clusions as to concealment of rates must be reached ordi-
narily, not by demonstration but by an argument from
probability. Words in a letter perhaps have two possible
interpretations; which is the probable meaning? The testi-
mony of a witness is decisive; is he probably candid? One's
judgment on any such uncertain facts, whatever their
connection, is sure to be influenced, and is in most cases
decided by presuppositions. To illustrate: in the trial
of Rose Callender before Sir Matthew Hale, on a charge
of witchcraft, it appears that John Soam's cart wrenched
the window of her house as he was passing with a load

Whether the report convicts the Standard Oil Company
of assisting in violation of the law as to publicity, I do not
undertake to decide. Some facts seem to tend strongly
toward that conclusion. No opinion on that point would
have value, however, unless it was based on a careful criti-
cism of the Garfield evidence-a study of the facts in the
light of information from other sources, as to railway usage
and recent railway history. The accusation is based chiefly
on an interpretation of correspondence and records in rail-
way offices. The words used in the records, in the haste
of business, are submitted to a sort of exegesis which would
permit a careful person to prove anything imaginable, by
sifting out whatever suits his expectations. It would take
perhaps 100 pages like these to consider that matter. I
have, however, examined somewhat carefully the evidence
in the Whiting case.
That case can be understood only if one realizes that
the railways of the United States are now passing through
a revolutionary change under the influence of regulative
legislation. The old obsolescent system of keeping records
and making and publishing rates has been characterized
by endless irregularity, carelessness and confusion. Far
back in the past there was hardly such a thing as a rate
definitely applicable to a certain shipment. More recently
it has not always been easy to say what is the proper rate.
The evidence in this trial showed that there might be sev-
eral rates, issued in succession for a certain shipment, with-
out at any point a cancellation of the preceding rates.
There might be on record two rates, when neither of them
conformed to the requirement of the law. Rates entirely
unobjectionable have not been posted as the law requires.
General tariffs have been issued including by classification
certain articles, as grain, coal and oil, when it was assumed


## p. 137 (#625) ############################################

PUBLIC OPINION AND THE STANDARD OIL COMPANY 137
(but only tacitly) that these articles would be given other
rates by special tariffs. The public, when it is said that a
rate paid was not the "lawful" rate, imagine a condition
of things in which there is no doubt as to what the lawful
rate is. In the Whiting case there was, between the sta-
tions in question, no rate on oil beyond objection as to
legality. The rate said by the prosecution to be the lawful
rate, existed only by construction from these materials:
(a) a tariff was filed showing a rate of 18 cents on fifth-class
goods to East Saint Louis from Chicago; (b) the Illinois
State classification put oil in the fifth class; (c) a statement
called an "application sheet" was filed with the Interstate
Commerce Commission, showing that the general tariff for
Chicago would apply also to Whiting. This rate was open
to question since the Illinois classification-necessary to the
legality of the 18-cent rate was not filed with the Com-
mission.
The 6-cent rate, actually paid and regarded by the
Government as illegal, was also constructive: (a) the rail-
way company gave the oil company a 6-cent rate, not by a
general tariff, but by a "special billing order," for ship-
ments from Chicago to East Saint Louis; (b) this was in-
terpreted as referring to shipments from Whiting by virtue
of the application sheet, which makes Chicago rates apply to
Whiting.
The 18-cent rate shows the slovenliness of method just
mentioned; a rate to be lawful must be filed with the Com-
mission-hence, if a rate is to be established by the sort of
patchwork here described, all the necessary patches (in-
cluding the Illinois classification) ought logically to be filed.
If the shipper is bound, then, at his peril, to know the
lawful rate and pay no other, he must, in such a case as
this, not only find out whether the order granting the 6-cent
rate was filed with the Commission, but he must also de-
cide (as the judge and jury happen to decide afterward),
that the omission to file the Illinois classification did not


## p. 138 (#626) ############################################

138
AMBROSE PARÉ WINSTON
invalidate the filed rate of which the classification was an
indispensable element. If he misses his guess on this point
he must pay a fine. The classification in evidence putting
oil in fifth-class was issued a year later than the 18-cent
class tariff; perhaps the shipper might doubt whether
the authors of the tariff intended to establish the fifth-
class rate of 18 cents for any article whatever, which
subsequent classification might assign to the fifth-class.
No court of law would permit such omissions and irregu-
larities in the filing of records; the Interstate Commerce
Commission, by thus acquiescing in the slovenliness of rail-
ways in conforming to the law, shows how hopelessly general
that laxity must have been. The prosecution assumed what
ought to be-one unmistakable rate for any article between
two specified points. The Oil Company assumed the fact;
they accepted the statement of the railway official that he
had conformed to the requirements of law; they did not un-
dertake to decide the questions of legal interpretation here
involved, and which kept the trial court busy for some days
or weeks, and on which the Supreme Court of the United
States might have divided five to four.
The company accepted the body of railway practices here
applying, lax and unsanctioned by the law as they were, not
attempting to reform what the Interstate Commerce Com-
mission had been obliged to accept. Among these established
usages was the practice of regarding Whiting (which is only
two miles across the State line from Illinois) as a part of
the shipping district of Chicago, so that the shipment
would be considered wholly within the State of Illinois,
not subject to the Interstate Commerce Act, and lawful.
It is true the president of the Standard Oil Company
of Indiana was unable to prove before the Grand Jury
that any other freight than oil was shipped from Whiting
under Chicago rates. Naturally so, if that practice was
criminal, both the shippers and the railways would conceal

One who is convinced that the propensities of the Oil

1. The 6-cent rate, though not filed, was in no other

2. The low rate could not injure any person whom the

Commissioner Smith, of the Bureau of Corporations, have

This statement is as clearly untrue as if they had said

the Standard now calmly designates as 'absence of dis-

thing.
To say that this rate had "produced a state of monopoly
in the vicinity of Chicago," means either that persons in
the oil business had been driven out or that persons wishing
to come into that business had been kept out. Neither of
these implications is true. No evidence has been offered
in this whole connection to show that any persons were

Whiting refinery was established, about 1890, or that any-

ing whether a rate is fair, one must be familiar with the

whether there have been attempts to conceal a rate, one
must, again, know thoroughly the business of fixing rates,
the method of book-keeping, of collecting charges, etc. All
these matters are intelligible only to one having experience
with them. The customs and methods of any profession—
that of the physician, the lawyer, the carpenter, or the
railway freight official-elude the apprehension of the out-
sider; they are misjudged by him almost as surely as the
customs of an East Indian hill tribe are misunderstood by
a British administrator. Colonial rulers have frequently been
taught the injustice and danger resulting from this diffi-
culty. In our dealings with railways we have assumed that
any intelligent, conscientious man is competent to make a
report on railway business. For guidance in matters of
law, the Government of the United States employs lawyers
of long experience. Yet the law is not occult; its vocabu-
lary is not extremely difficult, and its principles may be
found in treatises, statutes and decisions, and the appoint-
ment of an educated, intelligent layman to a position in
the department of justice would no more probably lead to
blunders than the attempt to make an official railway ex-
pert of one ignorant in such matters. In fact, as between
these two sorts of folly, the tyro in law would probably do
less harm than the made-to-order railway expert. The
Interstate Commerce Commissioners, by long service, over-
come in a measure their initial want of knowledge; a few
State officials are in the same way competent or partially
qualified; but in the appointment of most public officials
having to do with railways, general intelligence and good
character are usually thought sufficient (if not superfluous).
The Interstate Commerce Act specially provides that no
railway employee may be made a member of the Commis-
sion; that is, practically, no one having a knowledge
of railway business is qualified to exercise the immense

powers over railways entrusted to the Commission.
The danger of error in the criticism of railway business
is increased by the spirit of hostility with which the public
regards railways and other corporations. No undertaking
is more hopeful than the search for evil in conduct which
one does not understand.
Commissioner Garfield became chief of the Bureau of
Corporations with the measure of knowledge as to railways
which one may acquire by being a civil service commissioner.
His record as an honest and energetic official qualified him
as a railway expert no more than it qualified him to be
chief engineer of the Panama Canal. In preparing to dig
the canal he could have "read up;" and his policy there
would probably have been no worse than the set of maxims
which he prescribes as the whole duty of railways. He has
constructed a very brief, and therefore handy, set of rules
for rate making which-and no other-he assumes railways
must "normally" employ, and denounces as showing evil
intent whatever fails to conform to this strange thing that
never, in fact, was on sea or land. The report as a whole
is chiefly a complaint of rates lowered by competition of
railways at the point of shipment; if the legitimacy of
such rates, given and received, is admitted, there would
have been little purpose in writing the report. The
spectacle is here presented of a bureau chief inventing new
principles of commercial morality, denouncing as criminals,
those who have failed to conform to them, finding sup-
port in this from the head of the nation, and so from
the public who have not read the report and do not know
what it asserts. A parallel in the Isthmian Canal illustra-
tion would be an objection to using circular wheels on loco-
motives-they ought to be octagonal. This would be no
greater novelty than the demand that rival roads must not
compete.
The office of Commissioner of Corporations is itself a
singular innovation; that officer is not, it seems, like gov-

ernment statisticians heretofore, limited to collecting in-

it is also probable that few such officers will resist the
