one may feel sure that if his report on the Standard Oil
Company had, on any statement of facts, opposed the
popular opinion, his political future would have been much
darkened.
The Standard Oil fine has also its lessons:
1. It implies absurdly that the duty of maintaining freight
tariffs and publishing them according to law is not primarily
a duty resting upon the railway company; it is the shipper
who must beware; he must watch the railway company,
decide whether the railway officials obey the law, and not
accept their statement as to rates without an investigation
to make sure that the railway is within the law. If the rail-
way confuses its rates, through negligence or evil intention,
so that a prolonged judicial investigation is necessary to
determine which of two questionable rates is less dubious,
the responsibility rests upon the shipper to anticipate the
guess which an average jury will make in this question.
If the carrier goes wrong-by overestimating the intelli-


## p. 147 (#635) ############################################

PUBLIC OPINION AND THE STANDARD OIL COMPANY 147
gence of the jury or otherwise-he must pay. This priority
of obligation is shown by the fact that the shipper, not the
carrier, was prosecuted.
2. The greatest fine in the history of the world was
assessed for an act which, so far as anyone has shown, did
not deprive any person of any right. The low rate to East
Saint Louis probably worked to the disadvantage of rival
shippers on rival railways, but two Federal laws are meant
to maintain competition in rates between railways. The
rate was not secret in any such substantial sense that any
person wishing to ship at that rate would have been unable
to do so; for many years one of the three roads conformed
to the law as to filing the rate; the shippers were thus pro-
tected against any possible consequences of secrecy on the
other two roads. While there was thus no essential con-
cealment of the rate from any possible persons, there was
also no person who would have been injured by any im-
aginable concealment. No shipper, in all the preceding
years, asked for a carload rate on oil from any point of the
Chicago-Whiting district; while the same rate was in force,
according to law, on the C. & E. I., no shipper but the
Standard ever used it. No other defendant would have been
punished so severely under these circumstances.
I have talked of this subject with at least a dozen of my
most intelligent acquaintances, and their expressions almost
invariably exhibit two characteristics: (1) I find, with very
rare exceptions, the most confident belief that the Standard
Oil Company has been conspicuously a bad corporation;
(2) not one of these persons has been able to give a
definite statement of reasons for this belief; yet they do not
regard their lack of acquaintance with facts as a reason for
being less confident in the opinion. "Didn't Miss Tarbell
show this and that?" (though he hadn't read Miss Tarbell's
book, but had heard someone say it showed a bad record
for the Standard). "Where there is so much smoke there
must be some fire," etc.-which, being interpreted, means


## p. 148 (#636) ############################################

148
AMBROSE PARÉ WINSTON
that men have made up their minds, not by knowledge and
judgment, but by hearing a thing said many times. A
settled opinion is commonly a product of two factors; the
force of each impression multiplied by their number. A
weak argument, or mere assertion unsupported, if re-
peated often enough, serves effectively to persuade.
The prevalent opinion in the whole subject is merely a
repetition of current rumor; the remote sources of the
rumor are the Chicago prosecution with its tremendous
penalty for an act by which no one was hurt, the Gar-
field report, condemning low rates when railways compete,
and Miss Tarbell's jumble of contradictions.

PRESENT TENDENCIES IN DENTAL EDUCATION.*
J. H. KENNERLY
Professor of Chemical Dentistry in the Dental Department of Washington
University and Dean of the Dental Department.
Dentistry as a distinct profession owes its birth to the
foundation of the Baltimore College of Dental Surgery in
1839. The reason for the founding of this, the first dental
institution, by two distinguished doctors of medicine, was
that they at that early date realized the necessity for more
particular instruction in dentistry. The separation of the
medical and dental profession was not the creation of a
specialty in medicine, but it was the creation of a distinct
profession, which requires a definite course of instruction
especially adapted for its successful practice. The practice
of dentistry requires a combination of practical art and
science, with a superior proficiency of manual dexterity,
which is not needed in any other branch of medicine, unless
it be that of operative surgery. In fact, the dentist is the
composite of the artist and artisan. The oculist refers his
patient to the optician for the mechanical construction of
glasses; the orthopedist sends the necessary measurement
for artificial substitutes or mechanical appliances to the
artificial limb maker; but the major part of the work done
by the dentist is done by himself in the mouth of the
patient. The achievements attained by the dental pro-
fession as such are chiefly to be credited to the ingenuity
of the dentist himself and rarely to the man of medicine.
Ever since the separation of the schools of medicine and
dentistry, steps have been taken to reunite them, so as
to make dentistry a branch of medicine, placing it on the
same basis with ophthalmology, otology or any other speci-
alty of the mother science. The evidence that such a step
*Address as President of the National Institute of Dental Pedagogics. New
Orleans, La., December 31, 1907.


## p. 150 (#638) ############################################

150
J. H. KENNERLY
is retrogressive is amply illustrated by the fact that in
those countries where dentistry can only be practiced by
qualified medical graduates, very little progress has been
made in dentistry per se; in fact, a large part of the prac-
tice is carried on directly by what is known as technical
men, namely, men who have learned the laboratory technic
and have acquired certain operative procedures from ex-
perience. Such men are in frequent use in certain parts of
Europe to act as "straw men" in the dental practice of an
M. D. Recently much discussion has appeared in foreign
dental literature relative to the formation of so-called
stomatological societies. These societies are formed for the
sole purpose of trying to unite dentistry with medicine.
Agitation on this subject has gone so far as to exclude
dentists from attendance at international medical con-
gresses, in which there is a dental section, unless the at-
tendant holds the M. D. degree. Such was the case in the
one held in Lisbon in 1906, and again the same clause is
incorporated in the outline of the congress to be held in
Buda-Pesth in 1909. It seems timely, therefore, to suggest
some means which will establish our position very clearly
and definitely before the world at large.
It should be remembered that dentistry is a specific part
of the great healing art, which is practiced for the purpose
of doing the most good to suffering humanity. Conse-
quently, dental education is immensely concerned with the
means and methods which furnish the very best advantages
to the dental student in order that he may acquire a com-
prehensive knowledge of his chosen calling. To master the
entire field of medicine, including dentistry, in a given
period of time, would mean simply to possess a fair knowl-
edge of general medicine. Medicine of the present day is
so intensely complicated that a whole lifetime would be too
short in which to become master of its integral branches.
If we demand from the general dental practitioner a com-
plete medical education, it means retrogression, because


## p. 151 (#639) ############################################

PRESENT TENDENCIES IN DENTAL EDUCATION
151
the time required to complete the two courses, together
with the expenditure, would be prohibitive to many, and,
as a consequence, the public at large would be the sufferer.
Any law requiring the combined study would be in favor of
a few individuals only. However, dentistry is not studied
to suit the individuality of a favored few, but to do the
most good to humanity. Our object in teaching dentistry
is to make of our students competent dental practitioners,
and not half-educated medical men with a smattering
knowledge of dentistry. Froude has expressed this thought
very clearly: "The knowledge which a man can use is the
only real knowledge, the only knowledge which has life and
growth in it, converts itself into practical power. The rest
hangs like dust about the brain or dries like rain-drops off
the stones."
The best dental education is the one which will fit the
student in such a manner that he may render the best ser-
vices to his patrons. Actual experience of half a century
has amply, and beyond a shadow of a doubt, demonstrated
the fact that such an education can be best obtained in a
special dental school. It has also demonstrated the fact
that countries where the medical degree is a preliminary
essential for the practice of dentistry, have, generally speak-
ing, made very little progress, and that dentistry is often
practiced even at this late day in a very crude manner.
All unnecessary medical studies are a burden, which rob
the student of much valuable time in mastering the funda-
mental branches. Again, I make the statement that in the
actual practice of dentistry about nine-tenths of our labors
are mechanical. By this I do not mean to be understood
that our labor is the labor of a mechanic, pure and simple,
but that it has the same mechanical principles, based upon
scientific study, upon which the surgeon performs his opera-
tion.
An ideal course of study in dentistry should demand the
same entrance requirements as do the representative medi-


## p. 152 (#640) ############################################

152
J. H. KENNERLY
cal schools of the country. At present, a four years' course
in an accredited high school is generally regarded as suffi-
cient for entrance to the study of dentistry and medicine.
A few medical schools, namely, Johns-Hopkins of Baltimore
and Harvard University, require a B. S. degree or its
equivalent for admission, while a few others, among them
the University of Michigan, have arranged a six-year course
in which the B. S. and M. D. degrees may be obtained sim-
ultaneously. There is no doubt in my mind but that
dentistry will be compelled to follow in the advanced foot-
steps of the medical schools before the medical man will
look upon the dentist as being his equal. When they are
convinced that the study of dentistry is in every respect
equal to the study of medicine, our social recognition will
be equal to that of the medical men.
While dentistry is closely connected with general medi-
cine, a full and comprehensive knowledge of all branches
of the latter is not needed for its successful practice. At
the meeting of the F. D. I., held in Stockholm in 1906, the
following studies were selected as being essential to the
general education of the dentist: Physics, chemistry,
anatomy, histology and embryology, physiology, physio-
logical chemistry, bacteriology, materia medica and thera-
peutics, general and special pathology, general and special
surgery and physical diagnosis. These general medical
branches, together with the special dental training, will pre-
pare the student farbetter to enter upon the actual practice
of dentistry than would a complete knowledge of the whole
field of medicine. To complete a comprehensive course of
study successfully, as above outlined, a four-years' course
is essential. The writer is optimistic enough to prognosti-
cate the inauguration of a four-years' course in the near
future, in spite of the failure of this very proposition three
years ago. Individually, the four-years' course will mean
increased expense and lessened remuneration, and as a
natural sequence the non-endowed college will have a hard


## p. 153 (#641) ############################################

struggle to make both ends meet. The future dental edu-
cational institution will be a department of a fully endowed
university. Of the fifty-five dental colleges in the United
States less than a dozen have at present direct affiliation
with universities. The few simple facts, relative to dental
education, as outlined above, are the successive links in
dental evolution. They are bound to become true, and
the sooner we recognize these facts, the more service we
shall render to our profession.
We, as teachers of dentistry, are looked upon as the ones
who, to a large extent, shape the destiny of our profession.
The history of the Institute of Dental Pedagogics furnishes
the proof of this assertion. In this particular connection it
is interesting to observe certain phases of the proceedings
of the recent congress of stomatologists, held in Paris, Au-
gust 1-6, 1907. Among others the following resolution
was introduced by a member from Hungary: "The dentists
produced by the college system have always been a pro-
visionary substitute only. There is no reason why this
provisionary substitute should be further tolerated. It is
to the interest of the health authorities of every country to
abolish this system of education; the non-medical dental
practitioner should be placed, by employing suitable trans-
fer methods, upon the extinction list."
The absurdity of this dogmatism is amply illustrated by
the fact that any duly qualified medical practitioner of
Hungary without ever having acquired any special knowl-
edge in dentistry may style himself "qualified dentist." In
other words, he may foist himself upon the general public
as a person who possesses sufficient knowledge to prac-
tice dentistry as a specialty. Fortunately, the few men
calling themselves stomatologists will not shape the des-
tiny of the dental profession of the future. The pro-
fession has grown too powerful as a social institution to
be ruled or governed by a few who frequently, being
not even members thereof, take it upon themselves to


## p. 154 (#642) ############################################

154
J. H. KENNERLY
place the dentist produced by the college system upon
the extinction list.
From an etymological point of view, we understand by
the term "stomatologist" some one who is engaged in the
treatment of diseases of the oral cavity proper, which, of
course, includes the teeth, while a dentist is engaged in the
treatment of diseases of the teeth and their sequelæ.
However, we attribute to the term "dentist" a much wider
meaning at present. The United States Army regulations
require the following services of the members of the dental
corps: "The duties of the dental surgeon will ordinarily be
confined to the treatment of such cases as are directly asso-
ciated with the teeth and gums; but occasions may arise
when his services would be required as a specialist in the
treatment of diseases and injuries of the mouth and jaws;
such as cysts of the salivary ducts, empyema of the maxil-
lary sinus, fractures of the jaws, gingivitis, necrosis of the
jaws, facial neuralgia, stomatitis, and tumors of gums,
jaws, etc."
If the dentist in his routine practice is require to treat
the various ailments enumerated above, what is there left
for the stomatologist? It seems to me that the term dentist,
when employed to designate one's calling, is quite good
enough to distinguish us from the medical practitioner and
also quite sufficient to make the public understand what is
meant by it. Why then create a new title which, in reality,
seems nothing more nor less than what is expressed by the
simple term "dentist," and which only brings about confu-
sion in the minds of the laity and makes us the laughing
stock of our medical friends.

UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
THE WORK OF THE WASHINGTON UNIVERSITY
ASSOCIATION
Following the recommendation of the Annual Meeting of May 1,
1907, the efforts of the Lecture Committee of the Association have
been concentrated on lecture courses rather than on single lectures.
All the University Association lectures this year have been given at
the Y. M. C. A. Building, at the corner of Grand and Franklin
Avenues. This location, besides being better known and more
central than the Academy of Science, has also the advantage
of being much quieter, and the increased expense involved in such
a change would seem to be compensated for by the increased attend-
ance and interest manifested in the lectures. The following lecture
courses have been announced for the lecture season, of which the first
five have been given:
November 5, 12, 19, 1907.
Professor E. J. Swift.
The Improvement of Brain, by
December 3, 10, 17, 1907. Greece Past and Present, by Professor
F. A. Hall.
January 14, 21, 1908.
Bird Life, by Mr. R. N. Baldwin.
February 4, 11, 18, 1908. Astronomy, by Dr. G. O. James.
March 3, 10, 17, 1908.
Insect Life, by Professor J. F. Abbott.
Three Writers of the French Revolution,
April 7, 14, 21, 1908.
by Acting Chancellor M. S. Snow.
The attendance at each of these lectures has averaged about
sixty.
In addition a single lecture by Mrs. Fannie Macaulay (Frances
Little) on "Intimate Japan" has been announced for April. As usual,
fees have been charged to non-members for admission to all courses,
but an innovation has been introduced which seems to have met with
success and to have increased the attendance at the lectures. Early
in the season the Executive Council authorized the Secretary to issue
supplementary tickets at $1.00 each, to be purchasable by members
of the Association, and to admit a second person to any lecture, when
presented with a regular membership card. Over forty such tickets
have been purchased.
The Association treasury has borne all expenses this year, including
the rent of the lecture hall, but has been in receipt of a subsidy of $500


## p. 156 (#644) ############################################

156
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
from the University. This sum has been principally devoted to the
publication of the Bulletin.
The Bulletin of last year, being a semi-centennial number, was much
larger than usual, and was published in a larger edition. These volumes
have been distributed to practically all libraries, colleges and educa-
tional societies in the United States, and in Missouri in particular, the
University purchasing at cost a number of copies of the Bulletin for
such distribution. As a result, the Secretary has been in receipt of
many requests for back numbers of the Bulletin to complete files, and
in addition to the increased sales on this account, it would seem that
very good work is being accomplished by the Bulletin in advertising
the University and its work.
In addition to the regular lecture courses given in Saint Louis, the
following lectures have been given, under the auspices of the Committee
on Extension Work, in Belleville, Illinois:
October 25,1907. Heredity and Environment, by Professor E. J. Swift.
November 22, 1907. Age of Pericles, by Mr. William Schuyler.
December 20, 1907. The Modernism of the Ancients, by Professor
F. W. Shipley.
January 24, 1908. Life History of Our Continent, by Professor
W. E. McCourt.
February 28, 1908. Spain as a World Power, by Professor W. H.
Chenery.

THE CORPORATION

THE CORPORATION
The following are notes of the acts of the Corporation during the past
year:
APRIL 26, 1907
The resignation of Chancellor W. S. Chaplin was submitted and
accepted to take effect October 1, 1907.
MAY 3, 1907
The following preamble and resolutions were unanimously adopted:
"Whereas, The Directors of Washington University have received a
communication from Winfield S. Chaplin, tendering his resignation of
the office of Chancellor of the University, which he has worthily filled
since 1891, and requesting that said resignation be accepted to take
effect October 1, 1907, and
"Whereas, The Directors of Washington University feel that the six-
teen years of earnest, efficient and devoted service rendered to the
University by Chancellor Chaplin entitles him to the rest and relief
which he seeks by leaving the educational field; now, therefore,
"Be it Resolved, That Chancellor Chaplin's resignation comes to the
Directors as a complete surprise, for they had expected, from the very
cordial relations which have always obtained between him and the
Board, that his official connection with the University would continue
for many years;
"Resolved, further, That the Directors of Washington University,
in accepting with regret the resignation of Chancellor Chaplin, desire
to express their high appreciation of his character and of his unselfish
devotion to the best interests of the University, and to assure him that
he will carry with him their cordial wishes for his enduring happiness
and prosperity."
Mr. Robert G. Usher appointed Instructor in American History, vice
Mr. W. R. Smith, resigned.
Honorable Ethan A. Hitchcock elected a Director of the University.
MAY 23, 1907
Voted: to confer the degree of M. D. upon the members of the
graduating class of the Medical Department, fifty in number.
Voted: to confer the degree of D. D. S. upon the members of the
graduating class of the Dental Department, thirty-six in number.

The following is a condensed statement of actions of general interest
taken by the General Faculty at its meetings from March 1, 1907, to
March 1, 1908:
APRIL 1, 1907
The Faculty received a communication from the Corporation an-
nouncing that the latter had unanimously voted to adopt the suggestion
of the Faculty that the name of the Undergraduate Department be
changed to that of the Department of Arts and Sciences.
The High School of Little Rock, Ark., was placed upon the list of
accredited schools for the College and the School of Engineering and
Architecture.
The Faculty voted to place the schools approved by the Association
of Schools and Colleges of the New England States and by the Associ-

The Faculty decided that in reckoning the units of preparatory
work required for admission to the College and the School of Engineer-
ing and Architecture, a unit shall mean one year's work of five forty-
minute periods each week.
NOVEMBER 8, 1907
The Faculty received letters from Dr. and Mrs. Chaplin, expressing
their gratification upon receiving from the corps of instructors of the
Department of Arts and Sciences the gift of a silver service, upon the
occasion of Dr. Chaplin's resignation as Chancellor.
The Faculty received a communication from the Corporation an-

of the Faculty in regard to a rule for the administration of scholarships
in the Department of Arts and Sciences. The rule is as follows:
"That no student holding a scholarship in the Department of Arts
and Sciences be permitted to renew that scholarship at the end of the
year, if at that time there be a condition standing against that student
in any course he has taken."

FEBRUARY 5, 1908
The Faculty adopted the following rules, determining the eligi-
bility or ineligibility of students to participate in intercollegiate ath-
letics or debates, or in public dramatic performances:
1. All regular students in the Department of Arts and Sciences
who have been in residence for a full college year, and who have no
term conditions, shall be eligible, except as provided below.
2. A student otherwise eligible becomes immediately ineligible
for four weeks if his grades for any month show three D's, an E and a
D, or two E's.
11


## p. 162 (#650) ############################################

162
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
3. If his grades show a deficiency less than that named above,
he shall be warned by the Physical Director, the Chairman of the Com-
mittee on Intercollegiate Debates, or the President of the Dramatic
Club, respectively, that he is in danger of forfeiting his eligibility.
4. If in the same study a student has, for two successive months,
grades below C, he immediately becomes ineligible for four weeks.
5. A monthly or term grade of C or higher in any course cancels
at once all previous deficiency in that course.
6. A single "condition" on a whole term's work in any study at
once renders a student ineligible until such condition is removed, or
until he has, in good faith, entered upon the work of repeating the study
with a lower class.
7. A student getting a condition in a subject at the end of the first
term in the college year may have the privilege of removing the con-
dition at any time under existing rules governing examinations, but
shall be ineligible for athletics the first month of the second term of
the college year. In all other cases, removal of a condition at once
restores the student to athletic standing, provided monthly grades do
not interfere.
8. It shall be the duty of all professors and instructors to hand in
to the Dean monthly grades not later than the Monday following the
close of the four weeks to be covered, and the term grades not later
than the Monday following the close of the term.
9. It shall be the duty of the Physical Director, the Chairman of
the Committee on Intercollegiate Debates, and the President of the
Dramatic Club, to obtain from the Deans, on the first Tuesday follow-
ing the end of the month, the names of students belonging to their
respective organizations whose marks are below C, and then warn or
suspend students, as provided in the above rules.
THE COLLEGE FACULTY
The following record includes such actions of the College Faculty
for the year ending March 1, 1908, as appear to be of general interest:
The Faculty approved the following recommendations regarding
work in the Correspondence School:
1. That work in the Correspondence School, passed upon by the
heads of the departments involved, be accepted for an A. B. degree,
up to an amount not to exceed 60 units, 30 of which shall be in Fresh-
man studies.
2. That the candidate presenting correspondence work shall take
a full term's work in residence in the subjects presented, and not until


## p. 163 (#651) ############################################

FACULTY LEGISLATION
163
satisfactory completion of this work shall credits for correspondence
work be applied towards graduation.
3. Only such courses shall be offered for credit as are approved by
the heads of the departments in which the work falls.
4. No credit shall be allowed until the candidate has passed an
examination prepared by the instructor giving the course taken, under
supervision satisfactory to the University.
5. Credit records for the correspondence courses shall be kept in
the Correspondence School and shall be transferred to the College
records under the conditions specified in Article 2.
The Faculty also approved of the following recommendation,
which will be operative beginning with the next fall term:
That there be given, under the direction of the Director of Physical
Training, a series of courses in physical training open to all students,
which will be elective for all four years of the College, and for which
an aggregate of four units' credit may be earned; that is, one-half
unit for each term. The work shall consist of three hours' exercise
in the Gymnasium, or in the field, together with such supplementary
exercises as the Director of Physical Training shall deem best, and a
maximum of five unexcused absences is to be permitted each term.
The joint committee of the College Faculty and the Medical School
Faculty has agreed upon joint courses of study leading to the degree
of M. D. in six years. The details of this action will be found in the
records of the General Faculty. According to this course, the student
enters the College as a Freshman and does the first year's work, and
one-half of the third year's work in the College; the other two and
one-half years' work are done at the Medical Department. At the end
of the fourth year of such a course, a degree of A. B. will be given,
and at the end of the sixth year, the degree of M. D.
Since this arrangement involves a large amount of required work,
as well as on account of other considerations, the Faculty has decided
to adhere to a fixed schedule of exercises, instead of the changeable
program which has been in use heretofore.

OCTOBER 9, 1907
The following report of the Committee on the Course in Science
and Literature was adopted:
"Your committee appointed to consider and report upon a rear-
rangement of the work of Course VII in the School of Engineering
and Architecture (known as the Course in Science and Literature) begs
to make the following recommendation:
"That the statement now on page 175 of the catalogue be made to
read thus:
""The work of the Junior Year consists of ten courses which are dis-
tributed over five groups.
""The work of the Senior Year consists also of ten courses similarly
distributed. A thesis of literary or scientific character acceptable to
the Faculty will be required as one condition of graduation.
"The following subjects shall be open to students in Course VII:
German, French, Spanish, English, History, Economics, Pedagogy,
Psychology, Botany, Zoology, Geology, Drawing, Mathematics, Astron-
omy, Applied Mechanics, Physics, Chemistry, Civil Engineering 6 and 7,
or Civil Engineering 6 and 7-a, Civil Engineering 10, Mechanical Engi-
neering 1, 4, 9 and 20, Electrical Engineering 1 and 2, Architecture,
Anatomy, Physiology, Pathology and Bacteriology.'
"It is also the opinion of the committee that further courses in
Physics and Mathematics should be offered.
"Each student who desires to enter this course will be required to
select for his Junior and Senior Years two courses each that is, one
in each term, from one of the following groups, namely:
"1. Mathematics-Physics.
"2. Physics-Chemistry.
"3. Mathematics-Applied Mechanics.
"4. Botany-Zoology-Geology.
"He is advised, though not required, to retain this same principal
subject for both years. As to the remainder, that is, three courses per
term, he is free to choose them from the full list of electives as given
above."

probation] was amended so that it does not now apply to new Fresh-

DECEMBER 11, 1907
The following resolution was adopted: "That it is the sense of the
Faculty that it is contrary to good policy to grant certificates to special
students after two years, except in Architecture and Architectural
Engineering."
The following report was adopted:
"That a formal certificate be granted to properly qualified special
students in Architecture who shall have completed the equivalent of
two years of the regular course in Architecture, including at least fifty
credits in architectural subjects and twenty-two credits in other sub-
jects approved by the professor of Architecture. To be properly
qualified for candidacy for a special certificate, the applicant shall be
a college graduate, or he shall have reached the age of eighteen years
and shall have completed the equivalent of at least two years of a
regular high school course, and shall have had at least two full years'
experience as a draughtsman in an architect's office."
FEBRUARY 5, 1908
The subject, Economics 10, previously required in the schedule of
the course in Mechanical Engineering, was made an elective.
A committee was appointed to frame a permanent program for the
School of Engineering and Architecture.

UNIVERSITY CHAPEL
Last year a change of the Chapel period from a short fifteen minutes
before nine to the half-hour immediately succeeding the close of the
first class exercise, resulted in a most gratifying increase in the attend-
ance. During the fall of the present college year, however, a tendency
became manifest among the student organizations to use this half-
hour for the transaction of the necessary business of these activities.
To meet this situation, which so pointedly suggested the need of provid-
ing a period that would be available for the purpose indicated, it was
decided to omit the Chapel exercise on Monday of each week. This
action has been fully justified by an increasing interest in the services,
especially among the men. The attendance, excluding that of special
exercises, has averaged over forty since the new arrangement went
into effect. When it is remembered that no pressure, beyond
that of a cordial invitation, is brought to bear upon the students,
the present situation must be considered most encouraging. Follow-
ing is a list of chaplains officiating from April 8, 1907, to March 1,
1908:*
Week beginning Apr. 8, 1907, Rabbi Leon Harrison, Temple Israel.

UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
WORK OF THE DEPARTMENTS
The following reports are intended to cover only such features in
the work of the departments of the University as, by reason of their
novelty or their general interest, give especial occasion for some state-
ment concerning them.
DEPARTMENT OF CHEMISTRY
During the past year a research upon the detection of Ozone, Hydro-
gen Peroxide and Nitrogen Peroxide was carried out by Professor E. H.
Keiser and Dr. McMaster. The results of this work have been published
in the January number of the American Chemical Journal, Vol. 39, p. 96.
Another research upon the acid carbonates of Barium, Calcium,
Silver and Lithium is nearly complete, and it is hoped to have the
results ready for publication by April 1st.
Professor Keiser has devised a new method for the preparation of
Nitrogen Peroxide. Messrs. Hawkins and Meyer have been engaged
in the quantitative study of this method, and in devising an economic
method for the preparation of Sodium Nitrate from Chile Saltpeter.
Mr. H. E. Wiedeman has isolated a new compound of Acetylene
and Iodine Trichloride, and has made a study of its composition and
properties.
Other investigations have been in progress as follows:
Mr. W. A. Ruth: The preparation of a compound of Carbon and
Phosphorus by the interaction of Calcium Carbide and Phosphorus
Trichloride.
Mr. J. E. Kessler: A study of the vicosity of organic liquids.
Mr. P. E. Schuck: Spectroscopic analysis of the gases given off from
Aqua Regia.
Mr. F. Von Eschen: The effect of oxidizing agents upon the Silver
and Copper derivatives of Acetylene.
DEPARTMENT OF CIVIL ENGINEERING
In the early winter a considerable number of tests were made for a
local firm of engineers, by instruction of the Board of Appeals of the
Building Department of the city of Saint Louis, with reference to pos-
sible modification of certain features of the building laws of the city.
The purpose was to determine the strength of bond of concrete to em-
bedded steel. The results were quoted in several engineering papers.


## p. 189 (#677) ############################################

WORK OF THE DEPARTMENTS
189
Tests of a similar character, but more varied, will be made the subject
of one of the graduation theses; and another will investigate the
question of the prevention of porosity in concrete.
The equipment of the Laboratory of Engineering Materials is being
constantly augmented from the proceeds obtained from commercial
tests. Of the apparatus recently added, the device for testing the cold-
bending capacity of structural steel seems likely to be adopted and
secured by several of the larger institutions.
The increased number of students made impossible the further use
of the smaller drafting room, and made necessary the occupation of
the room originally planned for this purpose. This room is comfortably
filled with the thirty desks used by the upper classmen. Visiting gradu-
ates will be interested to know that the whole second floor of Cupples
No. I is now entirely used by the Civil Engineering Department. The
interest of graduates in addressing the Collimation Club from time to
time is thoroughly appreciated by the members.
The Department Library now numbers about 1,800 volumes. The
books added this year will number more than 400 volumes, but this
large increase arises from the gifts of 162 volumes by Chancellor Chaplin,
and 44 volumes by Professor Van Ornum.
DRAWING AND HISTORY OF ART
On account of the need of additional room on the part of the De-
partment of Civil Engineering in Cupples Building No. I, the students
in the various courses in instrumental drawing have been removed
from the rooms of that department, and are now temporarily installed
in certain rooms of the Department of Elecrtical Engineering in Cupples
Building No. II.
Through the thoughtfulness of the managers of The Pickel Stone
Company, the firm supplying the stone-work for the new buildings of
the Department of Arts and Sciences, the collections of the Drawing
Department have been augmented by full-sized models in plaster of
the ornamental details of buildings that have recently been erected.
After these models have been used by the stone-carvers they are pre-
sented to the Drawing Department, where they are of great service as
models for drawing, especially to the students in Architecture.
Upon the resignation of Mr. W. J. Brown, B.S., Washington Uni-
versity, Mr. G. A. Waters, E.E., Syracuse University, was appointed in
June, 1907, to the instructorship in drawing.
The collection of stereopticon slides used in illustrating the lectures
in History of Art, and those given in the Department of Architecture,


## p. 190 (#678) ############################################

190
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
has been steadily growing during the past few years, so that now it
numbers about 3,600 carefully selected examples.
GEOLOGY
The department occupies temporarily the upper floor of the Ridgley
Library. The lecture room is equipped with a new combination re-
flecting and projecting lantern. For use in this there is a collection of
between six and seven hundred slides. The Department Library is
furnished with sets of Government and State reports and a fair collec-
tion of general works on Geology-about a thousand volumes in all.
There are three laboratories. The laboratory of General Geology
and Physical Geography is equipped with a working collection of speci-
mens, maps and photographs. In the laboratory of Mineralogy and
Economic Geology one large, and two small, collections of minerals
have been arranged and catalogued for the use of students. A fine
petrographic microscope has been recently added to the equipment.
The third laboratory is devoted to chemical and blow-pipe analysis.
A working museum, with collections arranged for systematic study,
is in preparation.
DEPARTMENT OF GREEK
On the afternoon of March 7, the class in Greek 6 translated the
Electra of Sophocles in the presence of about eighty invited guests.
One of the features of the reading was the chanting of parts of the
choral passages in the original meter. The play was divided among
the members of the class, each one taking the part of a character. The
entire reading showed careful preparation and the translation was re-
garded as excellent by all who heard it.
The Greek Department has a valuable addition to its equipment in
the large collection of photographs secured by Professor Hall while in
Greece last year. There are more than three hundred of these, ranging
in size from eight by ten inches to two mammoth ones four by five feet.
The photographs were on exhibition for several weeks, and were viewed
by a large number of citizens as well as students. The various art
clubs of the city took much interest in the exhibition, going so far as
to have a united meeting of all the clubs at the University in order to
examine the photographs and discuss them. On the latter occasion
a brief informal talk was given to the members of the clubs by Professor
Hall. There have been added to the department, also, something over
four hundred lantern slides made from kodak views, many of them of
unusual scenes and unfrequented places in Greece.

DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY
No changes have occurred in the courses of study given in the De-
partment of History during the past year. Mr. Walter R. Smith, for
several years instructor in American and English History, resigned at
the end of the year 1906-07, and Dr. Roland G. Usher was appointed
in his place. Mr. Usher has received the degrees of A.B., A.M. and Ph.D.
from Harvard College, and has had special training in American History
under Dr. Edward Channing, whose assistant he was at Harvard for
two years before coming to us. On account of the temporary appoint-
ment of Professor Snow, the head of the department, as the Acting
Chancellor of the University, part of his work has been assigned for the
year to Mr. Squire F. Browne, who has taken the course in the History
of Greece, and to Dr. Usher, who is carrying on during the second term
the course in the Elements of International Law.
MCMILLAN HALL
A liberal education is much more than disciplining and developing
the intellect. It has to do with all the mental, physical and social ac-
tivities of life, and it should stand for the broadest culture and training
of the ethical as well as the intellectual side.
Since the opening of McMillan Hall, Washington University is no
longer merely a place for the academic instruction of its young women
students. It is also a home, in the broadest and truest sense, and as
such will increasingly become the center of their real life.
No small part of a college woman's training is the general culture
which it affords. And the cultural aspect of her education is not to
be undervalued by the woman, if she would fulfill and adorn life.
Throughout the various activities of humanity, culture has played a
winning part. It has not only added charm to character, but it has
laid its stamp on the choicest types of life.
The college-bred woman should have a social value. She should
represent a higher type of learning as well as living. She should be
not only informed and self-disciplined, but cultured, and the college
which does not concern itself with this phase of her life is not doing
her the largest possible service.
While home training is also a school which affords both discipline
and instruction, it is necessarily narrow in its influence. Its group is
small and the environment wearyingly monotonous. Besides, its best
interests are often blinded by the sympathy and indulgence of its too
nearly related members.


## p. 192 (#680) ############################################

192
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
Hence the college dormitory, if properly directed, meets the de-
mands for self-culture and discipline which the home lacks. Oppor-
tunities are greater for unity of life, for instruction in the social graces,
and for the cultivation of self-reliance; three important educational
elements in character building, or in preparation for serious living.
Since it is what we think and what we do that make us what we are,
the field for general development can not be too broad. The larger the
fellowship provided, the greater will be the variety and zest given to
individual expression. This, in turn, will enlarge and extend the means
of culture.
McMillan Hall is such a life center for the women of Washington
University. It combines with the home training a unity of spirit and
a share in the duties and responsibilities of its home life. By provid-
ing a larger circle of influence than the home, it gives each member a
larger contact, which tends to smooth the rough edges and to cultivate
by a wide yet intimate relation.
This cultivation is possible only through social intercourse and
fellowship, and in this way the educational and social value of the
personal relation is at the command of all. Furthermore, the Hall
provides a medium for receiving and communicating the spirit and
ideals of the institution.
Hence our problems will be worked out as our needs expand. The
first consideration is to secure the widest freedom for development that
is compatible with order and good government. To this end House
Government has been instituted. That is, the rules of the House are
drawn up by the students with the sanction of the Proctor. The ideal
being to secure expression from the students as to their wishes and aims,
and then to assist them in obtaining the better things.
Giving the members of the Hall a part in their own government
will increase the dignity and responsibility of their position. It will
also cultivate a sense of fairness and justice, and it stimulates considera-
tion for others.*
DEPARTMENT OF MECHANICAL ENGINEERING
Three students in this department, Messrs. R. C. Bulkeley, H. F.
Gauss and J. P. Polster, are making an investigation to determine the
relative cost of power from a Suction Gas-Producer Power Plant using
charcoal, pea-anthracite coal or coke as fuel.

McMillan Hall, in response to a request from the editor for some statement of the
policy and the aims of the new women's dormitory.

DEPARTMENT OF PHYSICS
In view of some of the recent results concerning the nature of an
electric discharge, Professor Nipher is making an attempt to determine
whether an electric current has true momentum. This idea was sug-
gested by Maxwell, and he seems to have examined the matter experi-
mentally but with negative results. Professor Nipher made an ex-
amination of the matter several years ago, and is now working with
greatly improved apparatus.
At Eads' Hall Professor Nipher has repeated the work of Wheat-
stone on spark discharge through half a mile of copper wire. There
are three gaps in the line, one being at each end and the other in the
middle of the line. The sparks in these gaps are on a spark-board, to
which the line is looped, and they are photograped by reflection from
a revolving mirror making 300 revolutions per second. Wheatstone
could only look at them, and such observation is not very satisfactory.
Professor Nipher has not been able to get a photograph of these sparks
which resembles what Wheatstone saw. He does find that, when one
end of the line is grounded, the sparks appear in regular sequence.
The one nearest the machine appears first and the one nearest the
ground appears last. The result is the same, whether the line is con-
nected to the positive or to the negative terminal. The one case cor-
responds to a compression wave, the other to a rarefaction wave.
The half-mile of wire is hung on silk cords in the long hallway.
The results were presented to the American Physical Society at its
January meeting.
DEPARTMENT OF PSYCHOLOGY
Professor Swift's book, "Mind in the Making," which is shortly to
be published by Charles Scribner's Sons, deals, among other things,
with the racial tendencies and nervous disturbances which occur dur-
ing the period of development. He is convinced that these factors
should receive more attention from those in charge of the education of
children than they usually receive. From a study of the childhood
days of a large number of eminent men and women, he finds that dul-
ness is not the simple matter which it is sometimes thought to be. The
school standard by which ability is estimated seems to be inadequate,
since so many of these eminent men and women were stupid in the
school. The rapid growth of American cities has centered attention
upon the machinery of the systems of schools, and the author of this
book believes that the time has now come to make the individual
13


## p. 194 (#682) ############################################

194
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
the basis of constructive pedagogy, instead of the school machinery
and the curriculum. He also urges such a flexibility in school organiza-
tion as shall so favor variation in children that they may develop what
is best in them, instead of being restrained within the mould which
schoolmasters have come to think is a proper shape and size for chil-
dren. The book is composed largely of original material gathered by
the author, or obtained from experiments which have been performed
under his supervision, and he is convinced that research and experi-
mentation ought to play more conspicuous parts in deciding the various
problems which the school teacher meets.
COMMENCEMENT 1907
The Commencement of June, 1907, celebrated the semi-centennial
of the inauguration of the University, and the exercises of the day were
planned with much elaborateness in honor of that occasion. The sig-
nificance of that fiftieth anniversary was dwelt upon at length by the
editor of last year's BULLETIN, so that the matter need not be further
expanded here. The ceremonies at the Commencement itself have been
recorded in an interesting, attractive little pamphlet, published by the
University last fall, which is to be had upon application. Any ex-
tended review of the exercises, such as the BULLETIN has been accus-
tomed to make, would be, therefore, merely a garbling of material
which has already appeared with excellent editing.
The presence of the recently appointed Ambassador from Great
Britain, the exceptional unity of purpose shown in selecting, as the
recipients of honorary degrees, men who mean something to Missouri
and to the neighboring States, and the intensely earnest address of
Chancellor Chaplin, made the exercises memorable in the history of
Washington University. The granting of degrees to the four college
presidents was particularly appropriate. Three of the men thus
honored are presidents of neighboring institutions-the University of
Missouri, Missouri Valley College, and William Jewell College; the
fourth was the newly-elected President Harry Pratt Judson of the Uni-
versity of Chicago. The address of Chancellor Chaplin was filled with
congratulation for the past achievement of the University and with
optimistic hope for the future; and it seemed, from its very earnestness
and broadness, to be the expression of a man who was viewing a work
which he had finished. Its full significance and the explanation of its in-
tense seriousness came with the later announcement of his resignation.


## p. 195 (#683) ############################################

GRAHAM MEMORIAL CHAPEL
The twenty-third of November, 1907, marked the laying of the
corner-stone of the thirteenth permanent building to be erected on the
campus, the Graham Memorial Chapel. The occasion proved attractive
to a large number of the friends of the University, who, together with
the Faculty and many of the alumni and students, heard the addresses
and witnessed the ceremony. The exercises consisted of the prayer
and the addresses which are here given in full:
PRAYER BY THE VERY REVEREND CARROLL M. DAVIS, DEAN OF CHRIST
CHURCH CATHEDRAL
"O Eternal God, without Whom nothing is strong, nothing is holy,
Author of all being and the fountain of all wisdom and knowledge, bless
this work, for which we are gathered together, to the honor and glory
of Thy great Name. Regard with Thy favor and visit with Thy bless-
ing this University, established for the promotion of sound learning.
Inspire its professors and teachers with a due sense of their solemn
charge and a suitable degree of wisdom and strength for its fulfillment.
Bless the students with health and give them a proper estimate of the
advantages they here enjoy. Grant them diligence in the pursuit of
knowledge, submission under discipline, and a readiness of mind to
follow the counsels of wisdom and experience. Fill their minds with an
ardent love for Thee and Thy truth. Guard their inexperience; keep
them from self-conceit; and shield their virtue from the assaults of
the world, the flesh and the devil.
"We give Thee thanks that Thou hast put it into the heart of Thy
servant to erect this building to Thy honor and glory, in living memory
of one who has gone before. Vouchsafe to grant that these walls now
begun may be built up an holy temple unto Thee. May the prayers
and praises of Thy people, here offered up, ascend to Thy throne. May
Thy true and lively word be set forth, and the glad tidings of reconcili-
ation in Thy Gospel be diligently preached.
"Direct those who design and those who superintend this building,
that it may be a house worthy of Thy holy Name. To Thy protection
we commend the workmen that shall be employed. Preserve them
from every vain and unholy thought and word.
"And, Almighty God, without Whom all our purposes are ineffectual
and all our efforts vain, grant Thy presence and blessing to Thy serv-
ants assembled here to lay the cornerstone of this edifice to be devoted.


## p. 196 (#684) ############################################

196
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
to Thy honor and the benefit of Thy people. Inspire our hearts
with a humbling sense of our dependence upon Thee at all times
and in all our undertakings. May the foundation of this institu-
tion rest upon Thy favor, and may its blessings be enjoyed by
many and conveyed to remote generations. Above all, may it be
an effectual means of advancing Thy name and praise among our
people.
"We give Thee thanks for the good examples of all those, Thy serv-
ants, who, having finished their course in faith, do now rest from their
labors, and we beseech Thee that Thou wilt hear in the name and for
the sake of Him who came into the world to reveal to us the knowl-
edge of Thy love and goodness.
"Our Father Who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name. Thy king-
dom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this
day our daily bread. And forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those
who trespass against us. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver
us from evil: for Thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory
forever and ever. Amen."
ADDRESS BY ACTING CHANCELLOR SNOW.
"Upon the desk in the handsome room over the archway of the en-
trance to University Hall lies a large Bible, handsomely bound. This
Bible was given to the Reverend Dr. Eliot on the 23rd of April, 1857,
by the students of the then infant University, for use in the daily re-
ligious exercises. For more than fifty years this copy of the Holy
Scriptures has been used on every working-day during each year, and
when the class of 1907 was about to leave the University last June
one of their gifts to the institution was the handsome binding which
now encloses the old Bible.
"During more than forty years of the history of the University a
brief morning service was conducted by the Chancellor or a member
of the Faculty. Since November, 1902, we have had the hearty co-
operation and assistance of the clergy of Saint Louis of all religious
creeds. Since that time it has been the custom for a clergyman repre-
senting some religious body to conduct the service during each morn-
ing of the week, a change in the officiating minister occurring every
week. Until twenty years ago attendance at this religious exercise
was compulsory; since that time it has been entirely voluntary. The
opportunity, however, is offered to all the students in the Department
of Arts and Sciences, who gather here for daily work, to participate in
such a service and to hear, from the best representatives of the clerical


## p. 197 (#685) ############################################

GRAHAM MEMORIAL CHAPEL
197
profession of this city, short sermons full of interest and value to stu-
dents and all others present.
"These services have necessarily been held in places not especially
adapted to such exercises. The time is now approaching when a
fitting place is to be prepared where it is hoped a service may be offered
which will be inspiring and attractive, and much more useful than has
been possible during these former years. By the gift of a generous
friend a beautiful building is now to be reared. It is of interest to all
of you, I am sure, to know something of the details of this new Chapel,
which before twelve months have passed will adorn this spot. Built
of the same attractive material used in the construction of the other
buildings, and of the same general style of fifteenth century Gothic
architecture, both exterior and interior will present perhaps as beauti-
ful an example of that particular style as may be found in any part
of this country. The interior dimensions of the Chapel are as follows:
length, 125 ft.; width, 45 ft.; height of the walls up to the spring of
the roof, 45 ft.: greatest height of the roof above the floor, 54 ft.; height
of the two octagonal towers at the west end, 84 ft. No wood will be
used in the construction of the building, with the exception of that to
be found in the doors and sills. The walls are to be cased in light
Bedford stone, and the floor is to be of gray Tennessee marble. A
feature of conspicuous beauty will be the eighteen windows, whose
stone tracery will be admired by everybody who visits the building.
These are some of the noteworthy features of this latest and crowning
addition to the pile of buildings of which we are all fond and proud."
ADDRESS BY MR. JAMES A. WATERWORTH
"Mr. Chancellor, Members of the Corporation and Faculty of Washington
University, Ladies and Gentlemen:
"The noble and philosophical address delivered on the occasion of
the laying of the cornerstone of the new Washington University, on
November third in the year nineteen hundred, was the expression of
the thought of a vigorous and enlightened mind on the ideals and scope
and uses of the modern university. It set forth with clearness the
conditions and problems which modern civilization imposes upon so-
ciety, and the demand that society makes upon institutions of learning,
that they shall assist in the elucidation of those problems and shall
educate their students in a sense of personal responsibility and prepare
them to become an active moral force in society. With prophetic
vision he saw these summits crowned with the halls of a great Uni-


## p. 198 (#686) ############################################

198
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
versity, the home of learning and culture, which should bear its part,
and that a mighty part, in aiding the onward and upward progress of
man, the triumph of right and the bringing in of the age of peace. In
that faith, the cornerstone of the new Washington University was
laid; and though the voice of the speaker on that memorable occasion
is hushed, its echoes still linger in these precincts, and the invigorating
spirit of his thought is present with us to-day as we prepare to complete
the great educational structure whose outlines he sketched with such
sure and vigorous strokes.
"Seven years have passed, and we see University Hill 'crowned with
its tiara of proud towers,' rising in all 'the grace, beauty and symmetry,
in all the dignity and strength' invoked upon them on their natal day.
The arts and sciences have entered into their halls and taken their ap-
propriate seats to dispense their several gifts of knowledge and skill
to their votaries. Opposed, in the distance, the Gymnasium rears its
massive front to testify that the development and training of the bodily
powers have been amply provided for. All things needful have here
been prepared with generous care for the culture of the physical and
intellectual faculties of the student.
"One structure is lacking to complete the harmonious design of
Washington University; a fane in which the moral and religious nature
of the student shall find nourishment and reinforcement, a school in
which an added strength and grace shall be given to character; and in
assembling here to-day to lay the cornerstone of the Graham Memorial
Chapel, we supply that want and place the capstone of fulfillment
on the great plan adopted by the University Corporation many years
ago.
"There has never been a people advanced so far in civilization as to
esteem the education of its youth an essential element of national great-
ness that has not laid special stress on the training and development
of the moral faculties as a chief part of that education. Whatever was
the quality of its religion, whatever its moral standards, the youth was
instructed in the highest and best elements of both. The Persian boy
was trained to manage the horse, bend the bow and speak the truth.
The education of the Greek boy was accompanied by religious cere-
monies until his graduation. Rome taught her youth the arts of gov-
ernment and of practical speech and reverence for the gods; and when
the Church became the custodian and teacher of Western learning,
religion divided with letters the education of the youth. For more
than a thousand years there did not exist a university without its chair
of Theology and its religious tests; and the system, narrow as it may
now appear to us, gave us New England, and New England gave the


## p. 199 (#687) ############################################

GRAHAM MEMORIAL CHAPEL
199
United States liberal education. By the concurrent testimony of man-
kind, the fundamental values of all education are moral values.
"The moral and religious culture of the student has always formed an
important part of the scheme of education of Washington University.
In fact, it may be ventured that Washington University would not have
been founded-certainly not by the men who did found it-unless the
moral training of the student had been shown well in the foreground.
It is true that the Charter of Washington University provides that 'no
instruction either sectarian in religion or partisan in politics shall be
allowed in any department of the University'; and in the wisdom of
that provision there are few who do not concur. But that it was thereby
intended that moral training should be prohibited, or that political
science should be excluded from the curriculum, is not for a moment
to be supposed. That were to defraud the student of instruction in two
departments of culture of vital importance to the man, and the State,
of the most valuable elements in the character of her citizens. Chan-
cellor Eliot persistently appealed for support, on the ground that 'the
direct influence of the higher institutions of learning upon the public
mind and morals cannot be overestimated'; he 'deemed no system of
education complete which did not look to Christian manhood and
womanhood as the end to be obtained'; he declared that 'a university
established on the broad foundation of unsectarian principles in the
heart of the Mississippi Valley might be called a Christian enterprise.'
'Let us still work,' said he, 'as heretofore, in the service of God and
humanity.'
"It is then with the avowed intention that the students of Washing-
ton University shall be instructed and trained to serve God and hu-
manity in the ordinary walks of life, that the University Chapel has
been placed at the head of the Broad Walk in the heart of the design,
supported by the Schools of Arts and Sciences and confronted by the
Gymnasium; a solemn declaration in stone that science and the arts
and physical culture can attain their own highest excellence and their
greatest usefulness only when joined with a high morality. This beauti-
ful building is erected, therefore, in all sincerity of purpose and as part
of the scheme of education which has prevailed in this University from
the beginning, for the instruction and training of the student body in
good morals and piety; and specifically for the cultivation of those
virtues for which society clamorously calls: honesty, courage, faith,
love and that reverence on which the grace and happiness of human
life and intercourse so largely depend. The times cry out for the old
Roman ideal:
'Justum et tenacem propositi virum.'


## p. 200 (#688) ############################################

200
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
or, let us say, for that equally glorious ideal of our own ancestorss
enacted into law a thousand years ago as the qualification for holder,
of offices of trust: 'Men who neither for money nor for love nor for fear
will depart from truth and right.' These are the moral standards of a
race preordained to empire and from whose hands, holding to these
standards, empire will never be withdrawn. Those who study the
forces at work in modern society and their outworking in daily life,
know that the man of integrity, the incorruptible man, can speak the
deciding word in almost all controversies between men, can out of vio-
lent contentions bring agreement and peace. And society is demanding
of its great institutions of learning that they cultivate such men; that
together with the technical training called for by the needs of this in-
dustrial age, and in order to give social value to that technical training
and to the general culture of the universities, they shall inculcate high
ideals of life and conduct, and shall graduate men and women whose
aims and employments shall not be determined solely by considera-
tions of money or power or promise of material success; men and
women who will become a moral force in their communities and help
to ameliorate the asperities of our changing social conditions.
"And where can high ideals of life and high standards of duty and
moral excellence be so efficaciously urged as in a seat of learning? That
has been the prophet's platform in all the centuries. Paul in Athens,
Savonarola in Florence, Luther at Wittemberg, Knox at Edinburgh,
from that coign of vantage shook the world and won for us intellectual
as well as religious liberty. Society to-day cries aloud for the prophet,
the man who shall awaken the social conscience and stir it to its depths
and summon the people to righteousness; and the most command-
ing height on which the prophet ever stood is the university pulpit.
There he addresses the most critical, the most generous, the most
receptive audience man can plead with; there he speaks in sympathetic
environment,
'Of truth, of grandeur, beauty, love and hope,
Of melancholy fear subdued by faith,
Of blessed consolations in distress,
Of moral strength and intellectual power,
Of joy in greatest commonalty spread';
there his pleadings receive the quickest response and inspire the most
generous enthusiasm.
"And why fear the cry of sectarianism? Why should there be any
taint of sectarianism in the inculcation of good morals and virtue? Is
there not matter enough for discourse and instruction in the creed of
humanity-the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, and


## p. 201 (#689) ############################################

GRAHAM MEMORIAL CHAPEL
201
the duties that arise out of these relationships? These beliefs are not
sectarian; they are catholic, they are universal.
"As its chief school for this moral culture, as a pledge that the educa-
tional system and discipline and influence of Washington University
shall forever be exerted on the side of personal and civic righteousness
and in defense thereof, the Graham Memorial Chapel is erected.
"And not for these alone. Religion must comfort as well as enlighten,
and youth, alas, has its soul tragedies as well as maturity and age.
There are sins and repentances, doubts and denyings, sorrows and dis-
appointments, maladies of souls standing irresolute between duty and
desire, known to none but God and the doubting heart, that call for
more than mortal sympathy and more than mortal help. For such
passionate debatings with self, this Chapel should furnish a privacy,
an oratory, and an oracle. To these troubled ones it should be their
Father's house, where a message of hope and encouragement might be
received, and where the benediction of His presence should always
envelop them. Here the highest standard of moral and spiritual excel-
lence should always be set forth. The Grecian youth were surrounded
by exquisite examples of the sculptor's art, that their taste might be
educated by the beauty of the statue and that even their physical
development might take form from emulation of the noble human
forms sculptured in marble. There is one Person of matchless moral
perfection, of infinite human tenderness, of sympathy closer and more
accessible than a mother's, for whom this Chapel should be a conse-
crated niche; that looking constantly upon Him, and studying His
gracious lineaments, and learning the lessons of His divine life, the
student of Washington University may develop more and more into
the likeness of Jesus Christ.
"On this day of the founding of this University Chapel, we breathe
the poet's prayer:
'Let knowledge grow from more to more,
But more of reverence in us dwell,
That mind and soul according well
May make one music.'
The Graham Memorial Chapel, of which we now lay the cornerstone,
is the gift of Mrs. Christine Blair Graham of St. Louis, to Washington
University, to be erected as a memorial of her husband, Benjamin
Brown Graham, a man known to all and of good report, a modest and
courteous gentleman, a merchant of unimpeachable integrity, a citizen
of sterling worth, a benefactor of Washington University; who, for his
honorable life and generous support of the higher education, is deemed
worthy to be thus honored and remembered."

THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION
This year the BULLETIN finds itself relieved of what has always been
an agreeable service, namely, the publishing of detailed information
concerning the activities of the Alumni Association-by the appearance
of the First Annual Bulletin of the Alumni Association of Washington
University, a very useful little volume of eighty-seven pages. The new
Bulletin publishes most of the happenings of interest in the history of
the Alumni Association during the past year, and will doubtless prove a
valuable record. It is to be regretted, however, that, although the
June dinner (celebrating the semi-centennial of the University) is
described at some length, the editors have not preserved the addresses
delivered on that occasion, all of which were interesting and some of
which were quite noteworthy. For the sake of record, certain of these
speeches are given below:
THE RIGHT HONORABLE JAMES BRYCE Spoke as follows:
"Mr. Chairman, I am the youngest graduate of this University, and I
am very glad of it. I take this opportunity to thank you, to thank the
University, to thank the Board of Directors, for their kindness in con-
ferring upon me the honor of a degree, of which I am very proud. It is
a great thing to have a degree conferred by an institution which belongs
to a great city; it is typical of your great city, with its fifty years of
splendid work behind it, but with no limit to the grander work that is
before it.
"The honor which has come to me is enhanced by two circumstances:
the one, that it was conferred by Professor Snow, whom I have known


## p. 203 (#691) ############################################

THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION
203
for twenty-six years; and the other, that I was associated as a recipient
with so many eminent men. There was the Secretary of the Interior,
for whom I have great respect; there was one of your judges, and there
were four or five eminent engineers and others, and four or five of your
eminent teachers a class for whom I have the most ardent respect
and affection. I have known people at close quarters who appeared
to be tremednous persons at a distance, but who, when you came to
know them, were ordinary persons, like the rest of us. I have known
four or five Archbishops of Canterbury; three or four Cardinals of the
Holy Roman Empire; four or five Prime Ministers; four or five Lord
Chancellors; six or seven Presidents of the United States; and there
are only three persons for whom I still preserve the veneration I first
felt for them, when I came to know them well; one of these is a college
president. I have had the honor to be closely associated with several
college presidents today, and I hope some of the glory which surrounds
the college president may be reflected upon me on this remarkable
occasion.
"I have had a most enjoyable visit through the West. I have had
the pleasure of visiting the most interesting and the most beautiful,
rich and promising of all territories, and I have also had the pleasure of
coming to know this University better than ever before-how large it
is. There are only two things that occur to me as being things that I
might say, if you will permit me to do so, to the graduating classes.
An occasion like this brings one to a realization of what his old college
friendships are to him. There is more in them for women than for men,
even. I think the experience of our co-educational institutions has
been that they hold nothing better than the opportunities which come
for making friendships which are founded upon real sympathy of
mind and taste, and, believe me, the longer you live the more you will
value the college friendships. They are about the best things that make
life worth living, and I hope that those who will be scattered out from
this University to-day will not fail to keep up the correspondence with
the friends formed here in college. There is nothing in life more precious
than the maintenance of the college classes, the love which we have
learned to feel for one another while at these institutions of learning.
"The other thought that occurred to me is the immense value of a
corporate institution like this University. It is an inspiring thought
that one is a member of an institution like this; and if you are a credit
to it, the college will feel that it has not labored in vain for you. And
I think it adds a certain dignity to our future individual lives. It
seems a small thing here, in the midst of these great buildings, but it
adds dignity to one's individual life to feel that you are a part of the life

future good.

University."
MR. WM. R. DONALDSON, A.B., '63, spoke for the Alumni Associa-

"Like the man at Gough's lecture on temperance, it would seem that

progress and development of the country up to that date, he said:
'It is not brute force nor material elements nor political influences by
which, in the last analysis, this all-important work has been achieved.
It is the sovereign power of the educated mind.'

anniversary of our Alma Mater, and to consider that, if it progresses as
it has in the past, we shall have a grand and a great institution at the

nings that we have ourselves seen, it has arisen by mighty strides through
this half century, we look with assurance to a still greater institution
of learning at the centennial of her life. Her benefactors will take up
the work and will carry this work on, so that it will not only take equal
rank with the venerable seats of learning in the East, but with all the
great universities of Europe.
"It is a good thing that in America it is expected of those to whom
fortune has been kind, not to say prodigal, that they shall give of their
substance to public uses. It is held a public duty that those stewards
of wealth shall give in their lifetime or bequeath at their death a part
of their substance for public purposes. What nobler monuments can
one erect to one's memory than these buildings that we see around us;
