PROFESSOR GEORGE R. CARPENTER, of Columbia University, New
York, spoke as follows:
"Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen: I consider it a privilege to
speak to you. This is a day of commemoration, a day of thanksgiving,
a day of reminiscences, a day for recalling all the anxieties, all the
yearnings, that for a half-century have centered around the building
of this great University. We hear in prose and fiction of the energy,
of the ambition, of the indefatigable forces that enter into the building
up of great railroads and great capitalizations; we do not hear often
enough of the energy and resistless activity that have entered into the
building up of great universities. Even the 'youngest graduate'
knows something of what forces, of what plans, have entered into the
building of the University during his own short period, and when one
thinks of the professors' point of view, of the alumni's point of view,
of the perpetual zeal that has built up a University like this, one is
astounded at the persistence, at the industry of such forces.
"I am called to speak, to say in words what President Butler entrusted
to a letter which I have delivered to the Chancellor. I was instructed
to bid godspeed to Washington University, to greet it with all kindness,
to wish it the highest prosperity and fortune in the half century to come.
It is a great regret to President Butler that he could not himself come
to visit you, and it is an additional gratification to me that in his place
I have had that privilege.
"In the second place, I am called to speak a word to you because of
my own personal pleasure in being here. The essence of our university
life I take it in this country, lies in the free interchange of thought
between students and professors and trustees. In the older days each
college stood by itself; people scarcely spoke of it outside of its own
private circle. All that is beginning to change. The graduate of
Washington University and the graduate of Columbia University have
everything in common; the trustees of the two institutions have every-
thing in common; and not only these two institutions, but most of
the institutions throughout the land. We are all working in the same


## p. 206 (#694) ############################################

206
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
province, and it is a great advantage to us to see what the others are
doing. It is a gratification to me to be here, to visit Washington Uni-
versity, to study, as far as I can, its methods, its policies, its plans-
because Columbia and Washington have, I think, the same problem
before them, the creation of a city university-Columbia in New York
and Washington in Saint Louis have the same difficulties, the same
dangers, the same doubts and I hope some of the same plans for ob-
taining the common good. It is a pleasure, I repeat, to have had this
pleasure of addressing you."
DR. HERMAN TUHOLSKE, of the faculty of the Medical Department,
spoke, in part, as follows:
"While we look with pride on the present status of our Alumni Asso-
ciation and our medical teaching, your admiration would be awakened
could you look back forty years with us and see the status of medicine
in this country. I do look back that far and I do know how, in the
years past, we had to make doctors to supply the want, absolutely
needed; we had not then the choice of selecting men of education to
practice our profession according to our ideal. But out in the West
people were suffering for want of care. Here were needed men, though
not necessarily competent to perform the rarest operations, to cure the
people of chills and fever, of malaria and infant diseases, because there
was no one near them to help them. While such men did not satisfy
our ideals, they filled the necessities that were as urgent as the need
of bread. I remember, some thirty-five years ago in college, a gentle-
man who dissected there. He was a man of sixty-four; he weighed
about 230 pounds and was six feet, four inches tall. I was about
twenty-two then, and I wondered how this old gentleman, with all the
operations that he had to perform, could at that age do that work. I
was young and he was old, and I approached him quite deferentially
and called him Doctor; and in return he used the usual term of that
time he called me 'Doc.' I said, 'Doctor, you are doing some very
good dissecting here; the way in which you dissected out the tendons
and ligaments was most beautiful; will you tell me what they are?'
Oh, Doc,' he said, 'I am not caring for the man; I just wanted to
see how them things looked with the skin off.' I asked, 'Will you
tell me how you came to study medicine?' He said, 'I will tell you
the truth. I was out in Idaho and was running a blacksmith shop,
and I got word that about fifty miles away, where they were setting
up a machine, a fellow had got his leg torn all to pieces. There wasn't
a doctor within a hundred miles of the place, and the men were figuring


## p. 207 (#695) ############################################

THE ALUMNI ASSOCIATION
207
where they might find some tools to take the leg off, and they brought
the man over to me and I took a saw and chisel and cut the leg off.
The fellow didn't die; he got well. So they commenced to call me Doe.
So I got me a book and read about it, and so I have been practicing
medicine for fifteen years, and I wanted to come to one of these schools
and see how they do the thing right.'
"We had to deal with men and conditions of that kind. Our men
went into the country with a pistol in one hand to defend themselves,
and a pill-box in the other, and a lancet to save life. Those were the
conditions that have happily disappeared. And none have made
better use of the years than our medical profession. No state, no city,
no community ever helped the onward course of the medical profession;
it all came out of the members themselves. Nobody legislated us into
a higher course of medicine, and, what is more, no one ever furnished
us with the means; we had to find them, go out and get them, get them
anyway, and the poorest financially among us were foremost in bring-
ing up an institution that was finally fit to take rank with the great
institutions of this country."
DR. EDMUND A. ENGLER, of the Worcester Polytechnic Institute,
spoke, in part, as follows:
"I was considerably interested, I might say stopped in my line of
thought, when I read on a train the other morning at Detroit in one of
the local papers, which purported to give the facts, or perhaps some
more tangible results which our distinguished guest of the day, the
British Ambassador, had secured from his recent trip through the
South and West. The editor remarked, in one sentence which I recall,
that the distinguished Ambassador had an imagination which was
capable of grasping the things that were, of setting them beside the
things that are, and of reasoning to the things that are to be. And
this homely phrase struck me as being one of great significance, and I
felt glad that the Ambassador from Great Britain had at least suc-
ceeded in impressing the editor of one of our local papers with his tre-
mendous ability, because, when I began to cast about in my mind
what the real meaning of that sentence was, I could not help thinking
that it really contained the whole summary of the modern view with
reference to everything that now exists, and with reference to all our
views concerning such things; in other words, it was simply a news-
paper statement of what is now commonly accepted as the theory of
development. It has not been so long ago that the world had not con-
ceived the meaning of the idea of development. It has not always been


## p. 208 (#696) ############################################

208
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
supposed that the things that are have come from the things that were,
and that the things that are to be must come from the things that are.
In science, in literature, in all branches of human activity, it is a com-
paratively modern notion that things grow from what they feed on.
It is a comparatively modern idea that the forces of nature are at work,
not only in the material world, but in the social world, in the develop-
ments which men make in social organization in the developments
which nations make as they grow-just as inexorably as they are in
the smaller things in which we commonly see them operate. As I
went on to think, it occurred to me that, while possibly we may have
the correct view, it frequently happens that, in taking account of the
things that are, we are prone to forget the things that were, and possibly
have not brains enough to reason correctly about the things that are
to be. As I sat this morning listening to the addresses, some of which
had a historical touch, I could not help but think that many of those
who sat in the large audience and listened to those addresses failed,
perhaps, to grasp the things that were failed, perhaps, to realize that
the things which are to be with reference to Washington University
are distinctly and inevitably the result of the things that are. It oc-
curred to me that many of us take what we find existing for granted,
much as the children of today take, for example, our electrical develop-
ment. I have seen children who have never seen a horse car; I have
seen children who accept the telephone as if it had always been; I
have seen children who have never seen a street gas light; they accept
what comes to them without question, without investigation. They
benefit by the results and do not stop to inquire how those results have
been achieved.
"We are only children of a larger growth. We, too, are so full of
ourselves and of the moment in which we live that we forget and fail
to take into account the things which were before us and the things
which are responsible for what we have to-day. And yet, when you
come to look at the future, wise men are they who would be able to
make anything like a definite forecast-wise men are they who realize
that forces are now in operation which are controlling not only the acts
of corporations, of universities, and of organized associations of men,
but are controlling even the most detailed, the most individual, the
most intimate thoughts of men. Wise men are they who recognize
that such forces do exist, who use their efforts to ascertain the laws
controlling those forces, and so conduct their lives as to harmonize with
the laws which they know must produce the final result.
"It is the work of the university to so direct men's minds that their
horizon shall be broader, that they will be able to think and walk


## p. 209 (#697) ############################################

INTER-COLLEGIATE GAMES IN UNIVERSITIES
209
straight where other men stumble. It is the function of the University
to so lead men, not only those within their walls, but those in the com-
munity in which the university exists, along paths which will develop
a higher order of citizenship-along paths which will develop a greater
sense of obligation and a greater appreciation of the things that have
been."
At the Annual Banquet of the Alumni Association of Washington
University, held February 22, 1908, the following address was delivered
by Professor Alexander S. Chessin:
SHALL INTER-COLLEGIATE GAMES BE ABOLISHED
IN OUR UNIVERSITIES?
"The current controversy regarding college athletics is not eon-
cerned with physical training in general. The maxim of 'a healthy
mind in a healthy body' is universally recognized to-day. The attacks
are aimed only at the branch of athletics known as inter-collegiate sports,
where abuse and corruption have become notorious. Presidents, facul-
ties, athletic boards have, without apparent success, endeavored either
to correct or to check these evils, and when the situation grew
from bad to worse, these gentlemen arrived at the conclusion that
salvation lies in the destruction of the whole fabric. Their motto
is: 'We believe in athletics but we do not believe in inter-collegiate
games.' Hence the clamor for the discontinuance of the pernicious
practice.
"This conclusion can hardly be called rational. No sane person
would advocate the abolition of an institution or custom because of
abuses which are not inherent in its nature, but are grafted upon it by
extraneous and corrupt influences. Yet this is what the authorities of
a number of American colleges avowedly contemplate. Indeed, in a
few among our universities inter-collegiate games have been actually
abolished. No doubt this remedy is simple. Many a Gordian knot
might be cut in a similar fashion. Old and decrepit people, who have
become a burden to the community, might be drowned like so many
rats, instead of being comfortably fed and housed; sufferers from con-
tagious and incurable diseases might be exterminated to safeguard the
rest of the community; criminals might be hung without the ceremony
of a trial: why waste the people's money on hospitals and prisons and
courts of justice, for the sake of apparently not only useless but
dangerous citizens?
14


## p. 210 (#698) ############################################

210
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
"While the case in point may not be exactly analogous, the con-
templated action of some of our universities suggests a whole class of
such 'simple solutions,' which might be called 'solutions by extermina-
tion.' It cannot be denied that whenever an institution or a custom
is known beyond all question to be an unmitigated evil, the solution by
extermination is not only the most simple but also the most rational
solution. But when extermination means elimination of the good with
the evil, then it is incumbent upon us to strain every effort in ridding
the institution or custom of its ills, before condemning it as a whole.
"Were there no other reasons for the maintenance of inter-collegiate
games than those commonly advocated; were we to consider only what
they contribute toward American manhood, what they mean to the de-
velopment of strength, courage, determination and endurance; had
we in mind nothing but the vast and popular interest displayed in these
vigorous and healthy outdoor sports, by old and young, in and out of
college; were we only to think of the unconquerable spirit of competi-
tion which is in the very blood of the Anglo-Saxon and which dominates
every phase of American life; there would be cause enough to halt in
the present reactionary movement and to ask ourselves: 'are we not
going too far in our denunciation?'
"But there is one point which, to my knowledge, has been over-
looked in the controversy, and which I wish to emphasize above every
other because it has a vital bearing on our national life. Even were
we to grant that the arguments generally resorted to, and which I have
briefly outlined here, are unconvincing, there would still remain one
paramount reason why inter-collegiate games should be not only main-
tained but encouraged. If you take them away from the college, you at
the same time take away from it one of the most precious opportunities
that are at its disposal to graft upon our youths and to strengthen in them
a great moral principle-the principle of fair play.
"In these days, when on one side the church has lost a large part of
its hold on the people, and on the other corrupt methods of business
and of politics have eaten their way into the heart of the nation, it is
imperative that our schools rally to the assistance of our chief executive
in the battle which he is waging for the moral regeneration of the busi-
ness world. 'A school,' says Bishop Spalding, 'is more safely judged
by those it fails to improve than by those it helps.' If we fail to make
use of a single opportunity, no matter how small, for the moral better-
ment of those entrusted to our care, we are not doing our full duty.
That every college does not embrace this opportunity in the proper
spirit is attested by the unfortunate vituperations of Chancellor Day.
But it is not my purpose to dwell on the manifold sources of moral influ-


## p. 211 (#699) ############################################

INTER-COLLEGIATE GAMES IN UNIVERSITIES
211
ence at the disposal of educational institutions. They are familiar to
every educator worthy of the name. Besides, they do not form the
subject of my discourse. What I want to impress upon you is the fact
that no phase of university life offers as great and as fruitful a field
for moral training in the practice of fair play as the institution of inter-
collegiate games.
"I know that the champions of what I have called the 'solution by
extermination' will seize upon every chance to misconstrue my re-
marks. I do not wish to be misunderstood. I am fully aware of the
abuses which permeate inter-collegiate sports. Nor do I claim that
these sports in themselves involve any morality beyond that which is
afforded by every form of discipline. But I do profess that they
offer a ground preeminently fitted for the infusion and dissemination
of certain moral ideas leading to a high conception of honesty and fair-
ness and to a better understanding of the principles which President
Roosevelt is championing in his unremitting and fearless campaign of
righteousness.
"Indeed, the 'square deal,' this by-word of the present administra-
tion, is but the moral counterpart, the twin brother, of 'fair-play.'
Both represent a principle which is deeply rooted in the body of Anglo-
Saxon civilization, and forms one of the fundamental virtues of a truly
free and liberty-loving people.
"The battle waged by our President is, before and above everything,
a battle of ethics. To quote his own words from his last message to
Congress: 'The opponents of the measures we champion single out,
now one, now another, measure for especial attack, and speak as if the
movement in which we are engaged was purely economic. It has a
large economic side, but it is fundamentally an ethical movement. It
is not a movement to be completed in one year, or two or three years;
it is a movement which must be persevered in until the spirit which lies
behind it sinks deep into the heart and conscience of the whole people.'
And a little further, 'On behalf of all our people, on behalf no less of
the honest man of means, than of the honest man who earns his day's
livelihood by that day's sweat of his brow, it is necessary to insist upon
honesty in business and politics alike, in all walks of life, in big things
and in little things; upon just and fair dealing as between man and
man.'
"This moral regeneration of the nation cannot be achieved without
the right education. American schools above all should therefore heed
the warning cry of the President. Every means, every resource at their
command should be taken advantage of, every influence should be
exercised, every effort strained to stimulate moral progress. Our


## p. 212 (#700) ############################################

212
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
American youth should be educated on the athletic field no less than
in the class room. Shall we throw away an opportunity so rich, so
full of latent, yet unused, power?
"I do not have in mind the actual participant in the game alone.
These sports command the widest, the most general interest among all
the members of the university. Back of the players looms up the moral
support of the entire college: students, faculty, alumni, even the august
body of directors and trustees. The players in a great measure reflect
the moral standards of the whole institution and react on it in their
turn. Good examples are contagious. A man who, either from inborn
rectitude or from a spirit instilled by right educational influences and a
clean college atmosphere, has learned to abominate foul play and the
taking of unfair advantage, be he a participant in the game or merely
a spectator, is not going to follow the methods of Standard Oil in after
days, when he enters the field of business.
"If you will pardon a slight digression, I am reminded to-night of
another banquet in another city. The speaker was Wu Ting Fang,
then ambassador from China. In a remarkable address, which was
severely criticized at the time, he drew a parallel between Confucianism
and Christianity. He professed a belief in the superiority of the former
as a practical religion, because in its code of ethics there was no room
for such extravagant, visionary doctrines as the one embodied in the
words of our Lord: 'But whosoever shall smite thee on the right cheek,
turn to him the other also.' Utterly lacking appreciation of their
symbolic meaning, he failed to see that what lifts Christianity far above
the religion of Confucius is its idealism. An ideal is a thing unattain-
able, it is akin to that infinity with which mathematicians are familiar;
a thing which you may indefinitely approach but never reach; some-
thing realizable and yet elusive, an image constantly spurring you on-
ward and luring you to greater heights. From its very nature it impels
and stimulates progress. That Chinese civilization came to a stand-
still ages ago is doubtless due to lack of idealism in the nation. A peo-
ple whose ethical ideas do not reach beyond a code of practical rules,
no matter how admirable, is bound to face cultural stagnation in the
end. Without an ideal, progress itself is impossible.
"And now were you to ask me by what means shall the reforms so
urgently needed in college athletics be effected, I would say to you:
The means lie in that opportunity which I have endeavored to describe.
By instilling in the American youth love of fair play and a determina-
tion to see justice and purity triumph on the athletic field, not for the
sake of an existing code of rules but for the sake of right and equity,
we set before him an ideal which he will constantly strive to attain.


## p. 213 (#701) ############################################

UNIVERSITY NECROLOGY
213
We would thus achieve a double purpose: we would rid athletics of all
abuse and at the same time contribute our share toward the moral
awakening of the nation.
"The task is not an easy one. As Mr. Roosevelt has said, it may not
be completed in a year, nor in two or three years. But I believe that
somewhere within every one of us lurks a divine spark, which often
needs but a little assistance, a right influence or an example, to awaken
our dormant conscience and start us on the road toward the ideal goal."

ALBERT H. ZELLER*
Albert Henry Zeller was born in Saint Louis January 20, 1867, and
died in Saint Louis on November 2, 1906. He was the second son of
Wm. Zeller and Christine Haarstick-Zeller. He is survived by his
mother, two brothers, William F. and Eugene, and one sister, Mrs. F. W.
Frerichs.
One of the most interesting facts in Mr. Zeller's career is the di-
versity of his early education. When but three years of age he was
taken to Germany for one year, and at that time it is said he began his
studies on the violin. One year after his return to Saint Louis he
entered Peabody School, remaining there until 1878, at which time he
was sent to a French school in Lausanne, Switzerland, where he took
a regular course. In 1880 he was again in Saint Louis attending Smith
Academy, from which institution he was graduated in 1883. Four
years later he received the degree of Bachelor of Science from the School
of Engineering of Washington University.
After graduation Mr. Zeller was engaged as draftsman and assistant
engineer with the Saint Louis, Iron Mountain & Southern Railroad,
until 1889, when he became an assistant engineer with the Saint Louis
Merchants' Bridge Terminal Railway, which position he held until
May, 1891, although seven months of this period were spent traveling in
Europe. On leaving the employ of the Terminal Railway Company,
he was engaged until November, 1892, in the designing department of
the Edge Moor Bridge Works, Wilmington, Delaware. From February
to May, 1893, he was principal Assistant Engineer in charge of the
*As announced in Volume V of the BULLETIN, this memorial reached the editor
too late for publication last year.


## p. 214 (#702) ############################################

214
UNIVERSITY CHRONICLE
erection of the train shed at the new Union Station in Saint Louis.
He was then appointed Engineer Assistant to Robert McMath, presi-
dent of the Board of Public Improvements of Saint Louis. This posi-
tion he filled for four years, resigning in 1897 to go abroad two years.
On his return, in 1899, he opened an office in Saint Louis for the general
practice of his profession, and he was engaged in this work at the time
of his death.
Outside of his profession Mr. Zeller was also active. He was a
member of the Saint Louis Club of Saint Louis, the University Club,
and the Saint Louis Field Club. In 1890 he was elected a Junior of
the American Society of Civil Engineers, and in 1897 became an Associ-
ate Member. He was also an active and loyal member of the Alumni
Association of the University.
Among the delightful impressions which Mr. Zeller left upon his
friends, one point in particular is brought out by his intimate acquaint-
ance, Mr. Chauvenet, that of a rare type of gentlemanliness. He was
a gentleman of the fast-fading old school, a man who, in performing
service for others, invariably made them feel that somehow he was
under obligations to the one he was helping, and who, in his associa-
tions with his fellows, was accustomed to think of the interests of others
rather than his own, rarely speaking of his own fortune, whether good
or bad, and invariably showing an active interest in the fortunes of
others, and a sure sympathy in times of loss, which made him one
naturally sought out by those in trouble.
WILLIAM S. LOVE
Died, December 12, 1907, at his home in Orange, N. J., after a brief
illness, Mr. William S. Love, an alumnus of Washington University.
This eminent engineer received both his secondary and his higher edu-
cation in Washington University. He entered the Manual Training
School with the pioneer class in September, 1880, and graduated from
that institution in 1883. A year later he entered Washington Uni-
versity, taking the engineering course, and received the degree of
Bachelor of Engineering in 1888. He engaged for a time in professional
work in Saint Louis, and then moved to a higher position in Chicago,
where he became the agent of the Wheeler Condenser and Engineering
Company. A year ago he was promoted to the management of the
New York office of the same company, which very responsible position
he had filled for one year.
In the death of Mr. Love the Alumni of Washington University and
the engineering profession have met with a great loss. As a student


## p. 215 (#703) ############################################

UNIVERSITY NECROLOGY
215
he was faithful and earnest. He became an accomplished engineer
and a remarkably successful business man, and, above all, he was a
perfect gentleman. He was the soul of honor, the embodiment of good
cheer, and was unflagging in his loyalty and devotion to Washington
University. A wide circle of friends in Saint Louis and Chicago mourn
his untimely death and unite in a feeling of profound sympathy for his
mother, his widow and personal friends.
ROBERT LUEDEKING
C. M. WOODWARD.
Doctor Robert Luedeking, Dean of the Medical Faculty of Washing-
ton University and Professor of Clinical Medicine and Diseases of Chil-
dren, died on February 29, 1908. Doctor Luedeking was born in Saint
Louis, November 6, 1853, the son of Carl Luedeking, who was a philoso-
pher and educator. The younger Luedeking passed through the public
schools of the city, graduating from the High School in 1871. Immedi-
ately afterward, he proceeded to Germany, first to Heidelberg, thence
to the University of Strassburg, where he received, in 1877, the degree
of Doctor of Medicine. Incidentally, he served as coxswain in an
American boat crew which defeated the English in a race on the Neckar.
After taking his degree, he proceeded from Strassburg to Vienna, but
returned in the same year to Saint Louis. Subsequently he has re-
turned frequently to Germany for the completion of special portions of
his work, but from this time his home was in Saint Louis.
Here he was dispensary physician from 1877 to 1879, during which
period he had opportunity to grapple with that giant among diseases,
yellow fever. After this he was for four years Secretary of the Board
of Health, and also acted at intervals as temporary Superintendent of
the Saint Louis City Hospital and Female Hospital. About this time
be became a lecturer at the Saint Louis Medical College. Subsequently
the college-after being first merged into the Missouri Medical College
became the Medical Department of Washington University. And with
the merging came about the valuable association of Doctor Luedeking
with the University. Since 1882 he has been lecturer on Pathological
Anatomy and Professor of the Diseases of Children, and Chief of the
Clinic for Children's Diseases at the O'Fallon Dispensary, another
branch of Washington University. Among his other activities he also
found time to act as member of the staff of Saint Luke's and the Jewish
Hospitals and the Bethesda Foundling's Home, to serve as examiner
for life insurance companies, and to edit the Saint Louis Medical Re-
view. In 1902 he became Dean of the Medical Faculty of the Uni-
versity, and in 1905 was conferred his final honor, which he was so

briefly to enjoy, that of Professor of Clinical Medicine and Diseases of
Children in the Medical Faculty of the University.
Doctor Luedeking was the author of many scientific papers. His
fame began with the publication, in early youth, while at Heidelberg,
of his Researches on the Regeneration of Unstriped Muscle Fibre. Other
papers of note are: Pathology of Pneumonia, Etiology of Gastric Carci-
noma, Heredity in Parthenogenesis, Cellular Agency in Disease, Notes on
Diabetic Coma, Perforative Inflammation of Diverticulum, and papers
on antistreptococcic serum, and the present status of serum-therapy.
